sx_pingyaowenmiao.name: Pingyao Confucian Temple
sx_pingyaowenmiao.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
sx_pingyaowenmiao.lede: Among all the Confucian temples of China, this is the only Hall of Great Achievement built in Jin timber: rebuilt in 1163, the third year of Dading, it keeps its original appearance. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof, and its bracket sets use the independent cantilever, a device rare in China; the terrace in front is railed in bluestone and the central ramp carved with two dragons playing with a pearl. The temple is said to have been founded early in the Zhenguan era of the Tang, and in 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage together with the ancient city of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall; later buildings in the compound are not included.
facts: Form: the Hall of Great Achievement is five bays wide under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof and stands on a terrace railed in carved bluestone, with a 'worship stone' carved with the character for longevity set in its centre and stone ramps in front and to either side, the front ramp carved with two dragons playing with a pearl; the bracket sets under the eaves use an independent cantilever structure, rare among surviving Chinese timber buildings.

Date: the Pingyao Confucian Temple was founded early in the Zhenguan era of the Tang; the hall was rebuilt in 1163 and is the only Jin-dynasty building in any Confucian temple in China. The name 'Hall of Great Achievement' dates from 1104, when a Northern Song edict renamed the Hall of King Wenxuan, barely sixty years before this rebuilding. In 1997 the temple was inscribed as World Heritage with the ancient city of Pingyao, Zhenguo Monastery and Shuanglin Monastery.

Significance: this is the earliest surviving hall in any Confucian temple in China; in the symmetrical plan of old Pingyao, 'Confucian temple on the left, temple of the god of war on the right, Daoist abbey east and Buddhist monastery west', the temple holds one end. The terrace and the two side galleries of nine bays each enclose the main court, the galleries housing the sages and worthies of the past, a well-preserved example of a county-level school-temple layout.
captions: Pingyao Confucian Temple · Front of the Dacheng Hall

yanshan.name: Yanshan Temple, Fanshi
yanshan.lede: Outside, Wenshu Hall is a Jin Buddhist hall five bays wide. Inside, its murals unfold another scale: cities, palaces and everyday activities set Buddhist stories within a human world. Wang Kui and other painters completed them in 1167; the timber hall later underwent Yuan repairs. Its single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, substantial brackets and wall paintings survive together. The framing records building practice, while the paintings reveal architecture and society, each with its own dating evidence.
facts: Timber: the hall is five bays wide and six rafter spans deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Its four-puzuo bracket sets project once. The framing and eaves supports retain the scale of the Jin structure, giving its simple form considerable presence.

Inscriptions: the hall survives from the Jin, while an inscription beneath a four-rafter beam records rebuilding in 1315. The murals were completed in 1167. Painting, construction and subsequent repair should therefore be treated as separate events.

Murals: the west wall depicts the Buddha’s life, the east the story of Prince Xusheti, and the north temple compounds and a maritime disaster. Buildings, streets and human activity make these religious paintings evidence for Song–Jin architecture and social life.
captions: Front of the Manjushri Hall, Yanshan Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site
Surviving Jin structure, restored in the 2nd year of Yanyou, Yuan (1315) · Five bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

hn_baima.name: Qiyun Pagoda of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.sub: White Horse Temple · Jin brick pagoda
hn_baima.yearNote: A Jin rebuilding stele states 1175 explicitly; this is not 68, the year White Horse Temple was founded.
hn_baima.place: Henan · Luoyang · East Pagoda Court of White Horse Temple
hn_baima.lede: The year of the White Horse Temple's founding, 68 CE (Yongping 11 of the Eastern Han), is often hung on the Qiyun Pagoda, but the tower in front of us is Jin: a Jin stele beside it, the Record of Rebuilding the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the East White Horse Temple on Left Street of Henan Prefecture, gives the rebuilding year plainly as 1175 (Dading 15). A square brick pagoda of thirteen dense-eaved storeys, its outline a parabola narrowing step by step from the sixth storey, topped by a vase-shaped finial, it is the oldest standing building in the Luoyang area. Originally the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda, it was renamed Qiyun ('level with the clouds') in the Kangxi era by the abbot Ruxiu, following the tradition that Emperor Ming had built the first tower. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: A square brick pagoda with thirteen storeys of corbelled dense eaves, about 25 m tall overall (35 m by another account); the base is a waisted sumeru pedestal 7.80 m on a side, 6.76 m at the waist. The body draws in storey by storey so that the outline forms a parabola, and a vase-shaped finial crowns the top.

Dating: Its predecessor, the Shakyamuni Relic Pagoda of the White Horse Temple, is said to date from the reign of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han and was destroyed by Jin troops at the end of the Northern Song; the present pagoda was rebuilt in 1175 (Dading 15 of the Jin), as recorded on the Jin stele of the rebuilding. A Qing abbot, Ruxiu, renamed it Qiyun on the strength of the record that Emperor Ming had founded the tower.

Significance: The Qiyun Pagoda is the earliest Jin-period building still standing in the Luoyang area, and its parabolic profile preserves the look of Tang pagodas. The pagoda court lies about 200 m south-east of the temple gate; enlarged in 1990 to one hectare, it is the only Buddhist nunnery in Henan. The White Horse Temple itself was listed among the first national protected sites in 1961.
captions: Qiyun Pagoda of White Horse Temple · Square thirteen-story multi-eaved pagoda
Rebuilt in the 15th year of Dading, Jin (1175)

hn_baolun.name: Baolun Temple Pagoda
hn_baolun.sub: Thirteen eaves drawn into a slender silhouette
hn_baolun.yearNote: Entered according to the surviving pagoda rebuilt in the Jin; the founding date of the old Tang temple is not substituted for the date of the pagoda.
hn_baolun.lede: Clap beneath the pagoda and it answers with a toad's croak—people in Shanzhou call it the Toad Pagoda, and it is counted with the Echo Wall of Beijing's Temple of Heaven and the Yingying Pagoda at Yongji among China's four great echoing buildings, the oldest of them. In 1177 (Dading 17 of the Jin) the monk Zhixiu rebuilt this brick tower on the site of a Sui timber pagoda: square in plan, thirteen storeys of corbelled dense eaves, 26.5 m tall, on a platform and pedestal, each storey opening an arched door, a niche or a window, with wind-bells under the corners. The old walled town of Shanzhou has long been abandoned; the pagoda stands alone on its terrace. The plate shows the south face.
facts: Form: A thirteen-storey brick pagoda with corbelled dense eaves, nearly square in plan, laid in grey-blue brick, 26.5 m tall (27.2 m by another account) and 21.6 m around the base, on a platform and pedestal; each storey opens a round-arched doorway, a Buddha niche or a window, the interior holds a chamber and a stair for climbing, and wind-bells hang beneath the corners of the eaves.

Dating: Its full name is the Three Sages Relic Pagoda of Baolun Temple. The temple pagoda is said to go back to 601 (Renshou 1 of the Sui), when the nun Daoxiu directed a timber tower; in 1177 (Dading 17 of the Jin) the monk Zhixiu rebuilt it in brick—the pagoda that stands today. It has survived more than ten earthquakes with only a slight lean.

Significance: The echo inside sounds like frogs, hence the nickname Toad Pagoda; with the Echo Wall of the Temple of Heaven, the Yingying Pagoda at Yongji and the stone 'qin' of Dafo Temple at Tongnan it is counted among China's four great echoing buildings, and is the earliest. Baolun Temple itself is gone; the pagoda now stands in the Pagoda Garden of Shanzhou Park, within the site of the old town.
captions: Baolun Temple Pagoda · South elevation
17th year of Dading, Jin (1177) · Square thirteen-story multi-eaved brick pagoda

wangbao.name: Erlang Temple of Wangbao, Gaoping
wangbao.sub: Jin opera stage · Gable facing forward
wangbao.lede: The stage at Wangbao’s Erlang Temple turns the gable of its hip-and-gable roof towards the audience. Four corner columns and substantial brackets carry the roof over a small, square, single-bay stage. The load-bearing arrangement is unusually clear. An inscription on the stone pedestal gives the year 1183 and names its masons. Facing the temple’s main hall, the stage places performance and worship in the same courtyard and preserves architectural evidence of village theatrical life.
facts: Structure: a square stage one bay wide has round columns at its corners and a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with its gable facing forward. Broad lintels and brackets carry the roof; two intercolumnar bracket sets on each side give the small building a complete structural hierarchy.

Dating: the pedestal inscription records the twenty-third year of Dading and the masons Zhao Xian and Zhao Zhi, dating the work to the Jin. Other temple buildings were largely rebuilt in the Ming and Qing; their dates do not replace that of the inscribed stage.

Performance: standing on the courtyard’s south side and facing the main hall, the stage links performance with ritual. It provides physical evidence for early temple-fair theatre, while its inscription ties the timber form to a recorded date rather than a foundation legend.
captions: Erlang Temple of Wangbao · Jin opera stage
Jin · 23rd year of Dading (1183)

jingtusi.name: Jingtu Temple, Ying County
jingtusi.lede: Jingtu Temple’s Mahavira Hall rewards looking up: caissons and miniature celestial pavilions spread across its ceiling, their columns, rails, eaves and brackets reduced to intricate joinery. The Jin hall is only three bays square, yet its interior constructs another architectural world above the worshipper. The temple was founded in 1124 and repaired in 1184, with later renovations. Here the structural frame and ornamental woodwork express architecture at different scales.
facts: Space: three bays wide and deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Caissons and miniature pavilions furnish its ceiling with tiny columns, rails and eaves. A restrained exterior contrasts with the intricate interior.

History: the Yingzhou gazetteer records foundation in 1124 and repair in 1184; the surviving hall is Jin. Major Ming repairs followed. Foundation, repairs and later decorative work should not be compressed into one date.

Joinery: the celestial pavilions are images of buildings attached to the ceiling, not rooms to enter. Their fine components give architectural form to Pure Land imagery and preserve evidence for Jin interior decoration and woodworking.
captions: Front of the Mahavira Hall, Jingtu Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site
Restored in the 24th year of Dading, Jin (1184) · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

hn_fengxian.name: Fengxian Temple, Jiyuan
hn_fengxian.yearNote: The Jin date of the surviving Sanqing Hall is used, not the founding of the temple in the 1st year of Chuigong in the Tang.
hn_fengxian.lede: A hall five bays wide whose entire roof rests inside on just two rear hypostyle columns—one of the clearest examples in China of 'column reduction'. The Hall of the Three Pure Ones at Fengxian Abbey in Jiyuan was built in 1184 (Dading 24 of the Jin): five bays wide, seven rafters deep, under a single-eave overhanging-gable roof. The Qianlong-era Jiyuan county gazetteer says its beams are of chaste-tree and persimmon wood and its columns of mulberry and jujube, hence the nickname 'Chaste-Tree Beam Abbey'. Liu Dunzhen, who saw it, praised its 'bold handling and extraordinary conception'. The plate shows the front of the hall; the Ming Jade Emperor Hall and the Qing gate of the abbey are not drawn.
facts: Form: The hall is five bays wide and seven rafters deep under a single-eave overhanging-gable roof; the plan uses column reduction, with only two rear hypostyle columns inside carrying the roof frame—a textbook case of the technique. The Qianlong-era Jiyuan gazetteer records that 'the beams are of chaste-tree and persimmon, the columns of mulberry and jujube, each two or three spans around and some two zhang long'.

Dating: Fengxian Abbey was founded in 685 (Chuigong 1 of the Tang); the two Daoist masters Lu of the Tang and Helan Qizhen of the Song practised here. The present Hall of the Three Pure Ones dates from 1184 (Dading 24 of the Jin). Ten Jin, Ming and Qing buildings survive, among them the Ming Jade Emperor Hall, three bays wide with an overhanging-gable roof, and the Qing gate, also three bays under an overhanging-gable roof.

Significance: Because its beams and columns use four woods rarely chosen for structural timber—chaste-tree, persimmon, mulberry and jujube—locals call it the 'Chaste-Tree Beam Abbey', and Liu Dunzhen praised its 'bold handling and extraordinary conception'. It is the most important of Henan's surviving Jin timber buildings and is often set beside the Hall of the Three Sages at Shanhua Temple in Datong, Shanxi.
captions: Sanqing Hall of Fengxian Temple · Five-bay hall with overhanging gable roof
24th year of Dading, Jin (1184)

hb_linji.name: Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple
hb_linji.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hb_linji.lede: Chengling Pagoda concentrates elaborate brick carving around its base and tall first section, then draws the eye upward through tapering eaves to its finial. It commemorates Yixuan, founder of the Linji school, but its present form mainly follows a major Jin repair rather than surviving unchanged from its Tang foundation. Blind doors, windows and brackets translate timber decoration into brick and give the memorial its distinctive texture.
facts: The solid octagonal brick pagoda has nine tiers, a double Sumeru pedestal and an upturned lotus base. Door-shaped arches on four principal faces alternate with blind windows; close eaves above the first section reproduce elements of timber architecture.

The early tower commemorated Yixuan, founder of the Linji school. Its present appearance chiefly follows the major repair of 1185. Yuan, Ming and Qing repairs followed; an earthquake damaged the finial in 1966, and it was reinstalled in 1985.

Carved doors, balustrades and brackets preserve finely differentiated components useful for studying Jin decoration and joinery. Comparing them with the closely stacked upper eaves reveals how monumental mass and intricate craftsmanship work together.
captions: Chengling Pagoda of Linji Temple · Octagonal nine-story multi-eaved pagoda
Jin · Major repair in 1185

bj_lugou.name: Lugou Bridge, Beijing
bj_lugou.era: Completed in the Jin · Ming–Qing repairs
bj_lugou.lede: Lions beyond counting: 281 balustrade posts, each capped by a large lion with cubs, plus those on the ornamental columns and at the bridgeheads, 498 by one count and 501 by another; even the tally is unsettled. Lugou Bridge was begun in 1189, the twenty-ninth year of Dading of the Jin, and finished in 1192, the third year of Mingchang: an eleven-arch stone bridge across the Yongding River, 268 m long and 9.4 m wide, its piers built with cutwaters on the upstream face and iron posts on the points to break the ice. The shots of 7 July 1937 rang out here; in 1967 it was turned into a road bridge, and only in 1987 was it returned to a stone bridge. The plate views it from a shallow angle, with all eleven arches open.
facts: Form: an eleven-arch stone bridge running east-west, 268 m long including the approaches (the bridge proper 212.75 m) and 9.4 m wide, the spans ranging from 11.4 to 13.45 m; the ten piers have cutwaters on the upstream face with triangular iron posts against ice. Along the deck stand 281 balustrade posts and 279 stone panels, the posts about 1.4 m high and topped with carved lions; a pair of ornamental columns stands at each end, with crouching lions at the east end and elephants at the west bracing the balustrade.

Dating: in 1189 Emperor Zhangzong of Jin ordered a stone bridge, completed in 1192 and first named Guangli Bridge; twelve recorded repairs followed in the Ming and Qing, and in 1751, the sixteenth year of Qianlong, the stele 'Moon over Lugou at Dawn' was set up. The foundations, parts of the structure and some of the carving remain Jin originals, while posts and panels have been replaced over the centuries.

Events and value: on 7 July 1937, after exercises north of the bridge, Japanese troops attacked Wanping and the bridge, and the Lugou Bridge Incident became the starting point of full-scale war against Japan; in 1967-1968 the deck was overlaid with reinforced concrete as a road bridge, and in 1987 the stone bridge was restored and closed to traffic. It is the oldest large multi-arch stone bridge surviving in Beijing, and 'Moon over Lugou at Dawn' is one of the Eight Views of Yanjing.
captions: Lugou Bridge, Beijing · Eleven stone arches
Jin · Completed 1192, repaired in the Ming and Qing

hongfu.name: Hongfu Temple, Dingxiang
hongfu.lede: Hongfu Temple’s main hall stands within fortified walls on a high platform. Its five-bay, overhanging-gable hall and enclosing walls work at different scales: fortress-like outside, Buddhist temple within. The surviving Mahavira Hall is identified as a Jin structure, without an inscription establishing an exact building year. Nine clay figures remain on a brick altar. Timber architecture, sculpture and successive repairs coexist here; their different dates should not be compressed into a single year for the whole temple.
facts: Form: the main hall is five bays wide, with seven purlins, a depth of six rafter spans and an overhanging-gable roof supported by brackets. The temple stands on a raised earthen platform within fortified walls, giving a religious courtyard a closed exterior.

Dating: the surviving hall belongs to the Jin, but its precise construction year is uncertain. Nor should the temple’s foundation be dated from legend. Repairs from later periods are separate events; a timeline placement does not date every timber component.

Sculpture: nine clay figures occupy a brick altar, arranged as principal figure, bodhisattvas, disciples and guardians. Local research describes them as Song sculpture. Their dating should be distinguished from that of the Jin timber hall.
captions: Front of the Mahavira Hall, Hongfu Temple · Redrawn from photographs of the site
Surviving Jin structure · Five bays wide, single-eaved overhanging gable roof

protection.scope: Hongfu Temple, Dingxiang · Dingxiang · Mahavira Hall

yanqing.name: Yanqing Temple, Wutai
yanqing.lede: Yanqing Temple’s Great Buddha Hall is only three bays wide, but its deep eaves give the small grey-tiled hall an expansive profile. A central plank door, flanking lattice windows and bracket sets reveal the column grid. The hall is identified as Jin, with no known exact building year. A Song stone scripture pillar in the temple predates the timber hall. Reading them separately shows a village temple’s long continuity without using the date of one earlier object for all its buildings.
facts: Form: three bays wide and six rafter spans deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of grey tiles. A plank door occupies the centre, with vertical-lattice windows beside it. Lintels connect the columns and brackets carry the broad eaves.

Dating: the surviving hall is Jin, with an uncertain construction year. The courtyard’s scripture pillar dates to 1035 under the Northern Song. Its inscription does not date the hall; different objects preserve different historical evidence.

Timber: column brackets project with an arm and a descending strut, while intercolumnar sets include diagonal arms. The exposed interior framing allows the eaves supports and roof supports to be examined separately, revealing the structure in its details.
captions: Front of the Great Buddha Hall, Yanqing Temple · Shanwen Village, Wutai
Surviving Jin structure · Three-bay hip-and-gable hall, with later beast masks on the column heads retained in its present state

protection.scope: Yanqing Temple, Wutai · Wutai · Great Buddha Hall

sx_taifu.name: Taifu Temple, Fenyang
sx_taifu.era: Jin · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
sx_taifu.yearNote: 1200 is an approximate sorting point for the period indicated by the altar record of the 5th year of Cheng'an; the main hall is dated to the Jin from its architecture and heritage sources, and the altar date is not forced on the hall as a precise completion year.
sx_taifu.lede: Taifu Temple’s Haotian Hall places a three-bay-square plan beneath a hip-and-gable roof. A plank door and vertical-lattice windows articulate a compact setting for worship of the Jade Emperor. The main hall retains Jin timber forms, while sculpture and other buildings include Ming and Qing layers. An inscription of 1200 records establishing a ritual altar, not necessarily completion of the hall. Structure, inscription and decoration each carry dates, revealing the gradual making of a religious site.
facts: Plan: three bays wide and deep, the nearly square hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. A central plank door and flanking vertical-lattice windows organise the facade. Worship of the Jade Emperor gives this compact hall its religious purpose.

Inscription: the Cheng’an fifth-year record concerns establishment of an altar, while the surviving hall is identified as Jin through its timber form. Setting up an altar and building a hall are separate events; the inscription does not precisely date every component.

Layers: other halls are largely Ming, while sculpture and painting include Ming and Qing work and repairs. The Jin main hall stands with later images and subsidiary buildings, revealing a site accumulated through construction, repair and continued use.
captions: Taifu Temple · Hall of the Haotian Jade Emperor
Jin · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.scope: Taifu Temple, Fenyang · Haotian Hall · Xinghua Village

yongle.name: Yongle Palace, Ruicheng
yongle.lede: The long eaves of the Sanqing Hall lift gently at both sides, and huge glazed dragon ridge-end ornaments guard either end of the main ridge. Inside, the mural Homage to the Primordial (Chaoyuan Tu) arrays hundreds of deities in a grand procession, so that Yuan timber architecture and murals reflect each other within a single space.
facts: Seven-bay hipped hall: The Sanqing Hall, also called the Wuji Hall, is the main hall of Yongle Palace, seven bays wide with a single-eaved hipped roof, and is dated to the 3rd year of Zhongtong (1262).
Chaoyuan Tu: The murals in the hall were completed in 1325 and are recorded separately from the construction date of the building.
Relocation for protection: For the Sanmenxia Reservoir project, the palace buildings and murals were moved to their present site in the 1960s, preserving the original halls and murals.
captions: Yongle Palace · Front of the Sanqing Hall
Seven-bay hipped hall · 3rd year of Zhongtong

hn_guanxing.name: Dengfeng Observatory
hn_guanxing.sub: Front of the platform and stone scale
hn_guanxing.yearNote: The date used is that of the main structure drawn or of the construction phase explicitly listed in this entry; later repairs are described separately.
hn_guanxing.lede: Dengfeng Observatory turns a solar-shadow instrument into a brick-and-stone building. Its square platform narrows upward, with a northern slot aligned to a long stone measuring rule and stairs leading to the top. Yuan observations directed by Guo Shoujing left a tangible apparatus here: astronomy also measured midday shadows to determine seasons and the length of a year.
facts: The brick-and-stone platform narrows toward the top. A measuring slot cuts through its north side, while eastern and western stairs ascend the platform. The stone rule extends northward beneath the slot to receive measurable shadows.

Built in 1276, the thirteenth year of the Yuan Zhiyuan era, the observatory was associated with Guo Shoujing’s survey of the heavens. The nearby Duke of Zhou shadow platform is a separate monument with a different building history.

Channels and pools beside the stone rule helped establish a level measuring surface and reduce error. This union of instrument and architecture shows how traditional calendars depended on repeated observation as well as calculation.

bj_miaoying.name: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing
bj_miaoying.era: Built from the 8th to the 16th year of Zhiyuan
bj_miaoying.lede: One of the first things to rise in the new capital of Dadu: in 1271, the eighth year of Zhiyuan, Khubilai Khan engaged the Nepalese craftsman Anige to direct the building of a stupa, eighty-five men worked for eight years, and it was finished in 1279, the sixteenth year of Zhiyuan, the earliest and largest Tibetan-style stupa surviving in China. It is 51 m high: a three-tiered base on a cross-shaped plan carries an inverted-bowl body 18.4 m across, above which rise the thirteen 'heavens', a bronze canopy 9.7 m in diameter and a four-ton gilt-bronze miniature stupa as the finial. In 1368 lightning fire destroyed the whole of the Great Shengshou Wan'an Temple around it, and only the White Stupa was untouched. The plate shows the stupa alone, without the halls in front.
facts: Form: a Tibetan-style brick stupa 51 m high, white throughout, in five parts, base, body, rings, canopy and finial; the base has three tiers on a cross-shaped plan, 810 square metres in area and 9 m high; above a lotus pedestal wound with five 'vajra rings' sits the inverted-bowl body 18.4 m across, bound with seven iron hoops; the thirteen rings carry a canopy 9.7 m in diameter hung with 36 wind bells, and the finial is a gilt-bronze stupa 5 m high weighing 4 tons.

Dating: begun in 1271 under Anige and completed in 1279, with the Great Shengshou Wan'an Temple then built around it; in 1368, the twenty-eighth year of Zhizheng, the temple burnt after a lightning strike and only the stupa survived. It was repaired in 1433, the temple was renamed Miaoying in 1457, 108 iron lamp niches were set around the base in 1465, and further repairs followed under Kangxi, Qianlong and Jiaqing.

Repairs and finds: during repairs in 1978 the top yielded deposits placed in 1753, the eighteenth year of Qianlong, including 724 cases of the Longzang Tripitaka, sutras and mantras in Qianlong's own hand, Buddha images and relics; the major repair of 2013-2015 removed and replaced about eighty percent of the surface brick, adding nearly ten thousand bricks. The guardian deities, five-Buddha emblems and other carvings that once decorated the base and body have almost entirely weathered away.
captions: White Pagoda of Miaoying Temple, Beijing · Inverted-bowl stupa

fenghuangsi.name: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque
fenghuangsi.sub: Hangzhou · Yuan hall of brick vaults and domes
fenghuangsi.era: Rebuilt in the Yuan · Repaired over the centuries
fenghuangsi.lede: Fenghuang Mosque’s prayer hall presents three pointed roofs outside but brick arches and domes within. A taller central roof and two smaller side roofs combine a West Asian worship space with Jiangnan tiled roofs and raised corners. Its surviving core comes from a Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din, followed by Ming, Qing and modern repairs. The building records the long local history of Hangzhou’s Muslim community through its architectural language.
facts: Form: brick walls and arches divide the hall into three transverse spaces, each covered by a dome. Pointed tiled roofs sit outside them; the taller central roof has double eaves, so the inner and outer roof forms differ.

Dating: the prayer hall survives from the Yuan rebuilding funded by Ala al-Din and predates the mosque’s other surviving buildings. Repeated Ming, Qing and modern repairs mean that not every present roof ornament is Yuan fabric.

Significance: arches, domes and local tiled roofs unite different construction traditions. The hall is also a historic setting for Hangzhou’s Muslim worship, significant both as architecture and as a continuing community space.
captions: Prayer Hall of the Phoenix Mosque · Roof group visible on site
Yuan core hall, repaired over the centuries · Three pyramidal roofs and upper walls

sx_jishi.name: Ji Family Residence, Gaoping
sx_jishi.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Zhongzhuang Village, Chenqu Town
sx_jishi.lede: The Ji family residence has no monumental temple facade, only three shallow bays with a recessed central entrance forming a small porch. Its importance lies beside the door: a stone doorway pedestal bears the thirty-first year of Zhiyuan, giving an ordinary house a recorded date. Beneath a low overhanging-gable roof, rough brackets and naturally curved timber retain Yuan building practice; the square-lattice windows were altered later. The dated structure and changing fittings show a historic dwelling shaped by continued use.
facts: Plan: three bays wide and six rafter spans deep, the house has a gently pitched overhanging-gable roof. Its recessed central entrance creates a porch and a slightly concave plan. The low roof, shallow porch and small bays serve domestic needs rather than temple ceremony.

Dating: a stone doorway pedestal records the thirty-first year of Zhiyuan, a jiawu year, corresponding to 1294. This direct evidence agrees with the timber construction. It should not be confused with dates under other reigns bearing the name Zhiyuan.

Components: the front column brackets are four-puzuo sets, with some pieces made from naturally curved timber. The window lattices were later changed to square grids. Yuan structural timber and altered fittings reveal the layers of time in a long-used home.

31st year of Zhiyuan · 1294

hn_yuzhoutianning.name: Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou
hn_yuzhoutianning.sub: Three-bay Yuan Buddhist hall preserved on a school campus
hn_yuzhoutianning.yearNote: The date of the hall's rebuilding is used; it was later restored in the Ming and Qing and was dismantled and repaired in 2013. The main gate is Ming in style and is not the subject of this plate.
hn_yuzhoutianning.lede: The main hall of Yuzhou’s Tianning Wanshou Temple survives within an old school campus. A three-bay grey-tiled hip-and-gable roof rests on brick walls and stone columns; brackets support its eaves, while exposed beams retain the curves of natural timber. Rebuilt under the Yuan and repaired under the Ming, Qing and in modern times, this modest hall reveals the continuity of local construction. Accounts of the temple’s origins should be distinguished from the date of this hall.
facts: Three bays wide and deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and four-tier brackets with one descending cantilever arm. Its exposed framing combines stone columns, brick walls and naturally curved timber.

The hall is dated to its rebuilding in 1299, the third year of the Yuan Dade era. It was repaired in the Ming Hongzhi and Jiajing eras and the Qing Daoguang era; the dismantling repair of 2013 was a conservation project.

The hall once served as school accommodation and survives alongside the temple gate. Its curved beams and regional techniques offer material evidence for comparing Song–Jin construction with later Ming–Qing buildings.
captions: Main hall of Tianning Wanshou Temple, Yuzhou · Present state, near-frontal view
Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Dade, Yuan (1299) · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

jiutian.name: Temple of the Holy Mother of the Nine Heavens
jiutian.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jianzhong Jingguo, Song · Yuan offering hall
jiutian.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Donghe Village
jiutian.lede: The offering hall at Jiutian Shengmu Temple is open on all sides. Stone columns carry timber beams and a roof, exposing their connections. Between the stage and the main hall, it fits into a close sequence of buildings whose eaves interweave within a compact courtyard. The surviving offering hall is identified as Yuan, not dated directly from the temple’s Song repair record. Ritual spaces, inscriptions and buildings of different periods reveal a village temple formed through successive campaigns.
facts: Openness: stone columns support a timber hall three bays wide and five deep, without enclosing walls. Adjacent buildings remain visible between the columns, and framing and eaves supports can be examined directly, unlike in the enclosed main hall.

Dating: the offering hall is Yuan, the main hall Song and the dressing tower Ming, while other parts contain Qing layers. Their close arrangement does not mean that all were built in the year recorded for a Song repair campaign.

Courtyard: the axis links gate-stage, offering hall and main hall, with subsidiary halls and galleries beside them. Worship and performance share the courtyard. Successive building inscriptions allow its spatial layout and written history to be read together.
captions: Line drawing of the offering hall · Side elevation · Five bays deep
Hipped roof · Main ridge along the depth · Yuan

hn_huishan.name: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng
hn_huishan.sub: Front of the Yuan main hall
hn_huishan.yearNote: The main subject drawn is dated to the Yuan; the numeric year is only an approximate sorting value.
hn_huishan.lede: Huishan Temple’s five-bay main hall spreads a broad façade at the southern foot of Mount Song. Layered brackets carry its hip-and-gable roof, with central doors flanked by window bays. The temple’s history predates this Yuan timber building, while inscriptions and subsequent repairs add further layers. Its broad roof, reduced interior columns and exposed framing explain how a hall could provide an open space for worship.
facts: Five bays wide and three deep, the hall has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with five-tier double-cantilever brackets. Reducing the number of interior columns enlarges the worship space beneath the broad roof.

The temple was founded and repaired over several periods. The surviving timber hall is assigned to the Yuan, but its exact construction year remains uncertain; the timeline position around 1300 is approximate.

Inscriptions record Buddhist activity and repairs from different periods, complementing evidence in the framing. The site illustrates the distinction between a temple’s long history and the date of one surviving building.
captions: Huishan Temple, Dengfeng · Front of the Yuan main hall
Yuan · Yuan period

hb_shijia.name: Sakyamuni Temple
hb_shijia.yearNote: Dated by the structure of the Yuan hall; the temple's other, Ming halls are not mixed into the main subject.
hb_shijia.lede: A broad central bay lies beneath the modest three-bay roof of Shijia Temple’s central hall. Its low, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and timber frame support a Yuan attribution. The temple later expanded, with neighbouring roofs arranged to echo the hall, while ridges and ceilings were repaired or added. The building therefore combines the core of a Yuan frame with a worship space repeatedly shaped in the Ming and Qing periods.
facts: The central hall, or Mahavira Hall, is three bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof on a brick terrace. Its broad middle bay creates a concentrated interior; three exterior bays do not necessarily mean a small chamber.

The provincial heritage authority identifies a Yuan structure from the frame and appearance; inscriptions also attest to a Yuan Shijia Chan Temple. Expansion followed in the Hongwu era, and parts of the roof and interior ceiling are later additions or repairs.

The neighbouring halls have gable roofs but add columns and extended eaves towards the central hall, creating similar front elevations. This visual dialogue organises the temple as a whole while showing that its buildings belong to different phases.
captions: Middle hall of Sakyamuni Temple
Front of the Yuan three-bay single-eaved hip-and-gable Mahavira Hall

sx_jiangzhou_datang.name: Jiangzhou Great Hall
sx_jiangzhou_datang.sub: Main hall of the prefectural office · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof
sx_jiangzhou_datang.era: Yuan · Main hall of the prefectural office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement for a surviving Yuan structure, not an exact completion year.
sx_jiangzhou_datang.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Jiangzhou Prefectural Office
sx_jiangzhou_datang.lede: Jiangzhou’s administrative hall stretches across seven bays and opens its interior through reduced columns and large longitudinal beams. Its official scale is expressed in the structure as much as the roof. The surviving core is identified as Yuan, though its exact foundation year is unknown, and Ming and Qing repairs followed. Substantial timbers and front brackets preserve the load-bearing logic of a local government building. A projecting porch has been lost; the broad hall still reveals a public space different from an ordinary dwelling.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and eight rafter spans deep, the hall has a single-eaved overhanging-gable roof and seventeen bracket sets along the front. Columns, lintels and beams organise a broad facade, with enclosed ends and central openings producing different degrees of openness.

History: the foundation date is uncertain. The surviving core is Yuan, with repairs under Hongwu, Qianlong and Guangxu. A three-bay projecting porch formerly stood at the front but is lost. The present building is not the complete state of any single building campaign.

Reduced columns: large longitudinal beams work with the transverse framing to carry the roof with fewer internal columns. This surviving government hall helps explain Yuan public architecture through the arrangement of structural timber rather than decoration alone.
captions: Jiangzhou Great Hall · Main hall of the prefectural office
Yuan · Seven bays, overhanging gable roof

sx_fusheng.name: Fusheng Temple, Xinjiang County
sx_fusheng.yearNote: 1300 serves only as an approximate sorting point for a surviving Yuan structure and does not claim completion in that year.
sx_fusheng.place: Shanxi · Xinjiang County · Guang Village, Zezhang Town
sx_fusheng.lede: Fusheng Temple in Guang Village unfolds tier upon tier with the terrain, and the Amitabha Hall organizes its inner and outer spaces with double eaves and a surrounding gallery. Its Yuan timber structure and the painted sculptures inside depend on each other, and the north elevation shows the layers of eaves, rear wall and gallery columns more clearly.
facts: Yuan hall: The Amitabha Hall preserves a Yuan timber structure and was restored in the Hongzhi era of the Ming; the temple's founding history cannot directly stand in for the date of the surviving hall.

Double eaves and gallery: The Amitabha Hall is five bays square, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a gallery all around; the ground level differs between the high platform to the south and the rear courtyard to the north.

Surviving painted sculpture: The hall preserves painted sculptures of Amitabha Buddha, attendant bodhisattvas, Guanyin Crossing the Sea and others, which have undergone various later repairs; this plate shows the north side of the hall.
captions: Fusheng Temple · North elevation of the Amitabha Hall

sx_zezhou_yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.sub: Fucheng · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.era: Yuan · Painted sculptures of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.yearNote: 1300 is only an approximate sorting point for the Yuan painted sculptures. Official sources give no exact date of making for the single figure selected; 1076 relates to the rebuilding of the temple and cannot substitute for the date of the sculptures.
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.place: Shanxi · Zezhou · Fucheng Village, Jincun Town
sx_zezhou_yuhuang.lede: At Zezhou’s Yuhuang Temple, the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions become clay figures with individual poses, robes and animal companions. Xu Ri Shu is one of them: human expression and rat imagery turn an abstract celestial name into an identifiable deity. Official material dates the group to the Yuan, but not this individual figure to a precise year. The temple’s Northern Song rebuilding does not date the sculpture. One figure’s details help explain how astronomy, religion and human character meet in the ensemble.
facts: Form: Xu Ri Shu combines a person with rat imagery; robe, gesture and expression give the stellar deity a character. It is one member of a twenty-eight-figure group, so its specific features should not be treated as a uniform design for every deity.

Dating: official material identifies the ensemble as Yuan. The individual figure’s exact production year is unconfirmed. The temple’s rebuilding during the Northern Song belongs to architectural history and should not be used as the statue’s date.

Cosmology: the lunar mansions belong to the Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird and Black Tortoise groups. Human and animal forms make their names visible. Celestial order and varied expressions allow the ensemble to be read both as a stellar system and as individual figures.
captions: Jade Emperor Temple, Zezhou · Xu Ri Shu
Yuan · Representative painted sculpture of the Twenty-Eight Mansions

hb_ciyunge.name: Ciyun Pavilion
hb_ciyunge.yearNote: Of the original Dabei Pavilion complex only this pavilion survives; it was rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade in the Yuan.
hb_ciyunge.lede: Ciyun Pavilion is small, yet its two storeys are supported through a remarkably compact arrangement. Broad eaves surround a nearly square three-bay frame, with hanging posts and diagonal corner beams helping transfer loads. Once called Dabei Pavilion, the surviving building is a Yuan reconstruction; most surrounding temple structures have vanished. The isolated pavilion still shows how Yuan carpenters organised complex support within limited space.
facts: The pavilion is three bays wide and three deep, nearly square, and two storeys high. Projecting eaves contrast with the compact body; the levels are not simply repeated, and the exterior silhouette works with the internal support system.

Its former name, Dabei Pavilion, referred to the bronze image of the Great Compassion Buddha inside. The surviving building was reconstructed in 1306. Only the pavilion remains from the former complex, and later repairs do not replace its Yuan attribution.

Tails of upper-eave bracket arms support a transverse beam, while hanging posts and diagonal beams handle the corners. These connections, easily missed from a distance, offer evidence of Yuan structural planning and craftsmanship.

Two stories, three bays · Rebuilt in the 10th year of Dade, Yuan

yongan.name: Yong'an Chan Temple, Hunyuan
yongan.sub: Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma
yongan.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan
yongan.lede: Chuanfa Zhengzong Hall anchors Yong’an Temple with a five-bay facade and a single-eaved hipped roof. Central entrances, large characters on the end walls and broad eaves create a ceremonial scale; water-and-land ritual murals fill the interior. The temple was founded in the Jin, while Gao Pu funded this surviving main hall in 1315 under the Yuan. Temple foundation and hall construction are distinct events. Timber structure and later paintings together preserve a space shaped by religious activity and repair.
facts: Form: five bays wide and three deep, the hall has a single-eaved hipped roof on a raised terrace, approached by a platform and stone steps. Its broad body, facade and eaves establish the spatial rank of the main hall.

Construction: the temple began in the Jin and was rebuilt after fire during the Yuan. Gao Pu funded this hall in 1315. The surviving main hall is Yuan; other Ming and Qing buildings and later repairs belong to separate phases.

Murals: water-and-land ritual paintings cover the interior walls, including Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist figures. They survive within the timber hall, but painting, repainting and hall construction are different events. The structure’s date does not automatically date every painted surface.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of the Orthodox Transmission of the Dharma · Five bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof · 2nd year of Yanyou, Yuan

yanfu.name: Yanfu Temple, Wuyi
yanfu.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in Jiangnan
yanfu.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Yanyou
yanfu.lede: Yanfusi’s main hall stands in a mountain village near Taoxi, Wuyi. Timber columns, curved beams and bracket sets support a spreading double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Some Song components were retained in the Yuan rebuilding, combining a Yuan structure with earlier construction practices. The fourth Yanyou year marks the start of a project that took several years. Later repairs preserve a layered example of the continuity between Song and Yuan timber architecture in Jiangnan.
facts: Form: bracket sets support the spreading double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Spindle-shaped columns and curved beams within create a light composition distinct from the heavier character of many northern halls.

Dating: monks Huaifa and Dehuan raised funds for a rebuilding beginning in 1317 and lasting seven years. Some columns survive from the Song, while inscriptions record repairs since the Qing; the hall contains fabric of several periods.

Significance: retained Song components within a Yuan frame document continuity in Jiangnan timber construction. Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin’s measured survey and photographs connect modern architectural scholarship with the hall’s preservation.
captions: Yanfu Temple · Main hall
4th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.scope: Yanfu Temple, Wuyi · Main hall · Yuan structure in Jiangnan

jinhuatianning.name: Tianning Temple, Jinhua
jinhuatianning.lede: Jinhua’s Tianning Temple hall preserves the detail of Song–Yuan timber construction within a compact three-by-three-bay building. Beams and brackets support its single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, while an ink inscription beneath a beam dates a Yuan rebuilding to 1318. The temple’s earlier foundation, reused Song components and later repairs are separate phases. Although only part of the old monastery remains, its timber and inscription still reveal the transmission of building practices.
facts: Form: three bays wide and three deep, the hall has a near-square plan and a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Integrated beams and bracket sets support a roof whose deep eaves extend beyond the compact body.

Dating: an ink inscription beneath a beam records rebuilding in 1318, the fifth Yanyou year. The Yuan work reused some Song components, and modern dismantling repairs followed; the inscription does not date every surviving material.

Significance: the dated inscription and surviving timberwork provide firm points for comparison. Song components within the Yuan rebuilding show how Jiangnan temples could retain earlier construction rather than replace everything during renewal.
captions: Tianning Temple, Jinhua · Main hall
5th year of Yanyou, Yuan · Single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.scope: Tianning Temple, Jinhua · Main hall · Three-bay Yuan structure

sh_zhenru.name: Main Hall of Zhenru Temple
sh_zhenru.sub: Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan timber structure
sh_zhenru.yearNote: 1320 corresponds to the construction inscription on the hall's timber frame; the present appearance was restored through repairs including those of 1963, which removed a later lower eave. The temple's other buildings and the new pagoda behind the hall are not included in this plate of the Yuan structure.
sh_zhenru.lede: A broad gray-tiled roof rests on the three-bay timber hall, with ridge-end ornaments curling skyward at both ends. The main hall of Zhenru Temple preserves Yuan Jiangnan timber construction within today's city, and an inscription among its beams still records its construction in the 7th year of Yanyou.
facts: An inscription on an interior architrave records that the hall was erected in the 7th year of Yanyou in the Yuan (1320); the hall retains Yuan timber members and is an important Yuan architectural survival in Shanghai.
Three bays wide, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; four columns across the front frame central lattice doors with windows at the sides, and ridge-end ornaments stand at both ends of the roof.

Repairs in 1963 removed a lower eave added later, restoring its single-eaved appearance. The plate shows only the main hall; the new pagoda behind it and the later buildings on either side have dates of their own.
captions: Front elevation of the main hall · Three bays wide
Yuan · 7th year of Yanyou (1320)

xiayu.name: Xia Yu Shrine
xiayu.place: Shanxi · Pingshun · Zhuozhang River valley · Houbi Village
xiayu.lede: On the Yuwang Hillock, the highest point of Houbi Village in the Zhuozhang River valley, a temple of a single courtyard packs Yuan, Ming and Qing timber buildings into 877 square metres: the gate is Ming, with a rear-facing stage on its upper floor looking straight at the Yuan main hall, while the side halls and wing rooms were added in the Qing. The plate shows the main hall, a surviving structure of 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan), three bays wide under a gable roof with a two-rafter-deep front porch; its framing of four-rafter beam against front ru-beam on four columns is a ready textbook for Yuan village temples of southeastern Shanxi.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, with a two-rafter-deep front porch; column-top bracket sets are four-puzuo with one downward ang, the three intercolumnar sets were added in the Qing; framing is a four-rafter beam against a front ru-beam, with four columns across the depth.

Dating: the shrine was founded in 1336 (2nd year of Zhiyuan, Yuan) and repaired repeatedly in the Ming and Qing; the hall keeps one Ming and two Qing inscribed wall stones and three stone offering tables of the Wanli reign; the gate is Ming, the side halls and wings Qing.

Layout: a single courtyard of only 877 square metres; the three-bay, four-rafter gate carries a rear-facing stage on its upper floor facing the main hall, and the convex altar terrace before the hall is carved in relief on three sides; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the site as "Yuan to Qing", three dynasties of timber work in one yard.
captions: Line drawing of the main hall · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Yuan

protection.scope: Xia Yu Shrine · Houbi Village

duanliang.name: Second Gate of Tiger Hill
duanliang.sub: Suzhou · Duanliang Hall of Tiger Hill
duanliang.era: Yuan · Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan
duanliang.lede: The main beam is 'broken': strictly, the ridge purlin is not a single timber but two round logs butted together at the middle, with the bracket sets and frames below spreading the load to either side, and it has held for more than six hundred years. The second gate of Tiger Hill is therefore called the Broken Beam Hall; rebuilt in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, it is three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with one round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. Built in the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan on Lake Tai, the two are Suzhou's firmly dated Yuan timber buildings.
facts: Form: three bays wide and two deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with a round-arched doorway at the centre of the front. The ridge purlin is made of two round logs joined end to end rather than one piece, hence the name 'broken beam'; the hall is neither beamless nor left hanging after a fracture.

Dating: the present second gate was rebuilt in 1338, the same year as the main hall of Xuanyuan Palace at Dongshan; the temple on Tiger Hill rose and fell repeatedly from the Five Dynasties and Northern Song onward, most of its halls burnt in the Taiping war of 1860, and the second gate survived as the earliest building on the hill after the Five Dynasties Yunyan Temple Pagoda.

Value: the broken beam is often called a 'miracle' of carpentry, but it is in fact a splicing technique that lets the frames and bracket sets on either side share the load, reflecting the Jiangnan craftsman's habit of using timber as it came; together with the Yunyan Temple Pagoda completed in 959-961 on the summit, it forms Tiger Hill's sequence of early buildings from the Five Dynasties to the Yuan.
captions: Second Gate of Tiger Hill · Front of the Duanliang Hall
Rebuilt in the 4th year of Zhiyuan, Yuan (1338) · Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

sx_doudafu.name: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan
sx_doudafu.sub: Offering pavilion and main hall · Shanglan Village
sx_doudafu.era: Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng
sx_doudafu.yearNote: Placed by the Yuan rebuilding date, the 3rd year of Zhizheng, of the surviving offering pavilion and main hall; neither the Spring and Autumn date of the person venerated nor the earlier history of the shrine is used as the date of the timber structures.
sx_doudafu.lede: Stout timber columns hold up deep eaves, and the offering pavilion joins the main hall behind it. Among the gray-brown old timbers, dark green glazed tiles outline the ridges and eave-tile ends; the Shrine of Grand Master Dou gathers its ritual space into a tight group of timber buildings.
facts: The shrine is dedicated to Dou Chou, a grand master of the state of Jin, and is also called the Lieshi Shrine and the Yingji Shrine; the early history of the shrine and the dates of the surviving buildings are described separately.

The surviving gate, offering pavilion and main hall were rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng in the Yuan (1343). The plate selects the offering pavilion and main hall and does not count the Qing side buildings as Yuan structures.

The hip-and-gable roof of the offering pavilion links with the overhanging gable roof of the main hall behind, and thick columns and massive bracket sets create a striking contrast of scale; the colored plate follows the surviving old timber, gray tiles and glazed tiles, and is not a reconstruction of historical painted decoration.
captions: Shrine of Grand Master Dou, Taiyuan · Front of the offering pavilion and main hall
Yuan · Rebuilt in the 3rd year of Zhizheng (1343)

bj_juyong_yuntai.name: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing
bj_juyong_yuntai.sub: Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage
bj_juyong_yuntai.era: Built from the 2nd to the 5th year of Zhizheng
bj_juyong_yuntai.lede: A stupa base whose stupas are gone: the Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass was built in 1342-1345, the second to fifth years of Zhizheng of the Yuan, as a street-spanning stupa gateway; the three Tibetan-style white stupas on top were destroyed early in the Ming, the Buddha hall later built in their place burnt in 1702, the forty-first year of Kangxi, and only this white marble platform remains. It is about 10 m high, 26.84 m along the base and 24.04 m along the top, tapering upward; a single arched passage runs through the centre from north to south, its vault folded into a half-hexagon, and its inner walls are covered with the Four Heavenly Kings, a thousand Buddhas and mandalas, together with scriptures in six scripts, Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese, Phagspa, Uyghur and Tangut, a stone dictionary of the Yuan empire's many written languages.
facts: Form: a white marble platform, narrower above than below, about 10 m high, 26.84 m east-west and 17.57 m north-south at the base, 24.04 m and 14.73 m at the top; a connected arched gateway opens at the centre of the north and south faces, 7.27 m high and 6.32 m wide. Two tiers of stone slabs project on all four sides of the top, carved with cloud scrolls, beast masks and tasselled pendants, carrying a stone balustrade, with dragon-head spouts beneath the posts and at the corners to drain the top.

Dating: begun in 1342 under four Tibetan designers and supervisors appointed by Emperor Shun, and finished in 1345 with three Tibetan-style white stupas on top; the stupas perished early in the Ming and a five-bay Buddha hall replaced them, rebuilt in 1443-1448, the eighth to thirteenth years of Zhengtong; in 1702 everything on the platform burnt and nothing has stood there since. Restoration began in 1993 and the site opened in 1998.

Carving and scripts: the vault of the passage bears five mandalas, the sloping faces the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, and a thousand Buddhas fill the spaces between; each side wall carries two Heavenly Kings, and between the four kings are the Dharani Sutra in six scripts, Sanskrit, Tibetan, Chinese, Phagspa, Uyghur and Tangut, and the Record of the Merit of Building the Stupa in five; the outer faces of the arches show the garuda with the whale, dragon children, boys riding beasts and elephants of the 'six ornaments', all in Tibetan style.
captions: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass · Surviving base of the street-spanning stupa
Yuan · Built 1342–1345

protection.scope: Cloud Platform at Juyong Pass, Beijing · Yuan base of a street-spanning stupa · Half-hexagonal arched passage

hb_beiyue.name: Beiyue Temple
hb_beiyue.sub: Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)
hb_beiyue.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau lists the present hall under the 7th year of Zhizheng (1347); the county gazetteer records completion in the 7th year of Zhiyuan (1270), so both construction phases need to be recorded.
hb_beiyue.lede: Dening Hall spreads broadly through two hipped roof tiers and a surrounding gallery. A high terrace and central stair elevate the ritual space, while Yuan murals fill its walls with mountain deities. Beiyue Temple served remote worship of Hengshan. Records give differing construction phases for the surviving hall; its architecture, murals and inscriptions together preserve successive traces of imperial mountain worship.
facts: The complete hall is nine bays wide and six deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof, surrounding gallery and central approach to a high terrace. Hall, gallery and platform combine into an elevation that expresses ritual status.

The hall is registered as Yuan. The provincial authority records rebuilding in 1347, while local gazetteer material also gives construction in 1270. These may represent different phases; neither is replaced by the temple’s Northern Wei origins.

The temple worshipped Hengshan from afar. Yuan murals survive on the eastern and western interior walls, alongside inscriptions of successive dynasties in the grounds. Timber, painting and text make the mountain cult spatially legible.
captions: Quyang · Dening Hall of Beiyue Temple
Yuan timber structure · Double-eaved hipped roof

protection.scope: Beiyue Temple · Front elevation of the Dening Hall (with gallery and platform)

xuanyuan.name: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace
xuanyuan.lede: A small hall at Yangwan on Dongshan by Lake Tai, three bays square, its hip-and-gable roof pressed low and its eaves reaching far out; it was once the Temple of King Xu, dedicated to Wu Zixu, and only in the Republican era was it rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and renamed Xuanyuan Palace. The main hall was built in 1338, the fourth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan, the same year as the second gate of Tiger Hill; it is 13.74 m wide and 11.43 m deep, with a ridge more than ten metres high. A major repair under Shunzhi in the Qing means that the Yuan frame and the traces of Ming-Qing repairs share the same building.
facts: Form: the main hall is three bays and 13.74 m wide, three bays and nine purlins or 11.43 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with a ridge over 10 m high; the body is nearly square and the eaves are deep. The plate shows the front of the main hall.

Dating: the founding date is unknown; it was repaired and renamed the Temple of King Xu in the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song, and the main hall was built in 1338; a further major repair followed in 1649-1655, the sixth to twelfth years of Shunzhi, so what stands today is not an untouched Yuan original. It was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

History: the site began as a shrine to Wu Zixu, who by tradition built the great city of Helü on the orders of the King of Wu; Suzhou's Xu Gate and Xukou take their names from him, and dragon-boat racing at the Duanwu festival in the Jiangsu-Zhejiang region is also seen as his commemoration. In the Republican era the temple was rededicated to the Yellow Emperor and first called Xuanyuan Palace.
captions: Yangwan, Dongshan · Main hall of Xuanyuan Palace
Three bays, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Yuan features alongside Ming–Qing building

protection.scope: Main Hall of Xuanyuan Palace · Suzhou · Yangwan, Dongshan

shisi.name: Shisi Temple, Jingning
shisi.sub: Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village
shisi.lede: Shisi Temple’s main hall stands among the historic buildings of Daji village in Jingning. Its timber body and layered double-eaved hip-and-gable roof retain the character of a Jiangnan Yuan hall. It dates to 1356, separately from the later Sanqing Hall and repaired bell tower. The temple’s links with the Mei lineage’s ritual and village life make the building an entry point into local religious and family memory as well as an architectural survival.
facts: Form: a timber frame supports the two tiers of eaves beneath a hip-and-gable roof. The main hall stands between the bell tower and Sanqing Hall within a compound of buildings serving different functions.

Dating: the hall was built in 1356, the sixteenth Zhizheng year. Ming and Qing expansion followed; the bell tower was repaired in 1646 and Sanqing Hall is later. One hall’s date does not describe the entire compound.

Significance: the Yuan hall alongside later buildings demonstrates the temple’s gradual growth. Its relationship with the Mei lineage joins religious space with family ritual, preserving several layers of local social history.
captions: Shisi Temple · Main hall
16th year of Zhizheng, Yuan · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof

protection.scope: Shisi Temple, Jingning · Main hall · Yuan structure in a mountain village

jijian.name: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple
jijian.lede: A small hall built in stone on the pattern of timber: stone columns, stone beams, stone purlins, even the roof is of stone slabs, and the back wall sits directly against the rock face of Tianchi Mountain. The stone hall of Jijian Temple, formerly Xitian Temple, was built in 1357, the seventeenth year of Zhizheng of the Yuan; it is three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a low, compact single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. To the east and west stand two small stone shrines built around Buddha niches, one inscribed 'Tushita Palace' and the other 'Garden of Bliss', and the standing images inside them are Yuan originals as well.
facts: Form: the stone hall faces south, three bays and 7.64 m wide, two bays and 5.52 m deep, under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; columns, beams, purlins and roof are all carved in stone in imitation of timber, and the back of the hall sits against the natural rock face. The plate shows the front of the stone hall.

Dating: the Jijian Hermitage was founded in 1357, and became a temple after the Ming; the surviving stone hall, niches and images all date from the Yuan, and the site was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Attached shrines: east and west of the hall stand two stone shrines built around Buddha niches in the manner of timber porches, each one bay wide and half a span deep: the west one has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and a standing Amitabha in its niche, inscribed 'Garden of Bliss'; the east one has a single-eaved roof and a standing Maitreya, inscribed 'Tushita Palace'. Yuan stone halls imitating timber are rare in the Jiangnan region, and this is a complete surviving group.
captions: Jijian Temple · Front of the Xitian Temple stone hall
17th year of Zhizheng, Yuan (1357) · Three-bay stone structure imitating timber

protection.scope: Stone Halls of Jijian Temple · Suzhou · Xitian Temple, Mount Tianchi

sx_jishan_qinglong.name: Qinglong Temple, Jishan
sx_jishan_qinglong.era: Late Yuan–early Ming · Middle hall murals
sx_jishan_qinglong.yearNote: The subject drawn is the middle hall murals, using the dating range of Sun Bo cited by the Yuncheng Museum; 1360 is only a sorting coordinate. It is not 1289, the completion year of the timber structure, and scholarly opinions on the dating of the murals still differ.
sx_jishan_qinglong.place: Shanxi · Jishan · Macun Village, Jifeng Town
sx_jishan_qinglong.lede: The earliest surviving wall painting of a Water-and-Land ritual in China is in the Middle Hall (yaodian) of Qinglong Temple at Macun: deities of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism parade in tiers, the Buddhas of the Three Ages enthroned at the top, drawn from the same southern Shanxi pattern books as the Yongle Palace one ridge away, yet in a manner of its own. An ink inscription of 1289 (26th year of Zhiyuan) under the hall's beams names the master carpenters; for the murals themselves there are two views, contemporary with the timber frame or repainted in the late Yuan to early Ming, and the timeline follows the latter. The plate redraws the Buddhas of the Three Ages in the upper part of the west wall and does not stand for all the murals and sculpture of the hall.
facts: Panels: each "Deities of the Three Realms" panel in the Middle Hall measures 223 cm high by 773 cm wide, principal Buddhas in the top register and lesser deities ranked below, linked by clouds; the line work is mainly iron-wire and nail-head-rat-tail strokes, the colouring based on azurite and malachite with vermilion, yellow, white and red.

Dating: the temple was founded in 662 (2nd year of Longshuo, Tang) and repaired repeatedly in the Yuan and Ming; an ink inscription under the ridge-brick tie beam of the Middle Hall reads "Great Yuan, 26th year of Zhiyuan, mid-autumn ... master carpenters ... respectfully recorded", i.e. the timber frame was completed in 1289; since Sun Bo's 2010 thesis the murals are dated to the Yuan, with a late-Yuan-to-early-Ming view as well.

Significance: the temple holds 196.38 square metres of Yuan and Ming murals; the Middle Hall cycle is regarded as the earliest extant Water-and-Land painting, its three-teachings pantheon leading on to Ming examples such as Pilu Temple; with the Sanqing Hall of Yongle Palace and the Mingying Wang Hall of the Water God Temple it belongs to the group of Yuan murals of southern Shanxi.
captions: Qinglong Temple · Buddhas of the Three Ages on the west wall of the middle hall (detail)
Late Yuan–early Ming · Mural redrawn in line

sx_pingyaowall.name: Pingyao City Wall
sx_pingyaowall.sub: Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
sx_pingyaowall.yearNote: 1370 is used for sorting by the phase of the wall's expansion; the gate tower and surviving wall faces include later repairs.
sx_pingyaowall.lede: After the enlargement and brick facing of 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming), this circuit of wall at Pingyao, over six thousand metres round and about twelve metres high, was never pulled down: six gates, four corner towers, seventy-two bastions and more than three thousand merlons can still be counted. It is the most complete county-town wall in China and the core of the "one city, two temples" World Heritage property of 1997. The plate takes the south gate, Yingxun Gate, where the arched passage, gate platform and double-eave gate tower stack into one group and the battlemented wall runs off east and west; both tower and wall surfaces include later repairs.
facts: Wall: about 6.4 km in circuit and about 12 m high, rammed earth faced with grey brick, paved on top with a horse ramp inside; a bastion with an enemy tower projects roughly every 50 m, 72 in all, with over three thousand merlons; the moat outside is about 4 m wide and 4 m deep.

History: tradition dates the first wall to King Xuan of Zhou; the present wall was enlarged and brick-cased in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming) on the old town, and dozens of later repairs kept the early-Ming scheme; part of the south wall collapsed in 2004 and was rebuilt in 2005.

Heritage: in 1997 the Ancient City of Pingyao, with Shuanglin and Zhenguo temples, was inscribed as World Heritage, the wall enclosing a 225-hectare property; nearly four thousand Ming and Qing shops and dwellings inside bear witness to the town's years as China's financial centre from the 19th to the early 20th century.
captions: Pingyao City Wall · Yingxun Gate and adjoining wall sections
Ming–Qing · Ming–Qing

sn_hancheng.name: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple
sn_hancheng.era: Rebuilt in the Hongwu era, maintained over the centuries
sn_hancheng.yearNote: 1371 is the recorded rebuilding of the Confucian Temple on its Yuan site; the Dacheng Hall retains Yuan building methods and has been maintained over the centuries, so not every surviving member can be assigned to 1371.
sn_hancheng.place: Shaanxi · Weinan · Old town of Hancheng
sn_hancheng.lede: Hancheng Confucian Temple’s Dacheng Hall presents three broad bays in its front porch but five in the main frame, balancing openness with finer subdivision. Rebuilt on a Yuan site in the Hongwu period, the single-eaved hip-and-gable hall retains earlier displaced-column techniques. Roof, porch columns and interior space reveal layers of Ming rebuilding and later repair rather than one construction date.
facts: The hall is five bays wide, with a three-bay front porch beneath a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Large lintels above the eaves columns support the upper structure. Broad open porch bays contrast with the more finely divided frame behind.

The provincial gazetteer cites earlier records for rebuilding the temple on its Yuan site in 1371, followed by repeated repairs. The hall retains Yuan building techniques; the rebuilding date does not establish the manufacture date of every surviving timber.

Some interior columns are displaced, freeing the principal space from an evenly divided column grid. As the main hall for Confucian worship, it combines ritual axial order with practical space. Timber details explain its construction more clearly than the roof alone.
captions: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple, whole hall · Line drawing
Ming · Rebuilt 1371 · Later maintenance

protection.scope: Dacheng Hall of Hancheng Confucian Temple · Five-bay hall · Timber front porch

yuhuang.name: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou
yuhuang.era: Founded in the 10th year of Hongwu
yuhuang.place: Hebei · Yu County · North city wall
yuhuang.lede: Jingbian Tower places Jade Emperor worship on Yuzhou’s northern city wall, giving a two-storey pavilion three eave lines. An intermediate eave links roof and galleries in strong horizontal bands, combining a frontier presence with temple dignity. Founded in the early Ming and repaired later, the building is best understood by separating roof tiers from usable storeys.
facts: Also called Yuhuang Pavilion, it stands on the northern wall with two storeys and three eave tiers beneath a glazed hip-and-gable roof. Galleries wrap the body; an intermediate eave adds a line without creating a third usable floor.

The provincial authority records foundation in 1377. Brackets and timber proportions retain Ming characteristics, but later repairs must be distinguished from the founding phase; not every visible component is an original early Ming piece.

The pavilion forms a religious precinct with the Heavenly Kings Hall and bell and drum towers, while the city wall gives it a prominent urban position. Frontier defence and Jade Emperor worship meet in the setting implied by its name Jingbian.
captions: Jade Emperor Pavilion of Yuzhou · Front
Three eaves, two stories · Five bays wide

xianwall.name: Xi'an City Wall
xianwall.sub: Arrow tower of Anding Gate · Ming rampart
xianwall.lede: Anding Gate’s arrow tower has a broad face pierced by firing windows, while one arch concentrates movement into a single entrance. Xi’an’s western gate developed during the Hongwu expansion, with arrow tower, inner gate tower and barbican forming successive defences. Repaired through the Ming, Qing and modern periods, the brick-faced earthen walls make a defensive plan tangible.
facts: The arrow tower stands on a massive gate platform, its walls densely pierced by firing windows. A central arch passes below it. A barbican connects it to the inner gate tower; the passage is only one component of this layered defensive space.

Local records associate Anding Gate with the expansion of 1374–1378. Repeated Ming and Qing repairs followed, and the outer gate tower was lost in the late Qing. The surviving arrow and inner towers still include later repaired brickwork and timber.

Gate defences had to accommodate both movement and resistance. Raised towers, narrow passages and enclosed courts worked together. Tracing a route from outside to inside explains the city’s defence better than treating its walls as one continuous barrier.
captions: Xi'an City Wall · Arrow tower and central arched passage of Anding Gate
Ming rampart · Ming, Qing and modern repairs

xianzhonggu.name: Bell Tower and Drum Tower of Xi'an
xianzhonggu.era: Founded in the Hongwu era · Moved in the Wanli era
xianzhonggu.place: Shaanxi · Xi'an · Center of the prefectural city
xianzhonggu.lede: The Bell Tower’s roof converges above a square plan, while the Drum Tower spreads beneath a long ridge. Their bells and drums once made the city’s hours audible. The Drum Tower began in 1380; the Bell Tower followed four years later and moved to today’s street junction in 1582. Comparing bases, passages and eaves reveals a shared timekeeping purpose expressed through different proportions.
facts: The Bell Tower has a square base, intersecting arched passages and three eaves beneath a pyramidal roof. The Drum Tower has a rectangular base, seven-bay frontage and surrounding galleries; its hip-and-gable roof and lower eaves emphasise width.

The Drum Tower was founded in 1380, and the Bell Tower in 1384 before moving in 1582. A new base was built for the relocated Bell Tower. Later repairs mean the foundation dates cannot be assigned to every surviving component.

Both towers announced time, linking sound with the main streets. Square and rectangular platforms, and pyramidal and hip-and-gable roofs, give one civic purpose distinct forms. They are juxtaposed here but are not immediately adjacent in reality.
captions: Xi'an Bell Tower · Drum Tower
Composite of two subjects, not adjacent in reality
