linggu.name: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple
linggu.lede: Not a single piece of timber: the Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple is built entirely of brick, three barrel vaults running side by side from east to west carry the roof, the central one spanning eleven and a half metres and rising fourteen, and the front and rear walls are four metres thick. Built in 1381, the fourteenth year of Hongwu of the Ming, it originally housed the Buddha of Infinite Life, Wuliang, and 'Wuliang Hall' became 'Wuliang Hall', beamless, in speech; it is the largest brick hall of its kind in China. In the Xianfeng era the temple was all but levelled in war and only this brick hall stood; in 1931 it became the memorial hall of the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army.
facts: Form: inside, five bays and 53.8 m from east to west, three bays and 37.85 m from north to south, with the roof 22 m high; a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in grey glazed tile carries three white glazed lama stupas on the ridge, the central one hollow at the base and open to the ceiling coffer inside to admit light. Three vaults run side by side, the middle one spanning 11.5 m and 14 m high, the side ones 5 m and 7.4 m; front and rear walls each open three doors and are about 4 m thick.

Dating: Linggu Temple was moved here from Dulongfu in 1381 and the Beamless Hall was completed the same year; in the Zhengtong era it housed three great Buddhas with the Twenty-four Devas along the sides and served as a sutra store, and it was repaired repeatedly under Jiaqing and Daoguang; in the Xianfeng era most of the temple's halls burnt in the fighting between Qing and Taiping forces, and only this brick hall survived.

Memorial hall: in 1928 the Nationalist government built the cemetery for fallen soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army on the old temple site, and in 1931 the restored Beamless Hall became its memorial hall, the Hall of Righteous Spirit; 110 slabs of Taihu bluestone set into the walls list 33,224 soldiers who fell in the Northern Expedition and in the fighting against Japan at Shanghai and in north China; the Nanjing municipal government restored it again in 1981.
captions: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple · Front of the brick-vaulted hall
Surviving Ming structure · Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with three pagoda-shaped ridge ornaments

protection.unitName: Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army
protection.scope: Beamless Hall of Linggu Temple · Nanjing · Brick-vaulted hall
protection.note: In 1933 the Beamless Hall was converted into the memorial hall of the Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the National Revolutionary Army; in the fifth batch the cemetery was incorporated into the first-batch listing of the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum. It is not a separately listed national protected site under the name “Linggu Temple.”

sx_chongshan.name: Chongshan Temple, Taiyuan
sx_chongshan.sub: Hall of Great Compassion · Early Ming official-style timber structure
sx_chongshan.era: Hongwu era, Ming · Hall of Great Compassion
sx_chongshan.yearNote: 1385 is only an approximate timeline placement within the Hongwu reign, not a precise completion year. Neither the temple's history nor its Qing main gate replaces the date of the Ming main subject drawn.
sx_chongshan.lede: In 1381 (14th year of Hongwu, Ming) Zhu Gang, Prince Gong of Jin, enlarged this temple for his late mother Empress Ma; at 140,000 square metres with six great halls on the axis it was once the largest in Shanxi. After a fire in 1864 (3rd year of Tongzhi, Qing) only the fifth hall on the axis, the Dabei Hall, was left. Seven bays wide under double eaves and nearly twenty metres high, together with its three Hongwu-era painted statues over eight metres tall, it is the most dependable specimen of an early-Ming official-style Buddhist hall in Taiyuan. The plate shows the front of the Dabei Hall.
facts: Dabei Hall: seven bays wide and four bays deep, double-eave hip-and-gable (xieshan) roof, nearly 20 m high overall; in the centre stands the Thousand-armed, Thousand-eyed, Eleven-headed Guanyin, flanked by the Thousand-bowl Manjusri and Samantabhadra, all three original Hongwu-period statues over 8 m tall.

History: according to the Daoguang-era Yangqu County Gazetteer the site was a travel palace of Emperor Yang of Sui and was called Baima Temple in the early Tang; the enlargement ran from 1381 to 1391 (14th to 24th years of Hongwu), and the present name dates from the Jiajing reign; after the fire of 1864, Zhang Zhidong in 1882 (8th year of Guangxu) turned the ruined front part into the Taiyuan Prefectural Confucian Temple.

Scale: in the Ming the temple had nearly a thousand bays of halls, the axis running through the Vajra, Heavenly Kings, Mahavira, Vairocana, Dabei and Jinling halls, the Dabei Hall second only to the nine-bay Mahavira Hall; today the temple measures 119.2 m east-west by 71.7 m north-south, covering 8,547 square metres.
captions: Chongshan Temple · Hall of Great Compassion
Hongwu era, Ming · Seven bays, double-eaved hipped roof

fj_chongwu.name: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City
fj_chongwu.sub: Granite gate platform · South gate wall section
fj_chongwu.era: City built in the 20th year of Hongwu, later repaired
fj_chongwu.yearNote: 1387 is the founding date of the Chongwu stone city and an approximate timeline placement; the surviving south gate section has undergone later repairs, and the upper gate tower seen in photographs is not labeled as original 1387 fabric.
fj_chongwu.lede: China's most complete surviving granite coastal fortress town. In 1387 Zhou Dexing, Marquis of Jiangxia, was ordered to build the Chongwu Battalion (qianhusuo) city on the Hui'an headland against pirate raids: a wall of some 2,500 metres, seven metres high, with gates on four sides and barbicans added to the east and west gates. The plate shows a section at the South Gate, a low, massive granite platform with the arched gateway in the middle; the gatehouse above is as it appeared after the comprehensive 1980s restoration 'to the original appearance', and should not be taken as early Ming fabric.
facts: Scale: the walls are built entirely of granite blocks, 2,567 m in circuit, about 500 m north-south and 300 m east-west, 5 m thick at the base and 7 m high; there were originally 26 guard huts, 1,304 crenels and 1,300 arrow slits, with a two- to three-tier rampart walk. The South Gate platform and its arch are one section of this.

History: begun in 1387 and completed in 1394; in 1558 pirates besieged the city for six days and nights and took it; in 1567 Qi Jiguang garrisoned troops here and reorganised the defences. Five major repairs followed between the Yongle and Daoguang reigns, and in 1983-1987 the State Administration of Cultural Heritage funded three phases of restoration, rebuilding 2,517 m of wall to the original appearance.

Comparison: Chongwu was a battalion city in the early Ming coastal garrison (weisuo) system of Fujian, and survives whole because its stone was quarried from local Hui'an granite; within half a square kilometre the town still keeps over twenty temples and nunneries, dozens of ancestral halls and more than two hundred old houses, a live example of the social structure of a southern Fujian military town.
captions: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City and a short adjoining stretch of wall · Line drawing
Ming · Founded 1387 · Repaired over the centuries

protection.scope: South Gate of Chongwu Ancient City · Granite gate platform · South gate wall section

sx_jiulongbi.name: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong
sx_jiulongbi.sub: Glazed spirit screen of the Prince of Dai's mansion · Nine-dragon relief
sx_jiulongbi.yearNote: The date given by the Palace Museum, the 25th year of Hongwu (1392), is used; the plate depicts only the surviving Nine-Dragon Screen and not the present-day reconstruction of the Prince of Dai's mansion.
sx_jiulongbi.place: Shanxi · Datong · Heyang Street, Old city
sx_jiulongbi.lede: Nine dragons twist among blue-green glazed tiles, with clouds and waves spreading along the long screen. The Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong contains its dense relief between a low coping and a layered Sumeru plinth, leaving behind the screen of an early Ming princely mansion.
facts: The Nine-Dragon Screen was originally the glazed spirit screen in front of the mansion of Zhu Gui, Prince of Dai. The Palace Museum records it as built in the 25th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1392), and it is assigned to the Ming according to the main body of the screen drawn.
The screen is about 45.5 m long and about 8 m high, with nine principal dragons arrayed along its continuous body; the hipped coping and the glazed Sumeru plinth form its upper and lower borders.

A spirit screen serves as a barrier and decoration in front of a building and is not a city wall or fortification. The plate removes the railings, trees and reflecting pool and simplifies the details of the cloud-and-dragon relief, while keeping the multicolored distribution of the actual glazes.
captions: Nine-Dragon Screen of Datong · Front of the glazed nine-dragon spirit screen
Ming · 25th year of Hongwu (1392)

shuanglin.name: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao
shuanglin.sub: Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture
shuanglin.era: Restored in the 2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi · Rebuilt in the early Ming
shuanglin.lede: It is the first thing you see inside the fortified gate: the five-bay, gable-roofed Hall of the Heavenly Kings, with four guardian Vajra figures three metres tall lined up in its front porch, the opening statement of Shuanglin Temple's more than two thousand Ming painted sculptures. The temple began as Zhongdu Temple; a Northern Song stele in the compound records a rebuilding as early as 571 (2nd year of Wuping, Northern Qi), while today's halls and statues mostly come from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing. In 1997 it was inscribed as World Heritage with Zhenguo Temple as part of the Ancient City of Pingyao. The plate shows the front of the hall and the porch guardians; the Maitreya, Indra, Brahma and Four Heavenly Kings inside are not in the picture.
facts: Hall of the Heavenly Kings: five bays wide and three deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof; four guardian Vajra figures about 3 m tall stand in the front porch; inside, the crowned Maitreya is 2.2 m high, the attendant Indra and Brahma about 1.75 m, the Four Heavenly Kings face inward from the south wall and the Eight Bodhisattvas line the sides.

Dating: the Gugu Stele of 1011 (4th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Northern Song) in the temple records that "Zhongdu Temple was rebuilt in the 2nd year of Wuping of Northern Qi (571)"; the Song renamed it after the Buddha's passing between twin sal trees; the existing halls and sculptures come mainly from a Ming rebuilding, repainted in the Qing, and the Ming rammed-earth enclosure with its battlements gives the temple the look of a fort.

Sculpture: ten halls hold 2,052 painted clay figures, 1,566 of them intact, the largest over 3 m and the smallest 30 cm, about three quarters modelled in suspended relief leaning forward 10 to 20 degrees; the clay is local red clay and the eyes are inlaid black glass.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of Heavenly Kings · Five bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Four vajra guardians in the front porch

protection.scope: Shuanglin Temple, Pingyao · Hall of Heavenly Kings · Painted sculpture

hb_zixiao.name: Zixiao Palace
hb_zixiao.era: Built in the Yongle era, Ming
hb_zixiao.yearNote: The Zixiao Hall is placed by its construction in the Yongle era of the Ming; 1413 is a sorting reference for this phase of the palace's construction and is not presented as the hall's exact completion year. It was later repaired, and the drawing shows the present state seen in research photographs. The Song founding history is kept separate from the Ming hall drawn.
hb_zixiao.lede: Zixiao Palace’s main hall stands on three stone terraces, with a five-bay timber body and green double-eaved roof. The steps turn mountain slopes into a solemn approach. The palace predates the Ming, while the surviving principal hall belongs to the Yongle emperor’s major building campaign and subsequent repairs. Brackets beneath the eaves and the rising platforms show how Wudang’s Taoist ritual order works with the terrain.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and five deep, with timber framing beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Three stone terraces raise it above the approach; stairs lead to the platform, creating an ascending sequence of foundations, columns and eaves.

The palace had a Song-period foundation and underwent major imperially ordered construction during the Ming Yongle reign; the surviving hall belongs to that phase. Later enlargement, beam inscriptions and construction records must be distinguished rather than applying the foundation date to everything visible.

Dedicated to the Supreme Emperor of the Dark Heaven, the hall was important in Wudang’s royal prayer system. Terraces adapted to the slope combine with ordered timberwork to organize worship and display the ritual and building practices of a Taoist palace.
captions: Zixiao Hall and front platform of Zixiao Palace · Line drawing
Ming · Yongle era, Ming

protection.scope: Zixiao Hall and front platform of Zixiao Palace

hb_jindian.name: Golden Hall of Wudang Mountains
hb_jindian.sub: Cast bronze, gilded · Double-eaved hipped roof
hb_jindian.yearNote: The drawing shows the surviving Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, placed at the 14th year of Yongle (1416); it is not to be confused with the ancient Yuan bronze hall moved into the Zhuanyun Hall. The formal national listing includes both the Yuan and Ming bronze halls; this plate shows only the Ming hall.
hb_jindian.lede: The Golden Hall on Wudang’s Tianzhu Peak resembles a small double-eaved timber sanctuary, but columns, beams, brackets, roof tiles, doors and windows are assembled from cast bronze and gilded. Built in 1416, it occupies the ceremonial heart of the summit complex. This surviving Ming hall must be distinguished from the older Yuan bronze hall moved elsewhere. Its metal imitation of timber joins imperial Taoist patronage with casting technology.
facts: The hall is three bays wide and three deep, following a double-eaved, hipped-roof timber form. Cast-bronze columns, beams, brackets, roof surfaces, doors and windows form a complete building while retaining traditional wooden architectural details.

The surviving summit hall was built in Yongle 14, or 1416. Components made in Beijing were transported to Wudang for assembly. The earlier Yuan bronze hall was subsequently moved and is a separate building from the present double-eaved Ming sanctuary.

The summit’s ceremonial centre reflects the scale of Ming imperial support for Taoism. Assembling metal components into a timber-like sanctuary also provides material evidence for historical transport, installation and building techniques.
captions: Ming Golden Hall on Tianzhu Peak, Wudang Mountains · Line drawing
Ming · 1416

tiantan.name: Temple of Heaven, Beijing
tiantan.sub: Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests
tiantan.era: Founded in the 18th year of Yongle · Rebuilt in the 22nd year of Guangxu
tiantan.lede: The Hall of Great Sacrifice was built in the 18th year of Yongle in the Ming (1420); in the Jiajing era it became a round, triple-eaved hall, and under Qianlong it received blue tiles and was renamed the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests. Struck by lightning and burned in the 15th year of Guangxu (1889), it was rebuilt to the original design six years later — what we see today is timber of 1896.
facts: Round, triple-eaved and conical, with blue glazed tiles and a gilded finial; 32.72 m in diameter and 38 m tall overall, it stands on a three-tiered round terrace of white marble.
Twenty-eight columns stand inside: four Dragon Well Columns represent the four seasons, twelve golden columns the twelve months, and twelve eave columns the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
The hall has no great beams; columns, tie-beams and bracket sets support the conical roof layer by layer, the pinnacle of Ming–Qing official-style timber construction.
captions: Line drawing of the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests · Round, triple-eaved
Conical roof · Three-tiered round terrace

protection.scope: Temple of Heaven, Beijing · Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests

hb_jimingyi.name: Jimingyi Post Town
hb_jimingyi.sub: East gate platform and flanking old city walls
hb_jimingyi.yearNote: 1420 is the founding year of the Ming post town recognized by the provincial cultural heritage bureau, with further construction in the Ming and Qing; this plate includes a gate tower restored in modern times, and its timber roof is not claimed as Ming original.
hb_jimingyi.lede: Jimingyi’s eastern arch compresses the road into a narrow entrance, then its brick platform and flanking walls broaden the view. The Ming and Qing postal and military station accommodated offices, horses and stores alongside residents. The gate gives that transport system a visible boundary. Ming wall history and the restored timber gatehouse belong to different phases, despite their coherent present silhouette.
facts: The nearly square station town has eastern and western gates and walls of rammed earth faced with brick. The eastern platform and adjoining wall sections define the entrance; their mass reveals defensive construction more directly than the timber superstructure.

The provincial authority dates the town’s foundation to 1420, followed by Ming and Qing repairs. The present timber gatehouse includes modern restoration: the founding date describes the station’s history, not the age of every visible timber component.

Offices, horse quarters and stores once stood alongside temples, shops and houses. This mix reflects the station’s role as a transport node; the eastern gate served both defence and the movement of official documents, horses and travellers.
captions: Jimingyi Post Town, Huailai · East gate
Gate platform and flanking wall sections; gate tower in its restored state

bj_changling.name: Ling'en Hall of Changling, Beijing
bj_changling.sub: Nine-bay nanmu hall · Double-eaved hipped roof
bj_changling.era: Built from Yongle to Xuande · Repaired over the centuries
bj_changling.yearNote: Palace Museum sources record that the sacrificial hall was completed in 1416 and the halls of the mausoleum precinct finished in 1427, while other accounts adopt 1427 as the completion of the hall. 1420 is only an approximate sorting point within the early Ming construction history of the hall drawn; the initial construction of the mausoleum in 1409 is not used as the hall's completion year.
bj_changling.lede: The scale of Changling's Ling'en Hall is easiest to grasp inside: sixty nanmu columns support a hall nine bays wide, with four particularly massive columns at its centre. It housed the spirit tablets of the Yongle Emperor Zhu Di and his empress and formed the ritual heart of the tomb complex. The hall and the whole complex were completed at different times. Palace Museum records date the worship hall to 1416 and completion of the complex's halls to 1427. Its double-eaved hipped roof and stone terrace still express the ceremonial rank of a Ming imperial tomb.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and five deep, the hall has a double-eaved hipped roof carried by sixty columns of solid nanmu timber. The four central columns are about 1.12 metres in diameter; their size and the broad facade convey the scale of the timber structure.

Construction: work on the tomb complex began in 1409. Palace Museum records date completion of the worship hall to 1416 and completion of the complex's halls to 1427. The hall and the larger complex therefore have distinct completion dates.

Ritual: originally called the worship hall, it housed imperial spirit tablets and hosted ceremonies at the tomb. It was renamed Ling'en Hall in 1538: ling evokes blessings received through sacrifice, and en the debt owed to one's parents. The name itself carries ritual meaning.
captions: Changling · Nine-bay Ling'en Hall
Yongle to Xuande, Ming · 1416–1427 construction history

protection.scope: Ling'en Hall of Changling, Beijing · Nine-bay nanmu hall · Double-eaved hipped roof

baoen.name: Pagoda of Great Bao'en Temple, Nanjing
baoen.era: Begun in the 10th year of Yongle · Completed in the 3rd year of Xuande
baoen.lede: Begun in 1412, the tenth year of Yongle of the Ming, and finished in 1428, the third year of Xuande, it had nine storeys and eight sides and rose 78.2 m, its body faced in white porcelain brick, its arched doorways set with lions, elephants and flying rams in five-coloured glazed tile, 152 wind bells hanging from the corner beams and more than a hundred lamps burning through every night; Europeans called it the Porcelain Tower of Nanjing and counted it among the seven wonders of the medieval world. It was blown up in 1856 during the Taiping internal purge at Tianjing, leaving only the finial and stone steles; the ink-numbered glazed components unearthed in 1958 and the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa found in the crypt in 2008 are what remain of it in physical form. The plate is based on a reconstruction model.
facts: Form: the glazed pagoda had nine storeys and eight sides and a total height of 78.2 m, visible from the Yangtze tens of li away; the body was faced in white porcelain, the arched doors framed in glazed tile with lions, white elephants, flying rams and other motifs in five colours; the finial was set with gold, silver and jewels, 152 wind bells hung beneath the corner beams, and the inner walls were lined with Buddha niches.

Dating: in 1412 the Yongle Emperor ordered the Ministry of Works to rebuild Tianxi Temple, and in 1424 he named it the Great Bao'en Temple and composed its stele text himself; the pagoda was begun the same year and completed in 1428, after nineteen years, reportedly under the supervision of Zheng He, then garrison commander of Nanjing. Fire at the end of the Jiajing era left 'only the pagoda, the meditation hall and the kitchen standing'.

Destruction and finds: in 1856, during the Taiping purge at Tianjing, the North King Wei Changhui ordered it blown up to deny the Wing King's troops a platform for cannon, leaving only the finial and steles. In 1958 a large number of glazed components bearing ink-written serial marks were unearthed around Yaogang Village, and tradition says three identical sets were fired; in 2008 an iron casket at the site yielded the Seven-Jewel Ashoka Stupa containing the 'Buddha's parietal bone relic', and the site park opened in 2015.
captions: Nine stories, eight faces · Drawn from the Tushanwan model of the old pagoda
Original pagoda destroyed · Not the modern glass tower

bj_zhihua.name: Zhihua Temple, Beijing
bj_zhihua.sub: Tathagata Hall · Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
bj_zhihua.era: Founded in the Zhengtong era · Surviving Ming halls
bj_zhihua.yearNote: Official descriptions give 1443 and 1444 respectively as the founding year of Zhihua Temple. 1444 is used for approximate sorting; the temple's founding year cannot be taken directly as the precise date of making of every surviving member.
bj_zhihua.lede: Beneath black glazed tiles, Rulai Hall and Wanfoge form a single two-storey Buddhist hall. The lower storey is five bays wide and the upper narrows to three, making the stepping back of walls and roofs especially clear. Zhihua Temple was commissioned by the Ming eunuch Wang Zhen. Official accounts describe construction beginning in 1443 and completion in 1444. Its densely arranged Buddha niches and surviving Ming timber structure make this temple tucked into a hutong a material record of Ming Buddhist architecture as well as a distinctive black-tiled building.
facts: Storeys: Rulai Hall below and Wanfoge above have separate names but form one building. The lower level is five bays wide and three deep; the upper is three bays square. The narrowing facade and rooflines clearly articulate the two levels.

History: Wang Zhen commissioned Zhihua Temple as his family temple. Beijing government material dates its beginning to 1443, while a municipal heritage research introduction dates completion to 1444. These refer to the building campaign, rather than independently dating every hall.

Details: black glazed tiles and dense rows of Buddha niches are prominent features. The surviving Ming timber halls, decorative painting and bracket sets also provide material evidence for studying the transition from Song and Yuan building traditions to those of the Ming and Qing.
captions: Zhihua Temple, Beijing · Tathagata Hall and Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion
Ming · Founded 1443–1444

protection.scope: Zhihua Temple, Beijing · Tathagata Hall · Ten Thousand Buddha Pavilion

hunyuanwenmiao.name: Hunyuan Confucian Temple
hunyuanwenmiao.place: Shanxi · Datong · Old town of Hunyuan · Yong'an West Street
hunyuanwenmiao.lede: At the prefectural school of Hunyuan below the Northern Sacred Peak, the Dacheng Hall is the one building in the compound with real presence: five bays wide and three deep, roofed in yellow and green glazed tile, its central and second bays fully fitted with six-rail lattice doors while the end bays are solid brick, and the brick rear wall carries the four large characters "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness". The gazetteer records a large-scale rebuilding in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming), and the surviving hall is generally taken as a Ming structure; the omission of the front interior columns and the plain four-puzuo bracket sets under the eaves keep an older feel. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall.
facts: Dacheng Hall: five bays and 27.6 m wide, three bays and 14.6 m deep, single-eave hip-and-gable roof in yellow and green glazed tile; four-puzuo bracket sets with two intercolumnar sets each in the central and second bays, the front row of interior columns omitted; the terrace in front is about 13 m long, 6 m wide and 1.5 m high, with a two-dragons-and-pearl imperial ramp in the middle.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Hunyuan Prefecture Gazetteer says the temple predates the Liao and Jin, was enlarged in the early Yuan, rebuilt on a large scale in 1472 (8th year of Chenghua, Ming) and completed in the Wanli reign; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing, and the hall itself has no firm completion date.

Layout: along the axis only the Ji Gate, Dacheng Hall, Zunjing Pavilion and Chongsheng Shrine survive, the pavilion a brick vault below and a timber loft above; the "loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness" brickwork resembles the carved brick inscriptions of nearby Yong'an Temple, whose glazed roof fittings also match those of this hall.
captions: Line drawing of the Dacheng Hall of the Confucian Temple · Five bays wide
Single-eaved hipped roof · Surviving Ming structure

protection.scope: Hunyuan Confucian Temple · Dacheng Hall

bj_zhenjue.name: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing
bj_zhenjue.era: Completed in the 9th year of Chenghua
bj_zhenjue.lede: The five small pagodas do not stand separately on the ground: they share a tall stone-clad platform, the distinctive arrangement of Zhenjue Temple's Vajra Throne. The platform has a brick core faced with pale grey stone, with closely spaced eaves rising on the pagodas above. The group gave the temple its popular name, Five Pagoda Temple. Completed in 1473, the throne draws on Buddhist architecture at Bodh Gaya in India. Buddha images, Sanskrit mantras and Tibetan benedictions carved into its surfaces brought that imported form into the Buddhist art of Ming Beijing.
facts: Form: the tall throne has a brick core clad in pale grey stone and carries five small pagodas with closely spaced eaves. A passage inside reaches the top, making the supporting platform itself a building that could be entered and climbed.

Dating: Zhenjue Temple was founded during the Yongle reign, but the surviving Vajra Throne was completed in 1473, in the Chenghua reign. Restoration during Qianlong's reign brought the name Zhengjue Temple. The temple's names and the throne's construction date are distinct matters.

Exchange: the pagodas draw on architectural forms at Bodh Gaya in India. Buddha images, Sanskrit mantras and Tibetan benedictions carved into the stone combine different languages and imagery in one religious setting, recording exchanges in Chinese and Tibetan Buddhist art during the Ming.
captions: Diamond Throne Pagoda of Zhenjue Temple, Beijing · South side
Ming · 1473

hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.name: Qingyuan Tower, Xuanhua
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.sub: Triple-eaved bell tower with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and brick platform
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.yearNote: Only one Xuanhua city tower is selected as representative; Zhenshuo Tower and the Five-Dragon Screen are not added.
hb_xuanhuaqingyuan.lede: A street passes beneath Qingyuan Tower’s lofty brick platform while the building spreads above it through a cross-shaped roof. Three interlocking eave lines produce a complex but ordered relationship between centre and wings. Founded in the Ming Chenghua era on Xuanhua’s central axis, the tower combines timekeeping, an urban landmark and frontier memory in glazed upper tiles, plain lower roofs and plaques facing four directions.
facts: The tower has three storeys, three eave tiers and a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof on a brick platform. A gallery surrounds the lower level, with panelled openings above; interlocking roof planes unite four elevations rather than simply stacking roofs.

Founded in 1482, Qingyuan Tower underwent successive repairs. Its present layout and form continue the Ming bell-tower tradition; the founding date should be separated from later replacements and repairs to roofing and timber components.

Glazed tiles cover the upper roof, with plain tiles on the lower tiers; plaques address all four directions. Material hierarchy and directional titles strengthen its street-centre role, organising urban views and preserving Xuanhua’s frontier associations.
captions: South side of Qingyuan Tower
Triple-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof and arched passage through the brick platform

protection.scope: Qingyuan Tower, Xuanhua · Triple-eaved bell tower with cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and brick platform

yn_jianshui.name: Jianshui Confucian Temple
yn_jianshui.sub: Hall of the First Teacher · Dacheng Hall
yn_jianshui.yearNote: 1495 is only an approximate sorting point within the Hongzhi era (1488–1505); dating follows the Hall of the First Teacher drawn, and the temple's founding date of 1285 is not substituted for it.
yn_jianshui.place: Yunnan · Jianshui · Old city of Lin'an
yn_jianshui.lede: Beyond Dacheng Gate, Xianshi Hall occupies a raised platform towards the rear of Jianshui’s Confucian temple axis. A single hip-and-gable roof covers its five-bay front. Stone exterior columns and carved wooden doors reveal local workmanship and cooperation between materials. The temple began in the Yuan period, but this hall is dated to the Ming Hongzhi reign; their histories should be distinguished.
facts: Xianshi Hall, also called Dacheng Hall, has a five-bay front and a single hip-and-gable roof supported by stone columns and timber framing. Its carved exterior columns and lattice doors reward close comparison of materials and details.

The temple was founded in 1285, while the hall is attributed to construction during the Hongzhi reign of 1488–1505. Its precise completion year is not established. The temple’s foundation and the later hall belong to different stages that can be read along the axis.

The principal hall for worshipping Confucius stands high towards the rear to emphasise its ceremonial role. Stone columns, carved timber doors and painted framing show how shared Confucian architectural conventions acquired local workmanship.
captions: Hall of the First Teacher, Jianshui Confucian Temple · Line drawing · Pending user review
Ming · Hongzhi era

protection.scope: Jianshui Confucian Temple · Hall of the First Teacher · Dacheng Hall

sx_yuci_chenghuang.name: City God Temple of Yuci
sx_yuci_chenghuang.sub: Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage
sx_yuci_chenghuang.era: Ming · Xuanjian Tower and music tower
sx_yuci_chenghuang.yearNote: Xuanjian Tower (1497) and the music tower (1511) are supported by stele records; the date of about 1523 for the stage in front is an inference by the cultural relics survey from a date on the screen wall.
sx_yuci_chenghuang.lede: Xuanjian Tower is not one building but a group stacked up by three generations: in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi, Ming) the five-bay, two-storey, triple-eaved tower, seventeen metres high, went up south of the main hall; later a music hall was fitted against its north eave, less than a metre between the two roofs, and a one-bay, round-ridged, hip-and-gable street stage pushed further north, flanked by Ming glazed-tile splayed screen walls. The peacock-blue glazed roofs rise and fall, and from the courtyard they read as a single whole. The plate shows this northern group; the main hall, Xianyou Hall, and the gate are not in the picture.
facts: Xuanjian Tower: five bays wide and four rafters deep, two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 17 m high overall, peacock-blue glazed roof, three hollow caisson ceilings inside; to the north adjoins the two-rafter-deep music hall, and beyond it a one-bay street stage with a single round-ridged hip-and-gable roof, flanked by glazed splayed screen walls under hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: the temple was founded in 1362 (22nd year of Zhizheng, Yuan), moved to the present site in 1431 (6th year of Xuande, Ming) and enlarged in the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns; the tower was built in 1497 (10th year of Hongzhi), the gate in 1509 (4th year of Zhengde), and the music hall and stage were completed by the early Jiajing reign (around 1523), giving the present scale.

Significance: roofs of three periods interlock, and the screen walls and music hall enclose an acoustic space, a model of the Ming city-god-temple composite of tower, music hall and stage; it became a national key protected site in 1996 and was placed on the World Monuments Fund Watch list in 2000.
captions: City God Temple of Yuci · North side of Xuanjian Tower
Ming · Music tower and pass-through stage

protection.scope: City God Temple of Yuci · Xuanjian Tower · Music tower and stage

zhaoling.name: Zhaoling Palace, Xianyou
zhaoling.era: Ming · Exact date to be determined
zhaoling.place: Fujian · Putian · Dingdonghu Village, Xiyuan Township, Xianyou
zhaoling.lede: Zhaoling Palace’s low hip-and-gable roof shelters a three-bay timber hall on a stone platform. Railings along the front and sides carry rain screens, combining circulation, seating and shelter. A county heritage notice records a mid-Ming foundation and subsequent repairs, with Ming stone column bases still present. Rather than enclosing the hall in high walls, its frame, railings and rain screens create a light appearance, revealing how village timber architecture responds to terrain and weather.
facts: The freestanding timber hall stands on a stone platform. Its main chamber is three bays wide and five purlin lines deep, with a hip-and-gable roof and mixed raised-beam and column-and-tie framing. Rain screens above front and side railings link the roof to the veranda edge.

The county government’s 2024 heritage notice records a mid-Ming foundation and repairs in December 1984. The exact original year remains unknown, and surviving components belong to different phases rather than all being Ming material.

Plain Ming stone column bases shaped like inverted bowls survive alongside timber framing, railings and rain screens. This county-protected building provides material evidence for regional small timber halls and adaptive construction in mountain villages.
captions: Zhaoling Palace, Xianyou · Front of the single hall
Ming (to be determined) · Single-eaved hip-and-gable roof

sn_yanan.name: Yan'an Pagoda (Lingshan Temple Pagoda)
sn_yanan.sub: Octagonal nine-story brick pagoda · Surviving Ming form
sn_yanan.era: Tang–Song history, restored in the Ming
sn_yanan.yearNote: The combined national listing marks it as Song; educational sources describe the surviving pagoda as a Ming building. The plate and timeline list it as Ming according to its surviving restored form; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point, not a confirmed rebuilding year.
sn_yanan.lede: Yan’an’s nine-storey octagonal pagoda belongs both to an old temple and to modern collective memory. A tall lower storey supports a narrowing stack, its brick eaves dividing the vertical mass clearly. Lingshan Temple Pagoda has Tang and Song antecedents, while the visible form is treated here as a Ming rebuilding. Later postage stamps record another layer of symbolic meaning.
facts: This nine-storey octagonal brick pagoda has a tall lower storey and progressively narrower upper levels. Projecting cornices alternate with openings and solid walls, creating a compact vertical outline recognisable from a distance.

Tang and Song antecedents are recorded, and the heritage listing says Song, while educational material identifies the standing structure as Ming. Its visible outline is therefore understood as a Ming rebuilding, with an unresolved exact date; earlier foundations do not date its present appearance.

The outline of Pagoda Hill appeared repeatedly on stamps depicting revolutionary sites, giving an old building new symbolic meanings. Its construction history overlaps with modern image circulation, making it both a surviving monument and a city emblem.
captions: Yan'an Pagoda (Lingshan Temple Pagoda), surviving whole pagoda · Line drawing
Ming · Ming restoration · Exact year undetermined

protection.scope: Yan'an Pagoda (Lingshan Temple Pagoda) · Octagonal nine-story brick pagoda · Surviving Ming form
protection.note: In the fourth batch, Lingshan Temple Pagoda was incorporated into the first-batch listing of the Yan'an Revolutionary Sites; the pagoda itself is not labeled as first batch.

gx_dashi.name: Dashi Pavilion of Yong'an, Hepu
gx_dashi.sub: Low front, high rear · Linked timber pavilions
gx_dashi.yearNote: Listed as Ming in the third batch of national protected sites; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point within the Ming, not an established construction year. The plate shows the linked front and rear pavilions; the incense-burner pavilions around them are not part of the subject drawn.
gx_dashi.lede: Dashi Pavilion joins two timber pavilions, lower at the front and higher behind. Open ground floors and boarded upper rooms reveal the relationships between columns, beams and projecting eaves. Ridge figures and painted decoration bring mythical subjects and flowers into the timber frame. The building is attributed to Ming and was repaired during the Qing Daoguang reign, without a confirmed construction year. Its name recalls the worship of Avalokiteshvara here.
facts: Two connected pavilions have open lower levels and boarded upper rooms with doors and windows. Columns rest on lotus-carved stone pads; mortise-and-tenon joints connect beams, while projecting beams carry broad eaves.

The pavilion is classified as Ming, with repairs recorded during the Qing Daoguang reign and later conservation reflected today. Its exact construction year requires further study; early carpentry techniques and later repairs should be distinguished.

Column supports, framing and projecting eaves preserve earlier southern carpentry traditions. Ridge figures and painting express local decoration. Worship of Avalokiteshvara gave the pavilion its name, joining religious use with structural continuity.
captions: Front pavilion and linked rear pavilion of the Dashi Pavilion, Yong'an, Hepu · Line drawing
Ming · Ming dynasty

protection.scope: Front pavilion and linked rear pavilion of the Dashi Pavilion, Yong'an, Hepu

gs_jiayuguan.name: Jiayu Pass
gs_jiayuguan.era: Built in the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns, Ming
gs_jiayuguan.yearNote: The drawing shows the Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and its gate platform. The tower was built during the Hongzhi to Zhengde reigns of the Ming and repaired continuously in later periods; 1500 is only an approximate sorting point and does not equal a completion year, nor is the establishment of the pass in 1372 used in place of the tower's date.
gs_jiayuguan.lede: A single arch pierces a massive gate platform, with the three-storey Jiayuguan Tower spreading three tiers of eaves above it. It marks the west-facing entrance of the outer enclosure, serving as both a lookout and a threshold within successive defences. The pass and this tower were established more than a century apart, within the gradual strengthening of Ming frontier defence.
facts: The western tower stands on the outer enclosure’s gate platform, above a west-facing arch. Each of its three storeys has eaves. Columns and galleries lighten the upper silhouette, while the substantial platform links entrance and curtain wall.

The fort was established in 1372, while the western gate tower belongs to construction in the Hongzhi–Zhengde period and underwent later repairs. Fort and tower did not originate together; a broad period attribution cannot replace precise construction evidence.

Jiayuguan, Rouyuan and Guanghua towers share an axis but occupy different gateways. Identifying them reveals how the outer enclosure, barbicans and inner city organised both passage and defence in successive layers.
captions: Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and gate platform · Line drawing
Ming · Hongzhi–Zhengde

protection.scope: Jiayuguan Tower on the west side and gate platform

gs_dafo_tuta.name: Earthen Stupa of the Great Buddha Temple, Zhangye
gs_dafo_tuta.era: Built in the Ming · Later restored
gs_dafo_tuta.yearNote: The earthen stupa was built in about the Ming dynasty; 1500 is only an approximate Ming sorting point. An earthquake in 1927 damaged the top, which was restored in 1986. The drawing takes the upper stupa body and finial visible in photographs and does not invent the lower base hidden by the front hall and courtyard walls.
gs_dafo_tuta.lede: A broad dome supports a niche-bearing section, followed by rings and a finial that stretch the outline upwards. The earthen pagoda at Zhangye’s Great Buddha Temple, also called the Amitabha Thousand-Buddha Pagoda, contrasts with the broad Buddha hall. This view shows the part visible above halls and enclosure walls. It is approximately Ming in date, with a repaired earthquake-damaged summit.
facts: The visible upper section combines a domed body, a Sumeru-base-like niche section, rings and a finial, echoed by small towers. Transitions between rounded mass and rectilinear niches distinguish its silhouette from a storeyed pagoda.

Local historical sources broadly attribute the tower to the Ming period, without a precise construction year. An earthquake damaged its summit in 1927, and restoration followed in 1986; the present finial includes repairs rather than entirely original fabric.

The pagoda and Buddha hall share a temple but use different architectural forms: the dome and rings rise to a point, while a timber hall shelters a reclining Buddha. Even the exposed upper section reveals the pagoda’s separate role.
captions: Exposed body and finial of the Amitabha Thousand-Buddha Stupa · Line drawing
Ming · Ming dynasty

protection.scope: Exposed body and finial of the Amitabha Thousand-Buddha Stupa

gongzhu.name: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi
gongzhu.lede: This small temple in Princess Village, named for a Northern Wei princess, keeps its interest indoors: the Mahavira Hall is only three bays wide under a gable roof, with not even bracket sets under the eaves, yet its four walls are covered with Ming Water-and-Land murals in which Buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas and Daoist gods assemble in tiers, a complete Ming mural cycle of this genre. Tradition credits the founding to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; the surviving halls are dated by a restoration of 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming), and the Mahavira Hall and the passage hall before it are the temple's only Ming structures. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall; the murals are inside.
facts: Mahavira Hall: three bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, no bracket sets under the eaves; the passage hall in front is three bays square under a single-eave hip-and-gable roof with five-puzuo bracket sets, and these two are the only Ming buildings left in the temple.

Dating: tradition attributes the temple to Princess Chengxin, fourth daughter of Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei; it was restored in 1503 (16th year of Hongzhi, Ming) and is registered by the National Cultural Heritage Administration as Ming to Qing; facing south with three courtyards, it covers 4,347 square metres with 1,116 square metres of buildings.

Murals: the Mahavira Hall preserves Ming Water-and-Land murals with Buddhist and Daoist deities painted in one assembly; the Qielan, Horse King, God of Wealth and Erlang halls on either side were all built in the Qing and belong to a different period from the murals inside.
captions: Front of the Mahavira Hall, Gongzhu Temple · Redrawn from photographs
Restored in the 16th year of Hongzhi, Ming (1503) · Three bays, single-eaved overhanging gable roof, no bracket sets under the eaves

protection.scope: Gongzhu Temple, Fanshi · Fanshi · Mahavira Hall

hb_xtkaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Xingtai
hb_xtkaiyuan.sub: Bodhisattva Hall of the old Kaiyuan Temple (third hall / Sakyamuni Hall), full facade and four coiling-dragon stone columns
hb_xtkaiyuan.yearNote: The Vairocana Hall burned in 1988 and was rebuilt in 1997, so it was not chosen. Instead the plate uses the Bodhisattva Hall, restored in the 13th year of Zhengde in the Ming, and its four coiling-dragon stone columns inscribed 1518. It must be distinguished from the new temple of 2013 on the east side.
hb_xtkaiyuan.lede: The four dragon-carved stone columns beneath Pusa Hall’s eaves invite closer attention than its five-bay roof alone. Dragons project from single stone blocks, surrounded by foliage and clouds, turning load-bearing members into sculpture. This third hall in old Kaiyuan Temple follows a Ming rebuilding phase; dated inscriptions on the columns anchor the visual impression in written evidence, distinct from the temple’s earlier origins.
facts: Pusa Hall, also called Shakyamuni Hall, occupies the third position on the old temple axis. It is five bays wide with a gable roof. Four dragon-carved front columns support the eaves, their varying relief adding depth to the elevation.

The hall is assigned to the rebuilding phase of 1518; the columns carry an inscription for their erection in the seventh month of that year. The earlier temple foundation is distinct, as is the rebuilding of a fire-damaged Pilu Hall.

Dragons, clouds and foliage surround the columns, while donor names and places of origin survive below. Sculpture and building inscriptions share the same stone member, documenting both craftsmanship and local participation in temple construction.
captions: Kaiyuan Temple, Xingtai · Bodhisattva Hall
Front of the five-bay flush-gable hall with four coiling-dragon stone columns

sx_jiexiu_houtu.name: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu
sx_jiexiu_houtu.sub: Sanqing Tower · Hall and stage combined
sx_jiexiu_houtu.yearNote: The construction of the Sanqing Tower and the Offering Tower in about the Zhengde period is used as the sorting point; the dates 1516 and 1519 in stele records and sources each refer to different things, and 1519 is not forced to stand as the completion year of every component drawn.
sx_jiexiu_houtu.lede: Jiexiu's Houtu Temple stacks hall, stage and tower into one building: the lower floor of the Sanqing Tower is the Sanqing Hall, the upper floor is wrapped by a gallery on three sides, and the back is a stage facing the Houtu Great Hall, thirteen metres high, the tallest surviving Ming theatre stage; the double-eaved splayed screen walls on either side were forced up to match, with a brick eave below and a timber eave above. The Jiexiu heritage office records its founding in 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming), and every roof in the temple is glazed, five-coloured except for the yellow of the Houtu Hall group; here glazed tile is not trim but the main event. The plate shows the stage on the north face of the Sanqing Tower with its splayed screen walls.
facts: Sanqing Tower: two storeys under three tiers of hip-and-gable eaves, 15.2 m high overall, with a two-storey, triple-eaved cross-ridged porch projecting in front to join the offering hall; the stage at the back is 13 m high, its lower level barely tall enough to stand in; the splayed screen walls on either side have double gable eaves, carved brick below and timber above, their bargeboards decorated with purple-and-white glazed "mice stealing grapes".

Dating: the Jiexiu heritage office dates the founding of the Sanqing Tower to 1519 (14th year of Zhengde, Ming); the restoration of 1516 (11th year of Zhengde) absorbed the Zhenwu Hall and Sanguan Shrine, the Earth God Temple of 1730 (8th year of Yongzheng, Qing) completed the layout of eight linked temples, and repairs followed in 1835 (15th year of Daoguang).

Glazed tile: all 29 buildings are roofed in glazed tile, the Houtu Hall group in yellow and the rest in yellow, green, blue, white and ochre, mostly replaced in Qing repairs, while a few Song tiles survive on the Sanqing Tower; the more than a thousand Ming Daoist painted statues inside are equally rare.
captions: Houtu Temple, Jiexiu · North stage of the Sanqing Tower
Ming–Qing · Stage and splayed screen walls

tiefo.name: Iron Buddha Temple, Gaoping
tiefo.era: Restored in the 1st year of Jiajing
tiefo.place: Shanxi · Gaoping · Mishan Town · Mixi Village
tiefo.lede: In the lanes of Mixi Village, the three-bay main hall of the Iron Buddha Temple is finished with an overhanging gable roof and glazed ridge ornaments. Step inside and the Twenty-Four Devas unfold along the walls — glaring, smiling, eyes lowered — their beards, hair and streamers held out on iron wire, giving the clay figures expressions on the verge of movement.
facts: The main hall is three bays wide and six rafters deep, with a single-eaved overhanging gable roof. The front-eave bracket sets are five-tiered (wucai) with double cantilevers (ang), and a glazed ornament of a lion bearing a treasure vase stands at the center of the ridge.

The Ming painted clay figures of the Twenty-Four Devas inside the hall are modeled in clay over wooden armatures; their beards, hair, headdresses and streamers are shaped with iron wire, making the details light yet full of tension.

The founding date is unknown. In the 7th year of Dading in the Jin (1167) an iron Buddha was cast and the temple restored; it was repaired again in the 1st year of Jiajing (1522) and the 3rd year of Wanli (1575) in the Ming, and in the Qing. The surviving buildings show a Ming–Qing style.
captions: Main hall line drawing · Three bays wide
Single-eaved overhanging gable roof · Ming

feihong.name: Feihong Pagoda of Guangsheng Temple
feihong.era: Begun in the 10th year of Zhengde · Completed in the 6th year of Jiajing
feihong.lede: Between 1515 and 1527 (10th year of Zhengde to 6th year of Jiajing, Ming) the monk Dalian raised funds for over a decade and set this brick pagoda, octagonal, thirteen storeys and over forty-seven metres high, at the very front of the axis of the Upper Temple on Mount Huo. Its outer skin, from eaves and bracket sets to Buddhas, guardians and coiling dragons, is entirely fired glaze in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, making it the largest and most complete glazed pagoda surviving in China. It stands on the site of a Yuan predecessor and later rode out the great earthquakes of 1556 in Guanzhong and 1695 in Pingyang. The plate shows the whole Feihong Pagoda.
facts: Body: octagonal in plan, thirteen storeys, 47.31 m high overall (47.6 m in another source), tapering sharply into a cone; the core is brick and stone, and on every storey the eaves, bracket sets, niches, figures and coiling dragons are glazed components in red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Dating: rebuilt on the Yuan site from 1515 (10th year of Zhengde, Ming) with funds raised by the eminent monk Dalian and completed in 1527 (6th year of Jiajing); it then survived unharmed the Guanzhong earthquake of 1556 (35th year of Jiajing) and the Pingyang earthquake of 1695 (34th year of Kangxi).

Connections: Guangsheng Temple was listed among the first batch of national key protected sites in 1961; the Yuan murals of the Lower Temple were sold in 1928 and are now divided among three American museums; the "Tang monk sweeps the pagoda" episode of the 1986 television series Journey to the West was filmed here.
captions: Line drawing · Octagonal, thirteen stories
Glazed tile · First-story gallery

hb_xianling.name: Ming Xianling Mausoleum
hb_xianling.sub: Lingxing Gate · Dragon and Phoenix Gate
hb_xianling.yearNote: The surviving Lingxing Gate belongs to the Ming stone remains of the Xianling; 1540 is only a broad sorting point within the Jiajing period, not the exact completion year of this stone archway. Only the stone archway and its linked glazed screen walls are drawn; the stele tower (minglou) restored in 1990 is not drawn, and the founding year of the imperial tomb is not applied to all of its buildings.
hb_xianling.lede: Lingxing Gate divides Xianling’s spirit way into three openings between six stone posts. Hou beasts, a flaming jewel and yellow-glazed screen walls mark a ceremonial threshold. Carved beams and panels imitate timber construction in stone. The gate belongs to the mausoleum’s Ming remains, but its precise completion year is unconfirmed. Repairs in 1996 reinstated displaced pieces, leaving the present appearance with a visible history of conservation.
facts: This soaring stone gateway has three openings, six posts and four small roof units. Cloud plaques, lotus bases, hou beasts and a flaming jewel crown the posts; adjoining yellow-glazed screen walls stand on moulded bases.

The stone gate belongs to Ming Xianling, in the historical setting of the Jiajing reign, without a confirmed completion year. Conservation in 1996 reinstated originals, supplied missing pieces and restored connecting walls.

The gateway turns the continuous spirit way into a ranked ceremonial threshold. Timber-like stone carving and yellow glaze express imperial funerary architecture; original pieces and repairs also reveal how its remains have been preserved.
captions: Stone archway of the Lingxing Gate and linked glazed screen walls, Ming Xianling Mausoleum · Line drawing
Ming · Jiajing reign

taimiao.name: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing
taimiao.lede: Eleven bays across, sixty-eight nanmu columns and a three-tier white marble terrace give the Imperial Ancestral Temple's front worship hall a scale comparable to the palace's great halls. For major ancestral rites, imperial spirit tablets were brought forward from the buildings behind it. The temple was founded in 1420, alongside the Forbidden City, while its principal surviving arrangement follows the reconstruction of 1545. The hall's scale and the division of duties among the buildings express dynastic ritual through architecture, rather than the needs of everyday residence.
facts: Form: the worship hall is eleven bays wide and six deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles on a three-tier white marble terrace. Sixty-eight solid nanmu columns support its timber frame; the broad facade and high terrace establish the rank of the ritual setting.

History: founded in 1420, the temple was rebuilt in 1545, restoring collective worship with separate chambers in one hall. The principal surviving arrangement follows this rebuilding. The foundation of the temple and the dating adopted for the present worship hall should be described separately.

Ritual: the front worship hall hosted major ancestral ceremonies, while the resting hall and the distant-ancestor hall had different duties in housing spirit tablets. Before a major rite, tablets were moved onto the worship hall's seats. The sequence of halls thus served a specific ritual process.
captions: Imperial Ancestral Temple, Beijing · Sacrificial Hall
Eleven bays wide · Three-tier Sumeru plinth

fuzhoubaita.name: White Pagoda, Fuzhou
fuzhoubaita.lede: The Black Pagoda is stone; the White Pagoda is brick. In 904 Wang Shenzhi built the Bao'en Dingguang Duobao Pagoda at the western foot of Yushan to earn merit for his parents, originally a seven-storey tower with a brick core and timber galleries. Struck by lightning and burnt in 1534, it was rebuilt in 1548, when the brick core was simply made the body of the pagoda itself, coated in white lime, octagonal and seven storeys high with a gourd-shaped finial. The clean, plain silhouette seen today is the Ming rebuilding.
facts: Form: an octagonal seven-storey pavilion-style brick pagoda, 41 m high, with plain white-limed walls and a gourd finial; the brick core contains a hanging-post spiral stair to the top. In 1963, while the surroundings were cleared, fifteen Tang-dynasty carved bluestone panels from a Sumeru-base waist were unearthed, with sea legends, lions and peonies, and are now set up on the spot.

History: the Shiguo Chunqiu records that in 904 Wang Shenzhi built the pagoda for his late parents; the original had a brick core with timber work outside. It was destroyed by lightning fire in 1534 and rebuilt as the present pagoda in 1548; the stair was replaced in a 1958 repair, and in 1991 it was listed as a Fujian provincial protected site.

Counterpart: it faces the Five Dynasties Black Pagoda at the eastern foot of Wushan across the old city; together they are the 'Three Hills and Two Pagodas' that have marked Fuzhou for a millennium, and the pairing of stone with brick, black with white, shows the different materials and methods of Five Dynasties and Ming pagoda building.
captions: White Pagoda, Fuzhou · Dingguang Pagoda
Seven stories, octagonal · Ming rebuilding

sx_haihui.name: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng
sx_haihui.sub: Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda
sx_haihui.yearNote: 1565 is only a sorting point for the construction period of the large Ming pagoda; sources give either 1561 or 1565–1568. The small pagoda was founded in the Five Dynasties and altered in the Song; the two pagodas were not built in the same year.
sx_haihui.place: Shanxi · Yangcheng · Pagoda courtyard of Haihui Temple, Daqiao Village
sx_haihui.lede: Two pagodas stand one behind the other, six centuries apart: the small one in front, hexagonal and ten storeys, is the relic pagoda built for the Chan master Shunmin in 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang), studded with little niches and leaning slightly west; the great one behind, octagonal, thirteen storeys and about fifty-seven metres high, was built between 1565 and 1568 (Jiajing to Longqing reigns, Ming) with over two thousand taels of silver donated by the merchant Li Sixiao, its lowest three storeys wrapped in a battlemented wall like a castle while the tenth storey throws out a ring of glazed hanging galleries. Among the storeyed pagodas of north China there is no second example. The plate shows both pagodas together.
facts: Two pagodas: the small pagoda is grey brick, hexagonal, ten storeys with corbelled eaves, about 20 m high, its outer walls covered with Buddha niches; the great pagoda is octagonal, thirteen storeys and about 57 m high, its bottom three storeys enclosed by a battlemented masonry wall, and at the tenth storey a glazed balcony gallery projects, three bays to a side, twenty-four in all, with glazed columns, balustrades and brackets.

Dating: the stele "Later Record of Longquan Chan Cloister" of 956 (3rd year of Xiande, Later Zhou) in the temple dates the small pagoda to 922 (2nd year of Longde, Later Liang); the stele by Wang Guoguang, Ming Minister of Rites, "Record of Rebuilding the Precious Pagoda and Buddha Hall of Longquan Temple", dates the great pagoda to the Jiajing-Longqing years 1565 to 1568, with another view favouring 1561 (40th year of Jiajing).

Assessment: the great pagoda is also called the Glazed Pagoda for its glazed eave edges and galleries, and Zhang Yuhuan ranked it "the crown of the famous pagodas of Shangdang"; the temple housed the Haihui Academy in the Ming and Qing, was among the first provincial protected sites of Shanxi in 1965, and became a national key protected site together with the pagodas in 2006.
captions: Haihui Temple · Small brick pagoda and large glazed pagoda
Five Dynasties–Song small pagoda · Ming Jiajing–Longqing large pagoda

protection.scope: Twin Pagodas of Haihui Temple, Yangcheng · Hexagonal brick pagoda · Octagonal glazed pagoda

gx_zhenwu.name: Zhenwu Pavilion on the Jinglue Terrace
gx_zhenwu.sub: Timber pavilion of Rong County · Triple eaves
gx_zhenwu.yearNote: 1573 is taken as the construction date of the Zhenwu Pavilion; the earlier history of the Jinglue Terrace is listed separately from the surviving pavilion, and later repairs do not amount to rebuilding the whole pavilion.
gx_zhenwu.lede: Zhenwu Pavilion projects three broad tiers of eaves above the older Jinglüe Terrace. Columns and beams meet visibly in the open lower level. Its most unusual detail is on the second level: four internal column feet stop above the floor, with loads transferred through interlocking timbers towards outer supports. The pavilion was built in 1573. Its date should be distinguished from the terrace’s earlier history; tracing the supports reveals more than counting roofs alone.
facts: Mortise-and-tenon joints connect hardwood components and broad eaves. Four internal columns on the second level do not touch its floor. Projecting beams use outer columns as fulcrums to connect the eaves and upper loads.

The surviving pavilion was built in 1573, the first Wanli year of Ming, to honour Zhenwu. The terrace has an earlier history. Later conservation continues the timber structure rather than necessarily creating a wholly new pavilion.

Suspended column feet belong to a structural system, not merely an ornamental curiosity. The framing joins eaves, inner columns and levels, illustrating the balance between projection and load-bearing in southern Ming timber pavilions.
captions: Complete Zhenwu Pavilion on the Jinglue Terrace · Line drawing
Ming · 1573

guanyintang.name: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi
guanyintang.lede: A small hall of three bays whose walls, roof frame and the spaces above doors and windows are entirely taken over by sculpture: Guanyin sits in the centre with Manjusri and Samantabhadra at her sides, celestial palaces rise tier upon tier behind her, the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment ring the room in layers, and on the top tier the south wall carries Daoist immortals, the north wall Confucian worthies, so that Sakyamuni, Laozi and Confucius share one hall. Over five hundred suspended clay figures of around 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) turn the belief in the unity of the three teachings into a visible world. The plate takes the central Guanyin and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Main hall: three bays wide and four rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof covered in yellow and green glazed tile with coiling-dragon and passion-flower patterns; inside are more than five hundred Ming suspended clay figures, gilded and painted, arranged in tiers on the walls, roof frame and upper parts of doors and windows.

Dating: the Guanyin Hall was built in 1582 (10th year of Wanli, Ming) and repaired in the Qing; the name board was written in 1583 (11th year of Wanli) by Gao Qin, Vice Minister of War; the temple faces west with two courtyards over 7,400 square metres, the main hall Ming and the rest Qing.

Subjects: the altar holds Guanyin, Manjusri and Samantabhadra, the rear wall shows the life of the Buddha, the sides carry the Eighteen Arhats, Twenty-four Devas and Twelve Bodhisattvas of Perfect Enlightenment, and the fourth tier has Daoist figures on the south wall and Confucian ones on the north, with Sakyamuni in the middle and Laozi and Confucius to either side, a physical record of the merging of the three teachings in a village temple.
captions: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi · Detail of Guanyin and the suspended heavenly-palace sculpture
Wanli reign, Ming · Painted and suspended sculpture

protection.scope: Guanyin Hall, Changzhi · Ming suspended sculpture · Liangjiazhuang

xuankong.name: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan
xuankong.sub: Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings
xuankong.place: Shanxi · Hunyuan · Jinlong Gorge, Mount Heng
xuankong.lede: The whole temple hangs in a recess halfway up Cuiping Mountain, its highest point more than ninety metres above the valley floor. It looks as if dozens of slender timber posts hold it up, but the real load is carried by twenty-seven beams driven into the rock; most of the posts are little more than reassurance. The north and south flying pavilions, three storeys and over ten metres high, float free on three sides and are linked by two plank walks wide enough for one person; the Three Teachings Hall on the top floor of the north pavilion seats Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi together. A Northern Wei founding has long been claimed, yet the surviving forty bays of timber work are all products of Ming and Qing rebuilding. The plate shows the two pavilions and the walkways between them.
facts: Structure: 27 timber beams about 50 cm in diameter, soaked in tung oil, are bedded under the temple, one end tenoned into the rock and the other carrying the buildings and projecting about 1 m to support the walkways; the temple has 40 bays and 152.5 square metres of timber building, the two flying pavilions each three storeys with nine-ridged roofs and posts more than ten metres long on the outer side.

History: one account has Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei found it in 491 (15th year of Taihe) to relocate the Celestial Masters' Daoist seat, another gives 398 (1st year of Tianxing); it was repaired in the Jin, Ming and the Tongzhi reign of the Qing, and most existing buildings are Ming and Qing rebuildings; the 1978 overhaul that replaced load-bearing beams reconfirmed the cantilevered-beam system.

Three teachings: the upper floor of the main hall holds the Three Buddhas Hall, Taiyi Hall and Guandi Temple; the south pavilion rises through the Chunyang Palace, Sanguan Hall and Leiyin Hall, the north pavilion through the Four Buddhas Hall, Three Sages Hall and Three Teachings Hall, where Sakyamuni, Confucius and Laozi share one shrine; the temple became a national key protected site in 1982.
captions: Hanging Temple · Cliffside building group
Ming–Qing structures · North and south towers and suspended walkway

protection.scope: Hanging Temple, Hunyuan · Pavilions on a sheer cliff · Unity of the Three Teachings

hn_bigan.name: Temple of Bi Gan
hn_bigan.sub: Memorial to loyal remonstrance, with temple and tomb joined
hn_bigan.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing structures. The expansion in the 7th year of Hongzhi in the Ming (1494) belongs to the history of the temple complex and is not taken directly as the construction year of every component of the front of the Sacrificial Hall drawn here.
hn_bigan.lede: Bigan Temple’s sacrificial hall opens a five-bay façade among old cypresses, while the tomb behind extends the memorial into the rear of the precinct. The commemorated figure belongs to the Shang, but the surviving buildings largely reflect Ming and Qing rebuilding and repairs. Gate, inscription corridor and hall form a route from worship to the tomb, and successive inscriptions reveal changing interpretations of loyal remonstrance.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with doors, windows and columns forming a broad front. Gate, inscription corridor, hall and rear tomb align to establish the sequence of ritual movement.

The temple’s history reaches back to the Northern Wei; it was enlarged in 1494. Surviving buildings mostly reflect Ming–Qing rebuilding and repairs. Around 1600 is an approximate timeline position, not the date of every hall component.

Cypresses, inscriptions and the temple-before-tomb layout preserve successive forms of commemoration. Traditions of loyal remonstrance and surname ancestry are later cultural memories rather than direct evidence for Shang events.
captions: Sacrificial Hall, Temple of Bi Gan · Visible front facade
Rebuilt and repaired in the Ming–Qing · Based on 2024 frontal photographs

protection.scope: Temple of Bi Gan · Memorial to loyal remonstrance, with temple and tomb joined

hb_wahuang.name: Wahuang Palace and Stone Carvings
hb_wahuang.sub: Front of the cliff-hugging Wahuang Pavilion
hb_wahuang.yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau lists the Wahuang Pavilion and other buildings on the mountain as Ming–Qing remains; Handan cultural tourism sources record that a three-story timber pavilion was added on the stone vault in the Ming. 1600 is used only as an approximate sorting value for the Ming–Qing pavilion, and the pavilion is not dated by the year of the Northern Qi carved sutras.
hb_wahuang.lede: Wahuang Pavilion is defined by a rock chamber, stone vault and timber storeys stacked against the cliff. Three upper wooden levels draw a tall silhouette unlike halls on level ground. The surviving pavilion belongs to Ming and Qing building and repair phases, while adjacent carved scriptures reach back to the Northern Qi. Their proximity records accumulated history, not a single construction date.
facts: A stone vault fronts the natural lower chamber, supporting three timber storeys above to form a four-level structure. Eaves, columns and galleries face outward from the cliff; rock, stone and wood together determine the pavilion’s form.

The provincial authority assigns the upper buildings, including Wahuang Pavilion, to the Ming and Qing periods. The exact date of this building remains unconfirmed. Northern Qi scriptures nearby are earlier and cannot date the surviving timber pavilion.

Mountain paths link lower precincts with the upper pavilions. Nüwa worship and Buddhist cliff scriptures survive in the same landscape; viewing architecture and inscriptions together reveals layers crossing periods and religious traditions.
captions: Wahuang Palace, She County · Wahuang Pavilion
Four eave lines of the three-story timber pavilion and lower front gallery

im_dazhao.name: Da Zhao Temple, Hohhot
im_dazhao.era: Founded in the Ming · Altered in the Qing
im_dazhao.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the Ming–Qing main structure and does not claim an exact completion year for the Mahavira Hall; the temple was completed in 1580, and the Qing expansion and the relaying of yellow glazed tiles are recorded separately.
im_dazhao.lede: Dazhao’s main hall stands on the temple axis, its broad roof, layered eaves and substantial body forming a solemn frontage. Also called Wuliang Temple, Dazhao was founded in the Ming period and enlarged and altered under the Qing. The hall combines Han Chinese and Tibetan architectural forms and participates in a sequence of worship spaces with the entrance and Heavenly Kings Hall. The temple’s foundation date does not date every surviving component.
facts: The main hall anchors an axis approached through the entrance, Heavenly Kings Hall and Bodhi passage hall. Its broad body and roof combine Han Chinese and Tibetan architectural forms.

Dazhao was founded in 1579 and renamed Wuliang Temple after repairs in 1640. Surviving halls reflect Ming and Qing construction and alteration; the approximate seventeenth-century placement is not a precise completion date for this hall.

Looking back from the hall reveals the progression from entrance to the core worship space. The building provides material evidence of Hohhot’s temple culture and exchanges between Han Chinese and Tibetan architecture.
captions: Mahavira Hall, Da Zhao Temple, Hohhot · Line drawing · Pending user review
Ming–Qing · Ming–Qing

protection.scope: Da Zhao Temple, Hohhot · Wuliang Temple · Mahavira Hall

gd_zumiao.name: Triple Gate of the Foshan Ancestral Temple
gd_zumiao.yearNote: 1600 is only an approximate sorting point for the surviving Ming–Qing main structure, not the exact completion year of the Triple Gate. The founding of the Ancestral Temple in the Northern Song, its rebuilding in the Hongwu reign of the Ming and the date of the Triple Gate's present form must not be conflated.
gd_zumiao.lede: The Three Gates of Foshan’s Ancestral Temple welcome worshippers through three arched openings. A continuous ceramic ridge turns stories and figures into a lively roof-top panorama. Its horizontal scale and dense ornament make the entrance both a ceremonial boundary and a display of craft. The temple developed from a Northern Song foundation through Ming and Qing work; modern repairs add further layers to the visible gate.
facts: Three arched openings pierce the central gate wall. A long ceramic ridge spans the roof, with gilded woodcarving beneath the eaves. Substantial masonry and densely modelled figures combine in a layered horizontal elevation.

The temple was founded under the Northern Song and rebuilt under the Ming. Its gate reflects Ming and Qing building work and later repairs, including the 2007–2010 conservation campaign. Neither the temple’s foundation date nor a single year describes its entire present form.

Ceramic and wooden narrative ornament links Foshan craftsmanship with worship of the Northern Emperor. The entrance is a threshold to the shrine and a visible meeting place of artisans’ work, stories and community ceremony.
captions: Facade of the Triple Gate, Foshan Ancestral Temple · Line drawing
Ming–Qing · Ming–Qing

sn_chongwen.name: Chongwen Pagoda, Jingyang
sn_chongwen.yearNote: According to the Record of the Permanent Fields Endowed for the Community of the Iron Buddha Chongwen Pagoda Temple, as cited in published reports, construction began in 1591 and was completed in 1608; other accounts give different dates. This drawing follows present-day photographs and does not add the earlier finial.
sn_chongwen.lede: Chongwen Pagoda stretches upward through thirteen brick storeys, with doors and niches staggered around its eight sides. Built during the Ming Wanli period, its recorded purpose encouraged learning, while Buddhist niches retained a religious setting. The Jingyang tower brings educational aspirations into a pagoda form. Its truncated summit and repairs also distinguish today’s fabric from its earlier appearance.
facts: The hollow octagonal brick tower has thirteen storeys and an internal brick stair. Except at the summit level, doors and Buddhist niches occupy its eight faces in staggered arrangements. Receding storeys and cornices create a slender rhythm.

A published report cites a temple land inscription recording construction from 1591 to 1608, the nineteenth to thirty-sixth Wanli years. Other dates circulate; the inscription provides construction evidence, while today’s fabric also incorporates later repairs.

The inscription links construction with encouraging local children to study, while stone Buddhist images occupy the niches. Educational ambition and Buddhist architectural form meet here. This dual context offers more than judging Chongwen Pagoda by height alone.
captions: Complete surviving Chongwen Pagoda, Jingyang · Line drawing

sx_yongzuo.name: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan
sx_yongzuo.yearNote: 1612 is only an approximate sorting point for the period in which the twin pagodas took shape; the two were built one after the other, and this year is not given as the founding year of both.
sx_yongzuo.lede: On the high ground southeast of Taiyuan two thirteen-storey brick pagodas stand shoulder to shoulder, forty-six metres apart and both around fifty-four metres tall, the tallest pair of twin pagodas surviving in China. The east pagoda, Wenfeng Pagoda, came first, built in 1599 (27th year of Wanli, Ming) under Fu Lin and his son Fu Zhimo as a geomantic tower to mend the city's literary fortunes; the west pagoda, Xuanwen Pagoda, followed more than a decade later, completed in 1612 (40th year of Wanli) for the Prince of Jin by the eminent Wutai monk Miaofeng, its eaves edged entirely in peacock-blue glaze and named for the honorific title of the Wanli emperor's mother. The plate shows both pagodas, each with its own finial and taper.
facts: Twin pagodas: both are octagonal thirteen-storey brick pagodas of storeyed type, hollow double-shell structures with spiral stairs inside; the west Xuanwen Pagoda is 54.78 m high and the east Wenfeng Pagoda 53.3 m, 46 m apart, and all thirteen eaves of the Xuanwen Pagoda are edged with peacock-blue glazed tile.

Dating: Yongming Temple was founded in 1597 (25th year of Wanli, Ming) and the east pagoda finished in 1599; in 1608 (36th year of Wanli) Zhu Minchun, Prince of Jin, invited the Chan master Miaofeng to enlarge it, and in 1612 (40th year) the west pagoda and the beamless brick hall were completed and the temple renamed Yongzuo; additions in the Shunzhi and Kangxi reigns of the Qing gave it its present form.

Conservation: the east pagoda once leaned 2.87 m and was righted and strengthened in 1995 to 1996, the west pagoda was strengthened in 1981 to 1984, and only the west pagoda is now open to climb; the pair has been the emblem of Taiyuan since 1985, and the temple also keeps a Ming beamless brick hall and more than 260 stone steles.
captions: Twin Pagodas of Yongzuo Temple, Taiyuan · Wenfeng Pagoda and Xuanwen Pagoda
Ming · Wanli reign

hn_luwang.name: Tomb of Prince Jian of Lu
hn_luwang.short: Tomb of the Prince of Lu
hn_luwang.yearNote: 1615 is only an approximate sorting point for the tomb's construction phase in the late Wanli reign; the conversion error found online, “the 40th year of Wanli (1615),” is not carried over as the exact construction year of the stone archway.
hn_luwang.place: Henan · Xinxiang · Southern foot of Mount Fenghuang, Fengquan District
hn_luwang.lede: The Lufan Jiacheng stone gateway marks the beginning of the Prince Jian of Lu’s funerary avenue. Its central opening rises above the side openings, and independent ceremonial pillars stand beyond the four main posts. Cloud-and-dragon carving gives the heavy stonework an upward movement. It belongs to the late Wanli-period tomb complex, serving as both passage and ritual marker leading toward stone figures, gates and the burial precinct.
facts: This outer gateway has three openings and four soaring posts, with the Lufan Jiacheng inscription above the higher central opening. Separate pillars flank it; cloud-and-dragon carvings cover posts and beams, while drum-shaped supports brace the posts.

The precinct is the Ming tomb of Prince Jian of Lu, Zhu Yiliu. The gateway is assigned approximately to the late Wanli period; around 1615 is a timeline position, not a verified completion year for this structure.

The avenue passes through the central opening toward rows of stone figures and the tomb gates. Comparing this roofless gateway with roofed examples inside the precinct reveals varied entrance forms within one mausoleum.
captions: Tomb of Prince Jian of Lu · Lufan Jiacheng stone archway
Wanli period, Ming · Three-opening stone archway and twin stone columns
