rulong.name: Rulong Bridge
rulong.yearNote: According to the county gazetteer it was built in 1625; later repairs do not mean that every component of the bridge is original Ming fabric.
rulong.lede: A long gallery spans the stream, a tall tower lifts its ridge at the bridgehead, and the timber arch traces a broad angular line beneath the board siding. Rulong Bridge joins the road across the stream with a gallery where people can linger; it is the Ming timber-arch covered bridge of Yueshan Village.
facts: Built in the Tianqi reign: the county gazetteer records that Rulong Bridge was built in the 5th year of Tianqi in the Ming (1625); it is one of the surviving Ming timber-arch covered bridges in Qingyuan.

Timber arch structure: the bridge spans the stream on a timber arch frame, its ends resting on masonry abutments; protective boards shield the arch frame, and the gallery shelters travelers from wind and rain.

Staggered heights: the bell tower at the north end, with a triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof, rises high and, together with the central roof and the south entrance, forms a layered outline along the long bridge.
captions: Rulong Bridge · Timber-arch gallery and bridgehead pavilion
Ming · Built in the 5th year of Tianqi (1625)

ln_dazheng.name: Dazheng Hall, Shenyang Imperial Palace
ln_dazheng.sub: Octagonal hall with double-eaved pyramidal roof
ln_dazheng.yearNote: 1625 is an approximate sorting point for the early Qing construction; the construction span of the whole palace complex is not taken as the exact completion year of this single hall.
ln_dazheng.lede: The octagonal Dazheng Hall rises to the point of a double-eaved pyramidal roof, while dragon-wrapped columns draw attention back beneath the eaves. Doors surround its timber frame on eight sides above a pedestal. Begun when the Later Jin court moved to Shenyang in 1625, it is an early focus of the palace’s eastern precinct; its relationship with the Ten Princes’ Pavilions brings banner politics and varied decorative traditions into the court.
facts: Two tiers of eaves rise above an octagonal plan and converge into a central roof point. Doors enclose each side. Dragon columns, brackets and column-head ornaments meet beneath the eaves, while the pedestal provides a solemn base for the timber structure.

The hall was begun in 1625 following Nurhaci’s move to Shenyang. It belongs to the palace’s early construction, but the complex continued to expand; its complete Qing-period layout was not all finished in that year.

The arrangement of the hall and Ten Princes’ Pavilions reflects the Eight Banners, while the decoration draws on several traditions. Recent conservation used historical evidence to restore flaming-jewel patterns between brackets, making small details clues to the early Qing court.
captions: Shenyang Imperial Palace · Dazheng Hall
Early Qing · Octagonal, double-eaved pyramidal roof

quanzhoukaiyuan.name: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou
quanzhoukaiyuan.sub: Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns
quanzhoukaiyuan.era: Ming · Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen
quanzhoukaiyuan.lede: Nine bays across the front under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof: the highest grade of Buddhist hall in China. The hall should hold a hundred stone columns, but to make room for the huge Five Buddhas and the worship space two rows of fourteen were omitted, leaving eighty-six, and the name 'Hall of a Hundred Columns' stuck anyway. More remarkable still are the twenty-four bracket sets carved as celestial musicians, kalavinka with human bodies, feathered wings and bird legs, holding instruments or scholars' implements: structural members that carry the beams and at the same time a scene of music before the Buddha. The present form dates from the rebuilding of 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others.
facts: Form: nine bays wide and six deep, about 1,388 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof about 20 m high; a palatial-type frame with two rows of 14 columns omitted in the middle, leaving 86 stone columns and 76 bracket sets; where the two central rows of stone columns meet the beams, the brackets are carved as 24 flying musicians.

History: founded in 686 (second year of Chuigong, Tang); the present plan and frame proportions largely follow the rebuilding of 1155 in the Southern Song, the outer eaves were extended in 1389, and the hall was rebuilt to its present state in 1637 by the general Zheng Zhilong and others. The Sumeru base of the terrace in front carries 73 panels of lions and sphinx-like figures, moved here during the Ming rebuilding from a Hindu temple abandoned at the end of the Yuan.

Plurality: the hall enshrines the Five Buddhas of esoteric Buddhism, each 6 m high; two Hindu stone columns under the rear gallery eaves were also reused in the 1637 rebuilding, nine of their 24 medallions showing Vishnu, Krishna and other myths. That a Buddhist hall was rebuilt with Hindu members is the most tangible evidence of the port's mixed cultures.
captions: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou · Mahavira Hall
Restored in the 10th year of Chongzhen, Ming · Nine-bay Hall of a Hundred Columns

protection.scope: Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou · Mahavira Hall · Hall of a Hundred Columns

xiaoxitian.name: Xiaoxitian, Xi County
xiaoxitian.sub: Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage
xiaoxitian.lede: The Mahavira Hall is under one hundred and seventy square metres, yet nearly two thousand painted figures are packed into it: celestial palaces rise tier upon tier above the main Buddha, twelve musician bodhisattvas dance on the balustraded platform in front, human-faced apsaras and divine birds perch on clouds, the largest over three metres, the smallest no bigger than a thumb. All are clay, gilded and painted, suspended between roof frame and walls, begun in the Chongzhen reign at the end of the Ming and finished under Shunzhi in the early Qing. Qianfo Nunnery itself covers barely eleven hundred square metres, two thirds of its halls built in two storeys with cave-like openings for doors. The plate takes the central shrine and part of the celestial palaces and does not stand for the whole hall.
facts: Mahavira Hall: five bays wide and six rafters deep, single-eave gable (xuanshan) roof, interior under 170 square metres; nearly two thousand suspended figures are arranged in tiers on the roof frame, walls and shrines, the largest over 3 m high and the smallest able to sit in a palm.

Dating: Qianfo Nunnery was founded at the end of the Ming by the Chan master Dongming; the suspended sculpture of the Mahavira Hall was begun in the Chongzhen reign and completed in the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, about thirty years in all; the temple faces east on the hillside in an upper and a lower court, and became a national key protected site in 1996.

Layout: the whole temple has little over 1,100 square metres of building, two thirds of its halls in two storeys, with cave-like doorways dividing the upper, middle and front courts; the upper court holds the Mahavira, Manjusri and Samantabhadra halls, the lower court the Wuliang Hall, Weituo Hall, Moyun Pavilion and the bell and drum towers.
captions: Xiaoxitian · Detail of the suspended sculpture in the Mahavira Hall
Late Ming–early Qing · Main niche and heavenly-palace pavilions

protection.scope: Xiaoxitian, Xi County · Hall filled with suspended sculpture · Thousand Buddha Hermitage

tj_wenmiao.name: Confucian Temple, Tianjin
tj_wenmiao.sub: Dacheng Hall of the prefectural temple · Central facade and ceremonial stair
tj_wenmiao.era: Founded in the 1st year of Zhengtong · Present form from Ming–Qing repairs
tj_wenmiao.yearNote: 1436 is the year the Confucian Temple was founded and is not used directly as the date of manufacture of all the surviving components of the Dacheng Hall drawn here. 1650 is only an approximate sorting point for the present form shaped by Ming–Qing repairs, not the exact completion year of the Dacheng Hall.
tj_wenmiao.place: Tianjin · Nankai · Inside the East Gate of the Old City
tj_wenmiao.lede: The central entrance of the prefectural temple’s Dacheng Hall is framed by yellow-glazed roofing, painted beams and dark red doors. A stone ceremonial ramp leads towards the ritual space. Tianjin’s Confucian temple and school developed together, later forming adjacent prefectural and county temples under Qing administration. The date 1436 concerns the foundation of the garrison school. The present hall reflects successive Ming and Qing repairs; its entrance offers a starting point for understanding temple and education together.
facts: Glazed eaves, painted beams and doors frame the central facade, with a stone ceremonial ramp in front. Entrance and terrace organize ritual movement. This central section does not establish the bay count of the complete hall.

Tianjin’s garrison school was founded in 1436, followed by hall construction and Ming–Qing additions and repairs. The school’s foundation and the hall’s development are separate phases; the initial date cannot date every surviving beam or column.

Dacheng Hall centres worship of Confucius. Adjacent prefectural and county temples and Minglun Hall express local administration and the link between temple and school. Steps and doors connect education and ceremonial movement in visible architectural space.
captions: Confucian Temple, Tianjin · Center of the Dacheng Hall and ceremonial stair
Ming–Qing structure · Temple founded 1436

xianshen.name: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu
xianshen.sub: Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion
xianshen.era: Qing · Late Shunzhi to early Kangxi
xianshen.lede: One building does three jobs: the street runs beneath it, making it the over-street tower of Shuncheng Gate Street; one floor up it is the gate of the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; above that a five-bay theatre stage faces back to the north, the whole stacking into a four-storey silhouette. It is also the only surviving building in China linked to Zoroastrianism, the carved bull-headed and camel-headed beasts under its eaves read by Jiang Boqin as incarnations of Zoroastrian deities. Tradition credits the temple to Wen Yanbo of the Northern Song; it burned in the early Qing, and the present tower is a rebuilding of 1660 to 1668 (late Shunzhi to early Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the finial of the music hall ridge. The plate shows the over-street tower and the music hall.
facts: Form: the plan is T-shaped, about 20 m deep in all; the over-street tower at the front and the porch before the stage are each three bays square, the stage block behind is five bays wide and four deep with a surrounding gallery; the lower floor is the gate, the upper floor the stage, and with the music hall and double eaves it rises four storeys.

Dating: the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers burned in the early Qing and was rebuilt from 1660 (17th year of Shunzhi) to 1668 (7th year of Kangxi), with an inscription of 1667 (6th year of Kangxi) under the vase finial of the music hall ridge and an offering pavilion added in 1786 (51st year of Qianlong); in 1985 the over-street tower was jacked up 1.5 m as a whole and the restoration was completed in 1987.

Zoroastrian link: the stele record says Duke Wen Lu (Wen Yanbo) of the Song built the temple for the Xian god, and a Jiajing-era magistrate of the Ming turned it into the Temple of the Three Sworn Brothers; Jiang Boqin judged from the bull- and camel-headed carvings under the eaves that it is the remnant of a Zoroastrian shrine, and Chen Mingda's 1951 survey already called its artistry outstanding and warned against dismissing it for its late date.
captions: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu · Street-spanning tower and music tower
Qing · Rebuilt late Shunzhi to early Kangxi

protection.scope: Xianshen Tower, Jiexiu · Street-spanning tower and music tower · Composite pavilion

gz_wenchang.name: Wenchang Pavilion, Guiyang
gz_wenchang.sub: East of the old city · Three stories, three eaves
gz_wenchang.era: Rebuilt in the 8th year of Kangxi
gz_wenchang.yearNote: First built in 1609; the entry is placed according to the surviving pavilion formed by the 1669 rebuilding and later repairs, as given in official Guiyang municipal sources, and the founding year is not substituted for the surviving main structure.
gz_wenchang.lede: Nine-cornered roofs spread across three eave tiers at Guiyang’s Wenchang Pavilion, distinguishing it from ordinary rectangular towers and neighbouring defences. First built in 1609 for Wenchang worship, it was rebuilt in 1669 and repeatedly repaired later. Its three-storey form preserves both the eastern old-city landscape and a tradition associated with learning.
facts: The pavilion has three storeys, three eave tiers and nine-cornered roofs. Repeated corners and stacked levels create its distinctive profile; the nearby city gate tower is a separate building.

Guiyang’s official account records construction in 1609 and rebuilding in 1669, followed by repairs and enlargement under later Qing reigns. The rebuilding dates the main surviving form, not every individual component.

Originally dedicated to Wenchang, it represents civic beliefs associated with examinations and learning. Its unusual roofs, old walls and gate setting make it a surviving reference for Guiyang’s historic urban layout.
captions: Surviving Wenchang Pavilion, Guiyang · Line drawing · Pending user review

yn_jindian.name: Golden Hall, Kunming
yn_jindian.era: Recast in the 10th year of Kangxi
yn_jindian.yearNote: The surviving bronze hall drawn here was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the bronze hall first built in 1602 and its relocation are recorded separately, and the Golden Hall of the Wudang Mountains is not mistakenly used as a reference.
yn_jindian.lede: Roof, columns and doors resemble a timber hall, but close inspection reveals cast copper. Taihe Palace’s Golden Hall on Kunming’s Mingfeng Mountain reproduces traditional building details in metal. A stone platform supports its darkened surfaces and double eaves. The surviving hall was rebuilt by Wu Sangui in 1671; the earlier Ming copper hall had a separate history of relocation.
facts: Cast columns, beams, brackets, lattice doors and roof tiles assemble into a timber-like hall with double eaves on a stone platform. Metal replaces wood, but the relationships between components retain timber architectural forms rather than making a simple copper shell.

The existing hall follows Wu Sangui’s rebuilding in 1671, the tenth Kangxi year, confirmed by an inscription cast on a beam. The copper hall first founded in 1602 was later removed, so its date does not describe the surviving building.

Part of the Daoist Taihe Palace, it preserves an example of casting joined with traditional hall design. It historically followed Wudang’s Golden Hall, but the surviving forms, treatment of materials and histories at the two sites must be understood separately.
captions: Surviving bronze Golden Hall, Taihe Palace, Kunming · Line drawing · Pending user review
Qing · 1671

hb_qingdongling.name: Eastern Qing Tombs
hb_qingdongling.sub: Stone memorial archway on the Xiaoling spirit way
hb_qingdongling.yearNote: The date 1672 is adopted for the stone archway drawn here: Wang Qiheng, on the basis of the Xiaoling drawings and the archives on the transport of stone, established that the components were transported at the end of 1671 and the archway completed in early 1672. The early main works of the Xiaoling in 1663–1664 and the traditionally recorded ancillary works of 1668 are not used as the date of this stone archway.
hb_qingdongling.lede: The stone archway at the southern end of Xiaoling’s spirit road establishes the scale of the Eastern Qing Tombs through five openings and a sequence of stone roofs. Eaves, beams and columns resemble timber but are carved in stone; eleven roofed elements rise around a clear centre. This was not among Xiaoling’s earliest completed structures: archival research places completion in 1672. The ceremonial approach unfolds northward from here.
facts: The timber-inspired stone archway has five bays, six columns and eleven roofed elements. Its central passage and side bays rise in a hierarchy; continuous columns, beams and roofs emphasise a broad ceremonial frontage rather than a single narrow gateway.

Wang Qiheng’s study of Xiaoling drawings and transport records finds the stone components arriving in 1671 and the archway completed early in 1672. This date is distinguished from earlier completion and burial phases of the mausoleum.

At the southern end of Xiaoling’s ceremonial axis, the archway precedes gates, stele towers and ritual buildings. Stone versions of timber roofs give lasting material form to imperial hierarchy and order the visitor’s movement from the entrance onward.
captions: Eastern Qing Tombs · Stone memorial archway of the Xiaoling
Front elevation: five bays, six columns, eleven roofs

protection.scope: Eastern Qing Tombs · Stone memorial archway on the Xiaoling spirit way

sd_mengmiao.name: Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, Zoucheng
sd_mengmiao.sub: Seven bays, double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Green glazed tiles
sd_mengmiao.era: Rebuilt in the 12th year of Kangxi, later repaired
sd_mengmiao.yearNote: The surviving hall is placed at 1673, when it was rebuilt five years after the earthquake damage of 1668; the comprehensive repair of 1736 and modern renovations are described separately. It is not the original fabric of the hall first built in the Northern Song.
sd_mengmiao.lede: Yasheng Hall’s seven-bay body is enclosed by two tiers of green glazed eaves, marking the principal hall for worship of Mencius. It retains the ritual position within his temple but is not the original Northern Song hall. Rebuilding followed the earthquake of 1668, with further Qing and modern repairs. Its scale and roof rank correspond to Mencius’s status as the Second Sage, making Confucian ritual visible in architecture.
facts: Form: the hall is seven bays wide beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with green glazed tiles. Columns enclose its broad body. Its scale and roof distinguish the ritual centre from the single-eaved subsidiary halls.

Dating: the earthquake of 1668 damaged the hall, which was rebuilt five years later; 1673 anchors the surviving building. A comprehensive temple repair followed in 1736, with later work continuing. This is not the Northern Song foundation hall.

Significance: roof form, tile colour and bay dimensions translate the honours accorded to Mencius into architectural hierarchy. The relationship between this hall and lesser buildings illustrates Confucian worship and ranked construction.
captions: Yasheng Hall of the Mencius Temple, Zoucheng, whole hall · Line drawing

daimiao.name: Tiankuang Hall of the Dai Temple
daimiao.lede: Tiankuang Hall’s nine-bay front and double-eaved hipped roof give worship of the Mount Tai deity a palatial scale. Its ritual position follows a Song foundation, while the surviving timber dimensions and methods reflect Qing repair. A Kangxi rebuilding inscription describes retained columns and beams alongside replaced timbers and newly fired tiles. Murals repainted in the early Qing show the deity’s procession and return, adding another historical layer.
facts: Form: the hall is nine bays wide and five deep beneath a double-eaved hipped roof with yellow glazed tiles. Its broad body and eaves establish the high rank of this mountain cult building, with columns and three walls enclosing the deity’s hall.

Dating: the Kangxi repair inscription records completion in 1677, retaining usable beams and columns while replacing decayed purlins, rafters, boards and tiles. Surviving work reflects Qing methods, with later repairs; the completion date does not date every component.

Significance: the procession and return murals were repainted in the early Qing on the basis of Song subjects, combining ritual, landscapes and buildings. Separate phases of timberwork and painting provide tangible evidence for the continuity of mountain worship.
captions: Front of the Tiankuang Hall, Dai Temple · Nine bays, double-eaved hipped roof
Founded in the Song · Surviving form from the Qing restoration

gugong.name: Forbidden City, Beijing
gugong.lede: The Hall of Supreme Harmony owes its imposing presence to an eleven-bay facade, a double-eaved hipped roof and a three-tier white marble terrace. Ten ridge beasts at the roof corners also proclaim its architectural rank. The hall seen today was rebuilt after a fire during the Kangxi reign and completed in 1697; it is not the original Yongle-period hall. Imperial enthronements, weddings and major seasonal ceremonies took place here. At the centre of the Forbidden City's Outer Court, it served grand state ritual rather than the routine conduct of government.
facts: Form: eleven bays wide and five deep, the hall has a double-eaved hipped roof covered with yellow glazed tiles and stands on a three-tier white marble terrace. Its broad facade, raised platform and layered eaves create the most conspicuous outline in the Forbidden City's Outer Court.

Rebuilding: its predecessor was founded in 1420 and destroyed by a lightning fire in 1679. Reconstruction began in 1695 and was completed in 1697. The surviving hall belongs to this Qing building campaign rather than the date of the original Ming foundation.

Rank: ten ridge beasts line the roof corners, expressing the decorative hierarchy of a high-ranking hall. Imperial enthronements, weddings, New Year and winter-solstice ceremonies were held here. Its scale served ceremonial occasions rather than daily office work.
captions: Forbidden City · Hall of Supreme Harmony
Eleven bays wide · Double-eaved hipped roof

protection.scope: Forbidden City, Beijing · Hall of Supreme Harmony

mimi.name: Mimi Temple, Fanshi
mimi.place: Shanxi · Fanshi · Yantou Township · Mimo Cliff
mimi.lede: Thirty-eight kilometres southwest of Taihuai on Mount Wutai, this temple below Mimo Cliff on Mount Weiping was once the place of the saying that to visit Wutai without the Dragon Cave was to see only half the mountain. Tradition takes it back to the Northern Qi; the Tang monk Mucha retreated and built here, and it flourished in the Tang and Song, leaving outside the walls the Tang-founded, Ming-repaired pagoda of Patriarch Mucha and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han). The halls themselves are Qing rebuildings, the main halls of the front and middle courts both five bays wide. The plate shows the front of the Manjusri Hall: five bays with a front porch, a central stair climbing to the raised platform, and Qing paintings surviving on the porch panels and inside.
facts: Manjusri Hall: as drawn, five bays wide with a front porch under a flush-gable (yingshan) roof, standing on a raised platform reached by a central stone stair; in the temple the main halls of the front and middle courts are both five bays, the north and south sutra lofts five bays each, and only a five-bay north pavilion survives in the rear court.

Dating: the Qingliang Shan Gazetteer records that the Tang monk Mucha founded the temple while in retreat at Mimi Cliff, and another account has a Northern Qi nun's hermitage before it; of thirty-two hermitages once here the front, middle and rear courts and the West and Middle hermitages remain; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it became a national key protected site in 2006.

Stonework: before the temple stand a Jin-dynasty stone pillar and two brick pagodas, the pagoda of Patriarch Mucha, Tang-founded and Ming-repaired, hexagonal, four storeys and about 10 m high, and the pagoda of Master Xuanjue of 963 (7th year of Tianhui, Northern Han), hexagonal and two storeys; the Golden Buddha Loft in the Middle Hermitage holds a stone Amitabha about 7 m high carved in 1535 (14th year of Jiajing, Ming).
captions: Mimi Temple · Front of the Manjushri Hall
Five bays, flush gable roof · Qing structure

hn_kangbaiwan.name: Kang Baiwan Manor
hn_kangbaiwan.era: Late Ming–early Qing · Extended over generations
hn_kangbaiwan.yearNote: The Zhengzhou Municipal Bureau of Cultural Heritage dates the manor as a whole to the late Ming–early Qing, with continued construction in later periods. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the manor's Ming–Qing structures; the storied cave dwelling shown in the photographs has as yet no exact construction date of its own, and neither the Kang family's move here nor any individual's life dates are used as the date of the building.
hn_kangbaiwan.lede: Kang Baiwan Manor combines cliff-side cave rooms with multistorey houses. Superimposed arched openings and inward-facing side buildings enclose a long courtyard. The estate accumulated through generations of the Kang family rather than a single building campaign, joining living and working spaces. Wood, brick and stone carving reveal household customs, while the architecture shows how builders in the Heluo region adapted housing to the terrain.
facts: Cave rooms were cut against the cliff and buildings erected along the streets, with residences arranged around quadrangular courtyards. Arched cave openings and inward-facing side houses connect underground spaces, upper floors and courtyard life.

Zhengzhou’s heritage bureau dates the estate broadly to the late Ming and early Qing, with later additions. Around 1700 is an approximate timeline position; the individual cave building has no verified construction year.

The estate includes residences, workshops and storage. Its wood, brick and stone carving also conveys ornament and family teachings, preserving evidence of family enterprise alongside regional domestic architecture.

gx_gongcheng.name: Dacheng Hall of the Gongcheng Confucian Temple
gx_gongcheng.sub: Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof · Main hall of the Confucian temple
gx_gongcheng.era: Built in the Ming–Qing · Later repaired and maintained
gx_gongcheng.yearNote: The sixth-batch list of national protected sites gives the Gongcheng historic building complex as Ming to Qing. 1700 is only an approximate sorting point for the surviving Ming–Qing main structure; the founding, successive restorations and the dates of the present hall's components are not merged into a single precise year.
gx_gongcheng.lede: Gongcheng’s Dacheng Hall stands on the ascending ceremonial axis of the Confucian temple. Its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof and lifted corners spread above a high terrace. Ridge figures, painting and carved doors make a ritual building a repository of local craftsmanship. The temple originated in Ming, but the surviving halls reflect Qing rebuilding and later repairs. The foundation of the temple does not date every beam and column visible today.
facts: The raised hall has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, carved doors and eaves, and painted ridge figures. Steps connect it with the ceremonial platform; elevation, roofing and ornament emphasize the hall on the axis.

The temple originated in 1410 and was rebuilt during the Qing Daoguang reign, followed by further repairs. The protected complex is dated Ming through Qing. Foundation and rebuilding must be distinguished; later repairs also leave surviving components of different ages.

The hall worships Confucius, translating ceremonial order into an axis and terraces. Ridge figures and carved and painted decoration place local craftsmanship within ritual forms, preserving Guangxi’s interpretation of Confucian temple architecture.

hu_zhanggu.name: Historic Buildings of Zhangguying Village
hu_zhanggu.sub: Ming–Qing dwellings · Linked roofs and skywells
hu_zhanggu.era: Built over generations in the Ming–Qing
hu_zhanggu.yearNote: The surviving dwellings form a complex built in multiple phases during the Ming and Qing; 1700 is only a broad sorting point and does not refer to the exact construction year of any single house. The drawing shows part of the roofscape visible in photographs; it does not claim to reconstruct the whole village, nor does it equate the date of the Zhang family's settlement with the date of the surviving houses.
hu_zhanggu.lede: One grey-tiled roof meets another at Zhang Guying Village, with courtyards and gable walls tucked between continuous ridges. This is only a portion of the residential complex, yet its connected halls, side rooms and covered passages make the larger organisation legible. Courtyards admit light and help drain water. Built and extended through the Ming and Qing periods, the intricate roofscape records the expansion of family life.
facts: Courtyards, halls and paired side rooms form basic units linked by covered passages and lanes. In this roofscape, flush gable walls, tile ridges and courtyard openings express the organisation of the living spaces below.

Construction began in the Ming period and continued through Qing extensions; the surviving complex includes several phases. The ancestors’ settlement history differs from the dates of individual houses and cannot assign every residence one foundation year.

Connected passages maintain links between households, while courtyards admit light and assist drainage. The clustered houses reveal a pattern of extended-family residence in which everyday movement and social contact are closely tied to the architecture.
captions: Part of the roofscape of the Ming–Qing dwellings, Zhangguying Village · Line drawing

yn_jingzhen.name: Jingzhen Octagonal Pavilion
yn_jingzhen.sub: Dai Theravada Buddhist temple · Ordination hall
yn_jingzhen.yearNote: 1701 is the year the Octagonal Pavilion was founded; later repairs, such as those of 1978 and 1993, are recorded separately, and the other, now destroyed buildings of Jingzhen Temple are not invented in the drawing.
yn_jingzhen.lede: Roof layers spread in eight directions and gather towards a pointed summit. Jingzhen’s Octagonal Pavilion combines a brick body with timber roofs into a light silhouette. Despite its name, it is a Theravada Buddhist ordination hall for monastic ceremonies. Founded in 1701 and repaired in modern times, it includes surviving and renewed details rather than an entirely untouched original.
facts: Timber roof tiers rise above a brick body in eight directions, converging at the summit. Decorations on walls and eaves are organised around the centre, giving a small building a richly layered appearance.

The pavilion was founded in 1701, the fortieth Kangxi year, and repaired repeatedly thereafter. Foundation and restoration are separate events; renewal of components does not mean that the whole building originated in modern times.

Within a Dai Theravada monastery, it serves ordination and uposatha ceremonies rather than primarily providing a scenic resting place. Reading its religious use together with the eight-direction roof explains its distinctive local form.

fj_chengqi.name: Chengqi Lou, Yongding
fj_chengqi.sub: Gaobei tulou cluster · Circular rammed-earth dwelling
fj_chengqi.era: Completed in the 48th year of Kangxi
fj_chengqi.yearNote: The completion year of Chengqi Lou, 1709, is adopted; the start of construction in the Ming and the completion in the Qing are described separately. The plate shows the surviving exterior and does not reconstruct the interior from postage stamps.
fj_chengqi.lede: 'Four storeys high, four rings round, four hundred rooms up and down; circle within circle, ring within ring, three hundred years of weathering.' The local rhyme describes Chengqi Lou: inside a round building 73 metres across sit three concentric ring-houses and an ancestral hall, the outer ring four storeys with seventy-two rooms to a floor, the second ring two storeys, the third one, each stepping lower towards the centre. The Jiang clan is said to have broken ground in the Chongzhen era and finished only in 1709, the 48th year of Kangxi; at its peak more than six hundred people lived here. The plate shows only the complete exterior, with no section cut.
facts: Form: a four-ring concentric earthen building, 73 m in diameter on a site of 5,376.17 square metres; the outer ring is four storeys and 16.4 m high with 72 rooms per floor, the second ring two storeys with 40 rooms per floor, the third ring a single storey of 32 rooms, and an ancestral hall at the centre, over four hundred rooms in all, with 3 main gates and 2 wells. The rammed-earth outer wall is 1.5 m thick at the base and 1 m at the top, and the eaves project nearly 4 m.

Dating: ground is said to have been broken in the Chongzhen era of the Ming and the building completed in 1709, spanning three generations and about half a century. More than six hundred people lived here at its height and some three hundred of the Jiang clan still do; the Fujian dwelling in the 1986 Chinese folk-dwelling stamp series is this building.

Comparison: Chengqi Lou is the core of the Gaobei tulou cluster, home of the Yongding Jiang clan, together with Wuyun Lou, Shize Lou and Qiaofu Lou; by size and number of rings it ranks among the foremost surviving round tulou and is called the 'king of tulou'. In 2008 the Gaobei cluster was inscribed on the World Heritage List as part of 'Fujian Tulou', six clusters and four single buildings.
captions: Complete exterior of Chengqi Lou, Yongding · Line drawing
Qing · 1709

hn_wuhou.name: Wuhou Shrine, Nanyang
hn_wuhou.sub: Honoring a worthy beneath the eaves
hn_wuhou.era: Qing structure · Repaired over the centuries
hn_wuhou.yearNote: 1711 — the comprehensive restoration of the whole shrine in the 50th year of Kangxi in the Qing, as officially recorded — is taken as an approximate sorting point, without asserting on this basis that the surviving Great Worship Hall was built entirely in that year. The construction of the main hall in the 11th year of Hongzhi in the Ming and the later Qing and modern repairs are recorded separately; the dates of the specific components beneath the eaves drawn here still need to be distinguished through measured documentation.
hn_wuhou.lede: Beneath the eaves of Nanyang’s Wuhou Shrine, columns, beams, doors and layers of inscribed plaques frame a place of worship for Zhuge Liang. The Great Worship Hall occupies the front precinct, contrasting with the commemorative cottage and pavilions behind. Ming, Qing and modern repairs shaped its present appearance, while plaques and inscriptions preserve later writers’ assessments. The historical figure’s lifetime and the shrine’s building dates must be distinguished.
facts: The Great Worship Hall is the principal ritual building in the front precinct. Plaques hang beneath the beams and inscriptions line the walls; images of Zhuge Liang, Zhuge Zhan and Zhuge Shang are enshrined inside.

Local records describe construction of a main hall in 1498 and a shrine-wide restoration in 1711, followed by later repairs. The 1711 campaign cannot date every surviving component beneath these eaves.

Front ritual halls and rear commemorative pavilions combine temple and memorial-garden functions. Plaques and inscriptions document continuing veneration, expressing later cultural memories of Zhuge Liang.
captions: Wuhou Shrine, Nanyang · Detail beneath the eaves of the Great Worship Hall
Qing structure, repaired over the centuries · Space of columns, beams and doors

sx_jiezhou_guandi.name: Guandi Temple, Xiezhou
sx_jiezhou_guandi.sub: Chongning Hall · Ancestral temple of Guandi
sx_jiezhou_guandi.yearLabel: Qing · Rebuilt after the Kangxi-era fire
sx_jiezhou_guandi.yearNote: 1725 is only an approximate sorting point for the rebuilding phase in the early 18th century, not the exact completion year of the Chongning Hall; 1702 is the year of the temple fire.
sx_jiezhou_guandi.lede: The ancestral temple of all Guandi temples, its main hall, Chongning Hall, is named for the title "Perfected Lord Chongning" conferred on Guan Yu by Emperor Huizong of Song in 1104 (3rd year of Chongning). The seven-bay hall under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof closes the axis of the front court, a ring of coiling-dragon stone columns in the gallery around it, and under its eaves hang imperial boards of four reigns: Kangxi's "righteousness lights heaven and earth", Qianlong's "divine valour", Xianfeng's "the pole of humanity for all ages" and Cixi's "awesome power shakes all". The temple was founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui); the existing buildings follow the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing). The plate takes the Chongning Hall alone; the Spring and Autumn Tower behind it is not in the picture.
facts: Chongning Hall: seven bays wide and six deep, double-eave hip-and-gable roof, with a surrounding gallery carried on coiling-dragon stone columns; a bell pavilion and a stele pavilion, added in the Qing, flank the front; inside and out hang the boards of Kangxi, Qianlong, Xianfeng and Cixi and dozens of late-Qing and Republican boards.

Dating: founded in 589 (9th year of Kaihuang, Sui) and rebuilt in 1014 (7th year of Dazhong Xiangfu, Song), the temple was destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly; the rebuilding after the fire of 1702 (41st year of Kangxi, Qing) produced today's front-court-and-rear-palace layout, and it became a national key protected site in 1988.

Layout: the temple covers 220,000 square metres; to the south lies the Garden of the Sworn Oath of 1620 (48th year of Wanli, Ming), to the north the main temple, whose front axis runs through screen wall, Duan Gate, Zhi Gate, Meridian Gate, Imperial Calligraphy Tower and Chongning Hall, while the rear palace centres on the Spring and Autumn Tower flanked by the Sabre and Seal towers; with over a hundred bays of halls it is called the crown of martial temples.

qufukongmiao.name: Temple of Confucius, Qufu
qufukongmiao.lede: Dacheng Hall locates the centre of Confucian worship in a nine-bay front, yellow glazed tiles and carved dragon columns. The colonnade beneath its double-eaved hip-and-gable roof joins the forecourt terrace to organize movement and ceremony. The surviving hall follows a rebuilding after the Yongzheng-era fire, continuing a much older ritual tradition without sharing the temple’s foundation date. Deep stone carving beside layered timberwork gives architectural expression to ritual rank.
facts: Form: the hall is nine bays wide and five deep, with a surrounding colonnade beneath a yellow-glazed double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Ten front stone columns bear deeply carved dragons; the terrace and stairs extend its ceremonial space.

Dating: rebuilding followed the fire of 1724 and finished in 1730, the eighth Yongzheng year. These dates concern the surviving main hall rather than the temple’s foundation. Later repairs form additional phases.

Significance: dragon columns, yellow tiles and the nine-by-five plan express the honours accorded to Confucius through architectural rank. The hall and terrace place offerings, ritual and spectators within an ordered setting, illustrating Qing official construction.
captions: Front of the Dacheng Hall, Temple of Confucius, Qufu · Redrawn from photographs

im_wuta.name: Five Pagoda Temple, Hohhot
im_wuta.yearNote: The completion phase of the pagoda's construction, 1732, is adopted; 1727 is the year construction began, and the restored temple halls are not entered as original Qing fabric.
im_wuta.lede: Five small towers rise from one broad vajra platform at Hohhot’s Five Pagoda Temple. Their close grouping matters more than individual height. Built from 1727 to 1732, the brick-and-stone reliquary tower bears Buddhist images and texts. A Mongolian astronomical chart behind it brings knowledge of the sky into a Buddhist setting.
facts: A base, vajra platform and five small towers form the monument, with the centre higher than the corners. Its arch inscription uses Mongolian, Tibetan and Chinese; images, texts and ritual objects cover the outer masonry.
The reliquary tower was built from 1727 to 1732. These dates concern the historic tower, not later reconstructed temple halls, which are not treated as original Qing buildings of the same campaign.

The shared-platform form draws on Bodh Gaya in India while using local masonry carving. Charts of the sky, Mount Sumeru and rebirth on the rear screen wall place learned knowledge alongside Buddhist belief.

hn_zkguandi.name: Guandi Temple, Zhoukou
hn_zkguandi.sub: Merchant guild hall of a trading port
hn_zkguandi.yearNote: The construction year of the gate drawn here, 1735, is adopted; it is not replaced by the dates for the guild hall as a whole, whether its founding in 1693 or its full completion in 1852.
hn_zkguandi.lede: Zhoukou’s Guandi Temple gate presents five bays, with three entrances and round windows at either side. Brackets, plaques and red doors articulate the space beneath its hip-and-gable roof. Behind lies a guild complex enlarged by Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants over successive reigns. The gate’s own Yongzheng date is distinct from that longer history; ritual halls and theatre spaces further inside recall the prosperity of the trading town.
facts: Five bays wide and three deep, the gate has a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with glazed ridge pieces. Three entrances and side round windows organize the front, beneath brackets, a gilded plaque and red-painted doors.
The gate was built in 1735, the thirteenth year of the Qing Yongzheng era. The complex began in 1693 and reached completion in 1852; those dates describe the whole ensemble rather than this gate.

Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants working in Zhoukou financed the complex as both Guandi temple and fellow-provincials’ guild hall. Axial halls and a theatre link commercial association, religious performance and urban life.
captions: Guandi Temple, Zhoukou · Front of the gate

hb_qingxiling.name: Western Qing Tombs
hb_qingxiling.sub: Front elevation of the Long'en Hall of the Tailing
hb_qingxiling.yearNote: The whole tomb complex forms one entry, represented by the Long'en Hall of the Tailing; the Palace Museum gives 1736 as the completion date, which is recorded separately from the burial in 1737.
hb_qingxiling.lede: Long’en Hall at Tailing marks the ritual centre of the earliest imperial tomb in the Western Qing group through double eaves, yellow glazed tiles and a broad terrace. A five-bay hall and side buildings form the court; worship space precedes the burial zone along the axis. Begun under Yongzheng and completed early in Qianlong’s reign, the mausoleum separates construction, ritual use and interment as distinct events.
facts: Long’en Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof in yellow glazed tiles. A terrace fronts the hall and subsidiary halls stand to either side, making the hierarchy of the ritual court visible.

The Palace Museum dates Tailing’s construction from 1730 to 1736. Subsequent interment is a different event; building history and burial ceremonies are recorded separately rather than used interchangeably to date the halls.

Behind Long’en Hall, gates and a sacrificial platform lead towards the square enclosure, spirit tower, burial enclosure and underground chamber. This sequence shows how imperial tombs link worship and burial while keeping their spaces distinct.
captions: Western Qing Tombs · Long'en Hall of the Tailing

feiyun.name: Dongyue Temple, Wanrong
feiyun.era: Restored in the 11th year of Qianlong
feiyun.lede: This three-storey timber tower in the county town of Wanrong stands 23.19 m high. Four through-columns run from the ground floor straight to the top, and 345 bracket sets and 32 upturned eave corners project tier upon tier, so that from a distance clouds seem to gather about the tower, hence the name Feiyun, Flying Clouds. The timber is left unpainted. It stands at the very front of the axis of the Dongyue Temple; its founding date is unknown, a repair stele of 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) already exists, and the present state is that of the repair of 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing). The plate shows the front of Feiyun Lou.
facts: Form: square in plan, five bays wide and deep, three visible storeys with five inside, three tiers and four eaves, crowned by a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; on the second and third storeys a hip-and-gable baosha projects on each of the four sides above a balcony. The whole tower is jointed without iron nails; the four cypress through-columns are 0.7 m in diameter and over 15 m tall.

Dating: the Qianlong-era Record of Repairing Feiyun Lou says the Dongyue Temple already existed in the 1st year of Zhenguan (627); the tower's own founding date is unknown, steles record repairs in 1617 (45th year of Wanli, Ming) and 1746 (11th year of Qianlong, Qing), and the present fabric follows the latter. Listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Assessment: Chai Zejun wrote that it 'holds an important place among surviving ancient storeyed buildings in China', and with the Yingxian pagoda it is called Shanxi's 'southern tower and northern pagoda'; behind it the Wumen gate and offering hall are Yuan structures, and the stone columns of the main Dongyue hall bear Ming inscriptions of the Zhengtong and Zhengde reigns, none of which is in the plate.

hu_tianhou.name: Tianhou Temple, Zhijiang
hu_tianhou.sub: Gate of the Tianhou Temple · Bluestone relief
hu_tianhou.yearNote: Placed by the construction date, 1748, of the surviving bluestone gate archway; the history of the Fujian Guild Hall from 1684 is listed separately. The drawing shows the stone archway and the steps immediately adjoining it, not the whole compound of the Tianhou Temple.
hu_tianhou.place: Hunan · Zhijiang · West bank of the Wushui River
hu_tianhou.lede: Figures, animals and plants unfold across stone-carved eaves and brackets at Zhijiang’s Tianhou Temple gateway, as if a journey had been inscribed into the building. A raised centre and lower side roofs organise its elevation, while carved bridges and towns recall the routes of Fujian merchants. The surviving gateway belongs to the 1748 construction campaign, serving both Mazu worship and the meeting of coastal culture with western Hunan.
facts: The blue-stone gateway imitates timber architecture with double-eaved hip-and-gable roofs and carved brackets. Its central doorway, plaque and dense reliefs are held within a clear framework of stepped rooflines.

The temple has a Kangxi-period history as a Fujian merchants’ guildhall. Merchants rebuilt on the site in 1748, the phase to which the stone gateway belongs. That earlier history and the present gateway must be distinguished, without treating the whole compound as original to one year.

Reliefs of Luoyang Bridge and the three towns of Wuhan recall merchants’ home region and travels. Popular stories appear alongside dragons, phoenixes and plants. Small carvings thus preserve memories of commerce and migration and show Mazu worship crossing regional boundaries.

hn_zhongyue.name: Zhongyue Temple, Mount Song
hn_zhongyue.sub: Central facade of the Junji Hall (detail)
hn_zhongyue.yearNote: 1750 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing appearance, not the exact rebuilding year of the Junji Hall; the hall underwent a major repair in 1986.
hn_zhongyue.lede: Junji Hall stands on a raised terrace within Zhongyue Temple. Central doors and stone steps emerge between old trees, while its double-eaved hipped roof extends to either side. The complete nine-bay hall is the ritual focus for worship of Mount Song’s deity; the visible centre is only part of its broad façade. Qing rebuilding and later repairs give architectural form to a much older mountain cult and culminate the sequence of axial courtyards.
facts: The complete hall is nine bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hipped roof of yellow glazed tiles and a raised front terrace. Its central five bays and steps reveal the main axis through the trees.

Many surviving buildings were rebuilt under the Qing and subsequently repaired. Around 1750 is an approximate position for the present appearance, not a verified rebuilding date; the earlier Taishi Shrine history does not date this hall.

The temple rises northward with the terrain. Gates, gateways, pavilions and halls create successive courtyards culminating at Junji Hall, joining the approach route to the ritual order of mountain worship.

sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.name: City God Temple, Jiexiu
sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate timeline position for the Qing building, not the exact completion year of the stage; the founding of the temple and the surviving Ming main hall have their own dates.
sx_jiexiu_chenghuang.lede: The stage of the Jiexiu City God Temple is built 'reversed' beside the gate: toward the courtyard it throws out a hip-and-gable baosha as the stage front, with a round-ridged flush-gable backstage behind. The roof is covered in blue-green glazed tile, and along the main ridge pavilions, vases and ridge beasts stand in a row; beneath the platform a passage is left, so one enters the temple under the stage. The Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau records that the founding date is unknown and that steles note four repairs from 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi, Ming) onward; the roof glaze is among the few Ming remains left in Jiexiu. The plate shows the courtyard face of the stage and its glazed ridge.
facts: Stage: the main body has a round-ridged flush-gable roof, with a three-bay hip-and-gable baosha projecting both toward the courtyard and outward, the inner one serving as the stage; the platform is raised with a stone balustrade in front and a passage below; bell and drum towers flank it, and as drawn the sparrow braces under the eaves are carved all over with flowers.

Dating: steles record repairs in 1495 (8th year of Hongzhi), 1572 (6th year of Longqing), 1724 (2nd year of Yongzheng, Qing) and 1814 (19th year of Jiaqing); Wikipedia additionally gives a founding in 1370 (3rd year of Hongwu, Ming). Listed in 2013 in the seventh batch of national key protected sites.

Glaze: the glazed ridge tiles, owl-tail finials, immortals and beasts, pavilions and vases on the roof are Ming remains, complete in colour and form; the main hall, seven bays wide under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, has slender columns and brackets of marked Ming character, and is not in the plate.

hb_bishushanzhuang.name: Chengde Mountain Resort
hb_bishushanzhuang.sub: Front elevation of the Danbo Jingcheng Hall
hb_bishushanzhuang.yearNote: The whole resort forms one entry; the founding of the hall in 1711 and the rebuilding of the present main structure in 1754 are kept separate.
hb_bishushanzhuang.lede: Danbo Jingcheng Hall balances palatial scale with restrained materials. Beneath its broad rounded hip-and-gable roof, nanmu columns, doors and ceiling retain their natural colour, giving dignity without dense painted ornament. Founded under Kangxi and rebuilt in nanmu under Qianlong, this principal palace hall hosted audiences and ceremonies, bringing the Mountain Resort’s landscape sensibility into imperial ritual.
facts: The principal hall is seven bays wide, with a single-eaved rounded hip-and-gable roof. Nanmu columns, panelled doors and ceiling largely retain their natural colour; the rounded roof without a sharp main ridge softens the broad elevation.

Resort records give a foundation in 1711 and rebuilding in nanmu in 1754. The surviving principal structure is dated to the rebuilding phase; the initial foundation year does not date every part of today’s nanmu hall.

Major ceremonies, official audiences and receptions for ethnic leaders and foreign envoys took place here. Restrained timber colour carried formal court functions, giving the resort palace a different material character from Beijing’s imperial courts.

im_wudang.name: Wudang Monastery
im_wudang.yearNote: The Suguqin Hall is a building of the Qianlong period of the Qing; sources differ between 1755 and 1757, and 1755 serves only as an approximate sorting point. The 1749 expansion of the monastery is not used to fix the completion of the hall drawn here.
im_wudang.lede: In a valley of the Yin Mountains, Wudang Monastery spreads its white-walled, flat-roofed Tibetan-style halls tier by tier along the slope. The Suguqin Hall at the front of the monastery is the space where the whole community gathers to chant sutras; its broad, steady mass contrasts sharply with the curved roofs of the timber halls of the Central Plains.
facts: Subject drawn: the Suguqin Hall, also called the Suguqin Dugong; it is not merged with the whole monastery or with the Nuni Hall rebuilt in 2005 into a single building.
Date: the monastery was expanded in the 14th year of Qianlong (1749); the Suguqin Hall is placed approximately in the Qianlong period, as sources differ on the hall's own construction year.
Form: a Tibetan-style flat roof, white walls, stepped terraces and a dark eave band; Wudang Monastery was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1996.
captions: Suguqin Hall, Wudang Monastery · Line drawing · Pending user review

hb_puning.name: Puning Temple
hb_puning.sub: Complete elevation of the Mahayana Pavilion
hb_puning.yearNote: The Chinese-Tibetan building complex forms a single entry, without a separate entry for the great Buddha statue; the Mahayana Pavilion is the representative.
hb_puning.lede: The six eave lines on Dacheng Pavilion’s south front are not six usable storeys. The tall building follows the terrain and houses a monumental wooden Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Guanyin; its sides and back show different tier counts. Built under Qianlong, Puning Temple combines a Chinese-style front axis with a rear layout drawing on Tibetan Buddhism. The pavilion brings sculpture, hillside space and timber architecture together.
facts: The south elevation has six eave tiers, the east and west five, and the north four, while the interior has three storeys. Eave counts respond to terrain and appearance rather than a uniform floor count; the large Guanyin stands at the centre.

Puning Temple was built from 1755 to 1758, with its rear layout drawing on Samye Monastery in Tibet. This is the history of a Qing temple, not the earlier date of the monastery that inspired its design.

Chinese-style timber construction and surrounding Tibetan-style halls and platforms form the worship space. The wooden Guanyin requires continuous internal height; differing eave and floor counts show coordination between sculpture, symbolic layout and building technique.
captions: Mahayana Pavilion, Puning Temple
Six-eaved tall pavilion and front stone steps

protection.scope: Puning Temple · Complete elevation of the Mahayana Pavilion

sx_dingcun.name: Dingcun Folk Houses
sx_dingcun.sub: Ding Kun Compound · Southern Shanxi courtyard house
sx_dingcun.era: Qianlong period, Qing · Ding Kun Compound
sx_dingcun.yearNote: 1760 is only for approximate sorting within the Qianlong period. The Ding Kun family built over three generations across about 50 years, and no precise completion year is invented for the hall drawn here.
sx_dingcun.lede: Dingcun lies on the east bank of the Fen River and keeps more than twenty Ming and Qing residences: the northern group are single-court siheyuan from the Wanli reign of the Ming onward, the central and southern groups two-court compounds of the Yongzheng to Xianfeng reigns of the Qing. The Ding Kun compound, now Courtyard No. 1 and the Dingcun Folk Museum, was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong, Qing); its owners Ding Kun and his son Ding Jialun both purchased the status of imperial student, and the grandson Ding Xilian purchased a sub-prefectural post in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong), whereupon the 'Xuandelang' archway was raised before the gate. The plate shows the three-bay hall inside the courtyard and the wing rooms on either side.
facts: Courtyard: as drawn, a three-bay hall with a front porch, with wing rooms on both sides enclosing a long narrow court; Dingcun houses are northern siheyuan of brick, stone and timber, richly carved on eave boards, sparrow braces, column bases and gate stones, and in one Qianlong-era house the railing panels of the central hall carry 'hundred plays' carvings such as 'Ningwu Pass' and 'Yue Fei's mother tattooing'.

Dating: the earliest house of the northern group dates to 1593 (21st year of Wanli, Ming), the central and southern groups to the Yongzheng-Xianfeng reigns of the Qing; Courtyard No. 1 was founded in 1745 (10th year of Qianlong), and the 'Xuandelang' archway was erected after Ding Xilian's purchase of office in 1795 (60th year of Qianlong). The Dingcun residences were listed as a national key protected site in 1988.

Value: Dingcun is a group of residences built continuously by one family in one village for over two hundred years; the Dingcun Folk Museum, opened in 1985, was China's first folk museum of the Han people. The Dingcun site on the Fen River terrace beside the village is a Palaeolithic site, protected separately from the houses.
captions: Dingcun Folk Houses · Hall inside the Ding Kun Compound
Qianlong period, Qing · Courtyard view

quanzhouwenmiao.name: Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple
quanzhouwenmiao.sub: Dacheng Hall · Qing structure in Song style
quanzhouwenmiao.lede: A Hall of Great Achievement for a prefectural school, yet roofed with a double-eave hip roof, yellow glazed tiles and stone columns carved with coiling dragons: extraordinarily rare among Confucian temples anywhere in China. The temple moved to its present site in the early Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and took its 'school on the left, temple on the right' layout after a rebuilding in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era and the present hall was thoroughly repaired in 1761, yet its column grid, beam frame and true cantilever brackets keep twelfth-century practice. The six relief dragon columns along the front eaves are known locally as 'six dragons bearing up the sage'.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and five deep, about 801 square metres in area, with a double-eave hip roof of yellow glazed tiles; the hall body is carried on 48 round white stone columns in a two-ring 'double-trough' grid, with six relief dragon columns at the front eaves and two more dragon columns inside; the bracket sets use true ang inside and out, the beams are fully painted, and the ridges carry cut-porcelain ornament.

Dating: moved to the present site early in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Northern Song and rebuilt in 1137; the hall was rebuilt in the Xianchun era (1265-1274), and the present hall is the product of a major repair in 1761 that kept its Song structural character. A 2014-2015 restoration to the original form and materials was named one of the outstanding heritage conservation projects of 2020 nationwide.

Significance: the Quanzhou Confucian Temple and its school symbolised the officials and scholars of Song-Yuan Quanzhou, and its building scale is the largest among Confucian temples in China's seven southeastern provinces; the waist of the Sumeru base of the terrace in front still carries Song bluestone reliefs of scrolling foliage. In 2021 it was inscribed as a component of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.
captions: Quanzhou Prefectural Confucian Temple · Dacheng Hall
26th year of Qianlong, Qing · Song-style double-eaved hipped roof retained

hb_putuozongcheng.name: Putuo Zongcheng Temple
hb_putuozongcheng.sub: Complete front of the Great Red Terrace and its surviving upper roofs
hb_putuozongcheng.yearNote: An independent temple complex forming one entry; it is not combined with the Xumi Fushou Temple into one entry, nor split into separate courtyards to pad the count.
hb_putuozongcheng.lede: The immense red terrace conceals halls behind its walls, while roof edges emerge above. White terraces climb the slope towards the central mass. Built under Qianlong with the Potala Palace as an important model, Putuo Zongcheng combines Chinese roofs and Tibetan-style terrace forms; its most revealing relationship is between the massive shell and the enclosed worship courts.
facts: The Great Red Terrace is the core, raised above stepped white terraces. Windows and central decoration divide the broad wall; roofs appear above, but the halls mostly lie within. This exterior is not an ordinary hall frontage.
The temple was built from 1767 to 1771, drawing on the Potala Palace. It is a newly built Qing temple: the antiquity of its model does not change the date of the surviving structure.

Wanfaguiyi Hall stands within the red terrace. Its Chinese-style double eaves and the Tibetan-style mass organise worship together; reading the rising exterior alongside enclosed courts explains the synthesis.
captions: Great Red Terrace, Putuo Zongcheng Temple
Exterior of the Great Red Terrace on the south side and the adjoining white terraces

protection.scope: Putuo Zongcheng Temple · Complete front of the Great Red Terrace and its surviving upper roofs

hn_kfhuiguan.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi-Gansu Guild Hall, Kaifeng
hn_kfhuiguan.sub: Front of the timber memorial archway
hn_kfhuiguan.yearNote: The subject drawn is dated to the Qing; the numerical year is only for approximate sorting.
hn_kfhuiguan.lede: The timber gateway of Kaifeng’s Shanxi–Shaanxi–Gansu Guild Hall welcomes visitors beneath five roofs of varying height. A broad central passage lies between two clusters of posts spreading forward and backward from carved stone bases. The gateway belonged to both the guild precinct and Guandi worship. Merchants of the three provinces used the hall for fellowship and assistance, while its carved stories and auspicious motifs expressed prosperity, moral aspirations and memories of home.
facts: The gateway has three openings, six posts and five roofs. The posts form two groups of three, spreading in a “chicken-foot” plan. The central roof rises above the flanking roofs, with drum-shaped braces and tall stone bases framing the passage.
Merchants from Shanxi, Shaanxi and Gansu founded the guild hall in 1776. The gateway is a Qing structure; its timeline position around 1780 is approximate rather than a verified completion date.

The guild combined Guandi worship, fellow-provincials’ association and relief. Carved historical stories and auspicious imagery at the gateway show how merchant architecture also expressed ethical ideals and regional identity.
captions: Shanxi-Shaanxi-Gansu Guild Hall, Kaifeng · Front of the timber memorial archway
Qing · Qing dynasty

sx_xinjiang_longxing.name: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County
sx_xinjiang_longxing.era: Qing · Qianlong restoration with added stories
sx_xinjiang_longxing.yearNote: This year is the date of the Qing restoration that added stories, producing the surviving thirteen-story exterior; neither the temple's Tang history nor early remains inside the pagoda are equated directly with the date of the exterior.
sx_xinjiang_longxing.lede: The Longxing Pagoda on the high ground north of the old Jiangzhou city is octagonal and thirteen storeys, over 42 m high, the highest point in the town. The pagoda originally had eight storeys; it collapsed in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong), cased in grey brick and raised to thirteen storeys, and the flat corbelled brick eaves and taper seen today were fixed then. The temple was founded in the early Tang as the Biluo Daoist abbey and renamed Longxing Temple in 670 (1st year of Xianheng); early remains inside the pagoda do not date its exterior. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: an octagonal brick pagoda of pavilion type, built of grey brick, thirteen storeys tapering upward, each storey divided by corbelled brick eaves, with brick-carved bracket sets under the first-storey eaves; its height is given as 42.4 m by one source and 43.7 m by another, and each storey carries a plaque, from 'one column holding up heaven' to 'ten continents and three isles'.

Dating: originally eight storeys, the pagoda fell in 1777 (42nd year of Qianlong, Qing) and was rebuilt in 1784 (49th year of Qianlong) at thirteen storeys; another account has it cased and heightened during the 1777 repair. Repaired in 1941, with a Record of Repairing the Longxing Temple of Xinjiang. The whole temple became a national key protected site in 2006.

Curiosity: the county gazetteer and steles record 'smoke rising' from the top of the pagoda on several occasions, in 1875 (1st year of Guangxu), 1937, 1971, 1976 and 1993, the 1971 episode lasting over ten days, its cause unexplained; the temple also holds a Yuan main hall and the Tang Biluo Stele, not in the plate.
captions: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County · Longxing Pagoda
Qing Qianlong restoration · Octagonal, thirteen stories

protection.scope: Longxing Temple, Xinjiang County · Longxing Pagoda · Jiangzhou city

hn_guanlin.name: Guanlin, Luoyang
hn_guanlin.yearNote: The plate takes the Qianqiujian Stage Tower and is dated by its construction in 1791; the history of the Guanlin hall complex from the Wanli reign of the Ming is not used for the coloring of this stage tower.
hn_guanlin.lede: Qianqiu Jian Theatre stands on a raised stage before Guanlin’s main gate, opening toward the square and temple. A hip-and-gable roof over the front stage joins a flush-gabled roof behind; together they resemble a double-eaved pavilion, although the two functional parts remain distinct. Built later than the Ming development of the main halls, the theatre shows how ritual precincts acquired new facilities as performance and Guandi worship became part of public life.
facts: The theatre has a projecting-front plan, joining a hip-and-gable stage roof to a flush-gabled backstage roof. Its raised platform faces Guanlin’s gate across a square used for performance and viewing.

Qianqiu Jian Theatre was built in 1791, the fifty-sixth year of the Qing Qianlong era. Guanlin’s hall complex has a separate Ming Wanli-period expansion history, which should not be used to date this theatre.

At the front of Guanlin’s axis, the theatre begins a sequence of gates, halls and a rear tomb with different functions. Performances offered to the deity extended temple worship into public gatherings and cultural activity.
captions: Guanlin, Luoyang · Front of the Qianqiujian Stage Tower
56th year of Qianlong, Qing · Hip-and-gable front combined with flush-gable rear

protection.scope: Guanlin, Luoyang · Qianqiu Stage Tower

hn_shedian.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Shedian
hn_shedian.yearNote: 1800 is an approximate sorting point for the Qing construction phase to which the Xuanjian Tower belongs. Officially reproduced material contains the conversion error “1st year of Jiaqing = 1786,” so that figure is not adopted as a precise completion year; 1756–1892 is the construction span of the whole guild hall complex.
hn_shedian.place: Henan · Nanyang · Shedian Town, Sheqi County
hn_shedian.lede: Xuanjian Theatre at Shedian’s Shanxi–Shaanxi Guild Hall rises beneath a central triple-eaved roof flanked by smaller towers. Wood and stone carving surround the stage. In a town where waterborne and overland trade met, merchants required Guandi worship, fellowship and ritual theatre. Built during an early phase of the repeatedly enlarged complex, the theatre turned merchant wealth into a shared cultural space, preserving the scale of Qing guild life.
facts: The theatre’s triple-eaved hip-and-gable roof joins symmetrical side towers. A raised stage and open performance area are enriched by carved beams and stone balustrades whose subjects relate to theatre.

The guild complex was built in phases between 1756 and 1892, with Xuanjian Theatre belonging to an early phase. Around 1800 is only a timeline position; available sources do not establish a separate completion year reliably.

Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants financed a complex combining a Guandi shrine with commercial fellowship. Historical and theatrical carving brought worship, entertainment and Confucian aspirations into their meeting place.
captions: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Shedian · Front of the Xuanjian Tower stage
Qing Jiaqing to Daoguang period · Triple-eaved pavilion

protection.scope: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Shedian · Xuanjian Tower · Merchant-guild opera stage

hb_jingjue.name: Jingjue Temple
hb_jingjue.sub: Xiangfu Palace and its projecting round-ridge front annex
hb_jingjue.yearNote: The provincial cultural heritage bureau identifies the surviving temple buildings as Qing; 1800 is only an approximate Qing sorting value. No precise construction year has been found for the Xiangfu Palace itself, and the tradition of a Tang founding is not used to date the present structure.
hb_jingjue.lede: Xiangfu Hall’s projecting rounded-roof porch extends a lower roof into the courtyard. Stone columns and timber framing join unequal roof heights, creating depth. Jingjue Temple’s surviving buildings chiefly belong to Qing repairs; the principal hall uses a suspended-beam and hanging-post arrangement. It differs from the double-eaved Mahavira Hall behind, rewarding close attention to roof connections rather than founding legends.
facts: Xiangfu Hall has a timber hip-and-gable roof and projecting rounded-roof porch. Columns connect porch and hall; the lower front roof creates depth and must not be confused with the rear double-eaved Mahavira Hall.

The provincial authority assigns the surviving temple to the Qing and records repeated repairs. No exact construction year for Xiangfu Hall is established; the temple’s early history is distinguished from the present frame.

Suspended beams and hanging posts organise the hall’s support, while brick, stone and wood carving display different crafts. The porch-to-hall junction offers a concrete way to study local adjustments of space and structure.
captions: Jingjue Temple, Yutian · Xiangfu Palace
Front of the main hall and its projecting round-ridge front annex

gs_fuxi.name: Fuxi Temple, Tianshui
gs_fuxi.era: Enlarged in the 10th year of Jiaqing, Qing
gs_fuxi.yearNote: The Ceremonial Gate was first built in 1523 and changed from three bays to five during the 1805 restoration; the drawing shows the surviving five-bay gate, dated by its 1805 form, and does not take the founding of the whole temple in 1483–1484 as the date of this gate. Repairs to the roofs and eaves, including those of the Ceremonial Gate, were completed in early 2026.
gs_fuxi.lede: Red columns carry a five-bay ritual gate, whose central passage links the forecourt with the main ceremonial courtyard. At Tianshui’s Fuxi Temple, successive gates and halls unfold along an axis, giving worship a measured pace. Originally a three-bay Ming gate, it was widened to five bays in the Qing period; its present breadth preserves that change.
facts: The ritual gate stands beyond the main gate and before Xiantian Hall, with a central passage in its five-bay front. A single roof and red columns extend sideways. This second courtyard gateway is smaller in scale than the principal ritual halls.

The gate was founded in 1523 and widened from three bays to five during repairs begun in 1805. Its broad present form reflects that later change, and the temple’s earlier Chenghua-period foundation does not directly date this gate.

Successive gates and courtyards organise Fuxi worship as a gradual progression, and this gate marks a significant transition. Its enlargement shows how ritual architecture could adapt to use over time.
captions: Ceremonial Gate, Fuxi Temple · Line drawing
Qing · 1805

protection.scope: Ceremonial Gate, Fuxi Temple

hb_dzgongyuan.name: Dingzhou Examination Hall
hb_dzgongyuan.sub: Complete front elevation of the Kui Pavilion and examination cells
hb_dzgongyuan.yearNote: The intention is to use the Qing enlarged form shown by the surviving Kui Pavilion and examination cells; the precise founding year of the individual building needs further verification at the photograph stage.
hb_dzgongyuan.lede: The Kuige and examination cells form a stepped mountain-like frontage, highest at the centre. They are not seven separate towers: a front pavilion and the gable ends of the examination building combine, with long windows lighting the interior. Founded under Qianlong and expanded under Daoguang, Dingzhou’s examination compound preserves rooms for candidates, officials and ritual as well as the history of the examination system.
facts: Kuige adjoins the south side of the examination building, following its gable profile through seven roof groups descending from the centre. Long lattice windows admit light; the silhouette is not a row of seven independent towers.

The compound was founded in 1738 and repaired and enlarged in 1834. Its present scale chiefly reflects the later expansion; these complex-wide dates do not establish the same building year for every individual structure.

Kuige honoured Kuixing, the cells accommodated examinations, the northern hall handled submitted and sealed scripts, and the rear building served examiners. Distinct functions translate scholarly ambition, ritual and administration into connected rooms and courts.
captions: Kui Pavilion and examination cells
Front composition of the central Kui Pavilion and the seven groups of roofs of the flanking cells
