sx_jishan_jiwang.name: Jiwang Temple, Jishan
sx_jishan_jiwang.sub: Offering Hall · Bell and drum towers
sx_jishan_jiwang.yearNote: The Offering Hall, bell and drum towers and Houji Tower drawn here are Qing rebuildings; the Yuan-dynasty Jiangyuan Hall in the temple is not drawn.
sx_jishan_jiwang.place: Shanxi · Jishan · West Street of the county town
sx_jishan_jiwang.lede: The sparrow braces under the front eaves of the offering hall of the Jiwang Temple carry no dragons or phoenixes; they show Hou Ji teaching the people to farm, spring sowing and the grain harvest. On either wing of this small three-bay hall stands a bell or drum tower, four metres square under a double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, and behind rises the thirty-metre Hou Ji Tower, three glazed roofs crowded together. The temple was founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), burned in the Daoguang reign of the Qing, and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by the magistrate Li Jingchun; all three buildings drawn belong to that rebuilding. The plate shows the offering hall and the bell and drum towers, with only the upper eaves of the Hou Ji Tower visible.
facts: Offering hall: three bays and 14 m wide, 10 m deep, roofed in coloured glazed tile, the roof described as overhanging-gable by one source and flush-gable by another; the sparrow braces under front and rear eaves are wood reliefs of farming, Hou Ji teaching agriculture in the central bay, spring ploughing in the east bay and harvest in the west bay. The bell and drum towers are 4 m square under double-eaved cross-shaped hip-and-gable roofs.

Dating: founded in 1345 (5th year of Zhizheng, Yuan), the temple burned down in the 10th year of Daoguang (some say the 16th) and was rebuilt in 1843 (23rd year of Daoguang) by subscription led by magistrate Li Jingchun; his seven-character poem on its completion is carved in the west gable wall, and the eight views of Jishan in the east. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Comparison: the temple is known for the 'three marvels' of glaze, wood carving and stone carving; the gallery of the Hou Ji Tower has twenty carved stone eave columns and fifty-two carved stone balustrade panels. The Jiangyuan Hall inside is a Yuan structure and the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers the temple as 'Yuan to Qing', but everything drawn is Qing.
captions: Jiwang Temple, Jishan · Offering Hall and bell and drum towers
Rebuilt under Daoguang, Qing · Upper eaves of the Houji Tower

protection.scope: Jiwang Temple, Jishan · Offering Hall · Bell and drum towers

xitai.name: Ancient Opera Stages of Ninghai
xitai.sub: Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Chongxing Temple · City God Temple
xitai.era: Qing to Republic · Aohu stage, 4th year of Xianfeng
xitai.lede: Ninghai County has 125 surviving old opera stages, ten of them listed as national protected sites, all built inside ancestral halls and temples between the Qing and the Republic. A stage one bay square is raised half a person's height into the air, the upturned corners of its hip-and-gable roof curling like ox horns, and inside a caisson ceiling spirals upward.
facts: Most stages are one bay wide, with the stage floor raised off the ground and a carved balustrade around the stage front; the column heads support the eaves with carved brackets (niutui, “ox legs”) rather than bracket sets.

Caisson ceilings are the specialty of Ninghai's stages: the stage of the Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu and its linking corridor have three caisson ceilings in a row, one of only three surviving “three linked caisson ceilings” in Zhejiang.

The Hu Clan Ancestral Hall in Aohu was built in the 4th year of Xianfeng in the Qing (1854); the stage connects with viewing galleries on either side, from whose upper floors the audience watched performances.
captions: Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Interior of the stage and linking corridor
Column frame · Ox-leg brackets · Caisson ceiling

protection.scope: Ancient Opera Stages of Ninghai · Hu Clan Ancestral Hall, Aohu · Chongxing Temple · City God Temple

qiufeng.name: Houtu Shrine, Wanrong
qiufeng.era: Qing · Rebuilt in the 9th year of Tongzhi
qiufeng.place: Shanxi · Wanrong · Ronghe Town · Miaoqian Village
qiufeng.lede: Emperor Wu of Han sacrificed to Houtu at Fenyin and, boating on the Fen, wrote the Song of the Autumn Wind; two thousand years later this tower still bears its name. It stands at the northern end of the Houtu Shrine on a brick-and-stone platform sixteen metres square, three storeys and over thirty-two metres high, galleried on all four sides under a cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof; the platform is pierced east-west like a street gate, with 'Gazing at Lu' over the east arch and 'Looking to Qin' over the west. As the Yellow River repeatedly shifted, the shrine was moved east again and again; the present site was rebuilt in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi, Qing) by magistrate Dai Ruzhen, and the tower was then moved to the rear of the temple. The plate shows the front of Qiufeng Lou.
facts: Form: platform 16 m square, tower of three storeys, 32.6 m high (33 m by another account), five bays wide and deep, cross-shaped hip-and-gable roof, galleries on each storey, a warrior figure on each upturned corner; inside the south gate of the platform a small niche is inscribed 'Sweeping-the-ground Altar', and the storeys hold, from bottom to top, modern, Qing and Yuan carvings of the Song of the Autumn Wind.

History: in the Yuan an Autumn Wind Pavilion behind the temple held the stele of the song carved in 1271 (8th year of Zhiyuan); in the Longqing reign of the Ming the pavilion was lost to the Fen and a tower built before the temple; in 1662 (1st year of Kangxi, Qing) the river breached and the tower was lost, and it was rebuilt elsewhere the next year; destroyed again in 1862 (1st year of Tongzhi) and moved to the present site in 1870 (9th year of Tongzhi). After the Guangxu-era Ronghe County Gazetteer.

Background: the Houtu Shrine at Fenyin was the imperial temple for sacrifice to the earth established by Emperor Wu of Han, and emperors of Han, Tang and Song sacrificed here in person; a temple-plan stele of 1137 (15th year of Tianhui, Jin) depicts the layout after the Northern Song enlargement. Apart from the Yuan gate, most of today's shrine is late Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 1996.
captions: Houtu Shrine · Front of Qiufeng Tower
Three-story tower · Qing rebuilding

protection.scope: Houtu Shrine, Wanrong · Qiufeng Tower

tj_shijia.name: Shi Family Compound, Yangliuqing, Tianjin
tj_shijia.era: Large-scale construction in the early Guangxu reign · Later repairs
tj_shijia.yearNote: 1875 is the starting point of the large-scale construction of the Shi family residence; the date of manufacture of the inner-courtyard gate drawn here as a separate element is unconfirmed, and this sorting point is not called the gate's exact completion year.
tj_shijia.lede: Gray-brick gateways recede one behind another along the axis of the nested courtyards, with dark red timber frames and pale drum-shaped stones finishing the entrance. The inner-courtyard gate and the receding gateway courtyards are chosen here; the stone lions and eave ornaments of another, outer gateway are not pieced into the same plate.
facts: The surviving Shi Family Compound is the Zunmei Tang residence; its large-scale construction began early in the Guangxu reign of the Qing (1875), and later conservation repairs have their own dates.

The plate is based on photographs of the inner-courtyard gate, keeping the low tiled roof, gray-brick gate piers, short walls on either side, drum-shaped stones and the gates of the nested courtyards behind.

Gray brick and gray tile, near-black reddish-brown door frames, dark red inset panels and a few ocher-gold edge lines are distinguished as they appear today; no bird's-eye view of the whole residence is drawn, and the outer gateway is not spliced in.
captions: Shi Family Compound · Inner-courtyard gate and receding gateway courtyards
Late Qing · 1875 as the start of large-scale construction of the residence

hu_yueyang.name: Yueyang Tower
hu_yueyang.era: Rebuilt in the 6th year of Guangxu, Qing
hu_yueyang.yearNote: Dated by the surviving tower form produced by the rebuilding of the 6th year of Guangxu in the Qing (1880); the 1984 dismantling and major repair continued the old form, and neither the Three Kingdoms legend of a troop-review tower nor the year of the Northern Song restoration is used as the date of this drawing.
hu_yueyang.place: Hunan · Yueyang · Shore of Dongting Lake
hu_yueyang.lede: Three storeys send their eaves outward, while the helmet-shaped upper roof curves inward, giving Yueyang Tower an outline both lively and steady. On Dongting Lake, timber columns and jointed beams carry the roofs, and galleries open the climbing experience toward the water. Its present form arose from the 1880 reconstruction and was retained in modern conservation; literary fame and the surviving building’s date need separate readings.
facts: The three-storey timber structure joins projecting eaves to a helmet-shaped roof. Beams and columns form a mortise-and-tenon framework. Open galleries, railings and raised corners maintain accessible, airy spaces beneath the substantial roofs.

The current form derives from the 1880 reconstruction. Later conservation included complete dismantling and reassembly, finished in 1984 with the earlier design retained. Older tower history and literary memories do not date every surviving timber component.

Views over the lake and the reading of Fan Zhongyan’s Account of Yueyang Tower bring landscape and literature together. The Qing design preserves that experience of ascent, but the essay’s Northern Song date cannot date the present structure.
captions: Three-story main tower of Yueyang Tower · Line drawing
Qing · 1880

protection.scope: Three-story main tower of Yueyang Tower

hu_nanyue.name: Nanyue Grand Temple
hu_nanyue.era: Rebuilt in the Guangxu reign, Qing
hu_nanyue.yearNote: 1882 is taken as the rebuilding date of the surviving main structures of the Nanyue Grand Temple; the Shengdi Hall later underwent changes such as repairs and column replacement. The drawing shows the present state as photographed and does not take the Tang founding of the whole temple as the date of this hall.
hu_nanyue.lede: Seven bays extend beneath the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of Nanyue Temple’s Shengdi Hall, where a stone-columned gallery opens the deep shade beneath the eaves. The palatial axis reaches a principal ritual space here, with timber, stone and carving shaping an orderly front. Its present principal fabric is dated to the Guangxu reconstruction, with later repairs altering details; the long history of mountain worship does not date every component.
facts: The hall is seven bays wide, with a stone-columned outer gallery beneath a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Roof, brackets and lower eaves extend in successive lines, while columns divide the broad front into clear bays and carving enriches the details.

The temple’s surviving principal buildings took shape after reconstruction in 1882, and the hall underwent subsequent repairs. Earlier temple history, Qing reconstruction and later conservation are distinct phases; today’s appearance cannot be described as an original Tang building.

This principal ritual hall gathers worship at the foot of the mountain before ascent. The axial palatial buildings stand beside the temple’s Buddhist and Daoist precincts, showing a setting where state mountain rites and local religious practice have long intersected.
captions: Shengdi Hall, Nanyue Grand Temple · Line drawing
Qing · 1882 · Later repairs

protection.scope: Shengdi Hall, Nanyue Grand Temple

gd_chen.name: Chen Clan Academy, Guangzhou
gd_chen.sub: Front gate · Lingnan ceramic sculpture and stone carving
gd_chen.yearNote: 1893 is the completion year of the Chen Clan Academy; the plate takes the present state of the central front gate, and components repaired later are not all regarded as original work of that year.
gd_chen.lede: The central entrance of the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall brings grey brick, stone columns and ceramic ridge figures into a richly layered facade beneath gabled roofs. Chen’s Academy was funded by Chen lineage groups across Guangdong, serving clan affairs and accommodating members visiting Guangzhou for examinations and other business. Completed in the late nineteenth century and repeatedly maintained, its entrance introduces both Lingnan craft and lineage organization.
facts: The central entrance has roofs ending at the gable walls, with stone columns and beams meeting grey brickwork. Ceramic ridge figures, brick reliefs and woodcarving concentrate different materials at the doorway in layers that invite close viewing.

Planning began in 1888. An inscribed couplet records completion of the principal complex in 1893, while some ridge inscriptions document work in the following year. The entrance and its ornament have since been repaired and are not all unchanged originals from one year.

Chen lineage groups jointly built the academy to accommodate members visiting the provincial capital for examinations, appointments and business. Its entrance concentrates regional carving and modelling while expressing a network of support across local clan communities.
captions: Facade of the central front gate, Chen Clan Academy · Line drawing
Qing · 1893

tj_guangdonghuiguan.name: Guangdong Guild Hall, Tianjin
tj_guangdonghuiguan.sub: Stage · Detail of the chicken-cage caisson ceiling
tj_guangdonghuiguan.era: Completed in the 33rd year of Guangxu
tj_guangdonghuiguan.lede: The Guangdong Guildhall’s stage projects towards its audience. Above it, a chicken-coop-shaped coffered ceiling spirals from a square frame towards a circular centre, combining carving and bracket work overhead. Two tiers of seating allow performances to be watched from three sides. Completed in 1907, the hall served Guangdong residents in Tianjin for gatherings and theatre, later becoming a theatre museum. Its stage connects migrant community life with the city’s theatrical memory.
facts: The projecting stage faces the audience on three sides without freestanding columns obstructing the front. Its square-framed, circular coffered ceiling uses spiralling interlocked brackets; two seating tiers surround the performance space.

The guildhall was completed in 1907, the thirty-third Guangxu year of Qing. After restoration it became a theatre museum in 1986. Initial construction, conservation and museum use represent separate phases.

The narrowing ceiling joins ornamental carpentry with sound projection, while the projecting stage brings performers close to spectators. This Guangdong community hall preserves the meeting of travelling merchants, theatre and Tianjin’s urban culture.
captions: Guangdong Guild Hall · Detail of the stage and chicken-cage caisson ceiling
Late Qing · Completed 1907

jl_wenmiao.name: Dacheng Hall of the Jilin Confucian Temple
jl_wenmiao.era: Main buildings completed in the 1st year of Xuantong
jl_wenmiao.yearNote: 1909 is the completion year of the surviving main buildings; 1736 is the founding of the Confucian temple, and the repairs of the 1920s and modern times are recorded separately, not merged into one year.
jl_wenmiao.lede: Eleven bays spread beneath yellow glazed tiles and double eaves, placing Dacheng Hall at the centre of Jilin’s Confucian ceremonial axis. It belongs to the main buildings completed at the relocated temple in 1909, not the original foundation of 1736. Republican and modern repairs add further layers to this late Qing educational landmark.
facts: The hall is eleven bays wide excluding the side corridors, with twelve front columns and a double-eaved yellow-tiled roof. A balustraded terrace with a central cloud-and-dragon carving emphasises the ceremonial axis.

The temple was founded in 1736, relocated for building in 1907 and completed its main halls in 1909. Repairs followed from 1920; foundation, surviving principal construction and later repairs are distinct stages.

The hall occupies the centre of a three-courtyard complex and serves Confucius worship. Its continuous columns and raised terrace direct visitors inward, expressing ritual hierarchy and local educational history.
captions: Jilin Confucian Temple · Eleven-bay Dacheng Hall
Completed 1909 in the late Qing · Later repairs recorded separately

gz_jiaxiu.name: Jiaxiu Tower, Guiyang
gz_jiaxiu.sub: Nanming River · Three stories, three eaves
gz_jiaxiu.era: Rebuilt in the 1st year of Xuantong · Later repairs
gz_jiaxiu.yearNote: The present appearance follows the 1909 restoration design and later repairs such as those of 1981; the Ming founding date does not replace the date of the surviving tower's form.
gz_jiaxiu.lede: Jiaxiu Pavilion stands on a rocky base in the Nanming River, its three storeys and three tiers of eaves rising to a pyramidal roof with four corners. Fuyu Bridge connects it to the banks, bringing pavilion, bridge and water into one urban landscape. Founded in the Ming period, it suffered repeated destruction and rebuilding. Its present form follows the 1909 reconstruction and a further twentieth-century restoration, preserving an older arrangement while recording Guiyang’s efforts to sustain its landmark.
facts: The three-storey pavilion has three tiers of eaves and a four-cornered pyramidal roof. Red lattice windows, stone eaves-supporting columns and balustrades stand above Aoji Rock; Fuyu Bridge connects the pavilion to pedestrian space on both banks.

Founded in the Ming Wanli period, Jiaxiu Pavilion was repeatedly damaged and repaired. Its present appearance follows the 1909 rebuilding and a further restoration in 1981, so all its materials should not be treated as Ming originals.

The name Jiaxiu expresses hopes for distinction in examinations and the emergence of talent. Long celebrated in verse, its combination of pavilion, river and bridge gives Guiyang’s educational ideals a tangible place in the city.
captions: Surviving Jiaxiu Tower, Guiyang · Line drawing · Pending user review
Qing · 1909

gx_chengyang.name: Chengyang Yongji Bridge
gx_chengyang.sub: Dong wind-and-rain bridge · Timber gallery with five pavilions
gx_chengyang.yearNote: Following volume 7 of Sanjiang Historical and Literary Materials, completion is taken as 1924; the proposal to build it in 1911 or the start of work in 1912 does not equal the completion year. The bridge has been repaired in later times, and the plate draws the complete bridge with all five pavilions as photographed today.
gx_chengyang.lede: Chengyang Yongji Bridge links five pavilions with a continuous timber corridor above stone piers and abutments. Tiered pavilion roofs turn the river crossing into an undulating line of buildings. Railings and benches provide places to pause, joining transport with shelter and social use. Local historical records give completion in 1924, separately from earlier proposals and construction. Later repairs continue a carpentry tradition rooted in the shared life of Dong villages.
facts: Stone supports carry a timber deck and five pavilions connected by a tiled corridor. Railings and benches run along both sides. Tiered roofs rise above the passage, with piers, framing and roofing forming the complete river crossing.

Sanjiang Historical Materials, volume seven, records a proposal in 1911 and completion in 1924; another account gives construction from 1912. Proposal, building and completion are separate stages, followed by later repairs.

The corridor shelters travellers and benches turn a route into a place for rest and interaction. Timber joints connect deck and pavilions, expressing Dong traditions that join daily travel, community life and architectural form.
captions: Whole Chengyang Yongji Bridge and its five pavilions · Line drawing
Republic of China · Completed 1924

protection.scope: Whole Chengyang Yongji Bridge and its five pavilions

gd_ruishi.name: Ruishi Lou, Kaiping
gd_ruishi.sub: Diaolou of Jinjiangli · Blend of Chinese and Western styles
gd_ruishi.yearNote: 1925 is taken as the completion year of Ruishi Lou, not the date of all the Kaiping diaolou; the national protected site listing falls under “Kaiping Diaolou,” and World Heritage inscription belongs to a separate system.
gd_ruishi.lede: Ruishi Lou rises above Jinjiangli village as a rectangular reinforced-concrete tower, topped by colonnades, rounded lookout turrets and ornamental pediments. Built between 1923 and 1925, it combined residence and defence while bringing materials supplied through Hong Kong and Western architectural tastes into the village. Traditional auspicious motifs in its plaster decoration reveal how emigrant-linked communities accommodated several architectural languages.
facts: The nine-level reinforced-concrete diaolou has colonnades and lookout turrets above a regular body, with Western-style window mouldings and pediments. Its simple lower volume and complex crown provide both domestic space and positions for observation and defence.

Local government sources describe construction in 1923–1925, commissioned by Huang Bixiu after prospering in Hong Kong and carried out by nearby craftsmen. Completion and commencement must be distinguished; these dates do not apply to other diaolou.

Building materials came through Hong Kong, while plaster decoration included traditional motifs of blessing, rank, joy and longevity. The tower brings together defence, overseas commerce and local craft, offering a concrete way to understand Kaiping’s emigrant-linked society.
captions: Complete tower of Ruishi Lou, Jinjiangli, Kaiping · Line drawing
Republic of China · 1925

protection.scope: Complete tower of Ruishi Lou, Jinjiangli, Kaiping

hlj_sofia.name: Saint Sophia Cathedral, Harbin
hlj_sofia.yearNote: The surviving brick church was begun in 1923 and completed in 1932; the early wooden church of 1907 is not used as the date of the plate's subject.
hlj_sofia.lede: A Latin-cross church of red brick: at the crossing four brick piers carry a drum 10 m across and a huge onion dome, above the main door rises a tent-roofed bell tower, and the whole stands 53.35 m to the top of the cross, the largest Orthodox church in the Far East. A wooden garrison church was first built here in 1907 and cased in brick in 1912; the brick building seen today was begun in September 1923 to the design of the Russian architect Oskolkov, modelled on the Epiphany Church in St Petersburg, and completed in November 1932. The plate shows the 1932 building and omits the modern ticket annex.
facts: Form: fair-faced red brick with a sheet-iron roof painted green; the plan is a Latin cross about 28 m north to south and 42 m east to west, with a floor area of 721 square metres holding 1,500 people. At the crossing four brick piers carry a drum 10 m in outer diameter and the onion dome; tent-roofed spires stand over the main door, the two transepts and the rear door, the central dome highest and the bell tower next.

Dating: built in March 1907 as a timber garrison church for the Russian 4th East Siberian Infantry Division and enlarged in August that year at the expense of the tea merchant Chistyakov; cased in brick in 1912 to become a brick-and-timber building; the cornerstone of the rebuilding was laid on 27 September 1923, the architect Oskolkov taking Kosyakov's Epiphany Church in St Petersburg as his model, and the work was completed on 25 November 1932.

Significance: it unites the centralised dome of Byzantine building with the onion domes and tent roofs of Russian vernacular timber architecture, and the Japanese architectural historian Nishizawa Yasuhiko judged it comparable in scale and conception to St Basil's in Moscow. It was listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996 and became the Harbin Museum of Architecture and Art in 1997.
captions: Saint Sophia Cathedral · Surviving 1932 structure
Red-brick walls · Onion dome and bell tower

protection.scope: Saint Sophia Cathedral, Harbin · Surviving brick church of 1932

guanque.name: Stork Tower, Yongji
guanque.sub: On the bank of the Yellow River · Contemporary reconstruction
guanque.place: Shanxi · Yongji · West of the old city of Puzhou
guanque.lede: The famous tower of Wang Zhihuan's poem stands again today on the bank of the Yellow River west of the old city of Puzhou. The present tower was rebuilt and completed in 2002: a high platform raises four tiers of eaves, and tier upon tier of colonnades bring the poetry of climbing high to gaze afar back into reality.
facts: Surviving tower: reconstruction began in December 1997, and the tower was completed and opened on September 26, 2002; this drawing and the timeline both register it under 2002.
Tang-style tower: externally it has four tiers of eaves and three stories, is 73.9 m tall overall and faces north, with Tang-style painted decoration and spreading eaves.

History of the old tower: the original tower was first built in the Northern Zhou, survived through the Tang and Song, and was destroyed by war in the early Yuan; its founding date and the surviving reconstruction are recorded separately.
captions: Front of the Stork Tower · Four eaves, three stories
Tang-style form · Rebuilt 2002

horyuji.name: Hōryū-ji
horyuji.era: Asuka period · Second half of the 7th century
horyuji.lede: Two tiled roofs rise above a lower board-roofed mokoshi at Horyuji’s Main Hall, whose deep eaves convey the timber architecture of the Asuka period. Slightly swelling columns support cloud-shaped brackets, and geometric upper railings add delicate detail between substantial roofs. The surviving hall belongs to the late seventh-century rebuilding of the Western Precinct, distinct from the temple’s foundation; its pairing with the pagoda preserves clues to early Buddhist planning.
facts: The main structure is five bays wide and four deep, with two tiled hip-and-gable roofs and a surrounding board-roofed mokoshi. Curving cloud brackets, swelling round columns and the upper railings establish a detailed rhythm beneath the deep eaves.

The temple’s early foundation is placed around the beginning of the seventh century. Records describe a fire in 670, followed by rebuilding of the Western Precinct. The hall is attributed to the late seventh century; the 607 foundation date does not date its completion.

In the Western Precinct, the hall stands to the east and the five-storey pagoda to the west within enclosing corridors. Their arrangement and cloud-shaped members preserve evidence of early East Asian Buddhist architecture and its wider cultural exchanges.
captions: Hōryū-ji · Front of the Kondō
Asuka period · Two-tiered irimoya roof and mokoshi

toshodaiji.name: Tōshōdai-ji
toshodaiji.era: Nara period · Second half of the 8th century
toshodaiji.lede: Eight round columns carry the broad single-eaved roof of the Kondō of Tōshōdai-ji, and the open portico in front adds a quiet layer of transition between the courtyard and the inner chamber where the Buddha images stand. After Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded the temple, his disciples completed this Kondō in the second half of the 8th century.
facts: Jianzhen (Ganjin) founded Tōshōdai-ji in 759, while the surviving Kondō was built in the second half of the 8th century; the temple's official account links its construction to his disciple Nyohō.
The Kondō is seven bays across the front and four bays deep, with a yosemune (hipped) roof covered in hongawara tiles; the front bay is left open to form a colonnade.

Three-stepped bracket sets (mitesaki kumimono) beneath the eaves carry the deep overhang, and the shibi ridge-end ornaments at both ends of the ridge and the broad single eave together define its exterior.
captions: Tōshōdai-ji · Front of the Kondō
Nara period · Seven-bay yosemune roof

byodoin.name: Byōdō-in
byodoin.lede: Across the Aji Pond, the central hall and its two wing corridors spread like a bird with outstretched wings, and twin phoenixes face each other on the ridge. The Amida Hall built by Fujiwara no Yorimichi in 1053 sets the Heian-period vision of the Pure Land above the waters of Uji.
facts: Heian structure: the Phoenix Hall was built in 1053 by Fujiwara no Yorimichi; the surviving central hall and wing corridors reflect the layout of an Amida hall of the late Heian period.

Twin phoenixes and two wings: the left and right wing corridors enclose the central hall, and a pair of phoenixes stands on the ridge; the name Phoenix Hall gradually came into use in the Edo period, and the phoenixes now on the roof are replacements installed in 1968.

Worship across the pond: the building sits in the west facing east, and worshippers on the east bank of the Aji Pond face west to venerate the Buddha; garden and hall together express the image of the Western Pure Land.
captions: Byōdō-in · Front of the Phoenix Hall and its two wings
Heian period · 1053

todaiji.name: Tōdai-ji
todaiji.lede: With round columns rising straight to the heights and tier upon tier of tie beams passing through them, the Nandaimon shows the structural power of the Daibutsuyō style. Three passages run beneath the broad double eaves, and Niō guardian statues on either side protect the entrance to Tōdai-ji.
facts: The surviving Nandaimon was rebuilt under the direction of Chōgen; its ridgepole was raised in 1199, and it was completed in 1203 together with the Kongō Rikishi statues within the gate.
The gate has an irimoya (hip-and-gable) roof, five bays across the front with three central doorways and double eaves; it is an important surviving example of Daibutsuyō architecture.
The gate has 18 great round columns in all, with six columns across the front dividing it into five bays; according to the temple, the gate is 25.46 m tall above the platform.
captions: Tōdai-ji · Front of the Nandaimon
Kamakura period · Rebuilt 1199–1203

kiyomizu.name: Kiyomizu-dera
kiyomizu.lede: Look beneath the stage first: zelkova pillars some 12 m long, interlocked with horizontal ties and not a single nail, carry a nine-by-seven-bay hall out over the cliff of Mt Otowa. This is the Main Hall rebuilt in 1633 at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu after the fire of 1629; its hipped, cypress-bark roof sends out hip-and-gable wing corridors at both ends, with the stage spread in front. The Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō architecture; it was designated a National Treasure in 1952 and inscribed with the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.
facts: Form: a kakezukuri (stilted) hall nine bays by seven, single-storey under a hipped (yosemune) roof of cypress bark, with lean-to mokoshi on the east, west and north sides, a hip-and-gable wing corridor at each front corner and a stage of about 200 sq m between them. Including mokoshi and wings the plan measures roughly 36 m by 31 m.

History: tradition dates the founding to 778 and the precinct burned repeatedly. The present hall was rebuilt in 1633 (Kan'ei 10) at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu after the fire of 1629; it was listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure in 1952. A twelve-year restoration begun in 2008 replaced all the cypress floorboards of the stage.

Value: judged by the Agency for Cultural Affairs a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō architecture, with gently curved roof planes and details that keep a Momoyama flavour. The stage rests on long zelkova pillars joined by through-ties without nails, the front row about 12 m long; the main halls of Hase-dera and Ishiyama-dera, also Kannon pilgrimage temples, use the same kakezukuri construction.
captions: Kiyomizu-dera · Main hall and Kiyomizu stage
Near-frontal view from the south · Edo period, 10th year of Kan'ei (1633)

toji.name: Tō-ji
toji.lede: At 54.8 m this is the tallest surviving wooden pagoda in Japan. Since Kūkai vowed to build it in 826 the Tō-ji pagoda has burned four times from lightning or fire; the present one is the fifth, raised after the 1641 fire at the expense of Tokugawa Iemitsu under the master carpenter Nakai Masazumi and completed in the seventh month of 1644. All five storeys are three bays square under hongawara tiles, without railings; the bracket sets are three-stepped and there is not one decorative nosing — the Agency for Cultural Affairs calls it a masterpiece of early-Edo revivalist wayō in Kyoto, designated a National Treasure in 1952.
facts: Form: a five-storey pagoda three bays square, tiled with hongawara, 54.8 m tall on a cut-stone podium. Every storey is three bays to a side with no verandah or railing; the brackets are three-stepped with intermediate strut blocks, the central pillar runs down to the first storey, and the details omit nosings and other ornament — robust, pure wayō.

History: the pagoda is said to date from the Tenchō era (824–834) but was actually finished around the end of the ninth century, and was then destroyed four times by lightning or fire. The present tower was rebuilt after the fire of 1641, begun that twelfth month and completed in the seventh month of 1644; listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and designated a National Treasure in 1952.

Esoteric space: on the first storey the central pillar stands for Dainichi Nyorai, with the four Buddhas of the Diamond Realm and eight bodhisattvas placed around it and the Mandalas of the Two Realms and the Eight Shingon Patriarchs painted on walls and pillars; the images date from 1643–44. Tō-ji (Kyōō-gokoku-ji), to which the pagoda belongs, was inscribed among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.
captions: Tō-ji · Five-story pagoda
Near-frontal view · Edo period, 21st year of Kan'ei (1644)

sd_guangyue.name: Guangyue Tower
sd_guangyue.era: Completed in the 7th year of Hongwu, Ming
sd_guangyue.yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving Guangyue Tower; repairs over the centuries and its completion in the 7th year of Hongwu in the Ming (1374) are described separately.
sd_guangyue.place: Shandong · Liaocheng · Old city of Dongchang Prefecture
sd_guangyue.lede: Guangyue Tower combines a substantial terrace with a timber tower at the old city’s centre. Arched passages connect the streets below, four levels of eaves change as they rise, and a cross-ridged roof crowns the top. Completed in 1374, it has undergone repeated repairs while preserving features of the transition from Song and Yuan towers to Ming construction. The relationship between the heavy base and open galleries links urban movement with ascent.
facts: Form: four timber storeys with surrounding galleries and projecting eaves stand on a square masonry terrace beneath a cross-ridged roof. Semicircular arched openings connect streets through the base, with separate stairs organizing ascent.

Dating: the tower was completed in 1374, the seventh Hongwu year, and repaired repeatedly. The city gazetteer records surviving early principal components, but the present fabric also includes repairs; not every timber is an original Ming piece.

Significance: the terrace, galleries, eaves and internal structure carry Song and Yuan traditions into Ming building practice. At the meeting point of the city’s streets, its form accommodates the functions of drum signalling, lookout and ascent.
captions: Guangyue Tower · Whole tower and base · Line drawing
Four-story timber tower · 7th year of Hongwu, Ming (1374)

protection.scope: Guangyue Tower, Liaocheng, whole tower and base

sd_yantai_huiguan.name: Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai
sd_yantai_huiguan.era: Begun in the 10th year of Guangxu · Completed in the 32nd year
sd_yantai_huiguan.yearNote: Begun in 1884 and completed in 1906; the drawing shows the street-front exterior in 2023 photographs, which predate the 2025 repairs.
sd_yantai_huiguan.lede: The street front of the Fujian Guild Hall brings a southern architectural outline to Yantai: red walls, firebreak gables and swallowtail ridges join around carved entrances. Fujian shipping merchants funded this Tianhou sanctuary, using materials selected and worked around Quanzhou before shipment north. It was completed in 1906. The frontage reveals only one edge of the compound, yet connects Mazu worship, maritime trade and the movement of craftsmanship between regions.
facts: Form: walls, gates and roofs form a continuous street front, with firebreak gables, swallowtail ridges and layered stone and timber decoration. A stage and main hall lie within; the frontage does not reveal the entire courtyard plan.

Dating: Fujian shipping merchants financed construction from 1884 to completion in 1906, with later maintenance and repair. Completion dates the original building campaign, rather than proving every component and surface of the frontage has remained unchanged.

Significance: the guild hall worships Mazu. Much of its brick, tile, timber and stone was selected and worked near Quanzhou before shipment, bringing southern craft north. Its entrance decoration and roofs record merchant organization, belief and interregional construction.
captions: Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai · Street-front exterior · Line drawing
Southern Fujian guild hall · 32nd year of Guangxu, Qing (1906)

protection.scope: Street-front exterior of the Fujian Guild Hall, Yantai

sd_jiuding.name: Nine-Top Pagoda
sd_jiuding.yearNote: 750 is used only to place it approximately in the Tang on the timeline, not as an exact construction year; the surviving pagoda includes later repairs, and the date of the folk-culture park is not counted as the date of the ancient pagoda.
sd_jiuding.lede: Jiuding Pagoda takes its outline from nine towers above one chamber: eight small square towers ring an octagonal platform, with a taller one at the centre. Corbelled brick courses project outwards and then recede to form their support. Construction style and associated finds generally place the main tower in the Tang period, without a secure year. Its complete outline also reflects later repairs rather than an untouched Tang appearance.
facts: Form: the main body is a single-storey octagonal brick pagoda. Corbelled eaves project and recede into an octagonal platform, carrying eight three-tiered square towers around a taller central tower: the nine tops named by the pagoda.

Dating: architectural form, sculptural style and associated finds support a Tang attribution, but the exact construction year is unproven. Later repairs are part of the surviving fabric; an approximate timeline date cannot substitute for an inscription.

Significance: one body supports nine towers, dividing the usual central summit into a surrounding ring and a raised centre. Small towers combined with a single chamber demonstrate variation in Buddhist pagoda form and brick construction.
captions: Nine-Top Pagoda · Octagonal brick pagoda · Line drawing
Nine small pagodas · Tang pagoda

protection.scope: Whole Nine-Top Pagoda, Jinan

sd_hongjialou.name: Hongjialou Catholic Church
sd_hongjialou.sub: Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus · Front elevation
sd_hongjialou.era: Completed in the 31st year of Guangxu, Qing
sd_hongjialou.yearNote: The date corresponds to the surviving church completed in 1905, distinguishing it from the earlier old church at Hongjialou and from later repairs.
sd_hongjialou.lede: The front of Hongjialou Cathedral repeatedly draws the eye upwards. Twin spires frame a central rose window; pointed entrances and tall windows echo one another, while masonry buttresses anchor the outline. The present Cathedral of the Sacred Heart was completed in 1905, distinct from an earlier destroyed church and later repairs. European church forms and decoration became part of Jinan’s architectural landscape through this building.
facts: Form: twin spires frame a symmetrical front with a central rose window and three pointed entrances. Masonry walls and buttresses create vertical lines that reinforce the upward rhythm of its Gothic architecture.

Dating: the earlier church at Hongjialou was damaged in 1900; the rebuilt cathedral was completed in 1905. That date concerns the surviving cathedral, not its predecessor or subsequent repair campaigns.

Significance: twin towers, pointed arches and a rose window combine European ecclesiastical forms within Jinan. The facade serves both as an entrance and a religious landmark, recording encounters between local construction and architectural cultures from elsewhere.
captions: Hongjialou Catholic Church · Front elevation · Line drawing
Twin spires · 31st year of Guangxu, Qing (1905)

protection.scope: Front elevation of the Hongjialou Catholic Church

sd_qingdao_catholic.name: Qingdao Catholic Church
sd_qingdao_catholic.yearNote: Begun in 1932 and completed in 1934; the date corresponds to the surviving St. Michael's Church and does not borrow the Qing-era dates of nearby German buildings.
sd_qingdao_catholic.lede: St Michael’s western front is organized by two bell towers and a central rose window. Pale yellow walls and red-tiled spires frame layered openings and crosses. Construction began in 1932 and finished in 1934, placing it in a later phase of Qingdao’s religious architecture rather than the dates of nearby German colonial buildings. Its symmetrical twin towers also differ clearly from the hall and single bell tower of the Jiangsu Road Protestant church.
facts: Form: the church has a cross-shaped plan, with symmetrical bell towers and crosses above their spires on the western facade. A circular rose window stands above the entrances; red tiles and pale walls distinguish roof, tower and openings.

Dating: construction ran from 1932 to completion in 1934, during the Republican period. Its location beside a former German colonial quarter does not place this church in the same period as nearby late-Qing buildings.

Significance: twin towers and a central window-and-door axis turn the entrance into an urban landmark. European church forms create a distinctive port-city streetscape; comparison with Jiangsu Road shows different periods and compositions of modern churches.
captions: Qingdao Catholic Church · West elevation · Line drawing
Twin bell towers · Completed 1934

sd_qingdao_christ.name: Qingdao Protestant Church
sd_qingdao_christ.sub: Jiangsu Road · Main hall and bell tower
sd_qingdao_christ.yearNote: The date refers to the main hall and bell tower built in 1908–1910; the church is kept separate from the Qingdao Catholic Church, completed in 1934.
sd_qingdao_christ.lede: The Jiangsu Road church combines its main hall and bell tower asymmetrically. A clock face and green spire mark the higher tower, while a red-tiled roof slopes towards the lower hall. Rough granite frames windows and corners, giving the masonry a castle-like weight. Built from 1908 to 1910 during German occupation, this individual building is distinct in both date and composition from the twin-towered Catholic church on Zhejiang Road.
facts: Form: the hall stands beside one bell tower, whose facade uses rough granite and semicircular window frames beneath a large clock. Steep red-tiled roofs and a green spire belong to separate volumes, creating an uneven outline.

Dating: construction began in 1908 and finished in 1910. Subsequent repairs include restoration and reopening near the end of the twentieth century. The dates concern the hall and tower, separately from the other church completed in 1934.

Significance: rough stone, red-tiled slopes and a clock tower introduce German architectural forms into Qingdao. The asymmetrical relationship joins a place of worship with a visible urban timekeeping landmark.
captions: Qingdao Protestant Church · Main hall and bell tower · Line drawing
Asymmetrical facade · Completed 1910

sd_yanmiao.name: Yan Temple of Qufu
sd_yanmiao.era: Fusheng Hall rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming
sd_yanmiao.yearNote: The plate corresponds to the seven-bay Fusheng Hall as rebuilt in 1507, which continued to be repaired in the Ming and Qing and in 1934, 1978 and 2006; neither the date of the Yan Temple's relocation in the Yuan nor the 1509 construction date of the stele pavilion is used to date this hall.
sd_yanmiao.lede: Fusheng Hall’s seven-bay front and two tiers of green-tiled eaves express Yan Hui’s place in Confucian worship. Four deeply carved dragon columns contrast with the other octagonal stone columns, while a terrace and colonnade extend the ceremonial space. The present scale follows the rebuilding of 1507, with Ming, Qing and modern repairs. Expansion from the earlier five-bay hall shows how changing honours entered architectural dimensions and decoration.
facts: Form: the seven-bay hall has a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with green tiles, surrounding colonnades and a front terrace. Four columns bear deeply carved dragons; eighteen other octagonal columns have shallow dragon, phoenix and floral carvings.

Dating: rebuilding in 1507 enlarged the earlier five-bay hall to seven bays, followed by repeated Ming and Qing repairs. Campaigns in 1934, 1978 and from 2006 replaced some timbers. Its present fabric is not an untouched Ming original.

Significance: dedicated to Yan Hui, the hall’s name and rank express the honours accorded to him. Expansion and carved dragon columns provide evidence for the development of sage worship and temple organization, distinct from Confucius’s Dacheng Hall.
captions: Yan Temple of Qufu · Fusheng Hall · Line drawing
Seven bays, double-eaved · Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Zhengde, Ming (1507)

sd_chongjue.name: Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple
sd_chongjue.era: Seven stories built in the 4th year of Chongning, Song · Two stories added in the 9th year of Wanli, Ming
sd_chongjue.yearNote: 1105 refers to the seven-story cast-iron main body of the Song; two stories and the finial were added in 1581, so the nine stories standing today cannot all be labeled as Song construction. The plate shows only the pagoda body and the upper platform visible in the photograph.
sd_chongjue.lede: Chongjue Temple’s iron pagoda imitates timber architecture in its cast exterior: brackets, eaves and railings taper upwards, with Buddhist images and blind doors on the octagonal walls. A brick core lies inside; the pavilion-like tower has no access for ascent. Seven lower storeys originated in 1105, with two storeys and a finial added in 1581. Its nine-storey outline thus joins different materials and two periods.
facts: Form: the octagonal nine-storey pagoda has an iron shell around a brick core. Cast brackets, eaves and railings imitate timberwork; blind doors alternate with Buddhist images. There are no internal stairs despite the pavilion-like exterior.

Dating: casting began with seven storeys in 1105, the fourth Chongning year. Two storeys and a finial were added in 1581. Cast inscriptions and dated finds from the added levels support these separate phases; not all nine storeys are Song work.

Significance: cast components turn timber eaves, galleries and brackets into metal surfaces carrying Buddhist imagery. Song and Ming phases show a votive project completed across centuries, with components and inscriptions preserving its building history after repairs.
captions: Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple · Body and upper platform · Line drawing
Seven stories built in the Song · Two stories and finial added in the Ming

protection.scope: Body and upper platform of the Iron Pagoda of Chongjue Temple, Jining

sd_xiaotang_shrine.name: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang
sd_xiaotang_shrine.sub: Eastern Han stone chamber · Modern shelter excluded
sd_xiaotang_shrine.yearNote: The plate shows the Eastern Han stone shrine itself inside its shelter; “about the 1st century” is an archaeological dating, not an exact construction year.
sd_xiaotang_shrine.lede: Xiaotangshan’s stone shrine translates a Han house into stone. Large slabs form walls and a pitched roof; a central column divides the open front into two bays, with roof surfaces imitating tile courses. Images and later inscriptions remain on the building, preserving both construction and the people who visited it. It is generally attributed to the early Eastern Han, around the first century rather than a precise year. Its traditional association with Guo Ju is not a proven identification.
facts: Form: the shrine is two bays wide and one deep, with an open front and a central column and stone beam supporting the roof. Large slabs form walls and projecting gables; carved tile courses reproduce the outline of a Han house in stone.

Dating: architecture, imagery and inscriptions generally place it in the early Eastern Han, approximately the first century. A visitor’s inscription of 129 proves it existed by then. Later supporting columns record additional repair phases.

Significance: interior images depict processions, daily life and mythology, while later inscriptions document viewing and maintenance. The traditional Guo Ju story must be distinguished from material dating; the shrine’s name does not establish its owner.
captions: Stone Shrine of the Guo Family Tomb on Mount Xiaotang · Line drawing
About 1st century

fj_qingjing_gate.name: Qingjing Mosque, Quanzhou
fj_qingjing_gate.era: Founded in the 2nd year of Dazhong Xiangfu
fj_qingjing_gate.yearNote: 1009 is the founding year of Qingjing Mosque; the surviving gatehouse has gone through a restoration in the 3rd year of Zhida in the Yuan (1310) and later repairs. The plate shows its present state and does not claim that every stone is Song work.
fj_qingjing_gate.lede: Entering from Tumen Street means passing through three successively narrowing pointed arches: this is the only surviving stone mosque gatehouse in mainland China. The mosque was founded in 1009, the second year of Dazhong Xiangfu of the Northern Song, under the Arabic name Masjid al-Ashab, the Mosque of the Companions; two lines of Arabic inscription above the arch record that a Muslim merchant from Shiraz rebuilt it in 1310, and the diabase-and-granite gatehouse seen today is essentially what that rebuilding left. The plate shows the gatehouse and the stone wall attached to it; the prayer hall inside is not included.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is 12.3 m high overall and 6.6 m wide at the base, built of diabase and white granite; it consists of three tiers and four connected pointed-arch openings, the first two passages pointed-arched with half-dome vaults and the third domed, with supports under the arches reminiscent of Chinese sparrow braces. The roof is a platform for sighting the moon during Ramadan, and its brick portions were rebuilt in the 17th-18th centuries.

Inscriptions: the Arabic inscription above the arch records that the mosque was built in AH 400 (1009-1010) as the first mosque of the local community, and that some three hundred years later Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Qudsi of Shiraz restored and renewed it, raising a dome, widening the passage and rebuilding the gate, completed in AH 710 (1310-1311). An imperial edict stele of 1407 (fifth year of Yongle) is set into the north wall.

Significance: one of the oldest surviving mosques in China, its gatehouse in West Asian mosque form is physical evidence of the Persian and Arab Muslim merchant quarter of Song-Yuan Quanzhou; the Stele on Re-erecting the Qingjing Mosque written by Wu Jian in 1350 is among the earliest datable Chinese-language stelae of any mosque in China. In 2021 it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site as part of 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.
captions: Qingjing Mosque, Quanzhou · Line drawing
Founded 1009, restored 1310

protection.scope: Surviving stone entrance gatehouse and attached stone walls

fj_anping_bridge.name: Anping Bridge
fj_anping_bridge.era: Begun in the 8th year of Shaoxing · Completed about the 22nd year of Shaoxing
fj_anping_bridge.yearNote: Begun in 1138; the Quanzhou Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism records its completion in 1152, while other sources record that it was finished in 1151. The plate shows only one section of the surviving deck and does not let this detail stand for the full length.
fj_anping_bridge.lede: 'No bridge under heaven is longer than this one.' In 1138 Huang Hu of Anhai and the monk Zhiyuan each gave ten thousand strings of cash and the monk Zupai directed the building of a bridge across the bay; both died midway, and work stopped for more than a decade until the prefect Zhao Lingjin took office in 1151 and took it over, finishing the bridge the following year. About 2,255 m long and known locally as the Five-Li Bridge, it is the longest surviving sea-crossing beam bridge in stone in China. The plate shows only a stretch of deck and a few nearby piers, not the whole bridge in miniature.
facts: Form: a stone beam bridge running east-west, about 2,255 m long with a deck 2.9-4 m wide, paved with stone slabs and railed in granite; 360 masonry piers of three types, rectangular, single-pointed boat-shaped and double-pointed boat-shaped, chosen to suit the depth and current of each channel, with huge stone slabs 5-11 m long laid across the piers as the deck.

Technique: the pier foundations use the 'sleeping timber' method, with timber piles driven into the seabed, a layer of timbers laid across them, and the stone piers built on top, saving stone and labour compared with the dumped-rock raft foundations of Luoyang Bridge; around the Shuixin Pavilion at mid-bridge survive 16 stelae recording repairs, the earliest the Record of Repairing Anping Bridge of 1459.

Significance: Anping Bridge was the overland node between Quanzhou and the Zhangzhou and Guangzhou regions to the south, built jointly by officials, monks, merchants and townspeople; the Ruiguang Pagoda at the east end, the Shuixin Pavilion at mid-span and the Wanggao and Tingchao gate towers at the two ends still stand. In 2021 it was inscribed as a component of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.
captions: Anping Bridge · Line drawing
Begun 1138, completed 1152

protection.scope: Representative section of the surviving stone-slab deck and piers

bj_yunju_north.name: Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple, Fangshan
bj_yunju_north.era: Founded in the Liao · Repaired in the Ming
bj_yunju_north.yearNote: The North Pagoda was founded in the Liao; its exact construction year has not been verified, and it was later repaired in the Ming and other periods. The start of sutra carving at Yunju Temple in the Sui is not used here as the date of the North Pagoda.
bj_yunju_north.lede: Yunju Temple's North Pagoda is difficult to describe as a single pagoda type: a pavilion-like lower section supports a rounded, stupa-like middle and a bell-shaped top. It is also called the Arhat or Relic Pagoda. Founded in the Liao period and repaired during the Ming, it belongs to a different time from the temple's sutra-carving enterprise, which began under the Sui. The pagoda survived modern warfare, and Buddhist verses on its bricks connect architecture with scripture. Its composite form and Liao date should be read alongside, but distinctly from, the earlier history of the stone sutras.
facts: Outline: a pavilion-like lower body, drum-shaped middle section and bell-shaped upper part combine several profiles in one pagoda. Also known as the Arhat or Relic Pagoda, it has more pronounced changes in mass than a conventional pagoda with many closely spaced tiers of eaves.

Dating: the North Pagoda was founded during the Liao and repaired during the Ming; its exact foundation year is uncertain. Jingwan began Yunju Temple's sutra carving in the Sui, and the work continued through several dynasties. That earlier beginning does not date this Liao pagoda.

Survival: the temple suffered damage during modern warfare, while the North Pagoda survived. Buddhist verses carved on its bricks make the building itself a carrier of religious texts. Together with the temple's stone sutras, they preserve scripture in different materials.
captions: Pagodas and Stone Sutras of Yunju Temple, Fangshan · Line drawing
Founded in the Liao, repaired in the Ming
