xz_jokhang.name: Jokhang Temple
xz_jokhang.sub: Present main facade · Buildings of several phases
xz_jokhang.yearNote: 647 is the traditional record of the temple's founding; the plate shows the surviving main facade, including expansions and repairs from many periods, and does not treat the whole golden roof and outer walls as original 7th-century fabric.
xz_jokhang.lede: Jokhang’s frontage opens toward Barkhor, its white walls, dark bands and golden roofs marking the centre of old Lhasa. Founded in the seventh-century Tibetan kingdom, the temple reached its present form through successive enlargements and repairs. The visible front is not an untouched survival of every founding component. Continuing worship and circumambulation give it further significance: building and streets together sustain the old city’s religious and social life.
facts: The main shrine faces west, with subsidiary halls organized around the central Buddha sanctuary. Walls, eaves and golden roofs build vertical layers; white surfaces and dark bands define the temple’s monumental silhouette.

Official accounts use 647 for the temple’s seventh-century foundation. Subsequent extensions and repairs created a frontage with several historical layers, whose components cannot all be treated as seventh-century originals.

The temple is revered across Tibetan Buddhist schools. The outer Barkhor circumambulation route connects with the old city’s streets, making Jokhang a centre for understanding Lhasa’s urban life as well as a place of worship.
captions: Jokhang Temple · Line drawing
Founded 647; present form of several phases

protection.scope: Surviving main facade (buildings of several phases)

hb_shanhaiguan.name: Zhendong Tower of Shanhaiguan
hb_shanhaiguan.sub: East Gate arrow tower · Gate platform and short wall sections
hb_shanhaiguan.era: Tower built in the Ming · Modern repairs
hb_shanhaiguan.yearNote: Shanhai Garrison was established in 1381, and the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau records that the pass fortress was built the following year. This plate shows the surviving Zhendong Tower and its gate platform; 1400 is only an approximate placement within the Ming, not the exact construction year of the timber tower. Repeated modern repairs are described separately.
hb_shanhaiguan.lede: Zhendong Tower stands on the eastern gate platform: the arch carries traffic and the two-storey arrow tower watches the approach. Its flanking walls and famous First Pass plaque make a defensive threshold into an urban symbol. The pass was established in the early Ming, but the complete present silhouette includes modern conservation. Both strategic setting and repeated repair are essential to understanding it.
facts: The eastern arrow tower rises above a through-arch, with two storeys overlooking the approach and adjoining walls spreading sideways. Gate, tower and wall form one defensive interface, not an isolated viewing pavilion.

Shanhai Guard was established in 1381 and the town built the following year. The surviving tower combines Ming heritage and later repairs; work continued after 1978, with a major repair in 1998. Town foundation and tower repair are separate dates.

The town controls a narrow corridor between mountain and sea, joined to barbicans, outer defences and the Great Wall. Zhendong Tower is one key node; its gate and wall connections reveal how defence regulated everyday movement.
captions: Shanhaiguan · Zhendong Tower and gate platform
Ming arrow tower · Repairs over the centuries and in modern times

protection.scope: Zhendong Tower with its gate platform and the short wall sections on both sides

hb_pule.name: Pule Temple
hb_pule.yearNote: 1766 refers to the construction of Pule Temple and Xuguang Pavilion; this plate shows only the round pavilion and the upper terrace directly supporting it, not the complete mandala platform.
hb_pule.place: Hebei · Chengde · East of the Wulie River
hb_pule.lede: Xuguang Pavilion’s circular double eaves and yellow tiles mark the centre of Pule Temple’s rear mandala precinct. A round timber pavilion rises on a square stone platform, contrasting spreading eaves with heavy masonry. Built under Qianlong, the temple places a familiar sequence of halls before a mandala space. The pavilion and its immediate upper platform alone reveal the meeting of Chinese timber forms and Tibetan Buddhist ritual.
facts: The circular pavilion has double eaves and a pointed roof in yellow glazed tiles on a stone platform. Its continuous eave line contrasts with the square support; this partial view cannot establish the number of tiers or buildings in the complete mandala precinct.

Pule Temple was built in 1766, with hall courtyards in front and a mandala precinct behind. Xuguang Pavilion is the rear core; its date and these two spatial systems explain the organisation of the Qing temple.

A three-dimensional mandala and circular coffered ceiling link the outer pavilion to internal religious symbolism. Its form invites comparison with the Temple of Heaven, but Buddhist use here must not be equated with that monument’s function.
captions: Pule Temple · Xuguang Pavilion and upper terrace
Double circular eaves · 31st year of Qianlong, Qing (1766)

protection.scope: Xuguang Pavilion and upper terrace

hb_anyuan.name: Anyuan Temple
hb_anyuan.yearNote: 1764 refers to the founding of Anyuan Temple and Pudu Hall; the surviving hall includes later repairs. Pudu Hall is also written with a variant character in its name, and that form is kept as a search alias.
hb_anyuan.place: Hebei · Chengde · East of the Wulie River
hb_anyuan.lede: Pudu Hall’s black glazed roofs are edged in yellow across three eave tiers, articulating a substantial square mass. Built on a hill east of the Wulie River, Anyuan Temple brought an Ili temple model to Chengde. Later repairs remain part of the surviving structure. Its seven-bay-square plan and encircling eaves deserve attention rather than being mistaken for a conventional elongated hall.
facts: Pudu Hall, also written with a variant final Chinese character, is seven bays wide and seven deep under three hip-and-gable eave tiers. Black tiles with yellow edging emphasise a nearly square body rather than a typical broad hall.

Anyuan Temple was built in 1764 for the Dashi Dawa community resettled in Chengde, using Guldja Temple in Ili as a model. Later repairs form part of the building; its founding date does not imply unchanged components.

The inner gate, Pudu Hall and an imperial poem stele survive. Ili’s architectural associations meet Chengde’s hillside setting, offering material evidence of Qing religious construction across regions.
captions: Anyuan Temple · Pudu Hall
Square triple-eaved hall · 29th year of Qianlong, Qing (1764)

protection.scope: Pudu Hall, entire hall

hb_zhili.name: Zhili Governor-General's Office
hb_zhili.sub: Main Hall · Five-bay principal hall of the office
hb_zhili.era: Surviving main structure of the Yongzheng reign, Qing
hb_zhili.yearNote: The Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau dates the surviving main buildings to the Yongzheng reign (1723–1735); 1730 is only a sorting point within that range and is not presented as the exact completion year of the Main Hall.
hb_zhili.lede: The five-bay principal hall, front gallery and open court express the administrative order of the Zhili Governor-General’s Office. Plain tile roofs direct attention to space rather than rich ornament. Major official and ceremonial functions occupied the front, with residences behind. Most surviving buildings date to the Yongzheng era and include later alterations; the hall’s position explains how official work and domestic life were arranged.
facts: The axial hall has five bays, a front gallery and terrace, with side buildings enclosing its court. Plain-tiled gable roofs emphasise the sequence of gates, halls and courtyards.

The site remained an administrative office from the Ming through the early Republic. Most surviving buildings date to 1723–1735; the approximate timeline placement must not turn 1730 into a precise completion date for this hall.

The hall hosted major official affairs and ceremonies; residences and family rooms lay farther along the axis. Successive courts mediated public administration and domestic life, revealing how a Qing provincial office functioned.
captions: Zhili Governor-General's Office · Main Hall
Five-bay principal hall · Yongzheng reign, Qing

protection.scope: Main Hall

hb_yongtong.name: Yongtong Bridge
hb_yongtong.sub: Zhao County · Single-span open-spandrel stone arch bridge
hb_yongtong.yearNote: According to the Hebei Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau, the bridge was built in the Mingchang reign of the Jin (1190–1195); 1192 is a sorting point within that range, and earlier legends are not used to date the surviving structure.
hb_yongtong.lede: Yongtong Bridge combines one large stone arch and four open-spandrel arches into a light silhouette. A gently rising deck carries continuous balustrades. Built in the Jin Mingchang era, it resembles but is smaller than nearby Anji Bridge, hence its nickname Little Stone Bridge. Studying the main arch and openings reveals its own construction rather than merely a reduced copy.
facts: The single main span is about 26 metres. Four smaller arches open the shoulders, reducing solid masonry and providing water passages. Parallel stone arch ribs support the deck, with posts and balustrades following its curve.

The provincial authority dates construction to 1190–1195. Earlier founding traditions do not establish the surviving bridge’s date, and an approximate timeline point is not evidence of a single completion year.
Both Yongtong and Anji use open spandrels, but differ in scale and river crossing. Carved balustrades combine ornament with engineering and reward study alongside the arch structure.
captions: Zhao County · Full side elevation of Yongtong Bridge
Single span, four small arches · Mingchang reign, Jin

protection.scope: Yongtong Bridge, Zhao County, entire bridge

hb_tiangong.name: Pagoda of Tiangong Temple
hb_tiangong.sub: Fengrun · Octagonal thirteen-story multi-eaved brick pagoda
hb_tiangong.era: Founded in the 8th year of Qingning, Liao · Later repairs
hb_tiangong.yearNote: 1062 is the Liao founding date; the surviving pagoda has been repaired in the Ming, Qing and modern times, and this plate registers it according to its preserved Liao form.
hb_tiangong.lede: Tiangong Pagoda concentrates brick sculpture on a tall first section, then tapers through thirteen close eave tiers. Dragon-wrapped attached columns, blind doors and brackets resemble timber architecture, though the body is solid. The temple has disappeared, but its tower survives on the old elevated site. Liao foundation, later repairs and excavated scriptures connect its form to a richer material history.
facts: This solid octagonal thirteen-tier pagoda has a Sumeru and lotus base. Blind doors, dragon columns and brick brackets decorate the first section; timber-like exterior details do not imply climbable interior storeys.
The tower was founded in 1062 and repaired in the Ming, Qing and modern periods. Its Liao attribution follows the preserved form, not a claim that every surviving brick is original.
Liao scriptures and images and Ming objects were recovered from the tower, informing religious and printing history. Such finds reconnect the isolated brick structure with its vanished temple.
captions: Tiangong Temple Pagoda · Whole pagoda
Octagonal, thirteen stories · Founded in the 8th year of Qingning, Liao (1062)

protection.scope: Pagoda of Tiangong Temple, Fengrun, whole pagoda

hb_shien.name: Shi'en Temple
hb_shien.sub: Main Hall · Qing round-ridge front annex
hb_shien.era: Founded in the 6th year of Chenghua, Ming · Front annex added in the Qing
hb_shien.yearNote: 1470 is the founding year of Shi'en Temple, and the surviving Main Hall retains Ming features; the five-bay round-ridge front annex was added in the Qing, so the whole ensemble is not dated as original 1470 fabric.
hb_shien.lede: Shien Temple’s high and low roofs reveal different construction phases. The rear hipped hall retains Ming characteristics, while a Qing five-bay rounded-roof porch extends it into the court. Most other temple buildings are gone, but this survivor is not an unchanged Ming image. Roof junctions and columns show how a later addition expanded shelter and usable space.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof and a five-bay rounded-roof porch. Two connected roofs of differing height should not be described as one double-eaved hipped hall.
The temple was founded in 1470. The hall retains Ming features, while the front porch is a Qing addition. Foundation and extension are separate phases, not one unchanged original construction.
The porch creates sheltered transition between hall and court. Despite the loss of the other temple buildings, this addition shows how religious architecture adjusted to use over time.
captions: Shi'en Temple · Main Hall and round-ridge front annex
Ming hall · Front annex added in the Qing

protection.scope: Main Hall and Qing round-ridge front annex

hb_dajingmen.name: Dajingmen Gate
hb_dajingmen.sub: Zhangjiakou · Arched gate and short wall sections
hb_dajingmen.era: Gate opened and built in the 1st year of Shunzhi, Qing
hb_dajingmen.yearNote: 1644 refers to the opening and building of the Dajingmen gate; the adjoining wall sections are Great Wall remains spanning several eras, and this plate does not attribute the whole stretch of mountain wall to 1644.
hb_dajingmen.lede: Dajingmen relies on a thick brick platform and arch, without a tall timber tower. Stone foundations and brick walls constrain the mountain route, while inscriptions turn the military gateway into civic memory. Officially opened in 1644, it joins walls with an earlier history. Gate and short wall sections reveal a boundary that regulated movement as well as defence and trade.
facts: A brick-vaulted gate stands on stone foundations with two timber doors clad in iron. The platform joins adjacent walls; masonry and the arch form a complete gateway without a timber tower.
The gate was formally opened in 1644. Connected Great Wall sections and earlier routes have separate histories, so this date must not be applied to the whole hillside wall.
Frontier markets and later trade routes connected with the gateway. Defence, inspection and transport shared the archway, showing that the Great Wall also accommodated exchange and passage.
captions: Zhangjiakou · Dajingmen and short wall sections
Gate built in the 1st year of Shunzhi, Qing (1644)

protection.scope: Arched gate of Dajingmen, Zhangjiakou, Hebei, and adjoining short wall sections
protection.note: The Dajingmen section was incorporated into the Great Wall in the seventh batch and placed under the fifth-batch Great Wall listing; the label is registered by the batch in which this section was included.

ah_xuguo.name: Xu Guo Stone Archway
ah_xuguo.yearNote: The construction year of the stone archway is used; the plate shows only the front elevation of one side of the eight-pillared, four-sided archway.
ah_xuguo.lede: Eight stone pillars enclose a four-sided memorial archway: the Xu Guo Archway turns a flat gateway into a stone space one can walk through. Beams, bracket sets and stone lions are all carved from the same gray stone, and it still stands at a street junction in the old Huizhou town.
facts: Built in the 12th year of Wanli in the Ming (1584) in honor of Grand Secretary Xu Guo, it is also called the Grand Secretary's Archway; it was listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level in 1988.

It has four sides and eight pillars: the front and back each have three bays, four pillars and three roofed tiers, and the left and right sides each a single bay, two pillars and three roofed tiers, together enclosing a rectangle; carving covers the stone beams and bracket sets that imitate timber construction.

The plate shows only the front elevation of one side, presenting four front pillars and three passages rather than lining up all eight pillars in a row; inscriptions and the street background are omitted.
captions: Xu Guo Stone Archway · Front elevation of one side
Ming · 1584 · Four-sided, eight-pillared stone archway

ah_zhenfeng.name: Zhenfeng Pagoda, Anqing
ah_zhenfeng.sub: Yingjiang Temple · Seven-story octagonal brick-and-stone pagoda
ah_zhenfeng.yearNote: The pagoda body drawn is dated to the Longqing reign of the Ming and placed at the commonly cited completion year of 1570; local records also give a completion date of 1572. The attached eaves, roofs and finial show the repaired state seen in the photographs.
ah_zhenfeng.lede: Zhenfeng Pagoda rises inside Yingjiang Temple in Anqing, its seven-storey octagonal profile narrowing upward. Eaves and platforms articulate the masonry body. Near the Yangtze, it is both a Buddhist tower and a landmark of the city’s riverfront. The usual completion date is 1570, under the Ming, followed by later repairs. Its changing levels and routes through the structure explain the late-Ming building more clearly than a height figure alone.
facts: The seven-storey octagonal masonry pagoda diminishes in plan and height upward, with eaves and platforms separating the levels. Stone steps wind through it, linking the exterior profile with the route of ascent.

Common accounts date completion to 1570, with later repairs to the surviving structure. This late-Ming placement is distinct from the temple’s history and does not imply that every present component has remained unreplaced.

Buddhist images and inscriptions preserve worship and local history within one building, while the riverside location makes it an Anqing landmark. Its proportions and layered profile illuminate the pavilion-style pagoda tradition.
captions: Zhenfeng Pagoda · Seven-story octagonal body and ground-level attached eave
Ming · Longqing reign · Present state after later repairs

ah_huaxilou.name: Huaxi Opera Tower, Bozhou
ah_huaxilou.sub: Great Guandi Temple · Courtyard opera stage
ah_huaxilou.yearNote: The year 1676, when the courtyard opera stage was added, is used rather than 1656, the founding year of the Great Guandi Temple; the woodcarving, painted decoration and roof have undergone later restoration.
ah_huaxilou.lede: The central stage of Bozhou’s Huaxilou stands inside the Guandi Temple, with an open stage front, eaves and carved timber focusing the performance space toward its audience. The complex was a guild hall built by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi, linking worship of Guan Yu, meetings among fellow provincials and theatrical entertainment. The temple’s foundation and the stage’s addition belong to different dates, with later embellishment as well. The stage shows how a trading community gave built form to belief, sociability and craft.
facts: The open stage faces the courtyard’s audience space, with its roof and carved timber beneath the eaves creating decorative layers. Inside the Guandi Temple, it forms part of a larger place for worship and communal meetings.

The Guandi Temple was founded in 1656. A 1676 inscription records construction of the theatre, followed by further repairs; the temple’s founding year should not be used as the stage’s completion date.

Merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi established the hall to honour Guan Yu and provide meeting and lodging space for fellow provincials. Theatre and carving turned trading networks into a culture that people could experience together.
captions: Huaxi Opera Tower · Central courtyard stage
Qing · Added 1676 · Later restoration

hn_miaole.name: Pagoda of Miaole Temple
hn_miaole.sub: Rebuilt in the Later Zhou · Square multi-eaved brick pagoda
hn_miaole.era: Later Zhou · Rebuilt in the 2nd year of Xiande
hn_miaole.yearNote: The Later Zhou rebuilding date of the 2nd year of Xiande (955) is used; the pagoda's earlier history is described separately, and legendary dates are not used for placement.
hn_miaole.lede: Miaole Temple Pagoda stands on the Wuzhi plain with a square body and thirteen diminishing brick eaves. Its finial and slender chains extend the solid profile upward. Although the temple setting has changed, the pagoda still reveals Five Dynasties brick construction. A recorded Later Zhou rebuilding date must be distinguished from earlier temple history and relic traditions; flood deposits also show that the monument has endured environmental change as well as time.
facts: The hollow square brick pagoda has thirteen closely spaced eaves formed by corbelled brickwork, diminishing upward. Southern niches and lower brick carving create varied rhythms; the finial is not counted as another eave tier.

The surviving pagoda is dated to its rebuilding in 955, the second year of the Later Zhou Xiande era, on a Sui–Tang predecessor. Earlier history and relic legends do not replace the date assigned to the surviving structure.

Repeated flood deposits raised the surrounding ground and buried part of the base, while the upper eaves and finial retained their profile. The site brings together brick-building technology, local hydrology and the fortunes of the temple.
captions: Miaole Temple Pagoda, Wuzhi · Thirteen tiers of multi-eaves
Later Zhou · Rebuilt 955

hn_fawang.name: Pagoda of Fawang Temple
hn_fawang.era: Tang · Exact year of construction undetermined
hn_fawang.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate timeline placement for a Tang survival and does not represent the exact year the pagoda was built; the Eastern Han founding date of the temple is not used. The plate omits the lower body and arched doorway hidden by trees.
hn_fawang.lede: The upper part of Fawang Temple’s Tang pagoda narrows into a gentle curve through fifteen closely spaced eaves. Light and shade on corbelled brick courses create a repeated rhythm around the square body. Its damaged summit survives without an intact finial. Other pagodas in the temple belong to different periods; the great pagoda is a Tang monument whose form is more securely understood than an exact building year derived from the temple’s founding traditions.
facts: The square brick pagoda has fifteen closely spaced eave tiers. Corbelled courses project and diminish upward in a roughly parabolic profile; small upper openings remain visible, but the crowning finial has been lost.

Zhengzhou’s heritage bureau assigns this large pagoda to the Tang, without specifying an exact year. Around 750 is an approximate timeline position; the earlier foundation date of Fawang Temple does not date this pagoda.

The group also includes single-storey brick pagodas and Yuan and Qing monuments. Their different forms and dates make the great pagoda’s square body and fifteen eaves a useful reference for comparing Buddhist tower types around Mount Song.
captions: Fawang Temple Pagoda · Fifteen multi-eaves and top, detail
Tang · Exact year of construction undetermined

hn_songling.name: Imperial Tombs of the Northern Song
hn_songling.yearNote: 1063 is the construction date of the Yongzhao Mausoleum, and the subject is an original stone civil official before the tomb; it does not mean that all the Song tombs were built in the same year, nor are the modern reconstructed gate towers counted as Song structures.
hn_songling.lede: Robes falling long and hands holding a tablet of office, the stone civil official stands at attention beside the spirit way of the Yongzhao Mausoleum. Weathering has softened the details but has not erased the solemn, quiet figure of a Northern Song tomb honor guard.
facts: Date of the tomb: The Yongzhao Mausoleum is the tomb of Emperor Renzong of Song, Zhao Zhen, begun in 1063; this entry uses its original stone carvings to represent the Northern Song imperial tombs, without counting the individual tombs separately.

Surviving carvings: The spirit ways of the Song tombs set out a ceremonial order with human and animal statues; the stone carvings are physical evidence for the study of Song sculpture and the imperial funerary system.

Plate scope: The plate shows the first stone civil official from the south in the east row at the Yongzhao Mausoleum; based on on-site photographs from 2025, it keeps the damaged crown, the tablet-holding pose and the stone base, and does not include the modern reconstructed gate towers.
captions: Yongzhao Mausoleum · Stone civil official (east row, first from south)
Northern Song · Tomb built 1063

hn_bixia.name: Bixia Palace, Xun County
hn_bixia.sub: Front of the main hall · Worship hall elevation
hn_bixia.era: Ming · Founded in the 21st year of Jiajing, with later repairs
hn_bixia.yearNote: 1542 is the founding date of the main hall recorded in sources, and repeated restorations in the Ming and Qing produced the present appearance; the plate shows only the front worship hall and does not include the unseen roof of the rear hall.
hn_bixia.place: Henan · Hebi · Mount Fuqiu, Xun County
hn_bixia.lede: A round-ridge roof spreads above woodcarving and painted decoration, and red door columns frame the dark entrance of the hall. With its worship hall joined to the main hall, Bixia Palace on Mount Fuqiu preserves the dense craftsmanship of a popular Ming–Qing temple.
facts: Construction and repairs: Sources record the main hall's founding as the 21st year of Jiajing in the Ming (1542), followed by many repairs and expansions in the Ming and Qing; the present appearance does not mean every member is original to the first construction.

Hall arrangement: A round-ridge hip-and-gable worship hall at the front joins a main hall with an overhanging gable roof behind; the woodcarving of the front eaves, pierced-carved windows and painted decoration make up a rich facade.

View notes: Drawn from a 2024 frontal on-site photograph of the front worship hall, omitting neighboring halls, trees, offering furnishings and text; the platform edge and side steps are generalized, and the hidden carved central imperial way is not reconstructed.
captions: Bixia Palace · Front worship hall elevation of the main hall
Founded in the Ming · Further repairs in the Ming and Qing

nx_xumishan.name: Xumishan Grottoes
nx_xumishan.sub: Cave 5 Maitreya Buddha · Chest and knees, detail
nx_xumishan.era: Tang sculpture · Grottoes begun in the Northern Wei
nx_xumishan.yearNote: 750 is only an approximate timeline placement for the Tang great Buddha of Cave 5, not an exact carving date; the Northern Wei founding of the grottoes is not used in place of the subject drawn.
nx_xumishan.place: Ningxia · Guyuan · Yuanzhou District · Mount Xumi
nx_xumishan.lede: The Buddha in Cave 5 at Xumishan is carved from the cliff, its full chest and seated knees lending a human scale to the rock face. This Tang-period Maitreya belongs to a cave complex begun under the Northern Wei and developed over several dynasties. The relationship between drapery and mass explains the statue more clearly than the complex’s foundation date alone. Weathering, losses and repairs also record its long exposure outdoors.
facts: Cave 5 contains a seated Maitreya roughly twenty metres high in a large rock niche. The chest and knees form full masses, while close-fitting robes and flowing folds soften the monumental figure.

The cave complex began under the Northern Wei, but the large Buddha in Cave 5 is Tang work. Its approximate eighth-century placement indicates a construction phase, not the founding date of the whole complex.

Guyuan lay on the northern route of the eastern Silk Road. The caves trace the spread and transformation of Buddhist art; this Buddha’s rounded modelling expresses Tang aesthetics, and its survival has depended on repeated conservation.
captions: Xumishan Cave 5 · Maitreya Buddha, chest and knees
Tang sculpture · Weathering kept as photographed

nx_xixialing.name: Western Xia Imperial Tombs
nx_xixialing.sub: Tomb No. 3 · Surviving rammed-earth tomb tower
nx_xixialing.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate sorting point for the Western Xia period, not the exact construction year of Tomb No. 3; Tomb No. 3 is generally considered to be Li Yuanhao's Tailing, but the attribution of its occupant is not treated as a proven conclusion.
nx_xixialing.place: Ningxia · Yinchuan · Xixia District · Eastern foot of the Helan Mountains
nx_xixialing.lede: The tower of Xixia Tomb 3 survives as a tall earthen mass, narrowing in stages and marked by channels of erosion. It is a remnant of an eleventh- to thirteenth-century cemetery, rather than a pavilion retaining its full eaves. Walls, gate platforms and ritual-building remains once formed a larger funerary enclosure. Tomb 3 is often tentatively attributed to Li Yuanhao, but that proposal should be distinguished from an established identification.
facts: The surviving tower is rammed from loess mixed with gravel and narrows upward. Its exposed earthen body has lost exterior decoration and should be understood with the surrounding enclosure and offering-hall remains.

The cemetery developed between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries. Tomb 3 is tentatively attributed to the founding emperor Li Yuanhao; neither that identity nor the tower’s precise construction year is established.

The cemetery plan, Tangut and Chinese stele fragments, and architectural finds illuminate exchanges among Tangut traditions, Chinese imperial ritual and Buddhism. The remaining rammed earth still preserves clues to that complex history.
captions: Western Xia Tomb No. 3 · Surviving rammed-earth tomb tower
Western Xia site · Not a reconstruction of the original

nx_108towers.name: One Hundred and Eight Pagodas of Qingtongxia
nx_108towers.sub: Top three rows of the group · Seven pagodas, detail
nx_108towers.era: Western Xia founding attributed · Later restoration
nx_108towers.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement based on the Qingtongxia municipal government's view that the pagodas were founded in the Western Xia, not an exact construction year. The 1988 national protected site list records the period as Yuan; the founding, later restoration and the surviving brick exterior must be considered separately.
nx_108towers.place: Ningxia · Wuzhong · Qingtongxia · West bank of the Yellow River
nx_108towers.lede: The 108 stupas spread in rows down a hillside beside the Yellow River. Individual towers are modest, but their ordered arrangement forms a strong triangular silhouette. The uppermost three rows contain seven stupas, arranged one, three and three, providing a starting point for understanding the whole group. Its origins are associated with Xixia Buddhist remains, although the exact founding year remains uncertain. Repairs also mean that every visible surface and component need not date to the same period.
facts: Twelve rows expand down the slope in an odd-number sequence, making 108 stupas in total. The top three rows contain seven towers, each combining a base, body and finial into a shared silhouette.

The local official account associates the group with the Xixia period, but its exact founding year remains uncertain and recorded datings differ. The approximate twelfth-century placement does not date all surviving towers to one construction campaign.

Bowl-shaped, gourd-shaped and other bodies occur within the ordered rows. Comparing individual forms with the hillside arrangement reveals a character that cannot be understood from a single stupa alone.
captions: 108 Pagodas · Top three rows, seven pagodas, detail
Western Xia founding attributed · Present state after later restoration

gs_mogao.name: Mogao Caves
gs_mogao.era: Cave 96 carved in the Tang; the nine-story building seen today is a later protective structure
gs_mogao.yearNote: 700 is only the approximate timeline position of the Tang colossal statue in Cave 96; the drawing shows the later protective pavilion seen today, and its exterior should not be taken as a Tang building.
gs_mogao.place: Gansu · Dunhuang · Eastern foot of Mingsha Mountain
gs_mogao.lede: Nine tiers of eaves climb the Mogao cliff, their red columns joining timber architecture to rock. This prominent building protects Cave 96’s giant Maitreya: the image originated in the Tang period, but the nine-storey exterior developed later. Distinguishing their dates makes the stepped roofs intelligible without mistaking the present building for Tang architecture.
facts: The building hugs the cliff, with nine roof tiers rising above the entrance to protect the cave and its giant image. Cave 96’s Maitreya was modelled against the rock; outer structure and inner sculpture are related but distinct parts.

Cave 96 originated in the Tang period, but its protective building was repeatedly altered, increasing from five storeys to nine in the twentieth century. The Tang image and today’s nine-storey timber structure have distinct histories; the image’s age does not date the exterior building.

This landmark shows how cave protection changed over time: storeys were added while the image remained within its original rock setting. Its recognisable silhouette also encourages separate readings of the cave’s ancient contents and later exterior.
captions: Exterior of Cave 96 · Line drawing
Present protective pavilion · Not an original Tang structure

protection.scope: Exterior of Cave 96

gs_yulin.name: Yulin Caves
gs_yulin.sub: Yulin River valley · Cave entrances, detail
gs_yulin.era: Carved continuously from the Tang onward
gs_yulin.yearNote: The drawing shows unnumbered cave openings in their present state, and the carving year of an individual cave cannot be determined from its exterior; 800 serves only for the approximate ordering of a cave group spanning several dynasties.
gs_yulin.lede: Cave entrances follow the sheer cliffs of the Yulin River valley, exposing how their openings meet the surrounding rock. Inside, paintings and sculptures reflect work across the Tang, Five Dynasties, Song, Western Xia, Yuan and later periods; entrances also changed later. No cave number is identified here, so the appearance of an opening cannot establish a single excavation date.
facts: The Yulin caves occupy cliffs on both banks of the river. Excavated into the rock with entrances facing the valley, they remain physically continuous with the surrounding cliff rather than forming freestanding buildings.

The research academy states that the earliest foundation date is unresolved, and surviving remains span Tang and later periods. This entrance’s cave number is unconfirmed, so it is understood within the group’s broad chronology rather than assigned an exact construction year.

Yulin and Mogao are important parts of Dunhuang art, preserving Silk Road culture through caves, paintings and sculpture. An entrance is a starting point for understanding the site, but cannot characterise all the differently dated works within.
captions: Valley cave entrances, detail · Line drawing
From the Tang · Interpretive drawing of present state

protection.scope: Valley cave entrances, detail

gs_maijishan.name: Maijishan Grottoes
gs_maijishan.sub: Cave 13 · Great Buddha of the East Cliff, detail
gs_maijishan.yearNote: The Great Buddha of the East Cliff in Cave 13 is a Sui clay sculpture over a stone core; its present state reflects repairs in later periods.
gs_maijishan.lede: The eastern cliff Buddha’s face and robes spread against Maijishan’s rock, yet their fine surfaces are modelled in clay. Cave 13’s main image has a stone core coated with clay, joining carving and modelling. It began in the Sui period and underwent later repairs, leaving work from several periods on its surface. This close view reveals its expression without representing the entire sculptural group.
facts: The main image has a rock core with clay modelling: the cliff supplies its foundation and the clay shapes face and drapery. These materials allow a monumental mass to retain a gentle, detailed expression.

The East Cliff Buddha originated in the Sui period, and Cave 13 is listed among caves substantially repaired from the Five Dynasties through the Song. Initial creation and subsequent conservation form distinct layers; not every visible clay layer or painted surface is Sui-period work.

Maijishan is renowned for sculpture, and this Buddha demonstrates monumental work against a cliff. The main image originally formed a group with two bodhisattvas. A close view reveals modelling skills while remaining distinct from the full ensemble.
captions: Great Buddha of the East Cliff, Cave 13, detail · Line drawing
Sui · Interpretive drawing of present state

protection.scope: Great Buddha of the East Cliff, Cave 13, detail

xj_kizil.name: Kizil Thousand Buddha Caves
xj_kizil.era: Cave group of the Kucha period
xj_kizil.yearNote: The drawing shows unnumbered cave openings in their present state; the date of a specific cave cannot be determined from its entrance, and 600 is only an approximate timeline position for the cave group.
xj_kizil.lede: Kizil’s cave entrances are cut into a cliff, where rock strata, openings and forecourts form the outward landscape. An important remnant of Buddhist art in ancient Kucha, the complex developed from about the third century to the eighth or ninth and once contained paintings and clay sculpture. This stretch of cliff has no securely identified cave numbers and must be understood within that multi-period history. Its approximate sixth-century placement is not a precise dating of each visible entrance.
facts: The caves are cut directly into the cliffs of Mingwutag Mountain, their entrances distributed across the rock face. The exterior shows their relationship with the mountain; paintings and clay sculpture form a further artistic space inside.

Official accounts place construction across roughly the third to eighth or ninth centuries. The exact dates of this unnumbered cliff section remain uncertain; its sixth-century placement is only an approximate point within the complex’s development.

Cave forms and paintings make Kizil representative of Kuchan Buddhist art and illuminate Buddhism’s movement along the Silk Road. Losses from the walls also show why caves and their paintings must be understood together.
captions: Cliff entrance, detail · Line drawing
Kucha-period cave group · Present openings

protection.scope: Cliff entrance, detail

xj_kumtura.name: Kumtura Thousand Buddha Caves
xj_kumtura.era: Cave group of the Kucha period
xj_kumtura.yearNote: The drawing shows unnumbered cave openings in their present state; the date of a specific cave cannot be determined from its entrance, and 700 is only an approximate timeline position for the cave group.
xj_kumtura.lede: Kumtura’s caves occupy cliffs on the east bank of the Weigan River. The valley and rock face provided connected spaces for Buddhist worship, while water continues to pose conservation challenges. This exterior section shows the relationship between entrances and rock strata, rather than the paintings and inscriptions inside. Construction extended from the fifth to the fourteenth century, leaving traces of successive religious activity. The approximate seventh-century placement represents only one stage of this long history.
facts: The caves are cut into the Queletag cliffs above the Weigan valley. Entrances penetrate conglomerate rock, and some caves are linked by corridors; the exterior cliff and interior worship spaces together form the site.

An official conservation report dates excavation across the fifth to fourteenth centuries. This unnumbered cliff section cannot be precisely dated cave by cave, and its approximate seventh-century placement is not the foundation date of the whole group.

Paintings, coloured sculpture and inscriptions in several scripts record extended Buddhist activity and cultural exchange. River erosion and vulnerable rock require reinforcement and water-level management, making the landscape essential to understanding the caves.
captions: Valley cliff face, detail · Line drawing
Kucha-period cave group · Present openings

protection.scope: Valley cliff face, detail

sc_huangze.name: Huangze Temple Cliff Sculptures
sc_huangze.sub: Cliff group of five figures, detail
sc_huangze.yearNote: The Huangze Temple cliff sculptures are characterized chiefly by Tang works; the exact carving year of the selected niche has not been determined from the image.
sc_huangze.place: Sichuan · Guangyuan · West bank of the Jialing River
sc_huangze.lede: On the cliff of the west bank of the Jialing, the 'group of five', a Buddha in the centre with disciples and bodhisattvas standing on either side, is the commonest arrangement at Huangze Temple, and the plate takes a detail of one such niche; the niche number has not been verified. The carvings were begun in the late Northern Wei, continued through Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui, and reached their peak in the early and high Tang; 57 niches with more than 1,200 figures survive. The temple takes its name from Wu Zetian, and here the caves came first and the temple later. The drawing follows a Tang niche and leaves out signboards and modern railings.
facts: Form: the main image sits in the centre of the niche with a disciple and a bodhisattva on each side, making a group of five; the largest, Cave 28 or the Great Buddha Cave, has Amitabha as its main image, about 6 m high, adds two guardians, and carries the Eight Classes of Beings on the back wall. The five figures in the plate are a detail of one such niche; its number and dimensions were not confirmed from the photograph.

Dating: carving began in the late Northern Wei and continued through Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui, peaking in the early and high Tang and declining after the mid-Tang; Yang Xiu, Prince of Shu and son of Emperor Wen of Sui, cut niches here. Listed in 1961 in the first group of Major National Historical and Cultural Sites, it is with Qianfoya among the earliest cave sites of Sichuan.

Significance: like Dunhuang, Huangze Temple had its caves cut before the temple was built; the temple is named for Wu Zetian and holds a stone image said to be her 'true likeness'. Published niche counts differ (47, 50, 57); this entry follows the survey of the Sichuan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, 57 niches and over 1,200 figures, with subjects including sutra pillars, multi-figure groups, Buddhas of the Three Ages and Sakyamuni and Prabhutaratna seated together.
captions: Cliff group of five figures, detail · Line drawing
Tang · Interpretive drawing of present state

protection.scope: Cliff group of five figures, detail

sc_qianfo.name: Thousand-Buddha Cliff Sculptures, Guangyuan
sc_qianfo.yearNote: Work on the Thousand-Buddha Cliff spans several dynasties; the niche drawn has not been confirmed from the photographs as a specific numbered niche.
sc_qianfo.place: Sichuan · Guangyuan · East bank of the Jialing River
sc_qianfo.lede: Along 388 m of cliff on the east bank of the Jialing, niches large and small are stacked one above another like a honeycomb. This is one of the earliest cave sites in Sichuan, begun in the late Northern Wei and most active in the Tang; when the Sichuan-Shaanxi highway was blasted through in 1935 about two thirds of the carvings were destroyed, yet more than 950 niches and 7,900 figures remain. The 146 inscriptions on the cliff run from the Wu Zhou period to the Republic, the best known being the merit cave of Wei Kang, inspector of Jiannan, dated 722 (Kaiyuan 10). The plate takes a seated Buddha with attendants from one niche and does not stand for the whole cliff.
facts: Form: the cliff runs 388 m north to south, closely packed with niches above and below; more than 950 niches and 7,900 figures survive, with subjects including Amitabha, Vairocana, Sakyamuni and bodhisattvas. The plate shows a detail of one niche, a seated Buddha with attendants on either side; its number was not confirmed from the photograph.

Dating: carving began in the late Northern Wei; the Northern Dynasties to the Tang were the main period, the Tang the richest, while the Five Dynasties, Song, Yuan and Qing mostly repainted. The cliff carries 146 inscriptions, the earliest of the Wu Zhou period (696–697); the inscription of Cave 513, the Wei Kang cave, is dated 'the seventh day of the sixth month of Kaiyuan 10', and Niche 211 was made by Su Ting. The site was called Baitang Temple in the Tang and renamed Qianfoya in the Yuan.

Significance: there were once more than 17,000 figures; in 1935 the building of the Sichuan-Shaanxi highway blasted away over a hundred metres of cliff, and Liang Sicheng reported to the government that year that 'about two thirds have been destroyed'. Listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites, it is the earliest cave site in south-west China and the largest cave complex in Sichuan.
captions: Cliff Buddha niche, detail · Line drawing
Tang (approximate) · Interpretive drawing of present state

protection.scope: Cliff Buddha niche, detail

sc_beishan.name: Beishan Cliff Sculptures
sc_beishan.sub: Beishan stone niche · Bodhisattva figures, detail
sc_beishan.era: Beishan begun in the late Tang · Carving continued in the Five Dynasties and Song
sc_beishan.yearNote: Beishan was begun in 892, and carving continued from the Five Dynasties to the Southern Song; the exact date of the niche drawn has not been confirmed from the photographs.
sc_beishan.lede: A seated central figure and attendants occupy a Beishan niche, their drapery, poses and faces engaging at close range. Compared with Baodingshan’s expansive cliff narratives, Beishan often draws attention to a single shrine and its details. Work began in the late Tang and continued through the Five Dynasties and Song. This niche has no confirmed number or precise date, so the site’s foundation cannot date it.
facts: This detail shows a seated figure with attendants in a limited rock niche, linked by poses and drapery. It belongs to Beishan, a separate site from Baodingshan’s Thousand-Armed Guanyin.

Beishan began in 892 and received further work through the Five Dynasties and Southern Song. This niche has no securely confirmed number or date. The mountain’s initial carving date cannot be assigned to every group of images here.

Beishan’s fine carving and figures trace Buddhist art from late Tang to Song. Close examination reveals drapery and expression, but secure dating still requires inscriptions, formal analysis and relevant research.
captions: Beishan stone niche, detail · Line drawing
Song (approximate) · Interpretive drawing of present state

yn_shizhong.name: Shizhongshan Grottoes
yn_shizhong.sub: Niche of the Nanzhao king, detail
yn_shizhong.yearNote: The niche drawn is traditionally called the Court Audience of Yimouxun; scholarship notes that this identification rests on early surveys and local legend and should still be treated with caution.
yn_shizhong.lede: A ruler sits with hands concealed in his sleeves, flanked by officials and attendants. Shizhongshan brings a scene of earthly court life into a Buddhist cave setting. Traditionally called Yimouxun Holding Court, this niche rewards attention to robes, seat and hierarchy. The identification as a Nanzhao ruler is relatively secure, but the individual king remains unsettled; a familiar title is not proof.
facts: The main figure sits within the niche, surrounded by an ordered group of officials and attendants. Round-necked, wide-sleeved robes, the folded hands and the seat describe individuals while making court hierarchy visible.

The cave group was excavated across the Nanzhao and Dali Kingdom periods. This niche is traditionally named for Yimouxun, but research traces individual royal names to early surveys and local tradition. The familiar name settles neither identity nor an exact carving date.

The carvings include rulers and secular life alongside Buddhas and bodhisattvas. Clothes, furnishings and attendants supply evidence for Nanzhao political culture, even while the precise identification remains subject to research.
captions: Niche of the Nanzhao king, detail · Line drawing
About 9th century · Interpretive drawing of present state

protection.scope: Niche of the Nanzhao king, detail

sn_beilin.name: Xi'an Stele Forest
sn_beilin.sub: Stone Terrace Classic of Filial Piety stele
sn_beilin.era: Stone Terrace Classic of Filial Piety stele, 4th year of Tianbao, Tang
sn_beilin.lede: The Stone Platform Classic of Filial Piety turns a book into a monument viewed from all sides. Four inscribed faces, a sculptured head and a raised base give the text a ceremonial scale. Emperor Xuanzong supplied its preface, commentary and clerical-script calligraphy; erected in 745, it later moved to the Stele Forest. The object brings together classical learning, imperial textual authority, calligraphy and stone carving.
facts: Four large stones form the inscribed faces beneath a carved head and above a stone platform. Walking around it is necessary to see the whole text. Its squared body and ordered lines establish a disciplined reading arrangement.

Emperor Xuanzong wrote the preface, commentary and clerical-script text, while Crown Prince Li Heng supplied the seal-script heading. Erected at Chang’an’s imperial academy in 745, it later moved to the present Stele Forest; this dates the object, not the entire collection.

Inscription fixed a Confucian classic in a form that could circulate through rubbings while preserving imperial calligraphy. Classical scholarship, writing and authority meet on its surfaces, distinguishing it from epitaphs and ordinary commemorative name inscriptions.
captions: Stone Terrace Classic of Filial Piety stele · Line drawing
745 · Interpretive drawing of present state

yn_cuanbaozi.name: Cuan Baozi Stele
yn_cuanbaozi.sub: Eastern Jin stele of Cuan Baozi
yn_cuanbaozi.lede: Compact, archaic characters fill a rectangular stone below its curved head. The Cuan Baozi Stele commemorates an Eastern Jin governor of Jianning, preserving clues to offices and local society. Erected in 405, its script belongs to the transition between clerical and regular writing. Individual strokes and the later, larger Cuan Longyan Stele invite comparison.
facts: A curved head and rectangular body contain separate sections for the title, main text and final list of officials. Closely arranged archaic characters give the stele both calligraphic and documentary significance.

The inscription uses the date “fourth Daheng year, yisi,” corresponding to 405, the first Yixi year of Eastern Jin. Rediscovered and moved for protection in the Qing period, it remains an Eastern Jin inscription regardless of its present display setting.

Its smaller size gives it the nickname “Small Cuan Stele”; together with the Liu Song Cuan Longyan Stele it forms the “Two Cuan.” They document local people and offices while allowing comparison of the transition from clerical to regular script.
captions: Cuan Baozi Stele · Line drawing
405 · Interpretive drawing of present state

yn_cuanyan.name: Cuan Longyan Stele
yn_cuanyan.sub: Southern Dynasties stele of Cuan Longyan
yn_cuanyan.lede: The Cuan Longyan Stele brings relief, calligraphy and biography together on one stone. Erected in 458 under Liu Song, it is larger than the Cuan Baozi Stele and thus called the “Large Cuan.” Weathering has not erased the distinction between head and text. Its transitional script rewards inspection, while family and regional history require comparison with other evidence.
facts: Animal and sun-and-moon motifs occupy the curved head above a broad inscribed body. Relief and text have distinct positions; a hole through the head is part of its form. Weathered surfaces still show their combination.

The stele dates to 458, the second Daming year of Liu Song, and records Cuan Longyan’s lineage and life. It is later than the Eastern Jin Cuan Baozi Stele. A shared family name and region do not make the two contemporary.

The Large Cuan preserves forceful transitional clerical–regular script, family genealogies and local careers. Reading it alongside the Small Cuan allows comparison of writing, scale and content, revealing the distinctions behind their joint name.
captions: Cuan Longyan Stele · Line drawing
458 · Interpretive drawing of present state

sn_yaowang.name: Yaowangshan Stone Carvings
sn_yaowang.sub: One niche of cliff-carved stone sculpture
sn_yaowang.era: Multiperiod carvings from the Northern Dynasties to the Tang
sn_yaowang.yearNote: The carvings span the Northern Dynasties, Sui, Tang and other periods; the single niche chosen for this plate lacks a confirmable exact date, and 700 serves only as an approximate placement.
sn_yaowang.lede: Yaowang Mountain contains more than medical prescriptions and memorials to Sun Simiao: Buddhist rock carvings preserve earlier layers of devotion. This niche contains a standing figure, its carved drapery contrasting with rough surrounding rock. The mountain’s sculptures and inscriptions span the Northern Dynasties, Sui, Tang and later periods. This particular niche lacks a confirmed exact date; neighbouring objects cannot date it.
facts: The standing figure occupies a niche cut into the rock face. Body, drapery and recess are carved from the same material. The projecting figure and recessed space contrast, while rough and smooth rock create changing light and shade.

Yaowang Mountain preserves Northern Dynasties, Sui and Tang sculptures alongside later inscriptions. They were not all made together. This niche’s number and exact date remain unconfirmed; an inscription on a neighbouring niche cannot determine them.

Cliff sculptures remain attached to their original rock, unlike freestanding sculptured stelae, offering different modes of viewing. Comparing religious images with later medical-sage themes reveals layers of devotional memory accumulated at one place.
captions: One niche of stone sculpture · Line drawing
Tang (approximate) · Interpretive drawing of present state

yn_duanshi.name: Stele of the Alliance between the Duan Clan and the Thirty-Seven Tribes
yn_duanshi.sub: Alliance stele of the Dali Kingdom
yn_duanshi.lede: The inscription records an alliance between the Dali Kingdom’s Duan rulers and thirty-seven groups at Shicheng. Erected in 971, it preserves oaths after military action and the granting of offices and rewards, revealing tenth-century political connections. Its plain stone and base invite attention beyond letterforms: a political event was made available for later scrutiny through an inscribed object.
facts: A stone base supports the surviving body and its dense writing. The restrained form gives priority to the record. Names and text preserve participants and alliance terms, which should be read together with the physical stone.

Erected in 971, the third Mingzheng year of the Dali Kingdom, it is also called the Shicheng or Shicheng Alliance Stele. After Qing-period discovery it was moved for protection; the present display is not the original alliance setting.

The text records military cooperation, an oath and the award of offices and rewards, providing evidence of relations between the Duan rulers and local groups. It shares Qujing’s collection with earlier Cuan inscriptions but documents a different polity and period.

gs_xixia_stele.name: Stele on the Restoration of the Responsive Pagoda of Huguo Temple
gs_xixia_stele.sub: Faces in Tangut and Chinese script
gs_xixia_stele.lede: One side of this stele is inscribed in Tangut and the other in Chinese, preserving the reconstruction of Huguo Temple’s Ganying Pagoda. Erected in Wuwei in 1094, it retains a recognisable head and rectangular body, while weathering reveals its long history. It documents the temple’s past and aids the study of Tangut writing; comparing the texts still requires specialist interpretation.
facts: A rectangular body, decorated head and closely arranged lines form the inscribed surfaces. Tangut and Chinese occupy opposite sides. Their different writing systems are essential to the object and should not be treated as a single Chinese script.

The stele was erected in 1094, the fifth Tianyou Min’an year of Western Xia, to record reconstruction of the Ganying Pagoda. This dates the inscription and event, not the temple’s earliest foundation or all related present-day buildings.

The two texts can be compared, making the stone important evidence for Tangut language, Buddhism and local history. Its content, as well as its calligraphic form, places a rebuilding project within a verifiable historical record.

js_suzhou_song.name: Song Stone Inscriptions in the Suzhou Confucian Temple
js_suzhou_song.lede: A city map carved in stone: on a slab 2.84 m high, the walls of Southern Song Pingjiang, its five land-and-water gates, 359 bridges, 61 wards and 264 lanes are all drawn in single incised lines, canals running parallel to streets in a double chessboard. Carved in 1229, the second year of Shaoding, it is the earliest surviving city plan in China; set against today's old city of Suzhou, Xuanmiao Temple and the twin pagodas of Luohan Cloister still stand where the map places them. The plate only summarises the structure of the map and is not meant as a legible reproduction.
facts: Form: the stele is 2.84 m high, 1.46 m wide and 30 cm thick, carved in single incised lines; the scale is roughly 1:2,500 north-south and 1:3,000 east-west, with walls, bridges and buildings drawn as simplified elevations at their plan positions. The original is kept in the Suzhou Confucian Temple, now the Suzhou Museum of Stone Inscriptions.

Dating: the stele bears no date; the modern scholar Wang Jian checked it against the rebuilding works of 1229 recorded in the Wujun Gazetteer, finding that everything built before that spring and summer appears on the map and nothing built after the autumn does, and so concluded it was carved in 1229, the second year of Shaoding of the Southern Song.

Content and value: the city is a rectangle longer north-south, with land and water gates drawn at each of the five gates, Qi, Lou, Feng, Pan and Chang, and the prefectural seat slightly southeast of centre; the map marks 359 bridges, 61 wards, 264 lanes, 24 alleys and 67 temples, many names still in use. Checked against archaeology and surviving buildings, it shows that Suzhou has been rebuilt again and again on the same site.

hn_xizhou.name: Bronze Pillar of Xizhou
hn_xizhou.era: Around the 5th year of Tianfu, Later Jin
hn_xizhou.lede: A slender bronze column preserves an oath made after war. The eight faces of the Xizhou Column carry continuous lines of text, while its damaged upper outline records its later history. Inscriptions and historical texts connect it with the 940 settlement between Chu and Xizhou. Both a large casting and a political record, it offers material evidence for local government, negotiated agreements and relations between communities.
facts: The column is an octagonal prism with inscriptions running continuously across its eight faces; its top is damaged. It is not an ordinary structural support. Its metal casting, distinctive form and written surface together define the monument.

Inscriptions and historical records describe peace between Chu and Xizhou and the erection of the column in 940. Original texts include an account, a eulogy and an oath, with separate Northern Song additions requiring distinct chronological readings.

The oath records political relations and agreed terms, providing material evidence for western Hunan’s history. Later moved from its former riverbank for preservation, the object is best understood in connection with the history of its earlier setting.

sc_emei_buddha.name: Bronze and Iron Buddhist Statues of Shengshou Wannian Temple, Mount Emei
sc_emei_buddha.sub: Bronze Samantabhadra riding a white elephant
sc_emei_buddha.yearNote: The cast-bronze Samantabhadra riding an elephant is a Northern Song survival; the name of the protected site also covers the other bronze and iron Buddhist statues in the temple.
sc_emei_buddha.lede: A bronze six-tusked white elephant carries the bodhisattva Samantabhadra; the elephant is taller than a living one, and image and mount together stand 7.85 m high and weigh about 62 tonnes. It was cast in 980 (Taiping Xingguo 5), when Emperor Taizong of the Northern Song granted the gold and sent the eunuch Zhang Renzan to Chengdu to oversee the work; it was cast in sections and carried up to a monastery a thousand metres above sea level, and how it was moved remains a puzzle. The wooden pavilion that once sheltered it burned in 1599 (Wanli 27), and two years later it was covered by the beamless brick hall that still stands. The plate shows this bronze inside the hall, not the modern colossus on the Golden Summit.
facts: Form: a bronze Samantabhadra riding an elephant, 7.85 m high in all and about 62 tonnes in weight; the bodhisattva is 3.64 m high, wears a two-tiered jewelled crown and sits cross-legged on a lotus seat on the elephant's back, the seat 1.39 m high and 2.22 m across; each of the elephant's four feet rests on a lotus. Above the lotus the alloy is brass, the elephant is bronze, cast in sections, and the elephant's belly and the figure are hollow to hold sutras.

Dating: the Southern Song Fozu tongji of Zhipan records that in the first month of 980 (Taiping Xingguo 5) Zhang Renzan was ordered to Chengdu to cast a gilt-bronze Samantabhadra; the Emei shan zhi says the monk Maozhen of Baishui Temple, after an audience at court, was granted three thousand liang of gold for the casting. Listed in 1961 as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site under the name 'bronze and iron Buddhist images of Shengshou Wannian Temple on Mount Emei'.

Significance: the beamless brick hall housing the bronze was built in 1601 (Wanli 29) with gold granted by the Empress Dowager Cisheng, a brick-vaulted structure in the manner of Indian temples using no timber at all; when Wannian Temple burned in 1946 this hall alone survived, and the bronze with it. The protected site also includes other bronze and iron images in the temple, none of which appears in the plate.

qh_taer.name: Ta'er Monastery (Kumbum)
qh_taer.sub: Great Hall of Golden Tiles · Present state
qh_taer.era: Founded in the Ming · Expanded in the Qing
qh_taer.yearNote: 1379 is one account of the monastery's first founding; 1700 is only an approximate timeline position for the surviving Qing Great Hall of Golden Tiles, not the hall's exact construction year.
qh_taer.lede: The Great Golden Roof Hall marks the religious heart of Ta’er Monastery with a gilded roof above a substantial Tibetan-style body. The monastery is associated with Tsongkhapa’s birthplace, while the hall’s present form emerged through Qing-period enlargement and subsequent repairs. Its roof, walls and silver stupa show how architectural traditions and Gelug devotion meet.
facts: A gilded copper roof rises above the hall’s substantial body. Its double-eaved, hip-and-gable profile reflects Chinese architectural practice, combined with a Tibetan-style building to form the monastery’s prominent central hall.

Repair histories record successive Qing-period enlargements: expansion in 1708 and conversion to three levels in 1711, followed by further rebuilding. The present hall has several construction phases; one date cannot describe every component.

Ta’er is an important Gelug monastery. Memories of Tsongkhapa’s birthplace and the silver stupa inside the hall form its devotional core. Its significance encompasses architecture, religious practice and continuing maintenance.

jx_nanchang_uprising.name: Former Headquarters of the Nanchang Uprising
jx_nanchang_uprising.sub: Facade of the old Jiangxi Grand Hotel building
jx_nanchang_uprising.lede: The former headquarters of the Nanchang Uprising was originally the Jiangxi Grand Hotel. Its four-storey brick-and-concrete building surrounds a courtyard, with regular windows and curved ornament on the street front. Completed in 1924, it became the uprising’s headquarters three years later. The surviving hotel connects the city’s commercial life with the revolutionary event commemorated here.
facts: The four-storey hotel is built of brick and concrete around an internal courtyard. Regular door and window openings, with curved Western-style cement reliefs above them, combine Chinese and Western features of modern hotel architecture.

Construction began in 1922 and finished in 1924. During preparations for the 1927 uprising, troops rented the hotel in the name of the First Division of the Twentieth Army, making it the uprising’s headquarters.

The site matters both as a setting of the Nanchang Uprising and as a surviving modern hotel. Its change from a commercial building to a military headquarters makes the connection between everyday urban spaces and major events tangible.

xj_jiaohe.name: Ancient City of Jiaohe
xj_jiaohe.sub: Surviving earthen remains of the Great Buddhist Temple
xj_jiaohe.era: Multiperiod site from Jushi to the Tang
xj_jiaohe.yearNote: The Ancient City of Jiaohe was in use over a long period, and the site contains several phases; 700 is only an approximate timeline placement and cannot be used to determine the construction year of the Great Buddhist Temple walls in the drawing.
xj_jiaohe.lede: Jiaohe’s Great Buddha Temple survives as earthen walls, raised platforms and niches, with roofs and most images lost. In the northern temple quarter, its position becomes clear when approached along the city’s central road. Jiaohe passed through periods including the ancient Jushi kingdom and the Tang dynasty; the surviving urban arrangement largely reflects Tang development. An approximate seventh-century placement does not precisely date every wall to a single year.
facts: Raised platforms, a central tower and niches preserve the temple’s scale in earthen remains, although most statues are gone. The central road leads to the northern temple quarter, retaining the connection between worship and urban streets.

Jiaohe developed from a Jushi capital into a Tang county town, and its surviving scale is broadly Tang. The Great Buddha Temple saw multiple phases of use; its seventh-century placement does not imply that all remaining walls were built together.

Jiaohe used several earthen techniques, including ramming, adobe and excavation that left standing walls. Not every ruin is rammed earth; the temple’s remaining spaces still make Buddhist worship within city life legible.
captions: Surviving earthen remains of the Great Buddhist Temple, Ancient City of Jiaohe · Line drawing

xz_potala.name: Potala Palace
xz_potala.sub: White Palace and Red Palace from the southwest, present state
xz_potala.yearNote: The timeline uses 1694, when the Red Palace was completed; the plate shows the multiphase White Palace, Red Palace and hillside stairways seen today, not a reconstruction of the 7th-century palace on Red Hill.
xz_potala.lede: Potala Palace rises along Red Mountain, with the White Palace spreading to either side and the darker Red Palace occupying the high centre. Stairs and massive walls bind it to the terrain. Its present scale chiefly took shape in the seventeenth century, rather than simply dating to its seventh-century origins. The White Palace’s residential and religious-administrative spaces differ from the Red Palace’s chapels and stupa halls. Seen from below, their layered walls and roofs connect landscape, religion and historical authority.
facts: The Red Palace occupies the centre, flanked by the White Palace. Thick walls and layered spaces rise with the mountain, while stairs link different levels into a continuous complex of palace rooms, chapels and ancillary buildings.

The main White Palace was completed in 1648. Work on the Red Palace began in 1690 and finished in 1694. The surviving principal scale reflects seventeenth-century rebuilding and later extensions, distinct from the earlier foundation.

The White Palace housed the Dalai Lama and religious-administrative activities; the Red Palace contains chapels and stupa halls. Their linked functions make the mountain complex a major witness to Tibetan architecture and religious history.
captions: White Palace and Red Palace of the Potala from the southwest, present state · Line drawing

js_zhuozheng.name: Humble Administrator's Garden
js_zhuozheng.sub: Hall of Distant Fragrance, present state
js_zhuozheng.era: Garden created 1509 · Most surviving buildings from the Qing
js_zhuozheng.yearNote: 1509 is the year the garden was created, and most surviving buildings were rebuilt after the 10th year of Xianfeng in the Qing; 1860 is only an approximate sorting point for the garden's present Qing state, not the exact construction year of the Hall of Distant Fragrance.
js_zhuozheng.lede: The Hall of Distant Fragrance is a 'four-sided hall': no walls on any side, only floor-length lattice windows, so that from inside the lotus pond, the islands and the two small pavilions become pictures framed in the openings. It stands on the site of the Ming Ruoshu Hall, three bays wide, with a broad terrace on the north reaching the water, and is the main hall of the garden's central section. The garden began in 1509, the fourth year of Zhengde, but most of today's halls were rebuilt after 1860: in the Tongzhi era the site served first as the Loyal King's palace, then became the Eight Banners guild hall, and was repaired again in 1887, the layout surviving since. It was inscribed as World Heritage in 1997.
facts: Form: a four-sided hall three bays wide, built on the site of the Ruoshu Hall of the Ming Wang family garden; floor-length lattice windows on all sides open the view in every direction, and a broad terrace on the north reaches the pond, facing across the water the two islands that carry the Xuexiang Yunwei and Daishuang pavilions. The name board was originally written by Shen Deqian of the Qing, destroyed in the Cultural Revolution, and is now a replacement by Zhang Xinjia.

Dating: the garden was founded in 1509; the central section is what survives of the late-Qing Eight Banners guild hall, established in 1872 and repaired in 1887, and most of the existing buildings were rebuilt after 1860, the tenth year of Xianfeng. The hall was shaken and damaged by bombing in 1937 and thoroughly repaired in 1980.

Value: the central section covers about 18.5 mu, centred on a pond that takes up roughly a third of the area, with every pavilion built at the water's edge, and it still keeps the solid, open and uncluttered layout of a Ming garden; it was listed among the first national key protected sites in 1961 and inscribed with the other classical gardens of Suzhou as World Heritage in 1997.
captions: Hall of Distant Fragrance, Humble Administrator's Garden, present state · Line drawing
Interpretive drawing of present state

sc_luding.name: Luding Bridge
sc_luding.sub: Iron-chain bridge span and abutments on both banks
sc_luding.era: Bridge built in the Kangxi reign · Battle of 1935
sc_luding.lede: Thirteen iron chains span the Dadu River, nine laid as the deck and four as rails, made of more than twelve thousand flat iron links; each chain is over 127 m long and weighs about two and a half tonnes, and its ends run into wells six metres deep behind the stone abutments on either bank, locked to cast-iron 'earth-dragon' and 'sleeping-dragon' piles. Work began by imperial sanction in 1705 (Kangxi 44) and the bridge was finished the next year; before it the river could only be crossed by bamboo or rattan ropes or by ferry. On 29 May 1935 twenty-two Red Army soldiers crawled along the chains to seize the bridge, and it entered another history. The plate shows the chain bridge and the abutments on both banks.
facts: Form: an iron-chain suspension bridge of 101.6 m span and 2.8 m width, its deck about 14.5 m above low water; of the 13 chains 9 form the deck and 4 the handrails, the deck chains 33 cm apart and covered with cross-planks and eight runs of longitudinal boards; each chain is 127.45 m long, weighs about 2.5 tonnes and is made of eight or nine hundred flat links. The abutments on both banks are of dressed stone, 20 m high, with timber bridge pavilions on top.

Dating: begun in 1705 (Kangxi 44) and completed in 1706 (Kangxi 45); because it was built by the Kangxi emperor's sanction it was once called the 'Imperial Bridge'. The eastern pavilion holds the Kangxi stele 'Imperial Record of Luding Bridge' telling how it was built, and on the west stands a stele with 'Luding Bridge' in the emperor's own hand. After a new bridge on the Sichuan-Tibet highway opened in 1950 it ceased to carry traffic, and the whole bridge was restored in 1977.

Significance: the chains are anchored in wells 6 m deep behind the abutments, to seven or eight 'earth-dragon' piles and a 'sleeping-dragon' pile weighing 1,800 jin, so that the mass of abutment and piles together takes the pull, the mature practice of Qing iron-chain bridges. On 29 May 1935 the Central Red Army 'took Luding Bridge by storm'; bridge and battle together were listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites.

bj_guozijian.name: Guozijian (Imperial Academy)
bj_guozijian.sub: Biyong Hall and stone bridges over the encircling moat
bj_guozijian.era: Completed in the 49th year of Qianlong
bj_guozijian.lede: A square hall encircled by a round pool, with four stone bridges approaching from four sides: this is the distinctive plan of Biyong at the Imperial College. A gilded finial rises above its double-eaved yellow-tiled roof, while hall and water form a precise geometric order. The college's history predates this building. Biyong was completed in 1784 for the emperor's ceremonial visits and lectures. Hall, pool and bridges gave physical form to ancient ideas about schools and ritual, bringing state education and imperial ceremony into the same space.
facts: Plan: the square hall has doors and verandas on all four sides and is surrounded by a circular pool with white marble balustrades. Four stone bridges lead to its four sides. A gilded finial crowns the double-eaved yellow-glazed roof; water and bridges organise the approaches.

Construction: Biyong was completed in 1784, while the Imperial College's history reaches back to the Yuan. Before this hall was built, emperors lectured in Yilun Hall. The institution's development should therefore be distinguished from the construction date of the surviving Biyong.

Lectures: Biyong served the ceremonial lectures delivered by an emperor visiting the college, and its surrounding water recalls ancient educational ritual. Square hall, round pool and four bridges create a legible spatial order and turn respect for teaching into architecture that can be walked through.
captions: Biyong Hall and stone bridges over the encircling moat, Guozijian · Line drawing

zj_yuefei.name: Tomb of Yue Fei
zj_yuefei.sub: Burial mound, tombstone and offering altar
zj_yuefei.era: Reburied in the Shaoxing reign, Southern Song · Later repairs
zj_yuefei.yearNote: 1163 is placed according to the official Hangzhou record of the reburial; the plate shows the burial mound, tombstone and offering altar seen today, whose stone elements have been repaired in later periods and are not regarded as entirely original Southern Song work.
zj_yuefei.lede: Yue Fei’s tomb beneath Qixia Ridge comprises a burial mound, stele and offering platform. Its meaning rests both on reburial after his rehabilitation in the Southern Song and on continuing repairs and commemoration. The tomb and neighbouring memorial temple have related but separate histories. The orderly appearance of today’s stonework does not establish that all of it is original Southern Song fabric; the burial site and its historical memory endure.
facts: Form: a raised mound, stele and stone offering platform define the centre of homage. The burial space is distinct from the neighbouring memorial temple, and its stone elements have their own repair histories.

Dating: Hangzhou’s official account records reburial here in 1163 after Yue Fei’s rehabilitation, and construction of the memorial temple in 1221. These are separate events; later repairs prevent assigning all current stonework to the Southern Song.

Significance: the tomb gives a physical location to a documented life, while subsequent rituals sustain public memory. Its reburial history and the material layers left by rebuilding both deserve attention.
captions: Tomb of Yue Fei, burial mound, tombstone and offering altar · Line drawing
Interpretive drawing of present state

jp_kinkaku.name: Kinkaku-ji
jp_kinkaku.yearNote: The timeline uses 1955, the year the surviving Shariden was rebuilt; the original structure from the time of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu burned down in 1950.
jp_kinkaku.lede: Three storeys, three idioms: a shinden-style ground floor in plain wood, a warrior-house second floor and a Zen-hall top floor, the upper two sheathed in gold leaf beneath a pyramidal shingle roof crowned by a bronze phoenix. The reliquary hall of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's Kitayama villa burned in an arson attack in 1950 and its National Treasure designation was withdrawn; the present Kinkaku was rebuilt in 1955 from the drawings of the 1904–06 dismantling repair and re-gilded with five-fold leaf in 1987. It is a faithful reconstruction, not a Muromachi original, which is why the timeline records 1955.
facts: Form: a three-storey wooden pavilion facing south over Kyōko-chi pond, formally 'two roofs, three storeys' because no eave separates the first and second floors. The lower two floors are five bays by four, the third three bays square; the roof is pyramidal and shingled, topped by a bronze phoenix. The ground-floor Hossui-in is plain shinden-style wood, while the Chōondō and Kukkyōchō above are fully gilded outside.

History: listed as a Specially Protected Building in 1897 and as a (pre-war) National Treasure in 1929; burned to the ground by an arsonist monk on 2 July 1950; rebuilt from the Meiji repair drawings from 1952 and dedicated in October 1955. The 'Shōwa Great Repair' of 1986–87 re-lacquered the building, applied about 200,000 sheets of five-fold gold leaf and replaced the phoenix. The garden became a Special Historic Site and Special Place of Scenic Beauty in 1956.

Caveats: before the fire only the third floor retained gold, and whether the second floor was ever gilded is disputed (Miyakami Shigetaka argues it was not); the rebuilding gilded the second floor entirely. The reconstructed pavilion is not itself a designated cultural property; Rokuon-ji was inscribed as a component of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto in 1994.
captions: Golden Pavilion of Rokuon-ji, surviving three-story Shariden reconstruction · Line drawing
Drawn from the surviving structure

jp_ginkaku.name: Ginkaku-ji
jp_ginkaku.yearNote: Temple records state that the ridgepole of the Kannon-den was raised in 1489 and that it was still unfinished when Ashikaga Yoshimasa died in 1490; the timeline marks the documented year of the ridgepole raising and does not presume a completion year.
jp_ginkaku.lede: There is not a flake of silver on it. The Kannon Hall of Jishō-ji is one of only two buildings surviving from Ashikaga Yoshimasa's Higashiyama villa; its pillars were raised and ridge set in the third month of 1489, and it was still unfinished when Yoshimasa died the following year. Two storeys under a pyramidal shingle roof: the lower Shinkūden is a residential, shoin-like room, the upper Chōonkaku has bell-shaped windows and panelled doors like a small Zen Buddha hall. About 8 m on a side, it is smaller and quieter than his grandfather Yoshimitsu's Kinkaku, yet it is the only original pavilion-in-a-garden of the Muromachi period.
