fj_luoyang.name: Luoyang Bridge
fj_luoyang.sub: Stone beam bridge · Run of piers (detail)
fj_luoyang.era: Completed in the 4th year of Jiayou
fj_luoyang.yearNote: Begun in 1053 and completed in 1059; the plate takes only one section and does not use this detail to represent the whole bridge.
fj_luoyang.lede: At the mouth of the Luoyang River the Song builders did three things that later generations never tired of praising: they dumped rock along the bridge line to form a low submerged dyke as a 'raft foundation', they farmed oysters on the footing stones so that the shellfish cemented the blocks together, and they used the rise and fall of the tide to float stone beams of more than ten tonnes on rafts and set them onto the piers. Begun in 1053 by Wang Shi and others, the bridge was completed in 1059 under the prefect Cai Xiang, and is the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China. The plate takes a stretch of several consecutive boat-shaped piers and their beams.
facts: Form: a stone beam bridge running northeast-southwest, now about 731 m long and 4.5 m wide, with 47 spans and 45 stone piers in the main section, built in two parts around the mid-river islet of Zhongzhou; every pier has a boat-shaped cutwater on the upstream side; the deck beams are single slabs of stone up to 11 m long, 0.98 m wide and 0.8 m thick, weighing over ten tonnes.

Dating: in 1053 Wang Shi, Lu Xi and thirteen others jointly began a stone bridge and failed to finish it in three years; between 1056 and 1059 Cai Xiang, twice prefect of Quanzhou, directed its completion and wrote the 153-character Record of Wan'an Bridge, carved on a stele. The bridge was repaired 27 times down to 1993 and came through the great Quanzhou earthquake of 1604 unharmed.

Significance: the earliest surviving sea-crossing stone bridge in China, it opened three centuries of bridge building in Song-Yuan Quanzhou; its raft foundations, oyster-cemented footings and tidal floating of beams were inherited by Anping Bridge and others. Seven stone pagodas from the Song onward and four guardian stone generals survive on the bridge and the islet, and in 2021 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.
captions: Luoyang Bridge · Stone beams and piers
Northern Song · Completed in the 4th year of Jiayou

protection.scope: Surviving section of the Luoyang stone beam bridge

fj_tianhou.name: Tianhou Temple, Quanzhou
fj_tianhou.sub: Main hall · Southern Fujian upswept ridges
fj_tianhou.era: Founded in the 2nd year of Qingyuan
fj_tianhou.yearNote: 1196 is the founding year of the Tianhou Temple; the main hall has been repaired in successive periods, and the plate shows its present state.
fj_tianhou.lede: Leaving Quanzhou by the south gate, Deji Gate, one came first to the Tianhou Temple and then went down to the Jin River to put to sea: this was the first stop for sailors paying their respects to Mazu in the Song and Yuan. The temple was built in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; in 1232 the prefect Zhen Dexiu came in person to sacrifice, bringing Mazu into the official cult, and in 1278 the court titled her 'Celestial Consort'. The main hall in the plate is five bays wide under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with steeply upturned ridges; its surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century, and it sits on a granite platform a metre high.
facts: Form: the main hall is five bays (24.6 m) wide and five bays (23 m) deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof with the high upswept ridges of southern Fujian; it stands on a granite platform 1 m above the ground whose four faces carry reliefs of carp turning into dragons, galloping steeds and cranes among clouds. The surviving main structure took shape in the 19th century.

History: founded in 1196 as the Shunji Palace; brought into official ritual after Zhen Dexiu's sacrifice in 1232; Mazu was titled Tianfei in 1278 and the investiture was conducted in 1281 by Pu Shiwen, superintendent of the Maritime Trade Office; Zheng He petitioned for repairs in 1407 and Shi Lang for the title 'Tianhou' in 1684; the hall was repaired to its original regulations in 1815 and 1821.

Layout: set at the southern end of the old city, linking the town within to the port without, the temple keeps a front-hall-and-rear-chamber layout formed before the 16th century, with gate, stage, worship court, main hall, rear chamber and dressing tower along the axis on a site of about 6,800 square metres; the rear chamber holds a reused pair of Yuan-dynasty sixteen-sided Hindu diabase columns. Inscribed as World Heritage in 2021.
captions: Tianhou Temple, Quanzhou · Main hall
Founded in the Southern Song · Later repairs

protection.scope: Front of the main hall of the Tianhou Temple, Quanzhou

fj_zhangzhou_paifang.name: Zhangzhou Stone Memorial Archways · Sanshi Zai'er Archway
fj_zhangzhou_paifang.yearNote: Sources differ on the exact construction year of the Sanshi Zai'er Archway, so it is placed approximately in the Wanli reign; the plate shows only this archway and does not represent the whole group of four.
fj_zhangzhou_paifang.place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Hong Kong Road, Xiangcheng
fj_zhangzhou_paifang.lede: On Hong Kong Road in the old town of Zhangzhou, two Ming stone archways face each other 28.5 m apart along a north-south line; this is the northern one. In 1619 the court raised it to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, together with his father and grandfather, three generations in all; the two faces of the tablet read 'Three Generations of Vice Ministers' and 'Served with Distinction in Both Capitals'. It is 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, built of alternating grey-green and white stone, a representative use of southern Fujian stone carving in a commemorative gateway.
facts: Form: a stone archway of three bays, five roofs and twelve columns, 8.09 m wide and 11 m high, oriented north-south; built of alternating bluestone and white stone, with fish-shaped ridge ornaments on the roofs, upturned eave corners, and beams and lintels dividing the tiers below the main tablet; brackets, sparrow braces, panels and hanging posts are all carved in stone.

Date: according to the Fujian Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau the archway was erected in 1619, the 47th year of Wanli, to honour Jiang Mengyu, Right Vice Minister of Personnel at Nanjing, and his father and grandfather; the main tablet is inscribed in regular script 'Sanshi Zai'er' on one face and 'Liangjing Yangli' on the other. The 'Minister and Third-Place Graduate' archway just to the south, for Lin Shizhang, is fourteen years older.

A set of four: the national heritage listing 'Zhangzhou Stone Archways' comprises the two Ming archways on Hong Kong Road and two Kangxi-era archways for military commanders on Yuekou Street; the panels of the latter even carry carved foreigners with curly hair and hats, a reflection of overseas trade in the Yuegang era. The plate shows only the Sanshi Zai'er archway.
captions: Sanshi Zai'er Archway
Wanli reign, Ming · Part of the Zhangzhou Stone Memorial Archways

protection.scope: Sanshi Zai'er Archway on Hong Kong Road, as a single structure

fj_jiangdong.name: Jiangdong Bridge
fj_jiangdong.yearNote: Built 1237–1241; the bridge was repeatedly repaired in later periods, and the plate shows a surviving section of stone beams and piers.
fj_jiangdong.place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · North Stream of the Jiulong River
fj_jiangdong.lede: Each stone beam is twenty-two or twenty-three metres long and weighs close to two hundred tonnes; how craftsmen eight centuries ago set them onto piers in a racing current was something the bridge engineer Mao Yisheng, writing in 1962, still called 'not fully understood'. Jiangdong Bridge, formerly Hudu Bridge, was rebuilt in stone after the timber bridge burnt in 1237, at the urging of the Zhangzhou prefect Li Shao, and took a little over three years. Today only five intact piers on the west bank, two spans of deck and nine ruined pier bases remain, with a 1970 road bridge carried above them. The plate takes a surviving stretch of beams and piers.
facts: Form: a multi-span stone beam bridge. Surviving are 5 intact piers, two spans of original deck, 9 ruined pier bases and the east and west abutment walls, a remnant 100.35 m long; the piers are built of interlocking stone blocks 0.35 x 0.4 x 5.2 m into a ship's-prow shape, 11.4 m long and 5.3 m wide; each span carries 3 to 5 stone beams 22-23 m long, 1.15-1.5 m wide and 1.3-1.6 m thick, weighing nearly 200 tonnes.

Dating: a pontoon bridge was laid here in 1190 and the prefect Zhuang Xia replaced it in the Jiading era with a timber bridge on stone piers; after the timber bridge burnt in 1237 the prefect Li Shao urged a stone rebuilding, completed in a little over three years. The Longxi County Gazetteer records it as 'twenty chi wide and two thousand chi long' with fifteen openings. In 1970 a reinforced-concrete road bridge was raised on top of the old bridge.

Significance: counted with the Luoyang, Anping and Longjiang bridges as the four great stone bridges of Fujian, its beams are of a size rare in the history of bridge building anywhere, and Joseph Needham's Science and Civilisation in China calls it 'an interesting historical problem'; Zheng Chenggong defeated Qing forces here in 1652, and Japanese bombing in the war of resistance left only the five piers on the west bank.
captions: Jiangdong Bridge · Stone beams (detail)
Southern Song · Jiaxi reign

protection.scope: Surviving part of the Jiangdong stone beam bridge

fj_dongshan_guandi.name: Guandi Temple, Dongshan
fj_dongshan_guandi.sub: Gate tower · Southern Fujian cut-porcelain ridge decoration
fj_dongshan_guandi.era: Founded in the 20th year of Hongwu
fj_dongshan_guandi.yearNote: 1387 is the temple's founding year; the plate takes the surviving gate tower and entrance, and the ridge decoration and buildings have been repaired.
fj_dongshan_guandi.lede: The temple gate is not a wall but a pavilion carried on six stone columns, known locally as the Taizi Ting. The three columns on either side lean slightly inward to form a triangular brace; above them close-set bracket clusters carry a palace-style pavilion roof whose ridges are covered in jianci diao, cut-porcelain mosaic: shards of coloured ware pieced into the Eight Immortals crossing the sea, auspicious beasts and figures from Tang and Song tales, their colours unfading. The temple was founded in 1387, the twentieth year of Hongwu, and was enlarged and rebuilt in the Zhengde and Kangxi reigns; it is the ancestral temple from which many Guandi temples in Taiwan drew their incense. The plate shows this gate pavilion and the stone steps before it.
facts: Form: the gate is of the pailou type, six round stone columns carrying tiers of brackets and a palace-style pavilion roof, the three columns on each side leaning inward for triangular stability; the roof and ridges are covered with cut-porcelain mosaic, the Eight Immortals and beasts such as qilin, elephant and lion on the front, Tang and Song story figures on the back. The whole temple is three bays wide and six deep, on a site of more than 680 square metres.

Dating: founded in 1387 (Hongwu 20), enlarged from 1508 (Zhengde 3) and completed in 1512 (Zhengde 7), rebuilt in 1680 (Kangxi 19); repeatedly added to since, so that the timberwork is partly Ming and partly Qing and modern. The halls still keep a carved wooden couplet composed by Huang Daozhou and a board inscribed by the Xianfeng emperor reading 'Wanshi renji'.

Significance: together with the Guandi temples at Yuncheng in Shanxi, Luoyang in Henan and Dangyang in Hubei it is counted among the four great Guandi temples of China, and it is the ancestral temple of nearly a thousand Guandi temples in Taiwan. The Taizi Ting, with its leaning columns and bracket sets, has stood through centuries of island typhoons and earthquakes, a representative work in which Minnan builders fused structural mechanics with cut-porcelain ornament.
captions: Guandi Temple, Dongshan · Gate tower
Founded in the Hongwu reign, Ming · Surviving facade

protection.scope: Front gate tower and stone steps

fj_eryi.name: Eryi Building, Hua'an
fj_eryi.era: Built in the 5th year of Qianlong
fj_eryi.lede: A huge ring 73.4 m across, four storeys and 16 m high, its outer wall 2.53 m thick at the base, yet not the gallery-type round house of the Hakka but a Minnan unit house: sixteen units, each with its own stair running from ground to top, divided from one another by walls and linked only by a concealed corridor along the outer wall. Jiang Shixiong of the fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan began it in 1740, the fifth year of Qianlong, and the work took thirty years. More than two hundred murals and as many painted panels survive inside. The plate shows the rammed-earth face of the outer ring.
facts: Form: a double-ring round tulou; the outer ring is four storeys, 16 m high and 73.4 m in outer diameter, with a wall up to 2.53 m thick. It is divided into 16 units with 213 rooms in all, each unit with its own stair; there is no continuous front gallery, but a concealed corridor runs along the inner face of the outer wall. The single-storey inner ring is joined to each unit by a passage.

Dating: begun in 1740 (Qianlong 5) by Jiang Shixiong, fourteenth generation of the Jiang clan and holder of the honorific 'xiangyin dabin', and completed around 1770 (Qianlong 34), after thirty years. Inside survive 226 murals, 228 painted panels, 349 wood carvings and 163 couplets, direct evidence for the mid-Qing date of its fittings.

Comparison: Eryi Lou combines features of the Hakka inner-gallery type and the Minnan unit type; in 1996 it became the first tulou listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site, and in 2008 it was inscribed as World Heritage together with the tulou of Yongding and Nanjing as 'Fujian Tulou', of which it is the largest single building by area.
captions: Eryi Building, Hua'an · Exterior
5th year of Qianlong, Qing · Round tulou

protection.scope: Round rammed-earth outer ring of Eryi Building, Hua'an
protection.note: Eryi Building was itself listed in the fourth batch and later merged into the Fujian Tulou; it is labeled with the batch in which it was first announced.

fj_hegui.name: Hegui Building, Nanjing County
fj_hegui.yearNote: Placed approximately in the Yongzheng reign of the Qing; the traditionally reported year is not treated as a verified construction date for each story.
fj_hegui.place: Fujian · Zhangzhou · Pushan Village, Nanjing County
fj_hegui.lede: A five-storey square building 21.5 m high, the tallest of all the Fujian tulou, yet built on a swamp. When the Jian clan of Changjiao raised it in 1732 they first drove more than two hundred pine piles into the soft ground, laid timber over them and built a cobblestone footing before ramming up the earth walls; after more than two centuries the building still stands level. Each floor has 28 rooms, 140 in all, with a single door in the middle of the front. The plate takes the five-storey earthen front and the low wall before it, without showing the inner court.
facts: Form: a square tulou of the inner-corridor type, five storeys and 21.5 m high, on a site of 1,547 square metres with a floor area of 3,574 square metres; 28 rooms per floor and 140 in all, one central door and a stair at each of the four corners; the massive rammed-earth outer wall is pierced by close rows of small windows, a defensive form different from the round tulou.

Dating: built in 1732, the tenth year of Yongzheng, by Jian Ciping of the thirteenth generation of the Changjiao Jian clan at a cost of fifteen thousand taels of silver; first raised to four storeys and given a fifth when rebuilt. It stands on marshland, on a foundation of more than two hundred pine piles and timber bedding with a cobblestone wall footing, which is why it has stayed sound for over two hundred years.

Comparison: Hegui Lou is known as the 'tallest' of the Fujian tulou, also called Shanjiao Lou, and is one of the few single tulou listed individually as World Heritage; in 2008 it was inscribed together with Huaiyuan Lou and the Tianluokeng and Hekeng clusters as the Nanjing portion of 'Fujian Tulou'.
captions: Hegui Building, Nanjing County · Front
Yongzheng reign, Qing · Five-story square building

protection.scope: Five-story square tulou of Hegui Building, Nanjing County
protection.note: Hegui Building is included under the fifth-batch Fujian Tulou listing and does not take the fourth batch of the original Eryi Building unit.

fj_hulishan.name: Hulishan Fort
fj_hulishan.yearNote: The plate shows part of the surviving Krupp gun emplacement; 1894 is an approximate placement for the fort's late Qing construction phase and does not mean all installations were mounted in the same year.
fj_hulishan.lede: A Krupp breech-loading coastal gun of 280 mm calibre, thirteen metres long and fifty tonnes in weight, still mounted on the emplacement it occupied more than a century ago: the largest surviving nineteenth-century coastal gun in the world. Hulishan Fort was built on the memorial of Peng Chuhan, commander of the Fujian naval forces, and Bian Baodi, governor-general of Fujian and Zhejiang; work began in the third month of 1894 and finished in the tenth month of 1896, a half-bunker, half-rampart fort commanding the entrance to Xiamen harbour. The plate takes only the Krupp gun and its emplacement on the east battery, not the whole fort.
facts: Form: a fort of half-bunker, half-rampart type with east and west batteries for the main and supporting guns, over 70,000 square metres in all, of which the citadel is over 13,000; the gun platforms are rammed from a mortar of camphor-tree sap, glutinous rice, lime, paper fibre and sand. The surviving east gun has a calibre of 280 mm, a length of 13.13 m and a weight of 50 tonnes, turns through 360 degrees and has a range of 16,000 m.

Dating: begun on the eighth day of the third month of 1894 and completed on the eighth day of the tenth month of 1896, a construction period of two years and eight months; the east gun is marked '28 cm K.L/40 C/87', made by Krupp in Germany in 1887; the west gun was scrapped in the Great Steel Drive of 1958, and the two 150 mm secondary guns were carried off by the Japanese occupying Xiamen in 1938.

Significance: in the late Qing four 280 mm coastal guns were bought from Krupp to strengthen the southeastern coast; the two at Dianguangshan at the mouth of the Min River are gone and this is the only one left at Hulishan, certified in 2000 as the largest surviving 19th-century coastal gun in the world. Its crossfire with the Yuziwei fort on the opposite shore closed the channel, a surviving piece of the Self-Strengthening Movement's coastal defences.
captions: Hulishan Fort · Krupp gun emplacement
Guangxu reign, Qing · Coastal defense remains

protection.scope: Surviving Krupp gun and part of its emplacement at the East Battery

fj_laojun.name: Laojun Rock Statue, Mount Qingyuan
fj_laojun.sub: Seated Lord Lao · Song stone carving
fj_laojun.yearNote: 1150 is only an approximate placement on the Song timeline, not a confirmed carving date for Laojun Rock; the subject is registered under the third-batch listing of the Laojun Rock Statue.
fj_laojun.lede: A single natural granite boulder, lightly carved to follow the shape of the rock, became a seated Laozi leaning on an armrest with his beard falling to his chest. The Quanzhou Prefectural Gazetteer puts it plainly: 'the stone image was formed by heaven; enthusiasts merely added a little carving.' At 5.63 m high it is the largest surviving Song-dynasty Daoist stone statue in China. A group of Daoist halls, the Zhenjun and Beidou halls, once stood below Qingyuan Mountain; the buildings are all gone, and only this Laojun remains seated at the foot of the hill, looking south over Quanzhou and the Jin River.
facts: Form: carved from one free-standing natural granite boulder, 5.63 m high, 8.01 m wide and 6.85 m deep; the Old Lord has a bald, high forehead, ears reaching his shoulders and a flowing beard, wears a Daoist robe with overlapping lapels and sits on the ground, right hand on an armrest, left hand on his knee, legs folded, the robe folds rendered in a few clear lines. The stone armrest shows Yuan-dynasty furniture features and is probably a later addition.

Dating: He Qiaoyuan's Minshu records that Zhu Xi visited this 'Yuxian Rock', so the statue existed by the 12th century; stone building members excavated around it, including cap-blocks with wedge tenons and arch keystones, match the work of the Southern Song twin pagodas of Kaiyuan Temple and the Liusheng Pagoda, the archaeological basis for dating it to the Song.

Significance: the largest surviving Song Daoist stone sculpture in China, which together with the Confucian Temple represents the native mainstream culture behind the Song-Yuan port of Quanzhou; it is the largest of the seven groups and nine Song-Yuan stone statues on Qingyuan Mountain, and in 2021 was inscribed as one of the 22 component sites of the World Heritage property 'Quanzhou: Emporium of the World in Song-Yuan China'.
captions: Laojun Rock, Mount Qingyuan · Seated figure
Song stone carving · Third batch, national protected site

protection.scope: Seated Laojun figure at Mount Qingyuan and the connected native rock
protection.note: The Laojun Rock Statue was itself listed in the third batch and later merged into the Mount Qingyuan Stone Statues; it is labeled with the batch in which it was first announced.

fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.name: Fuzhou Confucian Temple
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.era: Present structure from the Xianfeng reign
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.yearNote: The Confucian Temple has earlier origins; the Dacheng Hall is placed approximately by its 1851–1854 construction phase, and the plate shows its present state after the 2026 restoration.
fj_fuzhou_wenmiao.lede: In the eighth month of 1851 a fire destroyed the Fuzhou Confucian Temple; rebuilding began that twelfth month and was finished in the sixth month of 1854, and what stands today is that layout. The Hall of Great Achievement is seven bays wide and four deep under a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, on a stone platform a metre and a half high; a ring of twenty-two stone eave columns runs under the lower eaves, the eight stone interior columns weigh about nine tonnes each, and timber columns are jointed onto the stone column heads, a Fujian practice of mixing stone and timber. At the end of 2025 it completed its first major repair in the more than 170 years since the rebuilding.
facts: Form: seven bays wide and four deep, with a double-eave hip-and-gable roof, 19.6 m high, standing on a stone platform 1.46 m above the forecourt; the lower part of the column-and-tie timber frame is stone, 22 stone eave columns and 8 stone interior columns, with 18 full-height timber columns jointed above their heads; between the upper and lower eaves are 42 bracket sets of five tiers and eight layers, and the ceiling well is painted with a star chart.

Dating: in 773 the commissioner Li Yi moved the prefectural school here, a temple to Confucius was first made in the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song, and the Hall of Great Achievement was built in 1374; fire struck on the third day of the eighth month of 1851, and the surviving temple was built between the twelfth month of 1851 and the sixth month of 1854. The year-long major repair of 2024-2025 was the first in more than 170 years since the rebuilding.

Layout: the surviving temple covers 7,552 square metres with about 4,000 square metres of buildings; along the axis from south to north are the outer forecourt, Lingxing Gate, the half-moon pool, Dacheng Gate, the moon terrace and the Hall of Great Achievement, flanked by galleries, official halls and shrines to local worthies; the hall's floor area ranks among the largest of its kind in China, and inside stand bluestone seated figures of Confucius and his four attendants with the seventy-two disciples.
captions: Fuzhou Confucian Temple · Dacheng Hall
Xianfeng reign, Qing · Seven bays

protection.scope: Front of the Dacheng Hall of the Fuzhou Confucian Temple

tw_tainan_confucius.name: Dacheng Hall, Tainan Confucian Temple
tw_tainan_confucius.yearNote: 1665 marks the founding of the temple and school, and the Dacheng Hall was enlarged in 1712; the surviving hall was dismantled, restored and rebuilt in 1917, and the timeline is placed by the most recent large-scale restoration of the present main structure.
tw_tainan_confucius.lede: Dacheng Hall at Tainan’s Confucius Temple presents a solemn frontage with a broad roof and double eaves. The terrace, low enclosure walls and axial steps organize the ceremonial space before it. Founded in the Ming-Zheng period, the temple gained important forms through Qing reconstruction, while major repairs under Japanese rule shaped its current appearance. Education and ritual meet here: rooftop Tongtian vessels and continuing ceremonies keep cultural traditions visible in architecture and practice.
facts: The roof accounts for roughly half the hall’s total height. Double eaves and a rounded ridge emphasize its central status; an axial stair and terrace organize ceremony, with Tongtian vessels decorating the ridge.

The temple dates to 1665, while reconstruction of Dacheng Hall in 1712 established its double-eaved roof. Major repairs followed under Japanese rule, so the Ming-Zheng foundation date cannot date all present building materials.

The hall is used for rites honouring Confucius. The terrace axis and side passages express ritual hierarchy; the temple’s union of schooling and worship, and continuing ceremonies, sustain links with local educational life.
captions: Tainan Confucian Temple · Front of the Dacheng Hall
Temple founded 1665 · Dismantled and restored 1917

tw_lukang_longshan.name: Five-Door Hall, Lukang Longshan Temple
tw_lukang_longshan.yearNote: The temple moved to its present site in 1786, and the 1831 renovation established its scale; the plate shows the present state of the Five-Door Hall after component replacements in the 1960s and later restoration, and does not date every column and beam to the Qing.
tw_lukang_longshan.lede: The Five-Gate Hall at Lukang Longshan Temple faces an inner court, its entrances, dragon columns and layered eaves forming the temple’s inward threshold. Connected to a theatre, it serves circulation, worship and performances offered to the gods. The temple moved here under Qianlong, and Daoguang-period rebuilding established its present arrangement. Earthquake repairs and replaced components followed. Stone carvings and timber work show how Quanzhou immigrant beliefs became part of Lukang’s architectural traditions.
facts: The hall and theatre stand between the entrance gate and main hall. An extra front eave added to the double-eaved hip-and-gable roof creates three tiers; openings, dragon columns and side carvings organize the frontage.

The temple moved to this site in 1786, and rebuilding in 1831 established its main arrangement. Twentieth-century painting and replacement of columns and beams in the Five-Gate Hall mean its materials have not remained entirely unchanged since the Qing.

Paired dragon columns and dragon-and-tiger stone reliefs display refined carving. Quanzhou immigrants and Lukang merchants supported the temple; the shared passage and ritual theatre connect religious life, commercial communities and craftsmanship.
captions: Lukang Longshan Temple · Front of the Five-Door Hall
Relocated 1786 · Renovated 1831

tw_taipei_northgate.name: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City
tw_taipei_northgate.era: Completed in the 10th year of Guangxu (1884)
tw_taipei_northgate.lede: Taipei’s North Gate, also called Cheng’en Gate, has thick brick walls above a stone base. A single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and swallowtail ridge add lighter lines to its fortified body. Part of Taipei’s late-Qing city defences, it once connected the enclosed city with Dadaocheng. The walls and outer enclosure were later removed, leaving the gate among modern streets. Its closed form and former traffic role reveal both late-Qing defence and urban transformation.
facts: The enclosed gate combines stone blocks and brick, with two layers of walls inside and a traditional timber roof frame above. A single-eaved hip-and-gable roof and upturned swallowtail ridge contrast with the massive walls and stone arch.
Construction of Taipei’s city defences began in 1882 and finished in 1884. The North Gate’s inscription dates to 1882: gates preceded the walls, and 1884 marks completion of the city-defence project.

The gate once carried traffic toward Dadaocheng, while its enclosed structure answered the demands of firearm defence. Retaining its earlier outward form after the walls disappeared, it offers material evidence of Taipei’s growth.
captions: North Gate of Taipei Prefectural City · Cheng'en Gate
10th year of Guangxu, Qing (1884)

sc_leshan.name: Leshan Giant Buddha
sc_leshan.yearNote: The timeline is placed by 803, the year the Buddha statue was completed. The plate covers the surviving head down to the chest and abdomen and does not represent the complete 71-meter seated figure.
sc_leshan.lede: The head is 14.7 m high, the ears 7 m long, and 1,021 spiral curls are set in 18 rows, with a transverse drainage channel hidden in the 4th, 9th and 18th rows and a pair of connected tunnels cut behind the ears: the Tang builders put the drainage inside the Buddha's head, and so this 71 m seated Maitreya has held to its cliff for twelve centuries. The monk Haitong vowed to carve it in 713 (Kaiyuan 1); the work passed through Zhangqiu Jianqiong and was completed under Wei Gao in 803 (Zhenyuan 19), about ninety years in all. The plate takes the surviving head and torso down to the belly and does not draw the legs or the base.
facts: Form: a Maitreya seated with feet down, hands on knees, cut into the cliff of Lingyun Hill in an open-topped niche, 71 m high in all; the head is 10 m wide and 14.7 m high, the ears 7 m long, the nose 5.6 m, eyes and mouth 3.3 m each, the shoulders 24 m across; the 1,021 spiral curls on the head form 18 rows. The right ear and the nose are later repairs in timber coated with plaster, not original stone.

Dating: Haitong began carving in 713 (Kaiyuan 1) and work stopped at his death; in 739 (Kaiyuan 27) Zhangqiu Jianqiong, military governor of Jiannan, gave his salary to resume it, and it halted again in 746 at the knees; in 785 (Zhenyuan 1) Wei Gao gave his salary for a third campaign, finished in 803 (Zhenyuan 19), and Wei Gao's 'Record of the Great Maitreya Stone Image of Lingyun Temple, Jiazhou' was cut on the cliff to the right of the niche.

Significance: when finished the figure was painted and gilded and sheltered by a timber pavilion, already ruined by the early Northern Song; the pavilion was rebuilt under Renzong and later lost for good. In 1925 a red-sandstone mask was put over the face and removed in the 1930s. Around the Buddha some 206 niches with about 452 figures survive. Listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1982 and, with Mount Emei, as a mixed cultural and natural World Heritage site in 1996.
captions: Leshan Giant Buddha · Head to chest and abdomen
Begun 713 · Completed 803

protection.scope: Surviving cliff-carved head to chest and abdomen of the Leshan Giant Buddha
protection.note: Its first announcement in the second batch is explicitly confirmed by the State Council's sixth-batch merged list; only the surviving head to chest and abdomen of the Buddha is drawn, not the Lingbao Pagoda that was merged into the listing.

sc_baoen.name: Bao'en Temple, Pingwu
sc_baoen.yearNote: Work on the temple began in 1439, its main buildings had taken shape by 1446, and the whole was completed in 1460. The Mahavira Hall is placed at about 1450 within this construction period; no unconfirmed completion date is given for the single hall.
sc_baoen.lede: Deep in the mountains of north-west Sichuan, a monastery built by the local chieftain Wang Xi and his son uses glazed-tile roofs, nanmu timber throughout and more than two thousand bracket sets, official northern practice at every turn, which has earned it the name 'Forbidden City of the deep hills'. The Mahavira Hall is the main hall of the monastery, roofed in green glazed tile, with three gilded seated Buddhas inside and Ming murals on all four walls. Work began in 1440 (Zhengtong 5), the main halls were finished by 1446 (Zhengtong 11), and the sculpture and murals were completed in 1460 (Tianshun 4). The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall only, without the gate or side halls.
facts: Form: the Mahavira Hall is the principal hall, roofed in green glazed tile, its ceiling painted, with three gilded seated Buddhas at the front and Ming murals on the walls; every timber member in the monastery is nanmu, and the buildings use more than two thousand bracket sets of some forty types (counts range from 36 to 48), hence the name 'museum of dougong'.

Dating: begun in 1440 (Zhengtong 5) by Wang Xi, native chieftain of Pingwu, and his son; the main halls were finished by 1446 (Zhengtong 11) and the sculpture, murals and other ornament by 1460 (Tianshun 4); the great bell in the hall was also cast in 1446. The monastery faces east, 278 m from east to west and 100 m from north to south, with a built area of 3,518 square metres.

Significance: glazed roofs and dragon ornament throughout the halls belong to the official architecture of Ming north China and are rare in the hills of north-west Sichuan; the name 'Bao'en', repaying a debt of gratitude, was chosen to thank the court for permitting the building. The monastery also holds a nanmu Thousand-armed Guanyin and a revolving sutra cabinet, neither shown in the plate. Listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996.
captions: Pingwu Bao'en Temple · Mahavira Hall
Zhengtong to Tianshun reigns, Ming (1439–1460)

protection.scope: Front of the Mahavira Hall of Pingwu Bao'en Temple

sc_wuliang.name: Wuliang Pagoda
sc_wuliang.yearNote: The State Council's sixth-batch list dates it to the Song. The timeline position of about 1000 is for placement within the dynasty and is not a confirmed completion year; the traditional attribution to the Jianlong reign is not presented as a proven exact date.
sc_wuliang.lede: A plaque set into the tenth storey on the east face reads 'Pagoda of Ten Thousand Years of Jianlong', and for a long time the tower was taken to be a work of the Jianlong era of the Northern Song (960–963); yet its square plan and massive brackets look like a Tang pagoda, and recently some have pushed it, on the evidence of its imitation timber details, to the Jiading era of the Southern Song. Whichever view holds, it is one of the earliest Song pagodas in Sichuan. A square thirteen-storey brick pagoda of pavilion type, 39.56 m high, its walls carry columns, beams and bracket sets built in brick, and the first storey even has a flat plate-beam with camel-hump blocks. The plate follows the White Pagoda as it stands.
facts: Form: a square thirteen-storey brick pagoda imitating a timber pavilion, 39.56 m high, on a dressed-stone platform that was originally a Sumeru pedestal carved with dragon scales; each face is built with four columns and three bays, and the whole has 93 small niches, 10 doors and 9 windows. The brackets are four-step sets with a single arm or a single ang; the architraves of the lower three storeys are shaped like round timbers, only the first storey has a plate-beam with camel-hump blocks, and the finial is a cast-iron millstone shape.

Dating: the pagoda bears no construction date. A plaque on the east face of the tenth storey reads 'Pagoda of Ten Thousand Years of Jianlong', on which the New Gazetteer of Nanchong County dated it to the Jianlong era of the Northern Song; other views place it in the late Tang or Five Dynasties, or around the Southern Song Jiading era, and when listed as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 2006 it was dated Song. The base was repaired in 1641 (Chongzhen 14), and the platform and cracks in the body were repaired in 1981 and 1995.

Significance: the lower four storeys have a solid central pillar with brick stairs winding up around it, and from the fifth storey up the levels are joined by corbelling; it is a case study in the transition from Tang to Song pagodas and has been called 'the first Song pagoda of Sichuan'. The body is plastered greyish-white throughout, hence the name White Pagoda, while the imitation timber members are painted ochre; the plate follows the present colouring and does not reconstruct historical colours.
captions: Wuliang Pagoda · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
Song · Construction year undetermined

protection.scope: Surviving thirteen-story brick Wuliang Pagoda, Nanchong

sc_zhanghuan.name: Zhang Huanhou Shrine
sc_zhanghuan.yearNote: Diwan Tower belongs to the surviving Ming–Qing shrine complex; about 1600 is only a timeline placement, does not assert that all components were built in the same year, and is certainly not based on the year of Zhang Fei's death.
sc_zhanghuan.lede: The most striking thing in the shrine is not the main hall but the Diwan Lou behind the gate, a tower more than ten metres high: double eaves on a hip-and-gable roof, and beneath them every bracket set thrusts out a slanting ang at forty-five degrees, like a rack of halberds. The name takes up Zhang Fei's fame as 'a match for ten thousand', and the board reads 'Not ten thousand men could withstand him'. Zhang Fei died at Langzhong in 221 (Zhangwu 1) and was buried here, and the townspeople raised a temple before the tomb; the present buildings are the result of repeated loss and rebuilding in the Ming and Qing, and the Diwan Lou dates from the Ming. The plate takes the Diwan Lou and its attached front eaves only, without the main hall, tomb pavilion or tomb.
facts: Form: the Diwan Lou is over ten metres high with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, a pavilion storey above and a broad front eave below, and every bracket set under the eaves projects a slanting ang at 45 degrees. It is the second building on the shrine's axis, with the gate before it and the paired gateways and main hall behind; the red columns and the doors and windows between them in the plate are its lower front eave.

Dating: the shrine takes its name from Zhang Fei's posthumous title Marquis Huan; he was killed by his own officers in 221 (Zhangwu 1) and buried at Langzhong, and a temple has stood over the tomb for more than seventeen hundred years. The present complex of several courtyards is Ming and Qing rebuilding, with the Diwan Lou a surviving Ming structure. Listed as a Sichuan provincial protected site in 1991 and a Major National Historical and Cultural Site in 1996.

Significance: the shrine covers more than 6,600 square metres with over 2,400 square metres of buildings; along the axis stand the gate, the Diwan Lou, the gateways, the main hall, the rear hall, the tomb pavilion and Zhang Fei's tomb, whose mound is 8 m high, 25 m east to west and 42 m north to south. Langzhong is counted among the four great ancient cities of China, and this shrine is an important Three Kingdoms site within its walls.
captions: Zhang Huanhou Shrine · Diwan Tower
Surviving Ming–Qing buildings · Approximate date

protection.scope: Diwan Tower and connected front eaves of the Zhang Huanhou Shrine, Langzhong

sc_luodai.name: Luodai Guild Halls
sc_luodai.era: First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913
sc_luodai.yearNote: Yuwang Palace was first built in the Qianlong period of the Qing and rebuilt in 1913 after a fire in 1912. The timeline uses the rebuilding year of the surviving main structure and does not follow the parent unit's "Qing" label to mark the present gate tower as original Qianlong work.
sc_luodai.lede: Three arched doorways side by side, the middle one tallest, and above them the rolling, upturned outline of fire-walls topped with moulded clouds and dragons: this is the gate of the Huguang Guild Hall at Luodai. The hall is dedicated to Yu the Great and so is also called the Yuwang Gong, the place where Qing-era migrants of the 'Huguang fills Sichuan' movement met, worshipped and watched opera in the eastern hills of Chengdu. Built in 1746 (Qianlong 11), rebuilt in 1860 (Xianfeng 10), burnt in 1912 and rebuilt the next year, so that the gate seen today dates from 1913. With the neighbouring Guangdong, Jiangxi and Chuanbei halls it forms the group known as the Luodai Guild Halls. The plate shows the gate only.
facts: Form: a gate of pailou type with three arched openings, the central bay higher than the flanking ones, finished above with undulating fire-walls crested with moulded clouds and dragons. Inside lie the stage, courtyard and main hall, the central court framed in nanmu timber; the courtyard has no drains yet is said never to flood, which local tradition credits to the protection of King Yu.

Dating: the Huguang Guild Hall was built by subscription among migrants from Huguang in 1746 (Qianlong 11) and rebuilt in 1860 (Xianfeng 10); it burned in 1912 and was rebuilt in 1913, and the present gate belongs to that rebuilding. Listed as a Sichuan provincial protected site in 2002 and in 2006, together with the Guangdong, Jiangxi and Chuanbei halls under the name 'Luodai Guild Halls', as a Major National Historical and Cultural Site.

Significance: more than eighty per cent of Luodai's people are of Hakka descent, and four guild halls, Guangdong, Jiangxi, Huguang and Chuanbei, stand in one town, which has been called 'the home of guild halls', a material record of Qing migrant society in Sichuan. The Chuanbei hall originally stood at Wolong Bridge in Chengdu and was moved here in 1998. The plate omits the street shops and modern signs.
captions: Luodai Guild Halls · Gate tower of Yuwang Palace
First built in the Qing · Rebuilt 1913

protection.scope: Surviving gate tower of Yuwang Palace, Huguang Guild Hall, Luodai

sc_shenque.name: Que of Lord Shen
sc_shenque.era: Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date
sc_shenque.yearNote: The que is an Eastern Han relic; about 150 is a placement within the dynasty on the timeline, not a precise construction date from an inscription. The plate shows only one surviving main que and does not add the lost subsidiary que.
sc_shenque.lede: Of the seven Han que in Quxian only the Shen Fujun que survives as a pair, facing each other east and west some twenty-one metres apart, each 4.84 m high. Down the middle of each shaft runs a single line of clerical script: on the eastern que 'Spirit road of Lord Shen, Internuncio, Commandant of the Northern Camp, Marquis of the Left', on the western 'Spirit road of Lord Shen, Magistrate of Xinfeng, Commandant of Jiaozhi', in a free, flowing hand that keeps to no ruled line, a style of its own among Han clerical inscriptions. A red bird is carved in relief at the top of the shaft and a taotie mask below; on the inner faces the eastern que bears a green dragon and the western a white tiger. It dates from about the Yanguang era of the Eastern Han (122–125). The plate shows one of the two main pillars only; the attached child-pillars are lost.
facts: Form: a mother-and-child que in sandstone imitating timber construction; the two main pillars are each 4.84 m high, the shaft 1.10 m wide and 0.76 m thick, built up in four parts, base, shaft, storey and cap, with the shaft battered inward. Among the brackets of the storey appears a huagong, the only one on any Sichuan que. The outer faces of both pillars are rough and undecorated, proof that child-pillars once stood against them; they no longer survive.

Dating: the shafts carry no date. In form they resemble the Feng Huan que built around 121 (Jianguang 1) but are slightly later, and are generally placed in the Yanguang era of Emperor An of the Eastern Han (122–125); nothing is known of the Shen family who owned them. In 1849 (Daoguang 29) the magistrate Wang Chunyuan set up a 'Record of the Stele Pavilion of Lord Shen's Spirit Road' behind the western que. Listed in 1961 among the first Major National Historical and Cultural Sites.

Significance: the shafts are carved in relief with a red bird, taotie, green dragon, white tiger, door-ring masks and strongmen, and with stories such as riding a deer, playing with a tiger, Dong Yong serving his father and Yang Youji shooting the ape; the jade disc and white tiger on the inner faces are especially fine. The six sites and seven pillars of Quxian make up nearly a quarter of all surviving Han que in China, and since 2019 each has stood under a steel-and-glass shelter, which the plate omits.
captions: Que of Lord Shen · One surviving main que
Eastern Han stone que · Approximate date

cq_shibao.name: Shibaozhai
cq_shibao.era: Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing
cq_shibao.yearNote: Founded in the Wanli reign of the Ming and enlarged several times from the Kangxi to the Tongzhi reigns of the Qing; about 1800 places the surviving tower within the dynasty. Sources differ on when the top three stories took shape, and the whole present tower is not dated to 1956.
cq_shibao.lede: Red timber storeys climb the steep Yuyin cliff, narrowing beneath successive eaves and joining a three-storey Kuixing Pavilion to form Shibaozhai’s twelve-level silhouette. The building relies on the mountain, while stairs connect foot and summit. Ming and Qing projects shaped it over time; early photographs already show the upper pavilion, so its full height cannot be assigned a casual modern enlargement date.
facts: The lower nine storeys recede against the cliff and meet the upper three-storey Kuixing Pavilion. Mortise-and-tenon timber framing includes posts inserted into rock. Round and rectangular windows alternate, while building and mountain cooperate structurally.

Shibaozhai originated in the Ming Wanli period and was expanded repeatedly from Kangxi to Tongzhi; different phases shaped its present form. Accounts differ over the upper three storeys, but a 1909 archival photograph already shows them. The entire building cannot be dated to 1956.

The tower also serves as a route uphill, approaching the summit along the sheer cliff. Its adaptation of timber construction to terrain distinguishes it from a freestanding pagoda: the mountain is essential to its stability and spaces.
captions: Shibaozhai · Twelve-story fortress tower
Founded in the Ming · Enlarged in the Qing

protection.scope: Surviving twelve-story tower of Shibaozhai and the adjoining rock face

cq_huguang.name: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing
cq_huguang.era: Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign
cq_huguang.yearNote: The guild hall complex took shape in the Qing and was enlarged in the Daoguang reign; about 1846 places the surviving Qing structure, and the plate shows the opera stage as repaired in 2003–2005, without asserting that every beam and column is original 1846 work.
cq_huguang.lede: Carved balustrades front a raised stage, while columns and beams frame its open performance area and bring narrative carvings into spectators’ view. The theatre at Chongqing’s Huguang Guildhall belongs to a migrant communal setting where worship, deliberation and entertainment shared courtyard spaces. Qing expansions and modern conservation shaped the buildings; this single theatre front does not date every associated guildhall together.
facts: A raised stage, columns and carved rails organise the façade, with timber carvings beneath the eaves. Facing a courtyard and related to viewing halls and galleries, it forms one theatre within the guildhall complex.

The complex developed throughout the Qing period, with substantial Daoguang-period work; individual associations have different histories. Modern conservation also shaped its present condition. A building’s formation period does not date every surviving beam or column.

Migrant associations established shared places for worship, discussion and social contact away from home. The theatre added public performance to these activities, while carved stories and viewing spaces preserve aspects of migrant life in Chongqing.
captions: Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing · Front of the opera stage
Qing guild hall · Enlarged in the Daoguang reign

protection.scope: Front of the surviving opera stage of the Huguang Guild Hall, Chongqing

cq_diaoyu.name: Diaoyu Fortress Site
cq_diaoyu.era: Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later
cq_diaoyu.yearNote: 1243 is a key milestone in the building of the Southern Song defensive system at Diaoyu Fortress, and the timeline is placed by the site. The upper timber gate tower of Huguo Gate was built later, and not all the structure in the photographs is taken as original Song work.
cq_diaoyu.lede: A stone arch pierces a heavy wall, reached by stairs turning beside the cliff. Huguo Gate shows how Diaoyucheng’s defence used terrain directly. A later timber gatehouse stands above it, so the present structure is not entirely original Song work. An important construction phase took place in 1243, while the gateway reveals how wall, cliff and access route cooperate.
facts: The masonry arch forms part of the wall, with stairs climbing beside the cliff and terrain constraining the entrance. A later timber gatehouse adds a different historical layer above the heavy stone structure.

1243 marks a major phase in Southern Song defensive construction, followed by further extensions and repairs. It dates the site’s history, not every surviving component of this gate, especially its later timber gatehouse.

The fortress joins natural mountain obstacles to walls, organising limited access routes for defence. Huguo Gate makes that visible. Residential and administrative remains also show that resistance depended on sustained habitation and supplies.
captions: Diaoyu Fortress Site · Huguo Gate
Fortifications expanded 1243 · Gate tower built later

protection.scope: Stone gateway of Huguo Gate at Diaoyu Fortress, the later upper gate tower and the stone steps in front
protection.note: The place name originally announced was Hechuan City, Sichuan Province; it now belongs to Hechuan District, Chongqing. The upper gate tower was built later; the national protected site label corresponds to the main structure of Huguo Gate within the site.

cq_tongnan.name: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
cq_tongnan.era: Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151
cq_tongnan.yearNote: The Buddha's head was carved in the Tang and the body continued in the Northern Song, with the whole statue completed in 1151; the surviving gold leaf includes the results of conservation and restoration in the 2010s, and the timeline is not placed by the temple's founding year.
cq_tongnan.lede: Dark curls frame a golden face, with robe folds spreading over the broad body. Tongnan’s giant Buddha combines rock carving with gilded surfaces. Its head was carved first and its body later, across Tang and Song; the gold also includes later renewals and modern conservation. Reading face, gestures and drapery requires distinguishing the image from its changing surface decoration.
facts: The image uses the cliff as its core, with curls and a high cranial protuberance framing the face and robes covering the body. Its right palm faces upwards before the abdomen and its left hand rests on the knee. Gold contrasts with dark hair; the sculpted mass remains connected to the cliff behind.

The head was begun in the Tang period and the body continued in Northern Song, with the whole image completed in 1151 and subsequently gilded. Completion of the image and the temple’s foundation have distinct dates. Its hair and gold include later conservation.

Restoration research distinguishes rock, modelled hair repairs, lacquer and gold leaf as separate materials requiring care. Their layers form the present image, documenting both Tang–Song sculptural continuity and the evolving gilding tradition.
captions: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan · Surviving gilded Great Buddha
Head carved in the Tang · Whole statue completed 1151

protection.unitName: Cliff Carvings of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan
protection.scope: Surviving gilded seated Great Buddha of the Great Buddha Temple, Tongnan

sx_zishou.name: Zishou Temple, Lingshi
sx_zishou.sub: Front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings
sx_zishou.yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Hall of Heavenly Kings on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_zishou.lede: The front of the Heavenly Kings Hall of Zishou Temple is not a row of lattice doors but a solid wall of grey brick with a single doorway in the middle, over which hangs the plaque 'Secluded Delight of Hills and Woods'; the grey-tiled roof is edged in blue-green glaze and the main ridge is crowded with glazed pavilions and beasts. The temple is at Suxi village in Jingsheng town, Lingshi; steles record its founding in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), destruction by fire at the end of the Jin, rebuilding in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), large-scale repair in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and its present extent by 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi), the surviving halls all being Ming. The plate shows the front of the Heavenly Kings Hall.
facts: Heavenly Kings Hall: as drawn, a single-eaved hall whose front is a brick wall without lattice doors, with one central door, a pair of stone lions before it, bracket sets under the eaves, a grey-tile roof with glazed edging and a glazed main ridge; bell and drum towers stand to either side, and inside, along both sides, four Heavenly Kings about 3 m tall.

Dating: founded in 870 (11th year of Xiantong, Tang), burned at the end of the Jin, repaired in the Yuan, rebuilt in 1467 (3rd year of Chenghua, Ming), repaired in 1521 (16th year of Zhengde) and brought to its present form in 1622 (2nd year of Tianqi); about 17,000 square metres in two courts, front and rear. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Loss: the temple is known for its Ming painted sculpture and murals, with 248.34 square metres of murals and over a hundred statues; in 1993 the heads of its eighteen arhats were cut off, stolen and sold abroad, later bought back and returned by the Taiwanese businessman Chen Yongtai, one of the cases of lost Shanxi relics coming home.

sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.name: Ruicheng City God Temple
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.sub: Gable side of the main hall
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.era: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.yearLabel: Original Song structure · Repaired over the centuries
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.yearNote: 1100 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted gable side of the main hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_ruicheng_chenghuang.lede: The earliest surviving City God temple in Shanxi. Its main hall is a Song structure under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, with five-puzuo bracket sets and two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile on the front column heads; seen from the gable end, a Ming glazed panel of 'two dragons playing with a pearl' is set in the gable, the owl-tail finials and ridge ornaments are glazed too, while below is plain red wall. Known locally as the 'South Temple', it was founded according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired under the Yuan, Ming and Qing; on the axis the offering pavilion is Yuan and the offering hall and rear hall Qing, so four dynasties of carpentry stand in one court. The plate shows the gable end of the main hall.
facts: Main hall: five bays wide and three deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof; the front column-head bracket sets are five-puzuo with two downward cantilevers of split-bamboo profile and grasshopper-head beam ends; the gable carries a Ming glazed panel of two dragons playing with a pearl, the glazed owl-tails and ridge ornaments are bright in colour, and the red wall sits on a grey-brick dado.

Dating: according to the Republican-era Ruicheng County Gazetteer the temple was founded in the Dazhong Xiangfu reign of the Northern Song (1008-1016) and repaired in the Yuan, Ming and Qing; the main hall is original Song work, the offering pavilion Yuan, the offering hall and rear hall Qing, and the gate, stage and bell and drum towers recent rebuildings. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001.

Steles: the stele gallery displays 98 steles and image steles from the Northern Wei to the Ming and Qing, among them the Preface to the Jingyuan Daoist Hall of Mount Zhongtiao of 798 (14th year of Zhenyuan, Tang), composed by Wang Yan, prefect of Guozhou, and written by Yuan Zi; the offering pavilion, a four-rafter hall with two columns spanning the full depth, has massive architraves and leaning corner columns, typical of Yuan work, and is not in the plate.
captions: Ruicheng City God Temple · Gable side of the main hall

sx_qiao.name: Qiao Family Compound
sx_qiao.sub: Inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard
sx_qiao.yearNote: 1800 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_qiao.lede: The proper name of the Qiao Family Compound is Zaizhongtang, the residence of the Shanxi merchant Qiao Zhiyong. An eighty-metre stone walk divides six large courts into a northern and a southern row, and seen from above the whole house forms the character for double happiness; each court is a long narrow one like this, wing rooms on both sides closing in the yard and a two-storey main house at the far end. Building began in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), with enlargements in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns, and the present extent was reached only in the early Republic, so any single court can be dated only approximately. The plate shows the end house and the flanking wing rooms of one court of Zaizhongtang.
facts: Courts: Zaizhongtang covers 10,642 square metres with six large courts, twenty small ones and 313 rooms; the main gate faces east, an arched gateway with a tower above. As drawn, the two sides are single-storey wing rooms and the end house is two storeys with an upper gallery, grey brick walls, lattice doors and brick carving and painting under the eaves stacked tier on tier.

Dating: begun in 1755 (20th year of Qianlong, Qing), enlarged in the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns and completed in the early Republic; the courts were built in stages and no single court has a firm completion date. Listed as a national key protected site in 2001; made the Qixian Folk Museum in 1985 and opened the next year.

Family: the Qiaos rose from Qiao Guifa, who 'went west beyond the pass' to Baotou in the early Qianlong years and founded the Fushenggong firm, giving rise to the saying 'first Fushenggong, then Baotou city'; under Qiao Zhiyong the firm's branches spread far and wide. The Dexingtang, Ningshoutang, Baoyuantang and garden are recent reconstructions on their old sites and are not in the plate.
captions: Qiao Family Compound · Inner tower and flanking side rooms of the Zaizhong Hall courtyard

sx_wang.name: Wang Family Compound
sx_wang.sub: Courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort (detail)
sx_wang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted courtyard walls and roofs of Hongmen Fort on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_wang.lede: The Hongmen Fort of the Wang Family Compound is a fort in earnest: a wall eight metres high and two thick encloses a circuit of over six hundred metres, inside which eighty-eight courtyards climb the slope in four tiers with a single main street running up the middle, so that the plan resembles the character wang. Seen from above, grey-tiled roofs, brick courtyard walls, openwork screen walls and one small gatehouse after another pile up in layers, and that is the corner the plate takes. Hongmen Fort, also called Hengzhen Fort, was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing and housed eight generations of the Jingsheng Wangs, from the fourteenth to the twenty-first; the compound as a whole went up over nearly ninety years from the Kangxi to the Jiaqing reigns.
facts: Fort: Hongmen Fort, or Hengzhen Fort, is the west compound of the Wang Family Compound, laid out on the hillside in four tiers of courtyards from low to high, symmetrical left and right, with 88 courtyards and 776 rooms in all; the wall is 8 m high, 2 m wide and over 600 m round, and the south gate bears the stone plaque 'Hengzhen'. The plate shows the layering of roofs, screen walls and courtyard gates inside the fort.

Dating: Hongmen Fort was built in the Qianlong reign of the Qing, and Gaojiaya to its east in the Jiaqing reign by the brothers Wang Rucong and Wang Rucheng of the seventeenth generation; the compound was built mainly over nearly 90 years from Kangxi to Jiaqing, with 123 courtyards and 1,118 rooms. Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Family: the Jingsheng Wangs moved here as farmers in 1313 (2nd year of Huangqing, Yuan), took to trade in the Ming, grew rich on salt and tea in the Qing, and declined after the fall of Yangzhou in 1853 (3rd year of Xianfeng). The total area is given as 150,000 or 250,000 square metres, making it one of the largest Qing residential complexes in Shanxi.

sx_daixian_wenmiao.name: Dai County Confucian Temple
sx_daixian_wenmiao.sub: Front and platform of the Dacheng Hall
sx_daixian_wenmiao.era: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
sx_daixian_wenmiao.yearLabel: Ming–Qing buildings · Repaired over the centuries
sx_daixian_wenmiao.yearNote: 1500 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front and platform of the Dacheng Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_daixian_wenmiao.lede: The largest surviving prefectural Confucian temple in north China. The Dacheng Hall is seven bays wide and ten rafters deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof entirely covered in peacock-blue glazed tile, with nine-step bracket sets of one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves and a row of front lattice doors in twelve different patterns; it stands on a white-marble platform with stone balustrades on three sides and a carved dragon ramp in the centre. The temple is said to have been founded in the Tang; it was rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng, Yuan) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing, the surviving fabric being mainly Ming. The plate shows the front of the Dacheng Hall and its terrace, with the steles in the foreground omitted.
facts: Dacheng Hall: seven bays wide (five according to the Daixian county government page), ten rafters deep, single-eaved hip-and-gable roof in peacock-blue glazed tile; nine-step bracket sets with one upward and three downward cantilevers under the eaves; front lattice doors in twelve patterns; inside, a caisson ceiling converging on an eight-trigram apex, square, octagonal and round tiers carried on four layers of brackets.

Dating: traditionally founded in the Tang, destroyed by war at the end of the Yuan, rebuilt from 1367 (27th year of Zhizheng) and completed in 1369 (2nd year of Hongwu, Ming), enlarged in the Chenghua and Jiajing reigns and repeatedly repaired in the Qing; it survived after 1949 by serving as a granary. The National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Ming to Qing; listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: about 14,400 square metres in four courts, the axis running Wanren archway, Lingxing gate, Pan pool, Ji gate, Dacheng Hall and Jingyi pavilion, with the shrines of worthy officials and local worthies east and west of the pool; the Lingxing gate has six columns and five roofs, its side roofs set with glazed coiled-dragon roundels. The plate takes only the Dacheng Hall.
captions: Dai County Confucian Temple · Front and platform of the Dacheng Hall

sx_ciyun.name: Ciyun Temple, Tianzhen
sx_ciyun.yearNote: 1450 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the Mahavira Hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_ciyun.lede: The Mahavira Hall of Ciyun Temple is only three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, its bracket sets stepping out tier on tier beneath the eaves, and inside it keeps over fifty square metres of Ming murals: the twelve bodhisattvas of complete enlightenment on the main wall, the twenty-four devas and the eight classes of beings on the sides. The temple stands on West Street in the county town of Tianzhen; originally Fahua Temple, it was founded in the Tang according to the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer, repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao) and again from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming), when the chiliarch Xiong Liang petitioned for the name Ciyun Temple, 'the great monastery north of the pass'; today's layout is that left by the Xuande repair. The plate shows the front of the Mahavira Hall and the steps before it.
facts: Mahavira Hall: also called the Sakyamuni Hall, three bays wide and deep under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, standing on a high platform reached by a central stone stair, with dense bracket sets under the eaves as drawn; inside are over 50 square metres of Ming murals and a seated Sakyamuni flanked by the Medicine Buddha and Amitabha.

Dating: the Guangxu-era Tianzhen County Gazetteer records that the temple was 'built in the Tang, originally named Fahua', repaired in 1019 (8th year of Kaitai, Liao), rebuilt from 1428 to 1430 (3rd to 5th years of Xuande, Ming) and granted the name Ciyun Temple, with further repairs in 1539 (18th year of Jiajing, Ming) and 1761 (26th year of Qianlong, Qing). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Bell and drum towers: the bell and drum towers before the Heavenly Kings Hall are octagonal in plan with round domed roofs, a brick chamber ringed by eight columns below and an open railed storey above, a form found nowhere else among Yuan and Ming bell and drum towers in Shanxi; the bell tower hangs an iron bell of 1432 (7th year of Xuande, Ming). The temple has 31 surviving buildings on about 1.6 hectares.

sx_wuyue.name: Wuyue Temple, Jiexiu
sx_wuyue.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the opera stage on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_wuyue.lede: The Wuyue Temple of Jiexiu merges gate, stage and bell and drum towers into one building, known locally as the Haishen Lou, the 'mirage tower'. On the courtyard side the upper storey is five bays wide, the central bay pushed forward as the stage front under a small hip-and-gable roof, with the gables of the two wings turned to face front; below are five brick arches, the middle one the passage into the temple. The roofs are of peacock-blue glaze; Jiexiu calls itself the home of glazed tile, and the colour here is among the purest. The temple was founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing) and rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong), so the surviving buildings are Qing. The plate shows the courtyard front of the stage.
facts: Stage: built on a high platform, five bays wide, the central bay projecting one bay northward, with elaborate bracket sets under the eaves; the upper stage front has a wooden railing and the gables of both wings face forward, while below a central passage is flanked by four arched openings; gate, stage and bell and drum towers form one body, called the Haishen Lou.

Dating: according to temple steles, founded in 1456 (7th year of Jingtai, Ming), destroyed in 1750 (15th year of Qianlong, Qing), rebuilt in 1763 (28th year of Qianlong) and repaired in 2001; the National Cultural Heritage Administration registers it as Qing, and it was listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Glaze: the peacock-blue glazed roof ornaments are pure in colour and fine in form, and the Jiexiu cultural heritage bureau calls them another treasure of the 'home of glazed tile'; the temple faces south in two courts on 4,149 square metres, with 13 surviving buildings including screen wall, offering pavilion, main hall and rear hall, the main hall five bays under a flush-gable roof.

sx_pingyao_chenghuang.name: Pingyao City God Temple
sx_pingyao_chenghuang.sub: South face of the Zhaoge Lou stage tower
sx_pingyao_chenghuang.yearNote: 1750 is only an approximate position for ordering the depicted front of the front hall on the timeline, not an exact construction date; the founding, enlargements and later repairs are recorded separately.
sx_pingyao_chenghuang.lede: To enter the Pingyao City God Temple one first passes through a low gateway beneath a tower; over the passage hang the two characters 'Dare you enter', the 'enter' written like a knife. The tower is the stage, the Zhaoge Lou, double-eaved hip-and-gable and three bays wide; on its south face a hip-and-gable baosha projects above the passage, thick with bracket sets, and the bell and drum towers join it on either side. The temple's founding date is unknown; it was repaired after a fire in 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), another fire in 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing) left only the rear hall, and most of the surviving buildings date from the rebuilding of 1864-1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi). The plate shows the south face of this tower and the passage.
facts: Stage: two storeys under a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, three bays wide, glazed tile; the south plaque reads 'Dare you enter' and the north 'Zhaoge Lou', and the passage beneath leads into the front court; ten earthenware jars are buried under the stage floor to resonate with the ceiling. The bell and drum towers join it east and west; the plate shows the south face and the baosha.

Dating: founding date unknown; repaired after the fire of 1554 (33rd year of Jiajing, Ming), reduced to the rear hall by the fire of 1859 (9th year of Xianfeng, Qing), rebuilt from 1864 to 1869 (3rd to 8th years of Tongzhi), the Procession of the City God painted in the main hall in 1868 (7th year of Tongzhi). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Layout: the temple and the Pingyao county yamen stand on opposite sides of South Street in east-west symmetry; three courts on 7,302 square metres, the axis running archway, gate, stage, offering hall, main hall and rear hall, with the Six Bureaus and the Earth God shrine on the sides and the Kitchen God and God of Wealth temples east and west of the rear court, 'all the gods dwelling in one temple'.
captions: Pingyao City God Temple · South face of the Zhaoge Lou stage tower

sx_rishengchang.name: Former Site of Rishengchang
sx_rishengchang.era: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
sx_rishengchang.yearLabel: Former Qing draft bank · Surviving street frontage
sx_rishengchang.yearNote: 1823 is the commonly cited year the draft bank opened; the construction year of the surviving frontage itself is undetermined, and the timeline places it approximately by that period.
sx_rishengchang.lede: This row of shopfronts on the south side of West Street in Pingyao was the head office of China's first draft bank. The front is a run of dark wooden plank doors with a line of small painted panels above the lintels and a grey-tiled pitched roof above that, as unassuming as any shop; behind it two parallel courts face north, with a floor area of over 1,700 square metres. Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop; the customary date is 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang, Qing), though the steles allow the reorganisation to be placed only between 1819 and 1838, and no record gives the construction date of the shopfront itself. The plate shows the street front.
facts: Shopfront: the head office stands on the south side of West Street, facing north, with two courts side by side, on 2,324 square metres of land and over 1,700 square metres of floor area; as drawn the front is single-storey, a continuous row of plank doors with a line of small painted windows above and the plaque 'Rishengchang Ji' under the eaves.

Dating: Rishengchang was reorganised from the Xiyucheng dye shop of the Li family of Dapu, with the owner Li Daquan contributing 300,000 taels and Lei Lütai 20,000; a stele of 1819 (24th year of Jiaqing) still lists Xiyucheng and one of 1838 (18th year of Daoguang) no longer does, so the change fell between, conventionally in 1823 (3rd year of Daoguang). Listed as a national key protected site in 2006.

Influence: Rishengchang pioneered remittance between cities, with branches in Hankou, Tianjin, Shanghai, Guangzhou and elsewhere, and by 1891 (17th year of Guangxu) remitted thirty million taels a year; it was sealed in 1914 over a guarantee case and closed in 1932. Pingyao thereby became the financial centre of all China in the nineteenth century, and was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1997.

sx_pujiu.name: Pujiu Temple Pagoda
sx_pujiu.era: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
sx_pujiu.yearLabel: Rebuilt in the Jiajing reign (Ming) · Thirteen-story brick pagoda
sx_pujiu.yearNote: The surviving pagoda was rebuilt after an earthquake in the Jiajing reign of the Ming; sources differ on the exact year of rebuilding, and the timeline uses an approximate value of around 1560.
sx_pujiu.lede: In the Romance of the Western Chamber the student Zhang 'climbed the pagoda and walked the whole cloister'; this is that pagoda. A square brick pagoda of thirteen storeys with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, its eaves corbelled and its taper slight, it is close in form to the Great Wild Goose Pagoda of Xi'an. In 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) a great earthquake at Puzhou destroyed temple and pagoda alike; in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) the prefect Zhang Jiayin gave his salary to lead the rebuilding, and the pagoda rose six storeys higher than its Tang predecessor to thirteen, the present Yingying Pagoda. The other halls were later lost to fire and rebuilt from 1986 to 1990; the pagoda is the only Ming survivor. The plate shows the whole pagoda.
facts: Form: square in plan, a thirteen-storey brick pagoda with close-set eaves, 39.5 m high and 8.3 m on a side, with a door on the south; the first storey has no windows and a Buddha niche on the north wall, from the second to the ninth storey brick stairs spiral up inside the walls and each storey has window openings; the square cloister round it, eleven bays to a side, was rebuilt after 1986.

Dating: a Ming stele in the temple says Pujiu Temple was 'founded in the Sui and Tang', and an excavated sutra pillar is dated 872 (13th year of Xiantong, Tang); the pagoda fell in the earthquake of 1555 (34th year of Jiajing, Ming) and was rebuilt in 1564 (43rd year of Jiajing) by Zhang Jiayin, whose poem stele stands before it. The pagoda was listed as a provincial protected site in 1965 and a national key protected site in 2019.

Echo: strike a stone on the ground before the pagoda and it answers from within like a croaking frog, for which it is counted among China's four great echoing buildings; Ding Shizhang and others of Shanxi University found the cause in the eaves of each storey, unequal in length and concave, and the smooth surface of the body, which send sound waves back and forth around the pagoda into resonance.
captions: Pujiu Temple Pagoda · Yingying Pagoda, whole surviving pagoda

hb_bailinta.name: Bailin Temple Pagoda
hb_bailinta.yearNote: 1330 corresponds to the construction of the surviving Yuan pagoda of Bailin Temple; the timeline is not placed by the temple's traditional founding date.
hb_bailinta.lede: Bailin Temple Pagoda rises from layered lotus petals into seven tapering eave tiers. Brick balustrades, platforms and brackets evoke timber, while an iron finial contrasts with stone and brick below. Built in the Yuan, the tower should not take its date from earlier temple traditions. Close study of the base and eave details reveals how a substantial mass gains a finely articulated scale.
facts: The octagonal seven-tier brick pagoda stands on stone steps, a brick Sumeru base, timber-like platform and layered lotus petals. Close upper eaves lead to an iron finial with bowl, lotus, rings and jewel forms.
The provincial authority records construction in September 1330. The Yuan tower and earlier temple traditions have distinct chronologies, which later repairs do not erase.

Timber-like platforms, brackets and rafters become masonry details, with lotus ornament placed beneath the tower. Their material and component junctions offer a close view of Yuan pagoda construction.

hb_zdfuwenmiao.name: Zhengding Prefectural Confucian Temple
hb_zdfuwenmiao.yearNote: The surviving Halberd Gate is a Yuan structure whose exact construction year is unknown; 1300 is only an approximate timeline placement. The Prefectural Confucian Temple was founded in the 3rd year of Xining in the Northern Song (1070), and the two are recorded separately.
hb_zdfuwenmiao.lede: The five-bay Jimen Gate at Zhengding’s prefectural Confucian temple holds a ritual entrance beneath a low gable roof. Two bays of depth give it the scale of both gateway and hall. The temple originated in the Northern Song, but this timber building is Yuan. Its columns and eaves, rather than elaborate ornament, reveal the organisation of northern Yuan construction.
facts: The gate is five bays wide and two deep, with a single-eaved projecting gable roof in plain tiles. Internal central columns support the six-rafter arrangement; a broad front and shallow depth shape this gateway hall.
The temple was founded in 1070 and repaired and expanded under later dynasties. Jimen is separately identified as Yuan, with no exact building year; the Song foundation cannot date this frame.

Unlike a principal worship hall, the gate defines entry and movement between courts. Its Yuan column arrangement and frame show that ritual gateways are also valuable evidence for architectural history.
