hb_lingyan.name: Lingyan Temple, Yuzhou
hb_lingyan.era: Rebuilt in the 6th year of Zhengtong (Ming)
hb_lingyan.yearNote: 1441, the 6th year of Zhengtong in the Ming, is the date of the temple's rebuilding, and the hall depicted is the surviving Ming main structure; the record of a Liao founding is not used as the date of the surviving hall.
hb_lingyan.lede: Lingyan Temple’s Mahavira Hall spreads through a gentle roof slope and deep eaves. A hipped roof unites four planes, while bracket groups connect timber columns to the roof. Rebuilt in the Ming Zhengtong era, it also preserves painted ceilings and a refined coffer. Structure and decoration together show how a local Ming temple developed while retaining earlier techniques.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and four deep, with a single-eaved hipped roof and double-arm brackets. A gentle slope and deep eaves explain its substantial but unsteep appearance.

The provincial authority records destruction at the end of the Yuan and rebuilding in 1441. The surviving hall is Ming; an unknown earlier foundation cannot date it, and subsequent repairs remain distinct.

Coffers and Ming painted ceilings preserve interior craftsmanship, while the neighbouring Heavenly Kings Hall retains earlier methods. Together they show continuity in local building practice rather than an abrupt stylistic replacement.

hb_zhenwu.name: Zhenwu Temple, Yuzhou
hb_zhenwu.era: Ming–Qing buildings · Exact date of the gate unknown
hb_zhenwu.yearNote: The national protected site is dated to the Ming, and the temple was repaired in 1720; the exact construction year of the depicted gate is unknown, 1700 is only an approximate placement for the Ming–Qing buildings, and 1720 is not taken as the exact construction year of the gate.
hb_zhenwu.lede: The gate and stone steps at Zhenwu Temple make entry part of the religious setting: visitors climb before passing into the court, separating worship space from the street. The gate’s exact date is unconfirmed within a Ming–Qing temple context. Ming heritage attribution and Kangxi-era repairs indicate several phases, while the changing level and enclosed court establish a clear boundary between everyday streets and ritual space.
facts: The entrance consists of a gate, stone steps and a passage into the court. The climb and narrowed opening change the pace of movement, separating the worship precinct from the surrounding streets.

The temple is registered as Ming and a repair is recorded in 1720. The individual gate’s date remains unknown; neither the complex attribution nor a temple-wide repair establishes its precise foundation year.
Halls and subsidiary rooms form an enclosed court. The gate and steps regulate movement from street to worship, showing how a local temple establishes a ritual boundary within limited space.

hb_dzwenmiao.name: Dingzhou Confucian Temple
hb_dzwenmiao.yearNote: The surviving main structure is registered under the national protected site's Qing dating, and 1750 is only an approximate Qing placement; neither the Tang founding nor the Song rebuilding date of the Confucian Temple is taken as the exact construction date of the hall in the photographs.
hb_dzwenmiao.lede: Dacheng Hall at Dingzhou Confucian Temple organises the central worship court through a five-bay front and terrace, enclosed with side buildings. Although temple history reaches back to the Tang, the principal surviving fabric is Qing. The age of the ritual tradition is not the age of every column. The hall’s position explains how worship and education occupied connected but differentiated precincts.
facts: Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep. Its front terrace connects to the courtyard route, while side buildings enclose the central court. The hall’s bays, terrace and flanking buildings establish a clear focus for Confucian worship.

The site became a Confucian temple in the Tang, expanded in the Song, burned in the late Ming and was rebuilt in the Qing. The hall’s precise year is unknown; early temple dates do not replace its Qing attribution.

The central route serves worship, the western route includes teaching spaces such as Minglun Hall, and eastern courts contain ancestral and Kuixing shrines. Reverence, education and scholarly aspiration share the complex.

hb_xumifushou.name: Xumi Fushou Temple
hb_xumifushou.sub: Golden roof of the Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall and upper Great Red Platform
hb_xumifushou.yearNote: 1780 is the construction date of Xumi Fushou Temple and its main group of buildings; this plate shows only the golden roof of the Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall and the upper part of the Great Red Platform, not the lower base or the complete temple.
hb_xumifushou.lede: Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall’s gilded roof emerges above the Great Red Terrace, contrasting Tibetan-style mass with Chinese eaves. Gilded copper tiles and dragons make it a visible worship centre. Built to receive the Sixth Panchen Lama using his Tibetan residence as a model, Xumi Fushou Temple joins court ceremony and Tibetan Buddhism. This view concerns only the roof and upper terrace, not the entire temple.
facts: Miaogao Zhuangyan Hall sits within the Great Red Terrace. Its pointed gilded-copper roof and ridge dragons rise above the terrace; thick enclosing walls and exposed eaves reveal the layered space containing the hall.
The temple was built in 1780 to receive the Sixth Panchen Lama for Qianlong’s birthday, drawing on Tashilhunpo in Shigatse. The Qing date is not replaced by the earlier history of its Tibetan model.

Enclosed halls and the visible golden roof combine internal worship space with an exterior landmark, while the front precinct follows a Chinese axis. Materials and forms meet in the roof, though the full temple layout remains a separate subject.

hb_changping.name: Yuzhou Ever-Normal Granary
hb_changping.sub: Granary God Temple and connected opera stage
hb_changping.era: Ming granary system · Exact date of surviving temple and stage unknown
hb_changping.yearNote: The Ever-Normal Granary is registered as a Ming national protected site; the exact construction years of the Granary God Temple and the opera stage are unknown, 1650 is only an approximate Ming–Qing placement, and the date of the granary administration system is not taken as the exact construction date of the two buildings.
hb_changping.lede: The granary deity shrine and linked theatre at Changping Granary add worship and performance to a storage complex. Set between northern storehouses, the shrine faces a stage towards the court. Some granary frames retain Ming fabric, but the shrine and theatre have no confirmed individual date. This pairing shows that historical grain storage included protective ritual as well as practical management.
facts: The shrine stands between two northern storehouses with a linked theatre in front. Shrine and stage organise the court for worship and performance, functions distinct from ordinary grain storage.

The complex is registered as Ming, with original Ming timber in some stores, but no exact foundation year. The shrine and theatre are individually undated; the history of the storage system cannot date either building.
The paired ritual spaces show that grain storage accommodated beliefs concerning protection and safety. Their position among stores links everyday use, local ceremony and architectural organisation.

hb_daci.name: Daci Pavilion
hb_daci.yearNote: The surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Qianlong reign of the Qing, and 1760 is only an approximate placement within the 1736–1795 range; the 1227–1232 founding of the temple pavilion is not taken as the date of the pavilion in the photographs.
hb_daci.lede: Daci Pavilion rises from a high stone platform through three eave tiers, with steps making entry an ascent. A five-bay lower level supports the hip-and-gable roof; images and scripture storage give the storeys religious functions. The pavilion’s origins predate today’s Qing Qianlong rebuilding. Stone platform, timber body and worship space preserve a maintained monument rather than an unchanged early building.
facts: The pavilion has three eave tiers and a five-bay-wide, three-bay-deep lower level on a high balustraded stone platform. Steps and roofs organise movement from court to elevated hall.

Its foundation history reaches the thirteenth century, but the surviving pavilion was rebuilt during Qianlong’s reign. No single completion year is established; an approximate Qing date cannot be replaced by its early origins.
Guanyin occupies the lower level, with Buddhist images and scripture storage above. The high platform and roofs create an urban landmark while stacking different religious spaces within one building.

hb_puren.name: Puren Temple
hb_puren.sub: Gable and side eaves of the main hall (detail)
hb_puren.era: Founded in the 52nd year of Kangxi (Qing)
hb_puren.yearNote: Puren Temple was founded in 1713; the plate shows the gable pediment and part of the under-eave area of the surviving Qing main hall. This date corresponds to the building of the temple, and the plate does not show the complete hall.
hb_puren.lede: The gable panel and side eaves of Puren Temple’s principal hall bring monumental architecture into close detail. The triangular upper gable, supports and yellow glazed tiles reveal more than a distant roofline. Founded under Kangxi, the hall occupies a Chinese-style temple axis. This fragment shows how an early Chengde imperial Buddhist temple used traditional timber craft to create worship space.
facts: Ciwang Puyin Hall is seven bays wide and five deep, with a single-eaved yellow-glazed hip-and-gable roof. Its upper side gable and timber-supported eaves reveal how the triangular panel and sloping roof shape the side elevation.
Puren Temple was founded in 1713. The surviving Qing hall includes later repairs; the foundation dates a building phase, not every material visible in this close view.
An axial sequence of gate, Heavenly Kings Hall and principal halls follows Chinese temple planning. The gable and eaves reveal connections between glazed roofing, timber framing and worship space.

hb_xingwen.name: Xingwen Pagoda, Laiyuan
hb_xingwen.sub: Body and finial of the five-story octagonal brick pagoda
hb_xingwen.yearNote: The surviving pagoda is attributed to the Liao by its form, and 1050 is only an approximate placement; sources record a first construction in the 3rd year of Tianbao in the Tang (744), a Ming restoration in 1539 and modern repairs, and the founding date is not taken as the exact date of the surviving pagoda's form.
hb_xingwen.lede: Xingwen Pagoda’s five separated eave tiers express a pavilion rhythm more clearly than close-eaved towers. Octagonal walls and brackets imitate timber, but the solid interior is not climbable. It shares a high platform with neighbouring Taishan Palace, bringing Buddhist and Daoist buildings together. Tang founding records, Ming repairs and a Liao-form attribution are distinct evidence, not one precise construction date.
facts: The solid octagonal five-tier brick pagoda comprises a Sumeru base, body and finial. Timber-like brackets articulate each level; five exterior tiers are not five usable interior floors.

An embedded inscription records a Tang foundation in 744 and repair in 1539, while the provincial authority attributes its form to the Liao. These are distinct kinds of evidence; the surviving tower’s exact year is unsettled.

The tower and Ming-Qing Taishan Palace share a raised platform, with records of Buddhist and Daoist participation in repairs. Their setting reveals coexisting local religious spaces rather than an isolated monument.

hn_yanqing.name: Yanqing Daoist Temple
hn_yanqing.era: Surviving Yuan Jade Emperor Pavilion; approximate timeline placement
hn_yanqing.yearNote: Surviving Yuan Jade Emperor Pavilion; approximate timeline placement.
hn_yanqing.lede: Yuhuang Pavilion at Yanqing Guan rises from a square brick body to an octagonal upper level. Glazed details and layered eaves imitate a timber pavilion, but its structure relies on masonry. The surviving Yuan building also records the challenges posed by groundwater and foundation movement in Kaifeng. A conservation project raised the entire pavilion while preserving Yuan ground layers, allowing ancient construction and modern protection to be read together.
facts: Built entirely of grey brick without load-bearing timber beams, the pavilion appears three-storeyed, square below and octagonal above. Glazed ornament and masonry eaves reproduce the visual layers of timber architecture.

The surviving pavilion is assigned to the Yuan. Around 1280 is an approximate timeline position, not a verified completion year; changes in the monastery’s name and later repairs are separate from the building date.

An integral lifting project addressing cracking and foundation problems raised the pavilion by 3.1 metres while retaining Yuan ground layers. It illustrates conservation that protects both the monument and archaeological information beneath it.

hn_yuefei.name: Yue Fei Temple, Tangyin
hn_yuefei.era: Ming–Qing buildings and later repairs; exact construction year of the Second Hall unknown
hn_yuefei.yearNote: Ming–Qing buildings and later repairs; the exact construction year of the Second Hall is unknown.
hn_yuefei.lede: The second hall of Tangyin’s Yue Fei Temple presents five bays of red doors and windows beneath a grey roof. In Yue Fei’s home region, the temple sustains commemoration through buildings shaped by Ming–Qing construction and later repair; these are not a residence from the general’s Southern Song lifetime. Successive courtyards, inscriptions and commemorative writing reveal how later generations expressed the heroic image while giving the memorial architecture a history of its own.
facts: The hall’s five-bay front places doors and windows between columns beneath a single eave. Red-painted timber contrasts with grey brick and tiles, while the hall links preceding and following buildings within successive ritual courtyards.

The county government describes the surviving precinct as a Ming–Qing architectural group and records rebuilding in 1450. The second hall’s exact year remains unverified; around 1650 is only an approximate timeline position.

The temple is a public memorial to Yue Fei in his home region. Halls, inscriptions and writings preserve later expressions of remembrance. The buildings postdate his life by centuries, giving the memorial both personal and architectural histories.

hn_songyang.name: Songyang Academy
hn_songyang.sub: Front of the Qing main gate
hn_songyang.era: Surviving gate is Qing, with later repairs; approximately placed in the Kangxi period
hn_songyang.yearNote: The surviving gate is Qing and has been repaired; it is placed approximately in the Kangxi period.
hn_songyang.lede: Songyang Academy’s gate covers three openings with a low curved-ridge roof, modest stone columns and grey brickwork. Beyond it, the Hall of Former Sages, lecture hall, lineage shrine and library unfold along an axis, organizing reverence, teaching and books in successive courtyards. The academy is famed for Song scholarship, but its present gate and layout largely reflect Qing work. The unassuming entrance offers a human-scaled approach to these layers of educational history.
facts: The three-bay gate has a curved-ridge roof without a prominent ridge crest, framed by stone columns and grey brick walls. The axis beyond links the Hall of Former Sages, lecture hall, lineage shrine and library through successive courtyards.

Earlier religious institutions occupied the site, and the Song emperor bestowed the academy’s name in 1035. The surviving buildings and layout are largely Qing; around 1680 is approximate and is not replaced by the earlier foundation or naming dates.

The courtyards connect veneration of sages, teaching and book storage, preserving spatial evidence of traditional education. Proceeding inward from the modest gate, functional sequence conveys the academy’s character more clearly than lavish ornament.

hn_xiangguo.name: Daxiangguo Temple
hn_xiangguo.era: Qianlong rebuilding phase (Qing), not the Northern Qi founding year
hn_xiangguo.yearNote: The Qianlong rebuilding phase of the Qing, not the Northern Qi founding year of the temple.
hn_xiangguo.lede: In 1642 a breach of the Yellow River buried Kaifeng, and Daxiangguo Temple with it, under silt; the halls seen today follow the layout fixed by a rebuilding in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and a renovation in 1766 (Qianlong 31). The Daxiong Baodian (Mahavira Hall) shown here stands at the centre of the second courtyard: seven bays wide, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, set on a Sumeru-base terrace ringed by stone balustrades whose posts are carved with small lions. The Northern Song complex of sixty-four cloisters is long gone, but the scale of a Qing state-sponsored monastery remains.
facts: Form: the Daxiong Baodian is seven bays wide and five deep, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of yellow and green glazed tile and a total height of about 13 m. In front lies a Sumeru-base terrace; white stone balustrades surround hall and terrace, their post-heads carved with more than fifty small lions, no two alike.

History: in 712 (Yanhe 1) Emperor Ruizong of Tang bestowed the name Xiangguo Si. After the flood of 1642, the gate, Hall of Heavenly Kings and Daxiong Baodian were rebuilt in 1661 (Shunzhi 18) and renovated again in 1766 (Qianlong 31); the existing halls took their present form then, and Qianlong wrote the plaque 'Imperially Built Xiangguo Si'.

Fortunes: in 1927 troops of Feng Yuxiang destroyed every Buddhist image in the temple except the Thousand-Armed Guanyin and turned the temple into the Zhongshan Market; the main hall long stood empty and was used for exhibitions. In Northern Song the temple governed sixty-four cloisters on 540 mu of land; what stands today is only a corner of that core.

hn_zzchenghuang.name: Zhengzhou City God Temple
hn_zzchenghuang.era: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; exact construction year of the individual building unknown
hn_zzchenghuang.yearNote: Surviving Ming–Qing historic buildings; the exact construction year of the individual building is unknown.
hn_zzchenghuang.lede: The best-preserved group of Ming-Qing buildings in old Zhengzhou is not a government office but this City God Temple. The Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer records renovations led by seven prefectural magistrates between 1501 (Hongzhi 14) and 1890 (Guangxu 16), and the gate, passage hall, stage, main hall and rear chambers still line up on one axis. The three-bay front shown here, with its green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof, four small-octagonal stone columns in the central bay and three pairs of red plank doors, corresponds in the gazetteer's description to the temple's front gate hall; the main hall proper, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof, stands north of the stage.
facts: Form: the front shown is three bays wide and two deep, with a green glazed-tile overhanging-gable roof and seven-tier bracket sets with three ang under the eaves, the ang-tips shaped as triple clouds and the beam-ends as elephant trunks. Four small-octagonal stone columns stand front and back in the central bay; three pairs of solid plank doors hang on the through-columns, with a fan-shaped flight of six steps and a pair of stone lions before them.

History: originally named the Temple of the City God, Marquis Lingyou, it enshrines Ji Xin, a general of Liu Bang of Han, and was founded in the early Ming. According to the Republican-era Zhengxian Gazetteer it was repeatedly renovated by magistrates: Shi Chuncui in 1501 (Hongzhi 14), Liu Ru in Jiajing 6, Li Shixuan in Longqing 4, and others in the Kangxi, Qianlong and Guangxu reigns. A stele with the cursive 'Eulogy of Fortune' by the early-Ming deputy magistrate Zhang Dayou survives in the temple.

Comparison: on the axis, the stage is a two-storey hip-and-gable pavilion whose nineteen roof ridges cross and overlap; the main hall is three bays square under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof with gilt-style bracket sets in the central bay; the five-bay rear chamber has an overhanging-gable roof fronted by a rolled-ridge worship porch. With gate, tower, hall and chamber roof types all present, it is one of the larger and more complete surviving City God temples in Henan.
captions: Zhengzhou City God Temple · Front of the gatehouse

hn_jiawenmiao.name: Jia County Confucian Temple
hn_jiawenmiao.era: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; Five Dynasties founding year not used
hn_jiawenmiao.yearNote: Surviving Dacheng Hall with Ming–Qing repairs; the Five Dynasties founding year of the temple is not used.
hn_jiawenmiao.lede: The four front-eave columns of the Dacheng Hall are carved through their whole length with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as tiger heads, and the dragon columns are of wood: Qing wooden dragon columns of this kind survive nowhere else in Henan. The hall is five bays wide under a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, and the dragon slab before its terrace shows two dragons playing with a 'spider' rather than a flaming pearl. The temple began as a Kong family shrine completed in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou) and became the official Confucian temple in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin); the Dacheng Hall shown here is the Qing timber structure left by repeated Ming and Qing renovations.
facts: Form: the Dacheng Hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single-eaved hip-and-gable roof of green glazed tile, 15.5 m high and 19.7 m across the front. The four wooden eave columns are carved through with coiling dragons, their capitals cut as fanged tiger faces looking down on the dragons; the column bases are covered with auspicious scenes, and the architraves, bracket sets and sparrow braces are also pierced with figures, carts, birds, flowers and clouds.

History: descendants of Confucius built a family shrine here in 954 (Xiande 1 of Later Zhou); in 1206 (Taihe 6 of Jin) the magistrate Zhang Zhixing enlarged it on the same site into the official Confucian temple. The Dacheng Hall was restored and its dragon slab carved under the Yingzong emperor of Ming (1459); the temple was rebuilt eleven times, and the surviving Dacheng Hall, Ji Gate and side halls are all Qing timber structures.

Comparison: the wooden dragon columns are later than the Song dragon columns of the Sage Mother Hall at Jinci, yet they are the only surviving example in Henan. The outer bracket sets and purlins keep original painted decoration that is neither the Beijing 'palace style' nor the Suzhou-Hangzhou 'Su style' but a Central Plains local manner. The temple retains 22 buildings with 71 bays, laid out with the school on the left and the shrine on the right, serving as both Kong family shrine and county school.
captions: Jia County Confucian Temple · Front of the Dacheng Hall

hn_jiahuiguan.name: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Jia County
hn_jiahuiguan.sub: Gate tower with bell and drum towers
hn_jiahuiguan.era: Qing buildings; exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group unknown
hn_jiahuiguan.yearNote: Qing buildings; the exact dates of the individual buildings in the surviving group are unknown.
hn_jiahuiguan.lede: Seen from the street, the three-bay gatehouse is flanked by the bell and drum towers; its upper storey is the theatre stage, which faces north into the courtyard where the audience filled the open ground. The Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall of Jiaxian was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) by merchants from Shanxi and Shaanxi as a way-station and guild house where the old Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads crossed. Shown here are the gatehouse and the two towers: each tower stands on a 4 m base, with twelve round timber columns carrying a cross-beamed roof under two tiers of flaring eaves, rising above the ridge of the gatehouse.
facts: Form: the gatehouse is three bays wide, the central bay for passage and the side bays for gatekeepers and reception; the open three-bay upper storey faces north as the stage, its brick-carved ridge crowned at the centre by a qilin bearing a treasure vase. The bell and drum towers on either side stand on bases 4 m high, each with twelve round timber columns supporting cross beams, double tiers of flaring eaves and solid bracket sets.

History: the guild hall was founded in 1693 (Kangxi 32) with funds from Shanxi and Shaanxi merchants and is also called the Shan-Shaan Temple or Guandi Temple. It faces south over a watercourse on a site of 6,300 square metres; the river-guarding screen wall before the gate is 8 m wide, 7 m high and 1 m thick, with a brick-carved coiled dragon on a red-sandstone base.

Comparison: the east and west galleries have eleven bays each, the courtyard could hold a thousand spectators, and to the north stand the five-bay Guan Gong Hall and, behind it, the Spring-and-Autumn Pavilion. Jiaxian lay where the Nanyang-Luoyang and Xuchang-Luoyang roads met; the tea route north from Nanyang branched here toward Shanxi, and the hall is regarded as a surviving relic of the Qing 'Ten-Thousand-Li Tea Road' in Henan.
captions: Shanxi-Shaanxi Guild Hall, Jia County · Gate tower with bell and drum towers

hn_linfeng.name: Linfeng Fortified Village
hn_linfeng.sub: West Gate and connected red-stone wall
hn_linfeng.era: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi
hn_linfeng.yearNote: Red-stone walls rebuilt in the 1st year of Tongzhi.
hn_linfeng.lede: The red-stone plaque above the gate is cut with the two characters 'Linfeng', and the iron sheathing of the doors is chiselled 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu': this wall wears its own birthday on its face. Linfeng Fort was originally a late-Ming earthen stockade; in 1862 (Tongzhi 1) the villager Zhu Zifeng led its rebuilding in purplish-red ashlar, an oval ring 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and eight hundred merlons, and three gates set by the trigram directions to the north-west, south-west and south-east. Shown here are the west-facing Linfeng Gate and the wall joined to it.
facts: Form: the wall is stone outside and earth within, built of purplish-red ashlar on an oval plan 1,100 m around and 6.6 m high, with five watch-towers and 800 merlons. Each gate is a barrel-vaulted opening fitted with a pair of elm doors sheathed in 10 cm iron plate, with flood gates and drainage culverts outside; a moat 13 m wide circles the fort.

History: the Zhu clan is said to have moved here from Hongtong, Shanxi, in the Wanli reign of Ming and first raised an earthen stockade. In 1862 (Tongzhi 1) Zhu Zifeng, a native holding a purchased magistrate's rank, led the building of the red-stone fort; the words 'first year of Tongzhi, the year renxu' chiselled on the iron of the north-west gate are still legible. Inside survive one Ming courtyard house and more than a hundred Qing buildings with over four hundred bays.

Comparison: after 1949 village walls were pulled down across the region, but Linfeng's low-lying site and the need for flood defence saved it; Luo Zhewen called it 'the first red-stone fort of the Central Plains'. It was listed as a Chinese Historic and Cultural Village in 2005, among the first batch of Traditional Chinese Villages in 2012, and from 2014 the National Cultural Heritage Administration funded its overall restoration.

hn_gaoge.name: Gaoge Temple
hn_gaoge.sub: Pavilion and upper part of the high platform
hn_gaoge.era: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement
hn_gaoge.yearNote: Ming building with later repairs; approximate timeline placement.
hn_gaoge.lede: The one pavilion-hall left from a Ming princely palace. In 1404 (Yongle 2) the Yongle emperor enfeoffed his third son Zhu Gaosui as Prince of Zhao; the prince took up residence at Zhangde (Anyang) in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and turned the prefectural offices into his palace. The palace was abolished with the fall of the Ming in 1644, and by the Republican era only this Dashi Pavilion remained; because it stands on a brick platform about 8 m high it is known as Gaoge Si, the 'High Pavilion Temple'. The existing pavilion was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6), with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile; shown here are the pavilion body and its two tiers of eaves above the stone balustrade of the platform.
facts: Form: a pavilion on a high platform, more than 20 m in total height. The square brick platform is about 8 m high and 13 m on a side, with a flight of 32 stone steps on the south; white marble balustrades with carved lions line the steps and the platform top. The pavilion is three bays square, about 9 m each way, under a double-eaved nine-ridge hip-and-gable roof of glazed tile, with four round timber through-columns rising inside to the top beams.

History: Zhu Gaosui was made Prince of Zhao in 1404 (Yongle 2), took up residence at Zhangde in 1425 (Hongxi 1) and converted the prefectural offices into the Prince of Zhao's palace, of which the Dashi Pavilion was one hall; the existing building was rebuilt in 1470 (Chenghua 6). The Zhao line passed through eleven generations until the palace was abolished in 1644 (Chongzhen 17); by the Republican era its buildings had collapsed, leaving only this pavilion.

Comparison: most Ming princely palaces were demolished after the dynasty fell, and what survives elsewhere, such as the gate of the Jingjiang palace in Guilin, the Longting of the Zhou palace in Kaifeng or the Wangjing Tower of the Lu palace in Xinxiang, are fragments; Gaoge Si is the only building left of the Zhao palace. Twenty-five dragons carved in stone, interspersed with Sanskrit script, run around the outer walls of the pavilion, a rare decoration for a princely hall.

hn_wenzhige.name: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County
hn_wenzhige.sub: Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower
hn_wenzhige.era: Surviving pavilion rebuilt in the Kangxi period according to research, approximately placed on the timeline; the Ming date in the national list is for the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole
hn_wenzhige.yearNote: According to research, the surviving pavilion was rebuilt in the Kangxi period, and its timeline placement is approximate; the Ming date in the national protected site list refers to the city wall and Wenzhi Pavilion as a whole.
hn_wenzhige.lede: The east-west and north-south main streets of old Junxian cross here; the base is pierced by vaulted openings on all four sides, and carts and pedestrians pass beneath the pavilion. It is at once the bell-and-drum tower at the heart of the town and a gate-tower over the street. Originally called the Central Pavilion, of unknown founding date, it received the town bell after 1615 (Wanli 43) and has been known as the Bell-and-Drum Tower ever since; it burned in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and was rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge, 'Pavilion of Civil Rule'. Shown here are the brick base and the two-storey, double-eaved pyramidal-roofed pavilion that make up the surviving structure.
facts: Form: about 20 m high in all, in two parts, base and pavilion. The square brick base is about 12 m on a side, with an arched vault through the middle of each face so that the four openings align east-west and north-south. On top stands a two-storey square pavilion about 10 m high, with a double-eaved four-sided pyramidal roof, upturned corners and ornamental ridges trimmed with glazed tile; the lower storey opens on all four sides, and the platform is ringed by a gallery and a 1 m parapet with square openings.

History: the Jiaqing-era Junxian Gazetteer records that 'after the yimao year of Wanli (1615) the bell was moved to the Central Pavilion'. It was destroyed by fire in 1649 (Shunzhi 6) and rebuilt in 1709 (Kangxi 48) by magistrate Liang Tongluo, who renamed it Wenzhi Ge after the idea of 'ruling by civil virtue'; Zhang Xi wrote a 'Record of the Rebuilding of Wenzhi Ge'. The present pavilion is the structure left by that rebuilding, with later repairs.

Comparison: above the four vaults are Qing bluestone horizontal tablets, 'Red glow streams from the eastern wall' and 'Jade pours from the western hills' by Zhao Sulu on the east and west, 'Clear waters ring the Li' and 'Dark mist guards the Pi' by Zhang Zhe on the south and north. The pavilion is listed together with the surviving stretch of city wall on the Wei River, first built in 1370 (Hongwu 3), and is one of the heritage points of the Junxian section of the Grand Canal.
captions: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County · Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower
Qing · Surviving main structure

protection.unitName: Ancient City Wall of Xun County and Wenzhi Pavilion
protection.scope: Wenzhi Pavilion, Xun County · Surviving crossroads bell and drum tower

kh_angkor_wat.name: Angkor Wat
kh_angkor_wat.sub: Five central towers and adjoining terrace galleries
kh_angkor_wat.yearNote: Reign of Suryavarman II; 1125 is only an approximate timeline placement within the first half of the 12th century, and later conservation and restoration are recorded separately.
kh_angkor_wat.lede: Angkor Wat’s central tower and four corner towers rise from stepped terraces, organising stone architecture as a sacred mountain. The central towers and adjacent galleries form an inner area of worship within the larger temple grounds. Built under Suryavarman II in the first half of the twelfth century for Vishnu, it later continued as a Buddhist place of worship.
facts: A central tower and four corner towers form a five-tower plan above ascending terraces and galleries. From an oblique viewpoint towers overlap; the visible count differs from the complete plan.

APSARA dates construction to Suryavarman II’s reign in the first half of the twelfth century and records original dedication to Vishnu. Approximate dating distinguishes construction, later Buddhist use and conservation, without asserting one completion year.

Terraces and five towers express a sacred centre, while continuing Buddhist devotion keeps the former Hindu temple a living religious place. This continuity is more accurate than a story of complete abandonment and rediscovery.
captions: Angkor Wat · Five central towers and adjoining terrace galleries
First half of the 12th century

kh_bayon.name: Bayon
kh_bayon.sub: Central face towers and their supporting terraces
kh_bayon.yearNote: Angkor period; 1200 is an approximate placement at the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, and since the surviving towers have been repaired, they are not regarded as complete original fabric of a single year.
kh_bayon.lede: Great stone faces turn towards different directions above Bayon’s clustered towers, appearing and disappearing as visitors move. The central group developed around the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries in connection with Jayavarman VII’s Buddhist kingship. Conserved towers and their supporting platform create a shifting experience unlike Angkor Wat’s ordered five-tower plan.
facts: The central group combines towers of differing heights with their supporting platform. Monumental faces look in different directions, and nearby towers overlap; spatial relationships matter more than a theoretical total tower count.

APSARA places foundation under Jayavarman VII in the late twelfth century. Subsequent construction and changes support approximate dating around the turn of the thirteenth century, distinct from later conservation.

The faces turn architecture into sculpture, changing their relationships with each movement of the viewer. Their precise identity remains debated; they are not all asserted to be literal portraits of the king.
captions: Bayon · Central face towers and their supporting terraces
Late 12th–early 13th century

kh_banteay_srei.name: Banteay Srei
kh_banteay_srei.sub: Three central shrine towers and shared platform
kh_banteay_srei.yearNote: 967 is the dedication year recorded in inscriptions and is not the same as the completion date of every stone component; the surviving form also includes conservation and restoration.
kh_banteay_srei.lede: Fine carving interlaces the pink sandstone of Banteay Srei’s three central sanctuaries. Their modest scale concentrates elaborate door lintels and wall ornament on one platform. Towers overlap from an oblique view, rewarding close attention rather than sheer height. Dedication in 967 provides the date, not a claim that every stone was installed that year.
facts: Three central sanctuaries share a platform, with carved sandstone doorframes, walls and stepped superstructures. They form the core; libraries and gateways are separate, and this group is not the whole temple plan.
APSARA records dedication on 22 April 967 and inscriptions on central-group door jambs concerning the founder and his family. Dedication, construction stages and later conservation are distinguished.

A high official, rather than a royal foundation alone, sponsored the temple. Fine carving reveals the spread of courtly art to other patrons; the familiar name does not establish a queen’s residential palace.
captions: Banteay Srei · Three central shrine towers and shared platform
Dedicated 967

id_borobudur.name: Borobudur
id_borobudur.sub: Surviving main structure and complete base
id_borobudur.yearNote: UNESCO gives the 8th–9th century; 825 is only an approximate timeline position within this period. The surviving stonework underwent conservation and restoration in the 20th century.
id_borobudur.lede: Square terraces and carved galleries lead upwards to three circular platforms, where perforated stupas surround a great central stupa. Borobudur turns circumambulation into an expression of Buddhist cosmology. Built in the eighth and ninth centuries and conserved in the twentieth, its complete outline combines ancient design with continuing preservation.
facts: Five square terraces support three circular platforms and a central stupa. Seventy-two perforated stupas on the circular platforms contain Buddha images; relief galleries and the complete base frame the ascending route.
UNESCO dates building to the eighth and ninth centuries under the Syailendra dynasty, without one exact completion year. Major twentieth-century conservation restored and repositioned stonework.

Base, square terraces and circular platforms correspond to different Buddhist cosmic realms. Narrative reliefs give way to simpler upper stupas, turning movement through the monument into a passage towards open space.
captions: Borobudur · Surviving main structure and complete base
8th–9th century

id_prambanan_shiva.name: Shiva Temple of Prambanan
id_prambanan_shiva.sub: Single main Shiva temple and steps
id_prambanan_shiva.yearNote: On the same UNESCO page, the brief description gives the 10th century and the detailed description the 9th century; 900 is only for approximate ordering. The surviving main temple has undergone modern reconstruction and restoration.
id_prambanan_shiva.lede: A narrowing superstructure raises Prambanan’s Shiva temple about forty-seven metres above the central precinct. Entrance steps lead into concentrated stone ornament. The main temple and its base express the hierarchy of this sacred centre. Ninth-to-tenth-century dating is retained, and modern reconstruction forms part of the surviving structure.
facts: The central Shiva temple is the tallest principal shrine, about forty-seven metres high. Body, stepped crown and entrance stair form a vertical profile; Brahma and Vishnu temples beside it are separate buildings.

UNESCO’s summary uses the tenth century while its detailed account also refers to the ninth. A ninth-to-tenth-century range remains appropriate without an exact year, with restored stonework distinguished from the inherited design.

The group organises worship around Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, with the main shrine’s height emphasising Shiva’s central position. Its steep outline creates a different religious space from Borobudur’s spreading terraces.
captions: Shiva Temple of Prambanan · Single main Shiva temple and steps
9th–10th century

th_sukhothai_mahathat.name: Main Chedi of Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai
th_sukhothai_mahathat.sub: Lotus-bud main chedi and its supporting base
th_sukhothai_mahathat.yearNote: Reliable sources confirm the Sukhothai period and the lotus-bud form of the main chedi, but the precise year of its remodeling is unknown; 1350 is used only for timeline ordering, and the temple's founding year is not substituted for the age of the surviving main chedi.
th_sukhothai_mahathat.lede: A lotus-bud crown narrows into a fine spire above Wat Mahathat’s stepped base, expressing a distinctive Sukhothai form. Surviving masonry and stucco reveal the tower itself rather than lost hall roofs. The central chedi and its supporting base form the core of worship; the exact rebuilding year remains unconfirmed.
facts: The central chedi rises from a stepped base to a lotus-bud crown and slender spire, characteristic of Sukhothai art. Nearby hall columns and separate towers belong to the wider layout, not its direct body.

The Fine Arts Department suggests the tower may have been converted from an earlier Sri Lankan form. An exact rebuilding year is not established; approximate Sukhothai dating is separated from temple foundation and later repairs.

Stucco disciples on the base walk with hands joined in reverence, bringing devotional movement onto the building surface. Together with the lotus-bud crown, they show a local interpretation of external stupa traditions.
captions: Main Chedi of Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai · Lotus-bud main chedi and its supporting base
Sukhothai period · Approximate placement

th_chaiwatthanaram.name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
th_chaiwatthanaram.sub: Central prang, four corner prangs and shared base
th_chaiwatthanaram.yearNote: 1630 is the temple's founding year recorded in historical sources; the plate shows the surviving group of the central prang and four corner prangs, and given the discussion of earlier construction and the modern restoration, not all the brickwork is taken as built in the same year.
th_chaiwatthanaram.lede: A tall central prang and four corner towers share a broad brick platform at Wat Chaiwatthanaram, arranging a sacred centre as a temple-mountain. Chronicles record foundation in 1630, while modern conservation also shapes the surviving masonry. The central group shows how Ayutthaya Buddhism adopted Khmer tower forms to express cosmology.
facts: A high main prang and four smaller corner prangs rise from one platform, their narrowing bodies emphasising the centre. The outer gallery and eight tower-shaped chapels form a separate surrounding zone.

The anthropology centre cites several Ayutthaya chronicles for foundation in 1630 and records archaeology and restoration in 1987–1992. Foundation does not establish that all surviving bricks were laid simultaneously.

The study interprets the main prang as Mount Sumeru and its corner towers and gallery as the surrounding world. This shared Buddhist and Hindu cosmological pattern is expressed through the group, not height alone.
captions: Wat Chaiwatthanaram · Central prang, four corner prangs and shared base
Founded 1630

mm_ananda.name: Ananda Temple, Bagan
mm_ananda.sub: Whole temple body, central spire and projecting entrances
mm_ananda.yearNote: The Indian government's conservation project description gives the early 12th century; 1110 is only an approximate placement within that period, and none of the unverified exact years 1090, 1091 or 1105 is chosen. The surviving form includes later restoration.
mm_ananda.lede: Ananda’s broad body projects entrances in four directions, while terraces lift a golden central crown. This early-twelfth-century Bagan temple links interior devotion with an ascending exterior profile. Later repairs remain part of its walls and roofs; the whole body explains a shrine containing images and circulation better than a view of its crown alone.
facts: The cruciform body projects entrances in four directions, with terraces rising to the central crown. Four standing Buddhas face the cardinal directions within; the crown belongs to the temple body, rather than a separate stupa.

India’s conservation account dates building to the early twelfth century. Approximate dating is retained without choosing an unverified exact year; conservation after the 2016 earthquake contributes to the present appearance.
Unlike a solid stupa worshipped externally, Ananda contains images and circumambulation space inside its broad body. Four entrances and standing Buddhas connect devotional movement with orientation.
captions: Ananda Temple, Bagan · Whole temple body, central spire and projecting entrances
Early 12th century

la_xieng_thong_sim.name: Sim of Wat Xieng Thong
la_xieng_thong_sim.sub: The sim (main hall) and its supporting platform
la_xieng_thong_sim.yearNote: Official sources record its founding in about 1560; the main hall was repaired in 1928, in 1952–1960 and at other times, so not all the surviving decoration can be regarded as original 16th-century work.
la_xieng_thong_sim.lede: Three sweeping roof tiers descend over Wat Xieng Thong’s main sim, with gilding and glass mosaic adding close detail. Founded around 1560, it has been repeatedly repaired, so present ornament is not all sixteenth-century work. The hall and platform reveal Luang Prabang form through the relationship between low roofs and interior space.
facts: The sim has a central hall and side spaces beneath a low, three-tiered sweeping roof, with four decorated entrance columns. Its supporting platform belongs to the hall; the royal funeral-chariot building is separate.
The official tourism account gives foundation around 1560 and repairs including 1928 and 1952–1960. The founding period is distinguished from the age of present glass mosaic and gilded surfaces.

Low eaves and upturned finials define Luang Prabang hall architecture. Glass mosaics introduce daily and religious imagery, while inherited roof forms and later ornament sustain the building’s devotional use.
captions: Sim of Wat Xieng Thong · The sim and its supporting platform
About 1560

vn_po_klong_garai.name: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai
vn_po_klong_garai.sub: Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
vn_po_klong_garai.yearNote: Official Khánh Hòa Province sources give the late 13th–early 14th century; 1300 is only for approximate ordering, and the construction date of the tower is not inferred from the life dates of the king worshipped there.
vn_po_klong_garai.place: Khánh Hòa Province · Phan Rang–Tháp Chàm
vn_po_klong_garai.lede: Red-brick pilasters rhythmically divide Po Klong Garai’s main tower, whose narrowing superstructure rises above the hill. Its entrance and base form a central worship space, distinct from the gate and fire towers. Built around the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries and later associated with a revered ruler, it remains part of Cham ceremonial life.
facts: The central main shrine combines a square exterior with four diminishing levels and an east-facing entrance. Pilasters and niches articulate brick walls; the gate tower and elongated-roof fire tower are separate structures.
Khanh Hoa cultural and tourism sources date construction to the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The revered ruler lived earlier, so his lifespan is not used to date the brick tower.

Worship combines Shiva belief with the memory of a local ruler. Tower-opening, rain-prayer and Kate ceremonies continue, making both historic masonry and ongoing ritual essential to its community significance.
captions: Main Tower of Po Klong Garai · Surviving main shrine tower with entrance and base
Late 13th–early 14th century

vn_hue_ngo_mon.name: Meridian Gate (Ngọ Môn) of the Huế Imperial City
vn_hue_ngo_mon.sub: Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
vn_hue_ngo_mon.yearNote: 1833 is the construction date of the Meridian Gate; the surviving timber pavilion, roofs and platform have undergone later repairs, and there are also records of modern repairs.
vn_hue_ngo_mon.lede: Ngo Mon is the imperial entrance to Hue’s royal enclosure, formed by a substantial masonry platform and the Five Phoenix Pavilion above it. Five passages and layered roofs express a strict order of access. Built in 1833 under Emperor Minh Mang, the gate belongs to the ceremonial heart of the Nguyen capital. It combines the scale of a fortified entrance with separate routes for emperor, officials and attendants.
facts: The brick-and-stone platform has a recessed, U-shaped plan with five passages. Above it, the two-level timber Five Phoenix Pavilion has multiple roofs covered with yellow and green glazed tiles. Heavy masonry and lighter timber create clearly distinct lower and upper parts.

The present gate was built in 1833 under Minh Mang, replacing the earlier Nam Khuyet Dai. This date describes Ngo Mon’s construction phase, not the foundation of the entire imperial enclosure. The building has also undergone later restoration.

The central passage was reserved for the emperor; the others served civil and military officials, soldiers and attendants with animals. Used for access and royal ceremonies, the gate made Nguyen court hierarchy visible through its circulation routes.
captions: Meridian Gate of the Huế Imperial City · Complete gate platform and Five Phoenix Pavilion
1833 · Reign of Emperor Minh Mạng

ph_manila_san_agustin.name: San Agustin Church, Manila
ph_manila_san_agustin.sub: Surviving church facade and bell tower
ph_manila_san_agustin.yearNote: 1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
ph_manila_san_agustin.lede: Tiered orders of columns divide the doors and windows of the stone facade, a round window and a cross mark the triangular pediment, and the surviving bell tower adjoins it on the right. San Agustin Church preserves another architectural tradition of old Manila.
facts: The plate shows the surviving main facade and the single bell tower on the right; the low remnant of the lost left tower is kept and not reconstructed as symmetrical twin towers.

The National Museum of the Philippines records that the surviving stone church was completed in 1607; the original wooden church and later repairs are described separately, and the monastery as a whole is not drawn.

1607 is the completion date of the surviving stone church, as distinct from the earlier wooden churches. The bell tower and later repairs have their own histories, and the present building as a whole is not dated as original fabric of a single year.
captions: San Agustin Church, Manila · Surviving church facade and bell tower
Stone church completed 1607

kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.name: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.sub: Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.era: Hall built 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.yearNote: Hall built in 1308; the temple's founding is dated separately.
kr_sudeoksa_daeungjeon.lede: Sudeoksa’s Daeungjeon is a restrained timber hall with a three-bay front in a mountain monastery courtyard. Column-top brackets and the side framing are clearly exposed beneath its gabled roof. An ink inscription discovered during repairs dates its construction to 1308, giving this Koryo-period timber building unusually firm chronological evidence. Its columns, beams and roof invite close attention to construction rather than ornament.
facts: The hall is three bays across and four deep, with a gabled roof. Brackets are concentrated above the columns, while the side elevation exposes successive framing members. The load-bearing relationship between columns, beams and roof is readily visible.

An ink inscription found during repairs in 1937 establishes the hall’s construction date as 1308. This firm date belongs to the surviving hall; traditions about the monastery’s foundation and later repairs must be considered separately.

The restrained column-top brackets and open framing retain characteristics of Koryo timber construction. Its secure date makes it important for comparing early buildings. A view from the side reveals more of the builders’ methods than the front alone.
captions: Sudeoksa Daeungjeon · Single Daeungjeon hall and stone platform
Goryeo · 1308

kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.name: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.era: Surviving Muryangsujeon rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.yearNote: The surviving Muryangsujeon was rebuilt in 1376; the temple was founded in 676.
kr_buseoksa_muryangsujeon.lede: Muryangsujeon at Buseoksa is known for its broad five-bay front, gently swelling columns and restrained column-top brackets. A wide hip-and-gable roof covers the hall dedicated to Amitabha Buddha, creating a composed yet supple silhouette. Records describe rebuilding in 1376, while structural forms preserve earlier traditions. The surviving building and repeated later repairs together make up its historical layers.
facts: The hall is five bays wide and three deep, with a single hip-and-gable roof and column-top brackets. Columns swell gently at mid-height; their shape and generous spacing make the substantial roof appear both supple and stable.

Records describe damage in the fourteenth century and repair in 1376, followed by later repairs and dismantling restoration. Some structural forms continue earlier traditions, so every surviving component cannot be assigned to the same rebuilding year.

The hall houses Amitabha Buddha and is Buseoksa’s principal Buddhist sanctuary. The coordination of column shape, brackets and roof helps visitors understand Koryo timber traditions and the long continuity of monastery space through visible components.
captions: Buseoksa Muryangsujeon · Single Muryangsujeon hall and steps
Goryeo · 1376

kr_bulguksa_dabotap.name: Dabotap of Bulguksa
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.sub: Complete Dabotap stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.era: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.yearNote: Officially dated to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, and the pagoda's ordering year is approximately taken as 751.
kr_bulguksa_dabotap.lede: Square stone pillars support a pagoda body whose tiers keep changing form, while balustrades and an octagonal canopy shift its scale in the upper part. Carved from granite into a complex outline close to timber construction, Dabotap is entirely different from the common multi-roofed stone pagodas.
facts: Korean authorities officially date Dabotap to the 8th century, Unified Silla; 751 is a date associated with the building of Bulguksa, the ordering uses an approximate value, and no precise completion year is claimed for the pagoda.

Square stone pillars and stairways on four sides below combine with octagonal elements above, and official sources explain that its number of stories is hard to count in the way used for an ordinary pavilion-style pagoda.
Following its present state, the single surviving stone lion is kept, the lost lions are not added back, and the neighboring Seokgatap is not drawn.
captions: Dabotap of Bulguksa · Complete stone pagoda with stairways on four sides
Unified Silla · Approximate placement

kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.name: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.era: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.yearNote: The surviving Injeongjeon shown here was rebuilt in 1804; the palace's founding and successive fires are dated separately.
kr_changdeokgung_injeongjeon.lede: Injeongjeon at Changdeokgung stands on two stone terraces. Its five-bay front and two-tier roof command the ceremonial court, while the interior rises uninterrupted through both levels. The present timber hall was rebuilt in 1804 after a fire, and its interior retains early twentieth-century alterations. It records both Joseon court ceremony and the palace’s adaptation through successive building phases.
facts: The hall is five bays across and four deep, with a two-tier hip-and-gable roof and dense brackets above two terraces. There is no intermediate floor inside: tall columns and upper framing enclose a single lofty ceremonial space.

The hall burned in 1803 and was rebuilt the following year, reusing the existing stone terraces. The timber structure is principally dated to 1804, while its flooring and some interior decoration reflect early twentieth-century alterations.

Injeongjeon hosted court congratulations, investitures and important political ceremonies; rank stones organized officials in the courtyard. A low hill behind and corridors adjusted to the slope show how ceremonial order was reconciled with the terrain.
captions: Changdeokgung Injeongjeon · Injeongjeon hall and terrace
Joseon · 1804

kp_kaesong_namdaemun.name: Namdaemun of Kaesong
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.sub: Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.era: Inner-city gate first built 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.yearNote: The inner-city gate was first built in 1391–1393; the gate tower was destroyed in war in 1950 and rebuilt from 1954, a caption in the World Heritage nomination file records its restoration in 1955, and the timeline is placed by the surviving gate tower.
kp_kaesong_namdaemun.lede: Kaesong’s Namdae Gate has a granite base with a central arch supporting a single-storey wooden pavilion. It survives from the former southern entrance to the inner city. The gate originated in the late fourteenth century, but its pavilion was destroyed during the Korean War and reconstructed in 1955 using earlier images and architectural records. Old masonry and rebuilt timber together preserve its form and record destruction and recovery.
facts: The granite platform contains a central arched passage. Above it stands a timber pavilion three bays across and two deep. Its broad roof contrasts with the low, substantial masonry, making passage, platform and pavilion easy to distinguish.

The gate was first built in 1391–1393. Its timber pavilion burned during the Korean War and was reconstructed in 1955 using old photographs, drawings and surviving foundations. The present timberwork and earlier masonry belong to different phases.

The gate records the urban layout of Kaesong, capital of Koryo, and the postwar effort to preserve monuments. Distinguishing the early base from the reconstructed upper part shows how continuity can depend on reliable records as well as surviving fabric.
captions: Namdaemun of Kaesong · Stone gate platform and postwar rebuilt gate tower
Postwar reconstruction · 1955

kp_pothong_gate.name: Pyongyang Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.sub: Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower of Pothong Gate
kp_pothong_gate.era: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.yearNote: According to Kim Il Sung University sources, the surviving Pothong Gate was extensively repaired in 1473, with further repairs and extensions later; the Goguryeo origins of the city site are not used as the date of the surviving gate tower.
kp_pothong_gate.lede: Pothong Gate in Pyongyang combines an arched stone platform with a two-level wooden pavilion. Its broad double eaves once marked the city’s western entrance. The gate’s origins reach back to Koguryo, but its surviving form is chiefly associated with major repairs in 1473 and subsequent enlargement. Now standing apart from its former walls, it condenses memories of defence, travel and farewells in its masonry and timber silhouette.
facts: The granite base contains a central arched passage. Above it rises a wooden pavilion three bays wide and three deep, with two levels of eaves. Substantial stonework and the spreading timber roof create distinct layers.

The gate’s foundation is traditionally traced to the mid-sixth century under Koguryo. Its surviving form reflects major repairs in 1473 and later enlargement. The ancient origin of the entrance does not date every component of the present timber pavilion.

Pothong Gate was an important western route out of Pyongyang, serving defence, journeys and farewells. Although the city-wall layout has changed, the surviving gate still evokes the old urban boundary and the everyday movement of its inhabitants.
captions: Pyongyang Pothong Gate · Gate platform and double-eaved gate tower
Joseon · 1473

kp_sungyang_hall.name: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy
kp_sungyang_hall.sub: Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
kp_sungyang_hall.era: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.yearNote: The academy was established in 1573, and the lecture hall was repaired in the 17th and 19th centuries; the exact construction year of the surviving timberwork is undetermined, and about 1600 is only a timeline position within the Joseon period.
kp_sungyang_hall.lede: The lecture hall of Sungyang Academy stands on the highest of its stepped terraces, with a broad five-bay front facing the teaching courtyard and a shrine precinct behind. Established in the sixteenth century on the site of Jong Mong Ju’s former home, the academy combined Confucian education and commemoration. Repeated repairs complicate the hall’s precise construction date; its layout explains its use more clearly than a single year.
facts: The teaching precinct has three terraces. The lecture hall occupies the highest and is five bays wide by three deep; east and west student dormitories stand on a lower terrace. Walls and gates separate the shrine precinct behind.

The academy was established in 1573 on the site of Jong Mong Ju’s former home. Records describe repairs to the lecture hall in 1633 and to the whole academy in 1823. Its foundation date does not date every component of the surviving hall.

Teaching in front and worship behind combined Confucian learning with remembrance of Jong Mong Ju. Moving up the terraces reveals how courtyards, dormitories and the hall organized the academy’s educational and ceremonial life.
captions: Lecture Hall of Sungyang Academy · Five-bay lecture hall of the academy
Joseon · Approximate placement

kp_sonjuk_bridge.name: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong
kp_sonjuk_bridge.sub: Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
kp_sonjuk_bridge.era: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.yearNote: The nomination file says the bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, exact year unknown; about 1100 is an ordering position, 1392 is the year Jeong Mong-ju was killed, and the stone balustrades were added in 1780.
kp_sonjuk_bridge.lede: A short granite beam bridge spans a shallow stream, its deck enclosed by round-topped stone posts and rails. Sonjuk Bridge became a memorial site because Jeong Mong-ju was killed there, and the later balustrades also record its withdrawal from everyday traffic.
facts: The nomination file says the stone bridge has been in use since the early Goryeo, and its exact construction year has not been confirmed; about 1100 is an ordering position, and 1392 is the year of the killing.
The bridge is 8.35 m long and 3.36 m wide, with stone piers carrying stone beams topped by stone slabs; it is not an arch bridge. The surviving stone balustrades on both sides were added in 1780.
Only the old Sonjuk Bridge and its later balustrades are drawn; the separate bridge built alongside for traffic, the stele pavilion and the inscribed steles are not part of the subject.
captions: Sonjuk Bridge, Kaesong · Old stone beam bridge and 1780 stone balustrades
Goryeo · Approximate placement

jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.name: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1651 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_ueno_toshogu_karamon.lede: Ueno Toshogu’s Karamon concentrates splendour into a small entrance: a curved gable crowns its doors, with gilding and dense carving around the frame. The surviving gate belongs to the 1651 rebuilding. Only one bay across and deep, it creates a strong ceremonial boundary through elaborate curves. Roof and frame can be read before the dragon and bird decoration; repaired surfaces are not all original.
facts: The gate is one bay across and one bay deep, with a curved karahafu facing the approach and copper roof tiles. Its small structure supports dense ornament, contrasting the curved gable with upright posts and doors.

Heritage records date the surviving gate to 1651, and the shrine connects it with that rebuilding campaign. Subsequent repairs and surface maintenance mean that today’s gilding and paint cannot all be treated as original fabric.

Dragons by the posts and surrounding birds and flowers make the entrance a visual focus and express the sanctuary’s ceremonial status. The density of ornament shows how a small gate can acquire significance through detail rather than width.
captions: Karamon of Ueno Tōshō-gū · The Karamon alone
Edo period · 1651

jp_nezu_romon.name: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine
jp_nezu_romon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1706 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_nezu_romon.lede: Nezu Shrine’s gate concentrates entry into one central passage. Solid side bays give it gravity, while the upper balustrade draws a lighter line below the roof. This three-bay, single-passage romon has two storeys beneath one principal roof, unlike a gate with two large tiers of eaves. Built in 1706, its red frame and tiled roof make an Edo shrine entrance’s order easy to read.
facts: Three bays and one passage mean that only the central bay allows entry. The upper storey has a balustrade beneath a tiled hip-and-gable roof. Two storeys share one principal eaves line; storeys and roof tiers are different counts.

Heritage records date the surviving gate to 1706 as part of Nezu Shrine’s Edo-period buildings. This date applies to the gate itself; earlier shrine traditions and subsequent repairs form separate historical layers.

A central passage, enclosed side bays and an upper balustrade create a boundary between outside and inside, unlike a route through successive torii. Bay proportions and roof form show how a gate’s mass organises shrine space.
captions: Rōmon of Nezu Shrine · Three-bay, single-passage two-story gate
Edo period · 1706

jp_asakusa_jinja.name: Asakusa Shrine
jp_asakusa_jinja.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1649 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the shrine's founding.
jp_asakusa_jinja.lede: Asakusa Shrine’s low, broad timber worship hall contrasts with neighbouring Senso-ji’s postwar main hall. Tokugawa Iemitsu donated the surviving shrine buildings in 1649; they retained their early Edo form through fires, earthquakes and war. Painted mythical creatures and the red frame reward close attention. The shrine’s three deities also connect it with Senso-ji’s Kannon foundation legend.
facts: The shrine comprises a main sanctuary, offering hall and worship hall linked by corridors. The worship hall’s front faces approaching worshippers. Low eaves, doors and painted details establish the entrance, while corridors connect deeper ritual spaces.

The shrine records that Tokugawa Iemitsu established and donated the surviving buildings in 1649, and that they escaped subsequent disasters and war. Painted and lacquered surfaces were later repaired, so building dates and present coating dates should be distinguished.

The three people enshrined here belong to Senso-ji’s Kannon origin legend, linking neighbouring Buddhist and Shinto traditions. Mythical-creature decoration conveys auspicious wishes, serving both ritual and close visual inspection.
captions: Asakusa Shrine · Front of the worship hall
Edo period · 1649

jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.name: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1622 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_zojoji_sangedatsumon.lede: Sangedatsumon makes entry solemn through two deep eaves and a five-bay frontage. Three central passages occupy the ground floor, while the upper level houses Buddhist images. Zojo-ji dates the surviving rebuilding to 1622. Its early Edo scale gives passage the Pure Land meaning of leaving greed, anger and ignorance behind. Its complete outline also carries a conservation history; work began in 2025.
facts: This five-bay, three-passage gate has two storeys and two tiers of eaves beneath a hip-and-gable roof. An upper balustrade encircles it. The eaves distinguish lower circulation from the image-housing space above.

The temple records the earlier gate’s collapse in a storm in 1621 and rebuilding the following year; the heritage database separately lists 1621. The temple date and official record coexist; the discrepancy and ongoing conservation should be distinguished.

The name refers to release from greed, anger and ignorance, making passage a symbolic transition from ordinary life into the temple. Images above and entry routes below give the same gate both circulation and devotional functions.
captions: Sangedatsumon of Zōjō-ji · Five-bay, three-passage two-story gate
Edo period · 1622

jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.name: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.sub: Kannon Hall and the stage in front
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1631 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding. It was moved to its present site in 1694, and conservation repairs were completed in 1996.
jp_kaneiji_kiyomizu.lede: Kiyomizu Kannondo’s timber platform projects towards the Ueno slope, bringing worship and viewing together. Modelled on Kyoto’s Kiyomizu-dera, the hall has its own Edo history: Tenkai founded it in 1631, and later Kanei-ji construction prompted relocation. Red columns and the platform form one building. Its conserved appearance should not be confused with Kyoto’s much larger raised stage.
facts: A timber platform extends the hall towards the slope. Railings and supporting timbers join the red-columned hip-and-gable hall to an open viewing area, bringing the worship entrance close to the outlook.

Tenkai established the hall in 1631; it moved to its present site in 1694 for Kanei-ji’s main-hall project. Conservation finished in 1996, restoring its relocation-period appearance according to the temple. Foundation, relocation and conservation are distinct.

The hall adapted an image of Kyoto’s Kiyomizu-dera for Edo, adjusting its platform to local terrain. It shows how celebrated places could inspire another city while retaining each building’s own structure and history.
captions: Kiyomizu Kannon-dō of Kan'ei-ji · Kannon Hall and the stage in front
Edo period · 1631

jp_gokokuji_hondo.name: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji
jp_gokokuji_hondo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1697 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_gokokuji_hondo.lede: Gokoku-ji’s broad copper roof has turned green above a timber Kannon Hall from the Genroku period. The temple was founded in 1681, but this seven-by-seven-bay hall was built in 1697. A three-bay worship porch projects centrally. Approaching its steps and galleries reveals the scale of an Edo prayer temple through its nearly square mass and sweeping roof.
facts: The single-storey hall measures seven bays across and deep, with a hip-and-gable roof, a projecting three-bay worship porch and batten-seam copper roofing. Its square plan and broad eaves frame an emphatically central worship entrance.

The temple dates from 1681; the surviving Kannon Hall was completed in 1697, the tenth Genroku year. Temple foundation and hall construction are separate, and later roof and timber repairs cannot be attributed to the original foundation.

The broad hall accommodates collective Kannon worship and services, showing another scale of timber architecture beyond small refined structures. Its seven-bay body and three-bay porch reveal how a large mass focuses the direction of worship.
captions: Main Hall of Gokoku-ji · Main hall · Kannon Hall
Edo period · 1697

jp_ikegami_pagoda.name: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji
jp_ikegami_pagoda.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1608 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_ikegami_pagoda.lede: Ikegami Honmon-ji’s pagoda tapers through five dark tiled roofs beneath a finial. The temple records topping-out in 1607 and a dedication the following year, placing it in early Edo construction. Relocation and modern dismantling repairs are also part of its history: an intact outline does not mean every component is unchanged, and the temple’s earlier origins do not date this tower.
facts: Five progressively smaller roofs crown the timber pagoda beneath its finial, with a platform supporting the lowest level. Broad eaves alternate with a narrower body. Five roof tiers should not be assumed to mean five accessible internal floors.

The temple records topping-out in 1607 and dedication in 1608. The pagoda moved to its present location during the Genroku period and later underwent modern dismantling conservation. Its construction date differs from relocation and repair dates.

Japanese timber pagodas and Chinese brick towers both form layered vertical markers, but this tower emphasises deep eaves and intricate framing. Comparing its broad roofs with shorter brick cornices reveals how materials change related religious forms.
captions: Five-Story Pagoda of Ikegami Honmon-ji · Surviving five-story wooden pagoda
Edo period · 1608

jp_shofukuji_jizodo.name: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.sub: Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.yearNote: The timeline follows the 1407 construction date of the surviving structure depicted, rather than a legend of the temple's founding.
jp_shofukuji_jizodo.lede: Shofuku-ji’s Jizo Hall seems to have two roofs stacked above two storeys, but it is a single-storey hall surrounded by a lower mokoshi aisle. A 1407 ink inscription found during repairs gives this Kanto Zen hall a secure date. Wooden shingles on the main roof contrast with copper over the aisle; refined interior framing directs the eye upwards, inviting both exterior and interior readings.
facts: The three-by-three-bay hall has one storey and a surrounding mokoshi aisle. The main hip-and-gable roof is wood-shingled, while copper covers the lower aisle roof. Two eaves lines do not indicate two floors.

Repairs revealed an inscription for Oei 14, or 1407, on a support for the tail rafters. Heritage documentation uses it to establish the construction date. This physical inscription dates the hall more directly than temple foundation legends.

Heritage research compares it with Engaku-ji’s reliquary hall in Kamakura, showing the standardised design of Muromachi Zen halls. Dense brackets and framing rising towards the centre give a modest space a highly refined order.
captions: Jizō Hall of Shōfuku-ji · Single-story Zen Buddhist hall with mokoshi
Muromachi period · 1407

ln_wanfotang.name: Wanfotang Grottoes, Yixian
ln_wanfotang.sub: Western Cave 6 · Maitreya with crossed ankles
ln_wanfotang.yearNote: The western caves were excavated in 499, supported by Yuan Jing's dedicatory inscription; the eastern group has a separate inscription dated 502. Cave 6 lost its front wall and the statue stands exposed. Its body has later repairs and the halo was repainted; a 1930s photograph already describes recent repairs. The date marks excavation, not every surviving surface.
ln_wanfotang.lede: On the cliff above the Daling River, governor Yuan Jing sponsored the western caves in 499; Han Zhen and others continued the eastern group in 502. This is the earliest and largest grotto complex in northeastern China. Cave 6 has lost its front wall, leaving a Maitreya more than three metres tall exposed beneath a painted halo of lotus petals and small Buddhas.
facts: The western group's inscription dates it to 499, and the eastern group's to 502. Sixteen caves and nearly 500 sculptures survive. The complex entered the third national protection list in 1988.

The principal image in Cave 6 is a 3.05-metre Maitreya with crossed ankles, described as the largest Buddha-form Maitreya in northern and central Chinese grottoes. Its halo combines lotus petals, small Buddhas and scrolling ornament.

The collapsed front wall exposes the statue to the cliff face. Later repairs altered the body and repainted the halo. A 1930s photograph already records repairs, so the excavation date does not date all present surfaces.
captions: Wanfotang Grottoes, Yixian · Western Cave 6 · Maitreya with crossed ankles
Northern Wei · 499

protection.scope: Seated cross-legged Maitreya in western Cave 6, part of the grotto complex

ln_xingcheng.name: Xingcheng Old City
ln_xingcheng.sub: Chunhe Gate · East gate tower and barbican
ln_xingcheng.yearNote: The wall was begun in 1428 and completed in 1430. The date marks the start of wall construction. No reliable date was found for repairs or rebuilding of the surviving timber gate towers; the illustration follows the photographed condition of 2011 without claiming their original fabric survives.
ln_xingcheng.lede: The Ningyuan garrison city was begun in 1428. More than 3,200 metres of brick-faced walls still enclose all four sides, making it one of China's best-preserved Ming cities. Each gate has a semicircular barbican and a two-storey tower. The east-facing Chunhe Gate shown here rises between the barbican's wings above a vaulted passage.
facts: Liaodong commander Wu Kai and others petitioned to build the city in 1428; work finished in 1430. The walls entered the third national list in 1988 and were incorporated into the Xingcheng Old City designation in the sixth list in 2006.

The enclosure measures 821 metres north–south and 816 east–west, with a perimeter of 3,274 metres and walls 8.5–9.6 metres high. Each gate has a semicircular barbican and a five-bay, two-storey tower with a hip-and-gable roof and surrounding gallery.

The two-storey Chunhe Gate tower stands above the vaulted entrance, protected by the outer barbican's wings. The wall's founding date is documented, but the surviving timber tower's repair or rebuilding date remains unknown.
captions: Xingcheng Old City · Chunhe Gate · East gate tower and barbican
Ming · 1428

protection.scope: Chunhe Gate tower and barbican at the east gate, part of the city wall
